I believe an NHS workforce plan should prioritise people first, with robust digital infrastructure that supports safe, high-quality care. Interoperable, secure IT systems that connect GP practices, hospitals and community services would reduce duplication, speed up referrals and support safer decision-making. Key steps include a shared electronic patient record, real-time staffing and demand dashboards, and well-supported telemedicine that integrates with triage and appointment scheduling. Equally important is investing in staff digital training and dedicated digital health roles so clinicians can use tools confidently and safely. 

Crucially, we must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients: keep non-digital pathways, telephone triage, face-to-face clinics, and outreach through community hubs, interpreters and multilingual staff. For retention, offer clear career progression, mentoring, CPD, and pathways for return-to-practice, with manageable workloads and protected time for training. Staffing should reflect local need, with flexible hours and appropriate ratios across GP, nursing and mental health teams to keep care safe.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise tangible, funded career pathways that reliably bring people into healthcare and keep them there. This means funded training places for GPs, nurses, mental health professionals and allied roles, plus clear routes from education into practice—so young people and other new entrants can see a future in the system. Return‑to‑practice schemes must be protected and sufficiently resourced to bring experienced clinicians back safely. Protected CPD time and robust mentorship will help retain both early‑career staff and more senior colleagues who may be at risk of burnout. Streamlined systems for referrals, less duplicative paperwork, and better IT usability are essential so clinicians can spend more of their day with patients rather than on admin. It is also crucial to reduce targets that drive rapid throughput at the expense of safety and to ensure manageable workloads and reasonable triage processes.

A joined‑up approach with social care, mental health and community services—supported by joint funding and co‑design—would redistribute workload and improve holistic care, benefiting young people who often rely on multiple services. Practical examples include funded apprenticeships, back‑to‑practice programs, and dedicated CPD blocks that align with frontline needs while preserving high safety standards.

To ensure timely access while protecting patient safety,, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams that can safely redistribute GP workload. This means nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals working within clear, well-supervised scopes of practice, with strong training pathways and protected clinical supervision funded locally. By standardising induction, governance and supervision, these roles can handle triage, routine reviews, chronic disease management and elements of urgent care, freein GPs to focus on more complex cases without compromising quality. In our area, pharmacist prescribers and nurse-led clinics have already reduced bottlenecks when they operate within robust supervision and clear protocols. Extendingg this model—while ensuring safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving teams—would help maintain consistent patient experiences and safety. It’s important that staffing levels reflect patient needs, with predictable rosters and arrangements so patients see familiar staff where possible. We also need clear scope-of-practice definitions, revalidation processes, and indemnity arrangements, plus funded protected clinical supervision to support new roles and local governance. Ongoing safety monitoring and outcomee data should guide adjustments, ensuring access improvements do not erode clinical quality. Overall, a carefully regulated expansion of multidisciplinary teams, backed by training, supervision and robust safety oversight, should deliver faster access and safer care for patients.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe, the plan must prioritise practical staffing that actually works in communities, not more reorganisations. Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals, all with clearly defined roles and robust supervision so GP workload is redistributed safely. Give these teams protected time, governance oversight, and funded training pathways, so newer roles can confidently support chronic disease care and urgent triage without compromising quality. In my area, chronic disease reviews are delayed because we’re stretched; MDTs with proper supervision would improve access. 

Provide clear funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and support those re-entering the workforce. This needs visible progression routes, peer support and manageable workload expectations. 

Offer targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles. Pair these incentives with local workforce planning to fill gaps in GP practice, district nursing and community clinics. This approach protects safety and continuity and avoids simply shuffling staff between organisations.

Prioritise a well-supported NHS workforce: deliver tailored incentives for rural, urban deprived and coastal areas plus housing and transport support to recruit and retain staff; clarify scope-of-practice, provide revalidation and indemnity; fund protected clinical supervision; invest in interoperable IT and digital training for all, including alternatives for the digitally excluded.

i strongly believe a well-planned NHS workforce strategy should prioritise safety, sustainability and equity, while giving frontline teams the autonomy and support they need to deliver integrated care. In Wales, where demand is growing and services must operate closer to people’s homes, the plan must balance clarity about roles with real investment in people, systems and data. 

1) Clear scope of practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements. We need explicit, nationally agreed scopes of practice for new and extended roles (for example advanced nurse practitioners, physician associates and allied health professionals), with fatigue and risk-based supervision models. Revalidation processes should be streamlined and fit-for-purpose, not a barrier to service expansion. Indemnity coverage must be robust for all new roles and settings, including out-of-hours and community-based care, to protect patients and practitioners alike. This requires protected time for supervision, reflective practice and quality improvement activity, so safety is maintained as responsibilities grow.

2) Fund protected clinical supervision and supervision networks for new roles. Safe expansion hinges on protected clinical supervision that is itself funded. This should include regular mentorship, joint case reviews and access to senior clinical governance for MDT members. In rural and digitally underserved areas, supervision can be partly remote, but it must be reliable and synchronous to ensure patient safety and professional development. More explicit supervision frameworks will also help reduce miscommunication and variation in practice across teams.

3) Strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services. Distributing workload across sectors is essential to avoid burnout and to deliver holistic care. Jointly funded pathways, co-located teams where possible, and shared care plans can ease pressure on hospital and GP services while improving patient experience. For instance, social workers and community nurses co-located with primary care can manage social determinants of health and long-term care planning, freeing clinicians to focus on higher-risk cases open to urgent intervention.

4) Localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation. A transparent, localised data framework is critical. We need real-time dashboards on vacancies, nurse-to-patient ratios, turnover, vacancy fill rates, training uptake, and patient safety indicators. Predictive modelling should inform recruitment targets, service design, and budgeting, with explicit KPIs for equity—monitoring ethnicity, deprivation and rurality to ensure no group is disadvantaged. Evaluation frameworks should be embedded in every initiative, with learning fed back into planning cycles.

5) Career pathways, training and retention. The plan must create clear, appealing career ladders, with funded training places, mentorship, and opportunities to work across sectors. This includes bridging programmes for staff moving from acute to community roles, and incentives to work in underserved areas. Flexible working patterns, supportive supervision, and fair pay are essential to retain talent and reduce dependence on agency staff, which can undermine continuity of care.

6) Safe staffing levels and workload management. Staffing plans should be aligned with patient risk and complexity, not just activity targets. This means modelling demand at a local level and ensuring teams have the right mix of skills to deliver timely, high-quality care. In parallel, digital tools should support triage and decision-making without widening inequities for those with limited connectivity.

7) Governance, accountability and patient safety. Any expansion must be underpinned by robust governance, with clear accountability for patient safety, quality of care and strategic alignment with public health priorities. This includes safeguarding measures, consent considerations within diverse communities, and oversight to prevent new forms of gatekeeping in MDTs.

8) Practical examples we’d like to see scaled. Pilots that embed MDT clinics in GP practices with shared records and explicit referral criteria, plus parallel investments in community hubs and home-based care, show promise. Local authority and NHS boards should jointly fund pilot projects for home-based monitoring and proactive outreach by trained community link workers to prevent crises and reduce unnecessary hospital visits.

In short, an NHS workforce plan should prioritise clarity on roles and protections for staff, invest in supervision and joint funding with social care and community services, and build transparent, localised data and evaluation frameworks. If these elements are implemented thoughtfully, we can recruit, retain and support the right staff to deliver safe, high-quality care that is truly joined up for people across Wales.

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that recognises the realities on the ground and puts patient safety and high‑quality care at its core. From where I sit, the most important priorities are those that reduce avoidable workload, promote collaborative care across sectors, and make it easier for staff to do their jobs well without compromising their wellbeing or patients’ experience. I’ve seen how the pressures in primary care and community services ripple outward: more time spent chasing admin or juggling complex referrals means less time with patients who need real, hands‑on help. A thoughtful workforce plan should address that head‑on.

First, strengthen links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and improve holistic care. If district nursing, physiotherapy, podiatry, and mental‑health outreach are better connected to general practice, patients can be supported earlier in the care continuum and avoid hospital admissions. For example, when a community nurse can visit the same day or shortly after a GP contact, families feel reassured and a chronic condition is less likely to deteriorate. Shared funding arrangements and joint care pathways would enable flexible staffing and easier cross‑team referrals, reducing duplication and miscommunication that currently slow things down.

Second, deliver tailored incentives and practical supports to recruit and retain staff in hard‑to‑fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities in particular. Housing support, transport assistance, and targeted salary or retention bonuses can make a real difference. In my experience, promising a clear route for career development alongside local recruitment packages helps people stay long enough to build confidence in the role and the community. It’s not just about recruitment; it’s about staying where the need is greatest while maintaining quality of care.

Third, reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and streamline referrals. Clinicians are stretched not just by patient load but by administrative burden that doesn’t add value to patient care. A plan that simplifies IT systems, creates user‑friendly referral workflows, and shares high‑quality information across organisations would free clinicians to spend more time with patients. We know from everyday practice that efficient, integrated IT reduces delays in treatment, cuts frustration for patients, and lessens the risk of errors during transitions between services.

Fourth, invest in IT usability and digital tools that actually save time and improve decision making. A modern, interoperable electronic records system with decision support and simple, secure communication can cut down phone tag and repeat data entry. Streamlined e‑referrals and a reliable triage interface would enable quicker routing of patients to the right professional—whether that’s a GP, nurse, mental‑health clinician, or social‑care worker—without losing sight of safety and accountability.

Fifth, commit to robust staffing standards that protect safety and quality. Safe staffing levels, rotating rosters that acknowledge fatigue, and protected time for training and reflection are essential. Staff wellbeing programmes, access to mental‑health support for the workforce, and supervisory structures that encourage learning from near misses all contribute to a culture where people feel valued and able to deliver high‑quality care.

Sixth, enhance the training pipeline and career development opportunities. Long‑term planning should align undergraduate and postgraduate training with service needs, promote multidisciplinary teams (where nurses, physio, occupational therapists, social workers and mental‑health professionals work alongside GPs in integrated care), and create clear progression routes. When staff can see a future in the roles they’re in, turnover falls and expertise deepens, which in turn improves patient care.

Seventh, tailor measures to local circumstances while maintaining national standards. One size rarely fits all in a country as diverse as England. Local governance should have the flexibility to fund and shape incentives, community teams and care pathways that reflect local populations, housing constraints, and transport links, while upholding safety and quality benchmarks.

Finally, build the plan around the patient journey. If the workforce plan translates into smoother handovers, better access to community and mental‑health services, and support for carers and families, people will experience a more coherent, compassionate system. I’ve seen how disjointed care creates stress and deters people from seeking timely help; a plan that prioritises integration and practical supports for staff is, in effect, a plan to improve patient outcomes.

In short, prioritising joint funding and collaboration across social care, mental health and community services; targeted recruitment incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas; reducing admin and streamlining referrals; strengthening IT and data systems; safeguarding staff wellbeing and safety; and investing in training and career development will together create a more sustainable, patient‑centred NHS workforce. That approach will help maintain high‑quality care now and into the future, and it aligns with what people like me have been advocating through periods of pressure and change.”

A workforce plan for the NHS should start with clear, enforceable foundations that protect patient safety while making it easier to recruit, retain and develop staff across all levels. From where I sit as a patient who’s waited for timely GP access and has seen how care can deteriorate when roles aren’t well defined, the priorities must be practical and governed, not just aspirational. In particular, I’d push for four interlocking priorities, built on clarity, support and safety.

1) Clear scope of practice for every role with strong governance
- The plan must specify what each professional can and cannot do, and how they hand back to a GP when a problem sits outside their remit. For example, if pharmacists or physiotherapists handle routine issues under formal protocols, there needs to be explicit prescribing rules, escalation routes, and an accountable supervisor for the patient’s entire journey. Without that, you get fragmentation, duplicate tests, and patients retelling the same story to multiple clinicians.
- A formal, transparent scope also helps with recruitment. People joining the NHS need to know they won’t be overburdened by uncertainty over what they’re allowed to do, which is a real barrier in some teams.

2) Revalidation and continuing professional development that truly fits the role
- Revalidation processes must be efficient and proportionate to the level of responsibility. It’s welcome to widen who can contribute to care, but if revalidation becomes another bureaucratic hurdle, it undermines retention and confidence in new roles. The plan should guarantee protected time for CPD and annual revalidation activities, so clinicians aren’t pulled away from patients or forced to chase paperwork.
- Ongoing training should align with the expanded scope—hands-on mentoring, skills refreshers, and clear criteria for advancing within roles. This helps with retention because staff see a viable career ladder rather than a ceiling once they’ve qualified.

3) Indemnity arrangements that cover new and evolving roles
- Indemnity must match the scope of practice. When a workforce model relies on non-GP clinicians delivering care, there has to be clear, affordable, and accessible indemnity that travelers with those duties can rely on. Ambiguity here is a real deterrent to recruitment and a risk to patients if something goes wrong and there’s no clear coverage.
- The plan should include a mechanism that updates indemnity as roles evolve—so as new abilities are added, protection follows quickly, not months later.

4) Funded, protected clinical supervision and robust patient safety nets
- New roles and expanded teams require protected supervision time. That means funded sessions where less experienced staff can review cases with a more senior clinician, learn from near-misses, and establish safe practice in real time. Without protected supervision, new roles can drift, and patient safety can suffer.
- Supervision should be structured, with a named supervisor and a clear line of accountability. It also needs to be scalable to local needs; one area shouldn’t get a bare-minimum model while another has excellent mentorship. Evaluation should track improvements in safety, patient experience, and staff confidence.

Beyond these four pillars, the plan must be flexible enough to reflect local variation while ensuring core standards. Local pilots with rigorous evaluation are essential to prove that new roles actually save time, reduce delays and improve safety before rolling out widely.

In practice, this translates into concrete steps: (a) publish detailed role maps with responsibilities and escalation protocols; (b) set timelines and resources for revalidation aligned to scope, with protected time; (c) guarantee affordable indemnity for all tasks within defined scopes; (d) ring-fence supervision funding and embed safety metrics into every new pathway; (e) create clear career ladders and ongoing training opportunities to support retention; (f) involve frontline staff in co-design to ensure the plan reflects real patient care journeys rather than theoretical models.

With a climate of staffing shortages and rising demand, a workforce plan that foregrounds clarity, safety, and sustainable support will not only attract people to the NHS but also keep patients safer and more assured that someone knows their history and is accountable for their care. That consistency and governance are what will make broader MDT approaches work where they’re appropriate, without sacrificing the reliability of a steady GP relationship and timely care.

I think an NHS workforce plan must prioritise sustainable recruitment and retention by strengthening links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services. When we pool resources and responsibilities, teams can redistribute tasks like home visits, social prescribing and community outreach, freeing clinicians to handle complex cases and reducing pressure on GP practices. A shared funding approach could underpin integrated urgent response teams and ring-fenced slots for high-need patients, improving continuity of care.

Retention hinges on real flexibility and strong wellbeing support. Offering flexible hours, part-time roles, job-share options and phased retirement helps people balance work with family duties and reduces burnout. Practical measures such as childcare support and proactive mental health services for staff—counselling, supervision, and protected time for reflective practice—are essential to keep skilled staff and maintain morale.

From my experience, when care plans span primary, social care and mental health, patients move through the system faster and safety is preserved, while staff feel less fragmented. Ongoing training, clear progression pathways, and accessible telehealth options can broaden recruitment and sustain high-quality care, even in rural areas. A cohesive plan that aligns funding, staffing models and staff well-being will deliver reliable, safe care for patients and communities.

absolutely prioritise sustained, ring-fenced funding to create funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes; pair this with safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models and robust safety monitoring to keep care high-quality!

As someone living in Scotland, I think the NHS workforce plan must prioritise growing domestic supply and ensuring those trained stay in frontline roles, not just filling vacancies. The core priority should be to increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships so people see primary care as a viable, long-term career. This means more GP, nursing, pharmacy and allied health training places, linked to real primary care rotations and funded joint training programmes that include rural and deprived areas where shortages bite hardest. 

Alongside this, targeted financial incentives are essential: genuinely competitive pay packages and retention payments for staff in underserved areas and high-demand roles; relocation support to attract people to rural Scotland; and bursaries that cover training costs with obligations to serve in primary care for a set period. Build in flexible career ladders, protected supervision time and ongoing CPD, plus improvements in working conditions to help retention. 

Without a robust pipeline and meaningful incentives, we’ll keep chasing vacancies rather than addressing root causes of burnout and turnover. A workforce plan that pair expands training capacity with geographically targeted pay and clear career pathways would deliver safer, higher-quality care for patients.

As a young person living in England, I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three linked areas to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality. First, transparent, localised data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. If local systems publish clear staffing gaps, patient flow and outcome data, it would guide funding and help managers target shortages in GP and mental health services. In my area this could mean identifying where mobile clinics or extended hours are most needed and tracking improvements over time. Second, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, backed by staff digital training, while safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients. A common electronic record, shared referral pathways and a streamlined triage/booking flow would reduce duplication and misrouting that frustrates patients and staff alike. Third, flexible working to recruit and retain diverse staff—flexible hours, part-time roles, job-share, phased retirement and accessible childcare—plus proactive mental health support. Develop strong training pipelines, apprenticeships and rotations so teams stay cohesive in co-located hubs where GP, mental health and social care work together. This approach would help keep access reliable for students like me and families who depend on timely care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while preserving high-quality care, the plan should prioritise responsible overseas recruitment, streamlined visas and rapid credential recognition, plus strong integration support and safeguards for source health systems. In practice this means a clear visa route for NHS professionals, swift verification of qualifications, language and induction programmes, and mentoring in the first year to help navigate NHS norms. I've seen how stretched practices rely on temporary staff; ensuring a steady, well-supported intake is better for patients than panic hiring. At the same time, expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams is essential: empowering nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals to work at the top of their skills with proper training and supervision would ease GP workloads, reduce duplication and keep patients safer. For instance, pharmacist-led chronic-disease reviews or nurse-led triage in primary care can smooth pathways for those with chronic conditions. Finally, flexible hours, part-time options, job-share, phased retirement, childcare support and proactive mental health services are vital to retain a diverse workforce and guard against burnout.

Thank you for asking. Any NHS workforce plan should be practical, transparent and locally informed to keep care safe for all ages, especially in rural Northern Ireland. It should start with transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs, with a clear evaluation framework to tie funding to performance and patient outcomes. Regular dashboards at practice and health-board level would show vacancy rates, turnover, overtime and patient access times, enabling proactive action before gaps appear. Include ongoing engagement with GPs, nurses and allied health professionals, and community teams, so plans reflect real workloads.

Flexible working is essential: offer flexible hours, part-time options, job-sharing, phased retirement and accessible childcare support; provide proactive mental health services for staff and managers to prevent burnout. This will help retain experienced clinicians and reduce reliance on agency staff, ensuring safer, more stable care.

Expand training pipelines: increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships to grow domestic primary care capacity. In our area, protected nurse placements and GP training linked to a local university helped keep trainees in the region; continuing and expanding these arrangements will ease recruitment and sustain high-quality care across communities.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while preserving safe, high‑quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise flexible, family‑friendly working patterns and robust wellbeing support. I’ve seen how burnout and rigid hours push experienced clinicians away; offering part‑time roles, job‑sharing, and phased retirement would help keep skilled staff on board. Practical childcare support matters too—on‑site or subsidised provision, extended hours during school holidays, and predictable rosters that protect evenings and weekends for those with caring responsibilities.

We also need sustained investment in mental health for staff: confidential counselling, protected time for reflective practice, and proactive resilience training, so people aren’t quietly draining under pressure. Safe staffing ratios and constructive supervision are essential; these must be embedded in every team to maintain care quality under busy periods.

A strong, diverse recruitment drive is crucial. Targeted outreach to communities underrepresented in health roles, with language and cultural competency training for teams, will improve retention and patient trust. Use flexible digital tools for supervision and continuing education to reduce travel and enable flexible working. Overall, a plan that recognises staff as crucial partners—through flexible career paths, wellbeing support, and inclusive recruitment—will deliver safer, higher‑quality care for everyone.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams across all parts of Scotland, especially rural areas. This means clear role definitions for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates (PAs), paramedics and allied health professionals, with standardized training pathways and supervised practice to safely redistribute routine GP workloads. In practice, this could include pharmacist-led chronic disease clinics, nurse prescribers handling stable patients, and paramedics running same-day triage and home visits, supported by digital handovers and shared records to avoid gaps in care. Strong governance and ongoing CPD are essential to maintain safety and quality. 

Additionally, build stronger links with social care, mental health and community services with joint funding and integrated teams. This would enable holistic care and reduce hospital referrals. In my experience rural Scotland struggles with access; enabling local teams to manage a wider range of conditions would relieve pressure on GPs and improve continuity. Invest in training places, return-to-practice schemes, flexible contracts and rural incentives to attract and retain staff.

To keep care safe and timely, any NHS workforce plan should focus on making it easier for people to start, stay and progress in NHS roles here. I would like to see funded career pathways for all grades—reliable progression routes for nurses, therapists and GPs, with protected CPD time so learning continues even when workloads are high. Strong mentorship and formal return-to-practice schemes are essential so experienced staff can share what they know and newer staff aren’t lost to burnout.

Retention should also come from sensible staffing and workload planning, flexible hours, and recognition of the pressures on older patients and their carers. In my area, when teams lose experienced clinicians the impact on continuity and safety is clear.

I support overseas recruitment, but only if it’s responsible: streamlined visa processes, clear credential recognition, proper integration support, and safeguards to avoid weakening health systems in other countries. The emphasis must be on expanding training here while using international recruitment to cover gaps in the short term.

In short, fund training and retention, and recruit abroad only with robust safeguards—this will help ensure high-quality, safe care for patients who rely on prompt access to services.

The plan must prioritise expanding domestic training: increase undergraduate, postgraduate, and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships; ensure funded, geographically distributed placements to boost local workforce, alongside retention strategies and safe staffing to sustain quality care.

Second, reduce admin burdens that eat into patient care. Remove duplicated tasks, simplify referrals, and improve IT usability so clinicians spend more time with patients rather than chasing forms.

In practice, during winters I’ve seen how capacity and admin overhead push clinicians to the edge; a plan that grows capability while trimming bureaucracy would help Wales deliver safer, more timely care.

Prioritise expanding undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships, to grow domestic primary care supply; pair this with funded CPD and robust supervision to keep safe, high-quality care and good retention.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things: reliable, interoperable IT with strong cybersecurity; flexible working options to retain a diverse workforce; and responsible recruitment alongside a robust training and retention pipeline. Interoperable IT is vital so a named clinician can access a complete history and risk profile, creating a coherent plan in one visit. At the same time, we must safeguard alternatives for those who are digitally excluded—maintaining phone access, paper records where needed, and community hubs with staff who can support non-digital patients.

Flexible hours, part-time roles, job-share, and childcare support are essential to reduce burnout and keep experienced staff in post. I believe an NHS workforce plan should be built on two clear foundations. In short, prioritising honest local data and practical admin relief, backed by targeted, well-supported recruitment and development, will help recruit, retain and protect NHS staff while preserving the high quality, safe care patients deserve.

From my experience of dealing with local services, any NHS workforce plan will only work if it frees clinicians to care for people, rather than saddling them with bureaucratic tasks. In plain terms: reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated steps; streamline referrals and make IT usable. At the same time, we must fund real career pathways and practical retention measures so experienced staff and those starting out can build a sustainable career in frontline roles. Staffing decisions must be guided by solid local data and clear evaluation so resources actually match need.

Priorities I’d want to see prioritised include:

- Cut admin burden and improve information systems: clinicians spend too much time on administrative tasks that offer little direct benefit to patients. We need simpler, interoperable IT that reduces duplication across primary care, community services and mental health. Quick wins would be better integrated referral routes, fewer form-filling bottlenecks, and dashboards that show waiting times and capacity in real time. For example, when a patient needs a referral to a mental health service, the process should be straightforward and trackable, not a maze of emails and repeated data entry.

- Transparent, localised workforce data and evaluation: decisions should be based on what is really happening on the ground. Local authorities and NHS teams need accessible dashboards showing staffing levels, turnover, vacancy rates, and service delivery metrics. There must be evaluation frameworks that measure whether changes actually improve patient care, not just whether targets were hit. This means regular audits, independent oversight, and community input into what good looks like for different areas.

- Clear, funded career pathways and protected CPD: to retain talent we need visible routes from trainee to senior clinician with protected time for training and development. Mentorship schemes, structured return‑to‑practice programs for those who have left the profession, and funded continuing professional development should be the norm, not the exception. This is crucial for both mid‑career staff and newly qualified workers who need supportive induction and progression options.

- Supportive, moderated workload and working conditions: safe staffing ratios, reasonable shift patterns, and access to wellbeing resources are essential. Pair that with career progression that rewards expertise and leadership, not just productivity targets. Adequate staff wellbeing support helps prevent burnout and reduces avoidable turnover.

- Targeted recruitment and retention, with community fit: recruitment should focus on areas with the greatest gaps, including improving access in underserved communities. That means more local training places, sponsorships for students from diverse backgrounds, and roles that encourage experienced clinicians to stay in clinical practice through flexible working arrangements and career ladders that don’t push everyone into management paths.

- Mentoring, coaching and governance: formal mentorship and buddy systems can help new staff integrate quickly and build confidence. Governance processes must balance safety and learning, not punitive targets. Encouraging experienced clinicians to share best practices and provide supervision ensures safer, higher‑quality care.

- Cultural competence and language support as standard: a workforce plan should reflect the communities it serves, with multilingual staff, interpreters available in clinics, and training in culturally competent care. This complements the need for streamlined processes and better IT, because clear communication reduces avoidable visits and errors.

- Flexible, locally usable service delivery models: I’ve seen how mobile clinics, community hubs, and local outreach improve access in practice. A workforce plan should fund and enable these models where they’re most needed, and ensure staff have the tools and backing to work in these settings without being pulled back into centralised systems.

In short, I’d like the plan to couple practical fixes that free clinicians to care with strong career development and robust, local data to steer investment. If we get that balance right, we can keep high standards of safety and quality while making NHS jobs more sustainable and attractive. This aligns with what I’ve seen locally: improvements in IT usability and streamlined processes have the potential to free time for patient care, provided there’s also meaningful investment in people and in the systems that support them.

Overall, I’m leaning toward agreeing with a plan that prioritises reducing admin burden, investing in people through clear career paths and protected CPD, and using transparent local data to guide funding and performance monitoring.

I support a NHS workforce plan that prioritises expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams to safely distribute GP workload, while preserving continuity of care. To deliver safe, high-quality care, the plan should focus on: 
- clear governance and supervision: every new role operates within defined scopes with GP or senior clinician oversight, standard protocols, and safeguarding checks. 
- training, professional development and career paths: joint training across nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals; protected time for learning; robust return-to-practice routes. 
- roles and responsibilities: allow pharmacists to do medicines reviews and minor illnesses, nurse practitioners and PAs to triage, manage chronic conditions, and support prescribing under supervision; allied health professionals to handle wound care, rehab, and routine monitoring; all under transparent accountability. 
- recruitment and retention: competitive pay, manageable workloads, mentorship, and mental-health support; reduce admin burden; offer flexible working and rotation to retain staff. 
- patient-centered design: ensure non-digital access options, clear triage paths, and continuity with a named GP or care team; implement reliable digital tools that support, not replace, in-person access. 
- fair distribution: ensure rural and underserved areas get investment and training hubs.
In my practice we’ve seen a pharmacist and a nurse practitioner take on routine follow-ups with GP oversight; wait times improved while safety remained high. This kind of guarded rollout, with strong safeguards, could free GPs to focus on complex cases.

I strongly endorse an NHS workforce plan that puts stronger links with social care, mental health and community services at the heart of how we recruit, retain and support staff, while ensuring we maintain safe, high-quality care. My experience in older age ranges and trying to navigate services for family and myself shows that patients benefit when care is genuinely integrated, rather than passed from one silo to another. A workforce plan that funds and structures joint-work arrangements across health and care sectors would redistribute workload in a way that makes life easier for clinicians and steadier for patients.

Priorities should include real, joint investment in integrated teams. If joint funding is available for roles like care coordinators, social prescribers, mental health link workers and pharmacy support within primary care, we can shift routine, non-clinical tasks away from GPs and practice nurses. That would free clinicians to focus on urgent and complex problems. In practice terms, this could mean co-located teams with shared IT and a common care plan for patients with multi-mactor needs, so someone with diabetes, mental health symptoms and housing concerns isn’t bounced between services but has a coherent plan and a single point of contact.

We also need to reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. The current array of audits, forms and separate IT systems eats into time we could spend with patients. Streamlined referrals and better IT usability would be a major win. For instance, a simple, interoperable referral process between general practice, community nursing, and mental health services, with one electronic form and automatic progress updates, would cut down delays and reduce frustration for patients and clinicians alike. We should invest in user-friendly, reliable IT that supports clinical decisions rather than adds layers of bureaucracy.

A sustainable workforce plan must address recruitment and retention in practical terms. This includes flexible working patterns, clear career progression, and fair pay for the additional responsibilities that come with extended hours or team-based care. International recruitment can help, provided it’s coupled with robust language support, cultural onboarding, and a structured mentorship in the first year. Locums should not be a long-term substitute for stable teams; we need to offer genuine progression and a sense of belonging within the NHS.

Training pipelines and career pathways are essential too. A stronger pipeline for nurses, physician associates, and mental health workers, with opportunities for continued professional development and stepwise responsibilities, will help us keep good staff. In my area, when staff feel the organisation is investing in them and their wellbeing, they stay longer and provide more consistent care to patients.

Wellbeing and safe staffing go hand in hand with high-quality care. A plan must guarantee adequate staffing levels, protected supervision time for junior staff, and easy access to mental health support for clinicians. Reducing administrative burden, ensuring decent admin support, and providing well-functioning IT will all contribute to a healthier work culture and less burnout.

Finally, care should be truly team-based. Expanding the scope of practice for nurses, pharmacists and allied professionals, along with clear clinical governance and safe handover protocols, can improve access and keep patients safe. It’s not about cutting roles but about making the best use of the skills we have and ensuring all staff can do what they were trained for without bureaucratic bottlenecks.

In short, the plan should set out dedicated, long-term funding for integrated teams; streamlined, user-friendly IT and referral systems; a realistic workload that prioritises patient-facing tasks; robust training and clear career paths; and a strong focus on staff wellbeing. If these elements are funded, monitored and adjusted over time, we’ll see safer care, better access, and a more sustainable NHS for patients and clinicians alike.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe, the plan must prioritise flexible, sustainable working patterns and genuine wellbeing. First ensure varied hours and duties: part-time work, job-sharing, and phased retirement options so experienced clinicians can stay on, mentoring juniors and easing workload. Childcare-friendly policies—on-site or subsided childcare, predictable rosters—are essential to keep skilled people from dropping out when family needs change. Second, bolster mental health support and stigma-free wellbeing programs: confidential counselling, protected mental health days, supervision and peer support networks embedded in teams. Third, safer workloads and staffing: enforce safe staffing ratios, realistic rosters, limits on consecutive long shifts, and administrative relief so clinicians can focus on patients. Fourth, clear career development and return-to-work routes: funded training, leadership pathways, and reintegration programs after leave. Fifth, a commitment to diversity and inclusion so the NHS workforce reflects the communities it serves. Finally, bring technology to reduce admin burden without compromising patient safety, with options for flexible deployment and non-digital acces when needed. In my experience, flexible patterns and genuine support are key to preventing burnout and keeping good staff long-term.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable, high‑quality care by balancing recruitment with rigorous safety and ongoing support. Key priorities include: safe staffing ratios based on patient needs, with real‑time dashboards and protected supervision time so clinicians can train and supervise without compromising care; continuity and team‑based care, with stable core teams and predictable rosters to reduce frequent handovers and maintain clinical knowledge; responsible overseas recruitment: streamlined visa routes and credential recognition, strong integration support (language and cultural induction), mentorship, and well‑structured return‑of‑service terms that protect patient access without draining source health systems; local training and clear career pathways: expand placements in underserved areas, partnerships with universities, and progression routes that encourage long‑term NHS careers; pay and conditions: competitive pay, pension provisions, relocation support, and flexible working options (job‑share, part‑time) alongside adequate admin and IT support to reduce burden; wellbeing and safety: accessible mental health support, protected time for supervision, and proactive burnout prevention; safety monitoring: robust incident reporting, regular safety audits and transparent improvement plans; using technology to support care: smart digital triage and telemedicine where appropriate, ensuring tech relieves workload without compromising contact times. Pilot, measure outcomes, and scale what works.

From my perspective juggling work and family in Scotland, any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff must treat flexible working as a core design principle, not an afterthought. Priorities should include offering flexible hours, part-time and job-sharing options, and phased retirement to keep experienced clinicians on the books while reducing burnout. This would also help ensure continuity of care for patients. We should expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals—working under clear supervision to safely distribute GP workload. For example, with proper training, a nurse-led same-day clinic and a pharmacist-supported medicines review could handle many routine issues, freeing GPs for complex cases and reducing delays. Visible safe staffing ratios and ongoing safety monitoring are essential so access improvements do not compromise quality. In rural areas of Scotland, robust remote triage, integration with GP practices and home visit models can improve access while preserving safety. Invest in childcare and mental health support for staff to reduce turnover. In short, flexible, team-based, safety-focused planning is the path to sustainable, high-quality care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things. First, clear funded career pathways with protected CPD time, structured mentorship and return-to-practice routes to keep both experienced clinicians and newer staff in the service. Second, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding so trusts can recruit, train and plan with less policy volatility and staff churn. Third, cut unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and improve IT and referral processes so clinicians spend more time with patients. Concrete steps could include protected CPD blocks for doctors, nurses and therapists; formal mentorship schemes paired with return-to-practice incentives; longer-term training places; and streamlined e-referral systems with simpler admin. In practice, this would address the burnout I’ve observed among healthcare staff and help ensure timely care for older residents who rely on steady, local services. It should be complemented by flexible working patterns and safe staffing ratios, plus investment across community and hospital teams so the whole system supports patient-facing care rather than overload.

From my perspective, any NHS workforce plan should focus on attracting and keeping staff where care is most needed, while protecting continuity and patient safety. I’m not convinced that broad, rapid expansion of teams alone will deliver better care if it pulls resources away from core GP services. The priorities ought to create a steady, well-supported workforce that can sustain high-quality, safe care over time, especially in underserved areas and in high-demand roles.

Key priorities I’d want to see prioritised include:
- Targeted, market-competitive pay and retention incentives: ensure high-demand roles (GPs, district nurses, mental health professionals, allied health professionals) have explicit pay scales that reflect the workload and responsibility. Include retention payments for staying in post for a defined period, and relocation packages to attract staff to shortages areas. Also offer bursaries or signing-on incentives for students who commit to serving in underserviced locations.
- Stabilise frontline staffing to safe levels: reduce over-reliance on locums by guaranteeing predictable staffing levels per shift and clear accountability for patient care. Minimum safe staffing numbers should be defined for key roles and shifts, with contingency plans that don’t compromise continuity of care.
- Clear career paths and professional support: provide protected time for training, structured mentorship, and transparent progression routes. Address burnout and workload by offering flexible working options, robust mental health support for staff, and effective administrative support so clinicians can focus on clinical care rather than endless paperwork.
- Strengthen recruitment pipelines: develop partnerships with medical and nursing schools, allied health training programmes, apprenticeships and return-to-practice schemes. Include targeted international recruitment where appropriate, with strong retention measures and clear integration support to avoid long-term churn.
- Improve working conditions and infrastructure: reduce administrative burden through better IT and digital tools, streamlined consent and records processes, and modern, well-equipped workplaces. A well-supported team with better facilities makes retention more likely.
- Geographically targeted initiatives: fund and support small clusters or hubs in areas with the most acute access problems, but with robust governance and a named clinical lead to safeguard continuity and safety. These hubs should complement, not replace, strong, stable primary care in surrounding communities.
- Data-driven workforce planning: publish transparent dashboards on vacancies, turnover, training uptake and patient safety indicators. Use real-time data to adjust recruitment and retention strategies quickly, avoiding patchy coverage that harms care quality.
- Safeguard continuity of care: maintain a strong GP-led model where possible, with new staff integrated into clear care pathways and accountable teams. Avoid fragmentation that erodes safety and makes it harder for patients to build a trustworthy relationship with their clinician.

In my area, persistent GP vacancies and reliance on temporary staff have already affected continuity and trust. A relocation package for a nurse who moved 40 miles to fill a vacancy, combined with a targeted bursary for students willing to commit to practice in the region, would have a real, tangible impact. My experience tells me that targeted, well-supported incentives work better than broad promises of “more teams” that can destabilise existing services.

If done with care, a workforce plan that prioritises competitive pay, retention and relocation options, strong training channels, and safer staffing levels can help deliver safe, high-quality care without sacrificing continuity. It should be a long-term, data-informed programme that values the frontline staff as much as the patients they serve.

Prioritise flexible, well-supported roles—offer part-time and job-share options, phased retirement, childcare support—and invest in proactive mental health services to prevent burnout, maintain safe, high-quality care and attract a diverse, stable NHS workforce.

i really think prioritise flexible, family-friendly working patterns: part-time and job-share roles, phased retirement, and robust childcare support, plus proactive mental health services. These, alongside safe staffing and manageable caseloads, will attract and retain diverse NHS staff while safeguarding care quality!

I think we should prioritise reducing admin burden and duplications, streamline referrals and boost IT usability to free clinicians for patient care. Use overseas recruitment responsibly with fast visa processes, credential recognition and integration support. Build transparent local workforce data, KPIs and evaluation to guide planning and funding.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the plan must be built on transparent, localised data. Develop clear workforce modelling, KPI sets and evaluation frameworks that feed into planning, funding decisions and performance reviews so we can see what works where it is most needed and adjust quickly. Retention hinges on flexible working: offering part‑time options, job‑share roles, phased retirement, accessible childcare and proactive staff mental health support to keep a diverse workforce and reduce burnout. In many front‑line roles, modest shifts in hours can make the difference between staying and leaving. Real‑time staffing dashboards should monitor demand, absence and skill mix to safeguard safety. Invest in career progression, mentoring and CPD with protected time to develop skills and confidence. Local pilots that extend hours, provide flexible GP/nurse rotas and offer on‑site or subsidised childcare have shown promise; scale where effective, backed by solid data. Proactive wellbeing services and a culture that destigmatises mental health are essential pillars for both recruitment and retention and for sustaining high‑quality care.

From where I live in Scotland, a NHS workforce plan to recruit, retain and support staff must be genuinely place-based, long‑term and designed with the realities of rural, coastal and urban-deprived areas in mind. Short-term bonuses or one‑off recruitment drives don’t fix the gaps we see day to day. We need tailored incentives that recognise distance, housing, transport and the particular demands of delivering safe, high‑quality care in communities that are hardest to staff.

Key priorities I’d want to see:
- Place-based recruitment and retention packages: Develop tailored packages for rural, coastal and deprived urban areas that include relocation assistance, affordable housing options, and incentives that reflect local living costs. This should be paired with a clear, local career path so staff can see a future in the communities they serve rather than feeling they’re just passing through.
- Housing support: Access to affordable housing near hubs is essential. It could involve partnerships with housing associations or NHS-supported housing schemes, with prioritised allocations for new staff and options for temporary accommodation during settling-in periods.
- Transport and travel support: In our region a long daily commute, unreliable public transport, and limited parking create real barriers. A workforce plan must fund reliable travel solutions—subsidised local transport, longer-term travel allowances, and flexible hours aligned to bus routes—so staff can reach remote clinics without added stress or financial strain.
- Staffing models that prioritise safety and continuity: We need stable, multidisciplinary teams in local hubs rather than relying heavily on agency staff. Adequate staffing ratios, predictable rosters, and protected time for consultation, follow-up and handovers are crucial to maintain patient safety and reduce burnout among clinicians.
- Working conditions and workload management: Administrative burden is choking clinical time. The plan should boost non-clinical support, streamline digital systems, and ensure reasonable workloads so staff can deliver thorough, compassionate care without sacrificing their wellbeing.
- Local training, career progression and retention: Invest in local education pathways so people can train and remain in their communities. Strong mentorship, CPD opportunities, and clear routes for advancement help staff feel valued and less likely to move away in search of better prospects.
- Community integration and cultural competence: Recruitment must reflect community diversity. Fund interpreters and culturally competent training as standard, and build strong links with community organisations so staff feel connected to the people they serve and communities feel welcome accessing care.
- Infrastructure and digital backbone: Local hubs should be comfortable, accessible and well-equipped, with reliable IT and telehealth that supports, not replaces, in-person care. A robust digital and estates plan ensures clinics can operate safely even in adverse weather or staffing shortages.
- Local decision-making and accountability: Place-based workforce plans should be overseen by local NHS boards with clear milestones and public reporting on vacancy rates, turnover, and wait times. Plans must be reviewed regularly to adapt to changing needs and to learn what works in different communities.
- Cross-sector collaboration: Align housing, transport and employment policies with health service planning. Joint working with local authorities, transport providers and housing bodies makes incentives more effective and sustainable, rather than creating confusing, overlapping schemes.

In practice, I’ve seen how fragile the current system is when staffing levels dip. Neighbours endure longer waits or have to travel further because a clinic is short-staffed for weeks. A thoughtful, well-funded workforce plan that recognises the unique needs of rural, coastal and deprived urban areas—and links housing, transport and local training with stable, well-supported roles—would help deliver safer, higher-quality care for everyone. It’s not about a quick fix, but about building a reliable, locally rooted NHS workforce that communities can trust for years to come.

From where I stand, the biggest change we need in workforce planning is stability, clarity and real investment in people who deliver care every day. A workforce plan should explicitly prioritise growing the domestic supply of capable, well-supported staff in primary and community care, while safeguarding safe, high-quality care every day. I’m broadly supportive of increasing training opportunities—undergraduate places, postgraduate pathways for general practice, and apprenticeships—with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships. Long-term, ring-fenced funding is essential to keep the momentum going and to avoid the stop-start cycles that waste time and confidence.

Key priorities I’d want to see in an NHS workforce plan:

- Grow domestic supply through education, training and apprenticeships: Increase undergraduate and postgraduate places for GPs, nurses, district nurses, therapists and other primary care roles, with protected placements that ensure trainees gain real, hands-on experience in a GP or community setting. Apprenticeships can bring in people who might not have considered healthcare as a first career, creating a broader, locally rooted workforce. Strong university–practice partnerships should guarantee supervising clinicians, practical exposure and a clear pathway from student to practitioner.
- Stable, multi-year funding for training and workforce initiatives: Secure funding settlements that last several years, specifically ring-fenced for training capacity, supervision, and staff development. When funding is tied to annual cycles or policy shifts, those changes ripple through every practice and trust, disrupting mentoring, rotations, and retention. A steady financial base would enable trusts to plan staffing levels, invest in simulation and training facilities, and sustain mentorship schemes for GP trainers, district nurses and allied health professionals.
- Retention and wellbeing as core design features: It’s not enough to train more people; we must keep them. That means safe, manageable workloads, flexible patterns, opportunities for career progression, and accessible wellbeing and supervision support. If staff feel supported and have a clear route for development, they’re more likely to stay in primary care where their skills are most needed.
- Local workforce planning with protected career pathways: Local health systems should have a clear mandate to translate training capacity into real jobs. That includes ensuring sufficient scalable roles in GP practices, community teams and out-of-hospital services so trainees see viable career progression locally rather than having to move away. Local partnerships with universities and colleges should deliver targeted pipelines for areas with shortages.
- Multidisciplinary teams and role clarity: A strong plan would promote safe delegation and team-based care—pharmacists, physiotherapists, district nurses, mental health practitioners, andGPs working together with well-defined scopes. This distributes workload more evenly and supports more timely triage, in line with the improvements I’ve asked for previously, so patients can access the right professional quickly.
- Return-to-practice and diversification of routes into care: Include programmes for those returning to practice after career breaks, career changers, and internationally trained staff to complement domestic recruitment. Yet the emphasis should stay on growing domestic capacity first, with appropriate visa and immigration policies aligned to long-term workforce needs rather than reacting to short-term fluctuations.
- Data-driven planning and strong governance: Use real-time workforce data to anticipate shortages and to align training capacity with service requirements. Clear governance should ensure training outcomes translate into improved patient access and safety.
- Focus on patient-facing impact: Ultimately, more staff must translate into better access, safer care and shorter wait times. For example, with more trained nurses and district nurses, triage pathways and rapid home visits could be expanded, which would support the kind of integrated access system I described earlier and relieve pressure on GP appointments.

In my own experience, when practices are under pressure, it’s not just about more people; it’s about having the right mix, well supported and well led, with a predictable plan for development. A workforce strategy built on stable funding, strong training opportunities, and clear career pathways would help us move toward a healthcare system where timely access to care is more reliable, and where the care teams aren’t stretched to breaking point. I’m not asking for miracles—just a thoughtful, well-funded plan that grows our own talent, keeps people in the profession, and protects the quality and safety patients rely on.

Prioritise joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to share workload; deliver targeted rural, urban and coastal incentives, housing and transport; provide funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise integration and funding across health and social care so that care remains safe and high‑quality. Strengthening links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services would help redistribute workload, reduce bottlenecks and deliver holistic patient care. In practice this means care coordinators who can marshal GP, district nursing, social services and community support, plus more blended teams to support older residents at home. I’ve seen how lack of coordination can lead to unnecessary hospital visits or delays for someone needing both a nurse and a carer.

Second, expand education and training pipelines: increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and university–practice partnerships. This would grow domestic primary care supply and bring fresh skills into practices that are stretched, including rural and coastal clinics.

Third, tailor incentives to place staff where they are most needed: rural, urban deprived and coastal areas. Housing and transport support, secure accommodation near clinics, and targeted recruitment packages will help fill hard‑to‑staff posts and improve retention. Finally, fund and protect safe staffing standards and reasonable workloads to maintain quality and morale, building on the idea that well‑supported teams deliver safer, more compassionate care.

Agree. Any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safety as the starting point to keep access improvements from compromising quality. This means enforcing safe staffing ratios across GP, community nursing and mental health, with clear thresholds that trigger recruitment or temporary staffing so care remains sustainable. It also means continuity-preserving models: stable teams, the same clinicians seeing the same lists where possible, robust handovers and strong information systems so patients aren’t reassessed by strangers each visit.

Safety monitoring should be real-time and outcome-focused: dashboards that correlate staffing, wait times, clinical outcomes and patient safety incidents, with swift action when signals worsen. Beyond safety, targeted competitive pay and retention incentives are essential to attract and keep staff in underserved areas and high-demand roles—retention payments, relocation packages, bursaries, and local recruitment drives for GPs, practice nurses, therapists and mental health workers.

We also need to reduce non-clinical workload and admin burden through funded support roles and smart digital tools, enabling clinicians to focus on care. A clear training and career progression pathway, plus mentorship and culturally competent training, will help retention. All of this must be underpinned by stable funding and coherent integration across primary, community and social care.

I strongly support an NHS workforce plan that keeps safety at the centre as we extend access. Prioritising safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models will help ensure that improvements in access do not come at the expense of clinical quality. Where teams work with stable staff rotas and protected supervision, I see fewer missed details, fewer handoffs and better patient experience, even in busy times. 

We need transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks. Trusts should publish staffing by site, skill mix and patient acuity, linked to waiting times and outcomes, so commissioners can target funding where it will have most impact. Real-time dashboards would help managers anticipate shortages and deploy cover before problems arise. 

Clarifying scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements is essential, along with funded protected clinical supervision for new roles (e.g., physician associates, advanced nurse practitioners, pharmacists). That clarity reduces fear among staff and patients and supports safe expansion. In my practice, when supervision and clear protocols were in place, new roles helped with access without compromising safety. Integrated IT and shared records are also vital to keep continuity as teams grow.

From my experience in England, the NHS workforce plan should focus on three linked priorities that keep care safe and high quality while people can rely on non-digital options. First, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, plus thorough staff training in digital tools. Yet safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients—phone lines, walk-in hubs, and clear triage routes—so not everyone is pushed online. When NHS111 and digital booking fail, we mustn't trap people in delays. In my area, repeated callbacks and disjoint messages waste time; better IT must connect GP, out-of-hours and community teams so information travels without patients re-reporting their symptoms. Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied roles, with proper supervision to safely redistribute GP workload. This would bring more in-person slots and earlier access, especially for chronic care and urgent assessments. Third, develop transparent, local workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Local dashboards would show vacancies, training progress, and impact on patient outcomes, enabling adjustments before problems worsen. These steps together would support safe, high-quality care while avoiding a digital-only cure.

Agree. Any NHS workforce plan to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality must be built on transparent, localised data and clear evaluation. Local modelling of demand by geography and service, plus KPIs on vacancies, turnover, sickness and patient safety, should inform how funding is allocated and how teams are deployed. Sharing anonymised dashboards between trusts and local authorities would show where gaps cluster and whether retention schemes and training pipelines are actually working. In our area, GP vacancies and burnout are evident, so targeted recruitment drives, flexible hours and multidisciplinary teams can help—but only if the data show their impact. Robust evaluation should test new roles and models (for example pharmacist prescribers in community clinics) and identify schemes that fail to improve safety or access, so resources aren’t wasted. Importantly, data must guide staffing for both digital and non-digital access: keep phone lines open, maintain local hubs, and empower managers to reallocate staff as needed. A balanced, data-led plan supports staff wellbeing and development while preserving safe, high-quality care for everyone.

Prioritise expanding education pipelines—undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeships—with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships to grow the domestic primary care workforce, backed by CPD, return-to-practice schemes and adequate staffing to sustain safe, high-quality care.

Prioritise expanding training pipelines—undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeships—with protected placements and university-practice links to grow domestic primary care capacity. Also cut admin burden and streamline referrals; invest in user-friendly IT to free clinicians for patient care, ensuring safety and quality.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three interlinked strands: scalable training and career progression, responsible international recruitment, and strong wellbeing and governance. Locally, co‑located hubs have shown how integrated teams can reduce burnout and improve safety; the plan should seize this by expanding training places, return‑to‑practice schemes, apprenticeships and ongoing CPD so more staff are grown from within. 

International recruitment can help plug hard‑to‑fill posts, but only with streamlined visa routes, rapid yet rigorous credential recognition, and structured integration support—orientation, language basics, mentoring and clear supervision—to help newcomers settle and work safely. Importantly, safeguards must be in place to avoid undermining health systems in source countries, including transparent quotas, ethical recruitment standards and mutually beneficial partnerships.

Equally, ensure safe staffing through data‑driven workforce planning, sensible workloads, robust supervision and competency checks. Invest in flexible working, wellbeing, and a culture that values long‑term retention. When combined, these elements can extend the reach of local hub models nationwide while preserving high‑quality, timely care for patients.

A strong NHS workforce plan will determine whether we get timely, safe, high-quality care now and in the years ahead. It should prioritise three linked strands: responsible recruitment (including overseas routes), meaningful investment in digital systems and training, and genuine support for staff wellbeing, development and safety. In practice that means tackling shortages with a balanced mix of domestic growth and targeted international recruitment, but always with safeguards to protect source health systems and to support new arrivals so they can work effectively from day one.

- Safe, sustainable staffing as the foundation. We need clear, nationally informed staffing norms across GP practices, hospital teams and community services, plus the flexibility to adapt to local demand without overburdening staff. Flexible shift patterns, protected time for learning, sensible cap on consecutive hours, and robust mental health and wellbeing support should be built in. In my area, when teams are lean, patients lose out on timely access and clinicians burn out faster. A plan that funds resilient rosters, backfill for vacancies, and corridor-to-care coordination will protect patient safety and staff morale.

- Overseas recruitment done responsibly. I welcome a framework that makes it easier to recruit qualified clinicians from abroad, but with safeguards: streamlined, transparent visa routes; recognised qualifications and language support; structured induction and mentorship so newcomers integrate smoothly; and long-term partnerships with source countries to avoid pulling too many professionals away from their own health systems. There should also be limits and monitoring to prevent creating shortages elsewhere. In practice, overseas recruitment can fill gaps quickly, but it must be ethical and sustainable, not a quick fix that leaves ripple effects in other countries.

- Interoperable IT, secure systems and digital training. A workforce plan should explicitly fund interoperable electronic health records, decision support tools and real-time workforce analytics that remove unnecessary admin and help clinicians focus on patients. But new tech is only as good as the people using it: give clinicians protected time to learn, update skills, and work through onboarding; ensure systems are user-friendly and reliable; and provide ongoing technical support. At the same time, we must safeguard digitally excluded patients by maintaining non-digital routes to access care and ensuring staff can assist with digital literacy when needed.

- Career development, progression and leadership. A clear, funded path from entry to advanced roles helps retain staff. This includes placements across primary, community and hospital settings; opportunities for specialist training (nursing, allied health, midwifery, diagnostics, mental health); leadership and management development; and recognition of long-term service with fair pay progression. When staff see a future with learning and advancement, turnover drops and continuity of care improves.

- Attractive, family-friendly and fair working conditions. Recruitment is only part of the answer if we also keep people once they’re here. Flexible working, adequate rest periods, high-quality staffing environments, accessible childcare or carer support, and strong safety cultures are essential. Retention also depends on fair staffing levels, transparent workloads, and visible wellbeing support that reduces burnout.

- Local partnerships and pipelines. Strengthening connections with universities, colleges and training bodies to create apprenticeships, return-to-practice programs and student placements helps grow the workforce locally. Simultaneously, a targeted international recruitment approach can help fill shortages in the short term, while domestic training capacity expands for the medium and long term.

- Data-informed planning and accountability. Real-time workforce data—vacancies, turnover, sickness absence, cause of leave—should guide decisions at local and national levels. Frontline input matters: managers, clinicians and support staff should help shape deployment, training priorities and role design. There should be clear accountability when targets aren’t met, with practical improvement plans.

From my experience, a health system works best when staffing decisions are aligned with patient flow and service design. If NHS111, triage, booking, and care pathways are to stay accessible and safe, the people delivering those services must be adequately recruited, properly trained, and well supported. A workforce plan that combines ethical international recruitment with strong domestic training, robust IT, and a serious commitment to staff wellbeing will be more resilient, more capable of handling demand spikes, and better for patients and staff alike.

From my perspective, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three practical, linked areas. First, overseas recruitment done responsibly: streamlined visas, prompt credential recognition, strong integration support (language help, mentoring, and induction), and safeguards against depleting health systems in source countries. This is essential to help fill shortages without creating ethical or global harm. Second, sustained investment in interoperable, secure IT and comprehensive staff digital training, while preserving viable options for those who are digitally excluded—paper records and telephone triage must remain available where needed. Third, strengthen links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and deliver holistic care; this includes shared planning, clear career pathways, and wellbeing support so experienced staff stay and feel valued. In my area, co-located hubs with GP practices, district nurses and pharmacists show how collaboration reduces pressure and improves safety; dependable IT and upskilling amplify those benefits.
