A plan that combines responsible recruitment, inclusive digital capability, and cross-service collaboration will sustain safe, high-quality care for older patients like me.

From our experience, an NHS workforce plan should prioritise safety and quality just as strongly as recruitment. It must provide clear, well-supported pathways for new and expanded roles, otherwise gains risk fragility. First, define scope of practice for all extended roles with formal delegation, decision-support protocols, and guaranteed access to patient records to prevent fragmentation. Second, ensure revalidation and continuing professional development are workable: reduced administrative burden, protected time to learn, and alignment with local supervision. Third, guarantee indemnity arrangements for these roles, including consistent professional liability coverage for triage, prescribing under protocol, and remote consultations. Fourth, fund protected clinical supervision: protected time for senior clinicians to mentor, supervise and review cases, with documented governance and safe-guarding. Fifth, create clear career progression and training pipelines to recruit and retain staff, with competitive terms and opportunities in our area. Sixth, ensure digital integration and shared records so teams can work safely across disciplines. In pilots we’ve seen co-located hubs and pharmacist-led clinics reduce GP visits, but sustainability hinges on long-term funding and robust supervision.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Without that, investment in recruitment won’t reliably translate into safer, timely care. The plan should have two linked strands: robust data guidance and targeted pay and incentives to attract and retain staff in underserved areas and high-demand roles.

Key actions:
- Routine publication of local vacancies, turnover, caseloads and backfill duration, broken down by district and practice type.
- Local modelling of demand and capacity with clear milestones and independent evaluation of schemes.
- Targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to recruit into hardest-hit areas and roles (GPs, district nurses, mental health workers).
- Return-to-practice schemes, language and induction support for international hires, and funding to backfill so practices aren’t stretched.
- Flexible working and wellbeing offers to sustain recruitment.

From my experience, vacancies in my area mean longer patient waits and heavier admin on already stretched teams. A data-led plan with meaningful incentives is essential to keep high-quality care safe.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan must start with secure, multi-year, ring-fenced funding. Long-term funding gives NHS boards the certainty to build training capacity, expand clinical placements in primary and community settings, and stabilise staffing without the constant churn caused by short-term commitments. 

Second, invest in workforce development across all roles: more medical school and nursing places, funded return-to-practice routes, protected time for continuing education, and robust supervision and mentorship. Create clear progression ladders and leadership development to improve retention, especially for junior staff and those working in rural or remote areas. 

Third, align workforce planning with social care and mental health from the outset. Joint funding streams and shared recruitment pipelines can redistribute workload and enable holistic care. Practical examples include integrated community teams that span GPs, nurses, pharmacists, social workers and psychologists, with shared training posts and cross-sector supervision.

Fourth, fix working conditions and safety: predictable rosters, safe staffing levels, caps on excessive shifts and accessible wellbeing support, backed by data-driven planning tools to anticipate demand. 

Finally, tailor incentives for rural and remote settings and ensure continuity of care during transitions between posts. This set of priorities would create a more resilient NHS workforce able to deliver high-quality care now and in the future.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, an NHS workforce plan should do two things: grow domestic supply and ensure data-driven, locally tailored management. First, prioritise expanding undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships so students rotate through GP clinics, community teams and social care settings. This builds a home-grown workforce that understands local needs and reduces dependence on short-term staffing. In rural and outer-city areas, such continuity matters for safety and confidence in care.

Second, commit to transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks. Real-time dashboards on vacancies, turnover, sickness, workload, wait times and patient safety should inform funding and allocation decisions. Local NHS bodies must be able to see what works and adjust quickly, with ring-fenced funding tied to meeting safe staffing targets.

Additionally, ease the admin burden and protect time for training and supervision. Fast-track return-to-practice pathways, flexible training and strong development incentives will improve retention. Practical incentives—adequate pay, manageable workloads and access to well-being support—are essential to keep staff delivering safe, high-quality care at the point of need.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise flexible, sustainable roles to attract and keep people in care. This means more part-time positions, job-sharing, phased retirement options, and practical childcare support so staff aren’t choosing between family and career. Such measures would help retain a diverse workforce, reduce burnout and preserve career paths for younger staff like me who value balance and stability in their working lives. 

It should also strengthen links with social care and community services through joint funding and integrated teams. Shared rotas and pooled back‑office support would redistribute workload, cut unnecessary handoffs, and speed up patient care from GP clinics into community settings, improving overall outcomes for patients who rely on multiple services. 

Investing in interoperable IT and secure systems with ongoing staff digital training is essential. This includes seamless data sharing, e-prescribing, and effective telehealth, while ensuring alternatives for digitally excluded patients, such as in-person clinics or phone access. 

A plan that combines flexible working, cross‑sector funding, and digital readiness will help recruit, retain and maintain safe, high‑quality care for everyone who depends on NHS services.

An NHS workforce plan must prioritise sustainable recruitment, retention and support to keep care safe and high quality. In practice this means ensuring enough staff in general practice, community health and mental health services, with predictable workloads that allow continuity of care and the longer, deeper reviews patients need.

Key priorities include:
- Recruitment and progression: competitive pay, clear career ladders, protected time for training and supervision, and structured induction for new teams.
- Retention and wellbeing: manageable rosters, accessible mental health support for staff, safer working environments, and reduced unnecessary admin that pulls clinicians away from patients.
- Deployment and teams: expanding multidisciplinary teams so nurses, pharmacists, physios and physician associates work to the top of their skills, with strong leadership and supervision.
- Training and capacity: robust in-house training, local apprenticeships and faster credential recognition to bring skilled staff into frontline roles.
- Data-driven planning: use demand projections to align recruitment with anticipated need and avoid last‑minute shortfalls.

Overseas recruitment can help fill gaps, but it must be responsible: streamlined visa routes for qualified clinicians, rapid recognition of professional credentials, structured induction with language and cultural integration support, and ongoing mentoring. Safeguards are essential to avoid depleting source countries’ health systems — for example through caps, quotas, and bilateral capacity-building. In my experience, well-supported staff deliver better outcomes and reduce avoidable hospital visits.

Prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation; strengthen joint funding with social care and community services to share workloads and deliver holistic care; and expand education pipelines—undergrad, postgrad and apprenticeships—with protected placements and uni-practice partnerships to grow domestic primary care capacity.

AN NHS WORKFORCE PLAN SHOULD PRIORITIZE CUTTING UNNECESSARY ADMIN AND DUPLICATED TASKS, AND MAKING REFERRALS AND IT SYSTEMS EASIER TO USE SO CLINICIANS CAN SPEND MORE TIME WITH PATIENTS. IN PRACTICE, CLINICIANS TODAY SPEND HOURS ON PAPERWORK AND CHASING REFERRALS ACROSS MULTIPLE SYSTEMS; A SIMPLER, MORE USABLE IT ENVIRONMENT WOULD FREE UP VALUABLE TIME FOR ASSESSMENT AND FOLLOW‑UP, ESPECIALLY IN LONG‑TERM CONDITIONS AND MENTAL HEALTH. 

IT SHOULD ALSO STRENGTHEN LINKS WITH SOCIAL CARE, MENTAL HEALTH AND COMMUNITY SERVICES, WITH JOINT FUNDING TO REDISTRIBUTE WORKLOAD AND ENABLE HOLISTIC CARE AT SCALE. CLEAR SCOPE‑OF‑PRACTICE, REVALIDATION, AND INDEMNITY ARRANGEMENTS ARE ESSENTIAL, WITH PROTECTED CLINICAL SUPERVISION FUNDED TO SUPPORT NEW ROLES WITHOUT COMPROMISING SAFETY. 

FINALLY, INVEST IN PEOPLE: PROTECTED TIME FOR TRAINING, TRANSPARENT CAREER PATHWAYS, AND PREDICTABLE STAFFING SUPPORT TO IMPROVE MORALE AND RETENTION. A PLAN THAT REDUCES ADMIN, ALIGNS FUNDING ACROSS SERVICES, AND SAFEGUARDS PROFESSIONAL STANDARDS WILL HELP RECRUIT, RETAIN AND SUSTAIN HIGH‑QUALITY CARE FOR PATIENTS.

To maintain timely access while protecting safety and quality, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise targeted, well-funded recruitment and retention, especially for underserved areas and high-demand roles. This should include competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract GPs, nurses, mental health professionals, and care coordinators. Clear career pathways with funded training and supervision will help staff stay in the system and grow, reducing turnover that disrupts patient care.

Equally important is safe staffing and continuity. Set and enforce safe staffing ratios, promote continuity-preserving multidisciplinary teams, and implement robust safety monitoring and learning from incidents to prevent problems from escalating as access expands. In practice, that means flexible recruitment timelines, mentorship schemes, protected time for supervision and quality improvement, and wellbeing support to prevent burnout.

Finally, align workforce planning with the hub model discussed earlier: ensure co-located teams have enough staff to run same-day triage and integrated social and mental health services, with stable funding, flexible working options, and clear pathways for staff transferring into new roles or locations.

Prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, robust modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring; ensure regular review and responsive investment to support recruitment, retention and safe, high-quality care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise four linked areas to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality. First, establish clear scope‑of‑practice for expanded roles (advanced practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists, etc.) with straightforward revalidation and affordable, consistent indemnity arrangements. This helps people work to the highest safe level and reduces variation in care. Funding protected clinical supervision is essential: regular, protected supervision time and governance reviews so new roles are supported as they take on more responsibility. Second, use overseas recruitment responsibly: streamline visas and credential recognition, but couple this with robust integration support—mentoring, language and cultural onboarding, and practical help with housing—to prevent pressures on source health systems and ensure staff are retained long‑term. Third, underpin all with sustainable funding and working conditions: competitive pay, flexible rosters, wellbeing support, and clear career progression, plus strong local pipelines from universities and apprenticeships to address shortages in primary care and mental health. Fourth, basing decisions on real data, with transparent staffing standards and escalation pathways to maintain safe levels of care, and invest in leadership development so teams can adapt to changing needs. In my area, enhanced supervision for new clinicians could cut waits and improve safety while we expand access to timely services.

I think any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe staffing as the bedrock of both access and quality. Expanding access to services is important, but it must not come at the expense of patient safety or the consistency patients rely on. From what I’ve seen and heard in my communities, when staffing ratios fall, wait times lengthen, and the quality of care—especially in routine or complex cases—feels the impact. So the plan should set clear, funded requirements for safe staffing across primary, community, mental health and acute settings, with independent monitoring and transparent reporting.

- Safe staffing ratios and predictable staffing levels: Establish enforceable minimum staffing ratios that reflect the acuity and complexity of the setting. This would include not only doctors and nurses but allied health professionals in teams that are operating at the top of their training. For example, in practices where a multidisciplinary team is in place, having enough pharmacists, physiotherapists and physician associates to share routine workload keeps GPs free to manage higher-risk patients and diagnostics without compromising access.

- Continuity-preserving models: Patients value a reliable, named point of contact and a stable care team. The plan should promote continuity by funding small, consistent multidisciplinary teams in local hubs, with protected slots so patients aren’t shuffled between new staff every visit. In practice, that could mean a practice nurse who knows a family’s history works alongside a physician associate on follow-ups for chronic conditions, with a named GP for complex decisions. Continuity supports safer prescribing, better recognition of deterioration, and more confident care navigation.

- Safety monitoring and governance: Implement robust safety metrics and independent review mechanisms. Regular safety dashboards should track avoidable harm, wait times for high-priority conditions, appointment cancellation rates, and patient-reported safety experiences. If data show a pathway is compromising safety, the plan must allow rapid adjustments—retraining, staffing reallocations, or temporarily slowing expansion in that area until safeguards are in place. This ongoing vigilance is essential when changing models of care.

- Funded, clear career pathways and CPD protection: To recruit and keep skilled staff, there must be transparent, well-funded routes for progression. Funded protected time for continuing professional development, structured mentorship, and formal return-to-practice schemes for those who've paused clinical work are crucial. This helps retain experienced clinicians and supports early-career staff as they build confidence and competence. For instance, a GP practice that offers protected CPD time alongside peer mentorship is more likely to retain a nurse practitioner or a physician associate who might otherwise leave for better-supported roles elsewhere.

- Mentorship, return-to-practice and flexible careers: Establish national and local schemes that make it easier for experienced staff to mentor others and for clinicians returning after breaks to refresh competencies. Flexible working patterns, well-being support, and workload management that recognise family and study commitments will improve retention in a demanding sector.

- Clear progression tied to workforce design: Career ladders should be aligned with service changes—e.g., expanding MDTs and community-based care—so staff can move into roles that match evolving models without losing professional identity or supervision. The emphasis should be on safe delegation, defined scopes of practice, and robust supervision to maintain quality.

- Equity and geography: The plan must address rural and deprived urban areas where staffing pressures are higher. Use targeted training pipelines, local pipeline development, and rotational schemes to ensure a consistent standard of care nationwide, not just in pilot sites. Equity in access to safe staffing must be part of the success metrics.

In short, I’d like to see a workforce plan that treats safe staffing, continuity of care, and rigorous safety monitoring as non-negotiables, backed by funded career progression, CPD protection, mentorship, and accessible return-to-practice routes. That combination should help deliver real improvements in access while preserving the clinical quality and patient safety on which people rely every day.

i strongly believe a strong NHS workforce plan should align recruitment, retention and support with the reality that care happens in teams that span primary care, mental health, social care and community services. The aim must be to redistribute workload so clinicians can focus on safe, high‑quality care while patients get holistic support. In practice, this means several concrete priorities.

- Integrated, adequately funded workforce planning across sectors. Local areas should be encouraged to design teams that share roles and responsibilities across NHS, social care and community services. This can include joint recruitment campaigns, shared training budgets and pooled funding for community‑based teams (district nurses, social care practitioners, community mental health workers) so workload is distributed rather than transferred to a single service.

- Flexible, diverse working patterns to recruit and retain. Offering more part‑time roles, job‑share possibilities, phased retirement and formal childcare support helps attract a broader range of staff and reduces burnout. Flexible rotas must be paired with safe staffing norms and predictable planning to avoid gaps in care. Real‑world examples include evening clinics and weekend cover, where experienced staff can stay connected with patients without being pushed into unsustainable hours.

- Stronger focus on wellbeing, supervision and burnout prevention. A plan should guarantee accessible mental health support for staff, protected supervision, manageable caseloads, and administrative relief so clinical time isn’t swallowed by paperwork. Reducing burnout is as important as recruiting new staff, because turnover undermines safety and continuity of care.

- Streamlined training and clear career pathways. Create multidisciplinary training that enables nurses, GPs, pharmacists, social workers and allied health professionals to work effectively in integrated teams. Expand return‑to‑practice routes, apprenticeships and funded upskilling so staff can progress while staying in patient‑facing roles. Local career ladders should be explicit and attainable.

- Investment in digital tools without eroding human contact. Use technology to cut unnecessary admin, support triage, and enable flexible working, but preserve non‑digital options and in‑person support for patients who need it. Employ dedicated admin or care coordination roles to prevent clinicians from becoming data entry bottlenecks. A blended approach helps maintain safety and accessibility.

- Tangible support for rural and underserved areas. Local plans must address recruitment and retention in harder‑to‑staff locations with targeted incentives, supported remote and mobile services, and reliable transport solutions so patients can access care and staff aren’t deterred by isolation.

- Governance, accountability and measurable impact. Establish clear safety standards, workforce metrics (vacancies, turnover, burnout indicators, training uptake) and public reporting so services can adapt quickly. Continuous evaluation should inform how best to allocate joint funding and adjust rostering across sectors.

- A patient‑centred ethos in workforce design. Recognise that staff morale and capacity directly affect patient experience and outcomes. The plan should embed patient input into workforce models, ensuring teams are sized and composed to meet local needs and that flexible options don’t compromise care quality.

From my observations in our local area, a more integrated approach to staffing—where social care and community teams share capacity and resources with GP practices and local mental health services—could ease the pressure on individual clinicians and deliver more holistic care for patients with complex, long‑term needs. Flexible working patterns, backed by strong wellbeing support and sensible workload management, are essential to sustaining a diverse workforce willing to stay in front‑line roles. Overall, I’d like to see a workforce plan that prizes collaboration across sectors, supports staff with real, practical options, and measures outcomes for both patients and providers so money and effort genuinely translate into safer, higher‑quality care!

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high-quality, the plan should prioritise funded career pathways that keep experienced clinicians in frontline roles and provide clear routes for mid‑career progression. Protected CPD time and funding are essential so staff can stay up to date without having to sacrifice personal time or accept declining training quality as workload grows. Formal mentorship schemes linking seasoned clinicians with newer recruits and with those returning after a break should be standard, with dedicated time and measurable outcomes to track progress. Return‑to‑practice routes must be straightforward, with flexible options and supportive supervision during re‑entry to rebuild confidence after a pause.

Invest in whole teams—district nurses, community pharmacists, social prescribers, and mental health workers—so teams can share expertise and reduce bottlenecks that patients feel as delays. Ensure safe, realistic workloads, adequate admin support, and predictable rosters so burnout is not the price of higher access. Prioritise wellbeing resources and recognition for long‑serving staff, and align recruitment and training with the need to maintain continuity of care for older patients who may rely on non‑digital access.

In my area, I’ve seen how talent is lost when there’s no structured progression or mentorship; this plan would help keep experienced staff and newer entrants committed to high‑quality care.

From my experience in England, the biggest gains come when systems talk to each other. An NHS workforce plan should prioritise interoperable, secure IT and comprehensive staff digital training, with explicit support for those who are digitally excluded so they’re not left behind. Clinicians should be able to access shared care records, order tests and refer within one system, reducing duplication and delays. 

Crucially, we must reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. Streamline referrals and improve IT usability so time spent on admin is kept to a minimum, freeing clinicians for direct patient care. A real-world example: at my local practice, critical time is lost navigating incompatible systems and chasing results; a simpler triage and referral flow would release capacity for same-day advice. 

Invest in workforce models that support co-located multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and physician associates—within the hub approach, with clear career progression and protected time for professional development. Ensure training and supervision are available for all staff, and that backfill arrangements are planned so patient care remains safe during coverage gaps. 

Overall, a focus on usable IT, reduced admin burden and strong multidisciplinary teams will help recruit, retain and deliver high-quality care.

From where I sit, the NHS workforce plan must do more than fill vacancies for today; it should build a longer-term pipeline that sustains safe, high‑quality care in communities like ours. I strongly support increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships, to grow domestic primary care workforce supply. When training is done in real practice settings, with careful supervision and clear time for learning, staff stick around, know the community, and patients benefit from continuity.

First, expand the core pipeline. More medical, nursing and allied health undergraduates who gain early, meaningful exposure to general practice and community services will help demystify primary care and spark long‑term careers in the sector. Protected placements are essential: students must have learning time that doesn’t overly squeeze clinics or reduce access to appointments. I’ve seen how a well‑structured placement in a GP practice, with supervision and paid time for reflective learning, can be beneficial for both students and patients, not just for the practice’s day‑to‑day queue. Similarly, targeted postgraduate training, and enhanced GP specialty exposure in early career stages, helps new clinicians build confidence in independent practice more quickly.

Second, expand apprenticeship routes within primary care. Apprenticeships can bring local people into caring roles—navigators, care coordinators, social prescribers, and support staff—who then progress into higher‑level roles. These routes should sit alongside traditional routes, with clear progression ladders and funded time for study. In our hubs, a care navigator trained through an apprenticeship could provide outreach to older residents, help with transport to appointments, and coordinate social support, freeing GPs to focus on clinical care while preserving the personal touch that matters to patients like us.

Third, cement strong university–practice partnerships. Joint curricula, shared governance, and funded placements mean training happens without compromising safety or service quality. Universities should work with NHS employers to ensure supervisors are trained, protected time is provided, and learners contribute meaningfully to patient care rather than becoming a burden. Rotations across primary care, district nursing, mental health liaison, and social care within a hub can create well‑rounded practitioners who understand the realities of integrated care and can work across disciplines when needed.

Fourth, keep retention at the heart of the plan. It isn’t enough to recruit; staff must have opportunities for career progression, mentoring, and CPD that fits with their workloads. That includes flexible working arrangements, robust wellbeing support, reasonable workloads, and appropriate remuneration. We also need real pathways for experienced clinicians to take on leadership and teaching roles, which gives them purpose and stabilises services in the long term.

Fifth, tailor workforce planning to local needs and protection of safe care. Use workforce modelling to predict where shortages will occur and align training capacity accordingly. In rural and underserved urban areas, provide targeted recruitment campaigns, return‑to‑practice initiatives, and incentives to attract people to primary care. Staff must be able to deliver high‑quality care without being stretched to breaking point; protected time for supervision, case discussions, and joint assessments should be baked into every expansion plan.

Sixth, ensure the infrastructure supports training and safe care. Invest in training facilities within or near hubs, robust supervision models, and digital tools that enable remote supervision and learning without compromising patient access. Shared electronic records and consent processes help learners follow real patients through their care journeys while maintaining privacy and safety.

Finally, keep patients and communities involved. People like us value predictable, compassionate care, and we want to see patient representatives involved in workforce planning so training aligns with community needs and concerns. In the long run, a well‑grounded pipeline of domestically trained primary care staff will support the cohesive, locally rooted hubs we need to deliver timely, high‑quality care.

In short, prioritising education, protected placements, and strong university–practice partnerships isn’t a nice‑to‑have; it’s essential for a future NHS that can recruit, retain and sustain a capable primary care workforce capable of delivering the integrated care models we’ve discussed.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping high-quality, safe care, the plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams and making sure they are properly trained and supervised. This would allow nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles to take on well-defined, supported tasks from GPs, freeing doctors to focus on complex care and urgent cases. Key elements: clear scopes of practice, formal supervision structures, and robust clinical governance; planned career pathways and protected funding for MDT roles; accessible continuing training, including culturally competent care and digital tools to support decision-making; fair, predictable rostering and safe staffing levels to reduce burnout; and strong integration with GP practices, community services and social care through shared records and joint planning. In practice, I’ve seen GP waiting times grow as workloads rise; MDTs could help with routine reviews, medication management and triage, but must be introduced with safeguards to avoid fragmentation. With proper oversight, this approach could improve access while preserving safety and quality.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan should prioritise people, not just processes. Flexible, staff‑centred working patterns must be a core element: more part‑time roles, job‑share, phased retirement options, and practical childcare support so people can stay in health careers across life stages. This would help reduce burnout and widen the talent pool, including students and those returning after a pause.

Second, proactive mental health and wellbeing services for staff: confidential counselling, stress management, and peer support embedded in every organisation, with protected time for wellbeing.

Third, transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks: real‑time dashboards on vacancies, skill mix, sickness absence and workload, plus regular local reviews to inform funding, recruitment and training.

Fourth, sustained investment in training, supervision and progression: robust preceptorships, return‑to‑practice schemes, mentoring and clear career pathways to retain skilled staff.

Finally, ensure safe staffing and manageable workloads by aligning rosters with patient demand and ensuring appropriate supervisory capacity.

Prioritise transparent, local workforce data with KPIs and evaluation; clear scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements; protected clinical supervision; and multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain training and safe care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise freeing clinicians to care for patients rather than chase ever more paperwork. It must recruit, retain and support staff, but in a sustainable way that keeps safety and high‑quality care at the centre. Key priorities: reduce unnecessary targets, duplicative tasks and bureaucracy; streamline referrals; improve IT usability and interoperability so GP surgeries, hospitals and community teams share records and orders without re-keying data. This would free time for consultation, triage and follow‑up.

Invest in staffing with flexible working, manageable workloads and clear career progression, including mentoring for younger clinicians and strong wellbeing support to prevent burnout. A workforce strategy should include stable, adequately funded budgets, with ring‑fenced funds for recruitment, training and IT upgrades. Workstreams should be integrated with primary care so mental health, social care and community services can act as one system. Consider targeted international recruitment with robust induction, and expanded roles for allied health professionals to support GP‑led care.

In my experience, when systems become overburdened by admin, patient care suffers; simpler processes and better IT would make a tangible difference to safety and morale.

Prioritise more training places with protected placements and uni-practice partnerships, clear funded career pathways with CPD and mentorship, and expanding multidisciplinary teams to safely share GP workload while maintaining quality.

From a local perspective, any NHS workforce plan should be built on transparent, locally gathered data, solid modelling and clear KPIs, with evaluation frameworks that feed funding, planning and performance monitoring. Without close, current insight, staffing decisions can miss needs and risk safety. Priorities must include growing the domestic primary care workforce by expanding undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship placements, with protected slots and strong university–practice partnerships to ensure real, funded placement opportunities in GP practices and community teams. This should go hand in hand with clear career progression, retention incentives and support for staff balancing heavy workloads. 

Investing in interoperable IT and secure systems is essential, together with ongoing digital training for staff. At the same time, we must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients, keeping reliable phone triage and in-person options, and simple, consistent workflows. Our experience shows that when digital tools work without leaving people behind, access improves; when they don’t, delays grow. 

Practical staffing must also focus on safe, sustainable teams: appropriate staffing levels, manageable workloads, strong clinical governance, mental health and wellbeing support, and ongoing CPD. Embedding pharmacists, physiotherapists and nurse practitioners within local teams helps reduce GP workload while preserving high-quality, safe care.

From where I sit, in England, any NHS workforce plan must be practical, safe and sustainable. We’ve seen how staffing pressures ripple through every part of the system, from a delayed GP appointment to a crisis point in mental health care. A plan that genuinely prioritises recruitment, retention and support for staff, while keeping care safe and high quality, would make a real difference to people like me who rely on services being there when needed.

First, the core must be safe, predictable workloads. It’s not enough to shout about more staff; we need clear staffing models that ensure enough GPs, nurses, district nurses, therapists and social care colleagues are consistently on duty in the places that patients actually use them. That means transparent, locally agreed safe staffing levels, realistic rosters, and protection against burnout, so appointments aren’t rushed or cancelled because someone has to clock off early. In our town I’ve seen practices run on a skeleton team, which makes same-day slots a rarity and longer waits the rule. A workforce plan that guarantees safe staffing, with a mechanism to flag and address shortfalls before patients feel the impact, would be a real improvement.

Second, expand multi-disciplinary teams in primary care and community hubs. If practice-based pharmacists, physiotherapists, and occupational therapists work alongside GPs with proper supervision, triage becomes quicker and follow-ups more efficient. A patient could get a home visit that includes an assessment and a simple treatment plan from a nurse plus advice from a pharmacist in one visit. That kind of integration reduces pressure on doctors and speeds up care for people who don’t need hospital admission. We already know how valuable neighbourhood hubs would be for older residents who struggle with transport—bringing more expertise into the community would keep people well at home longer.

Third, invest in retention, development and flexible working. We’re living longer with chronic conditions, so career pathways for NHS staff matter. The plan should guarantee protected time for continuing professional development, clear routes for career progression, and flexible working options that allow experienced staff to stay in the service without burning out. That means part-time roles, job sharing, and appropriate supervision so newer staff aren’t left to shoulder heavy caseloads alone. I’ve spoken with a few long-serving nurses who’ve considered leaving because the pressure becomes intolerable; a steady, supportive environment with opportunities to grow would help keep skilled people at the bedside.

Fourth, recruit and support staff with wellbeing at the centre. Access to mental health support for staff, leadership that listens, and practical measures to ease administrative burdens will pay off in safer, higher-quality care. I’ve heard about colleagues who delayed seeking help for burnout due to stigma or long wait times for counselling. A plan that normalises help-seeking, accelerates access to support, and provides supervision for staff in high-stress roles would protect both workers and patients.

Fifth, reduce admin burden while preserving patient-friendly contact. Digital systems should ease clinicians’ workloads, not create new bottlenecks. We must maintain non-digital channels—phone lines and in-person contact—for anyone who struggles with online systems, especially older patients. A workforce plan should fund dedicated admin time and smarter IT that automatically flags care gaps, reminds patients of follow-ups, and routes referrals to the right team without endless chasing.

Sixth, local planning with a forward look. Demography, geography and local needs differ; a successful plan should translate into local workforce strategies, with pipelines for recruitment from the communities served, and strong links to education and training providers. That means apprenticeships and local career-pathways that bring in new blood while valuing the expertise of long-standing staff. Integrated care won’t happen by chance; it needs deliberate, cross-sector workforce planning that aligns NHS capacity with social care and voluntary sectors.

Finally, the plan must acknowledge prevention and community resilience. A well-supported workforce can deliver more effective prevention, social prescribing and community health initiatives that reduce demand on urgent services later. We can’t keep throwing money at short-term fixes; investing in staff, proper supervision and collaborative care today should save money and keep people living independently at home tomorrow.

Budgets are tight, yes, but a plan that prioritises staffing safety, stable teams, development and wellbeing will yield safer care and better outcomes. That’s not just about keeping appointments; it’s about keeping people well and connected to their communities for longer.

In Wales, prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving care, with robust safety monitoring and realistic workloads; invest in recruitment and training to keep high-quality access without compromising care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise closer integration with social care and community services, supported by joint funding, to rebalance workload and deliver more holistic care. This means co-funded posts and seamless career pathways that span hospital, community and care‑home settings, so staff can move between settings and share responsibilities without losing continuity. Expand and stabilise community mental health teams and crisis support with protected time for supervision, training and clinical development, and longer appointments where appropriate. Invest in multidisciplinary training across health, mental health and social care to build a common approach to complex, long‑term conditions. Improve workforce resilience with flexible, predictable rotas, strong wellbeing support and stable contracts to reduce turnover. Use shared planning dashboards and data to align recruitment with local demand and discharge planning needs. In my area, stronger joint working between GP practices and social care reduced discharge delays and avoided unnecessary visits, showing how joint funding can free up scarce staff for safer, higher‑quality care.

I agree that an NHS workforce plan must prioritise how we recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care. Practically, that means investing in interoperable, secure IT systems and giving staff the training and protected time they need to use them effectively. Shared, longitudinal records across GP, hospital, community and mental health teams should cut duplication and support continuity of care, so patients aren’t bounced between clinicians. Staff require ongoing digital skills training, with strong emphasis on cybersecurity and data protection, plus dedicated roles (digital champions) to help clinics implement tools smoothly. 

Crucially, we must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients: maintain reliable non‑digital access such as in‑person appointments, telephone triage, printed summaries, and local digital hubs for those without devices or connectivity. IT funding should be stable and ongoing, not just pilot projects, and must go hand in hand with staffing: safe ratios, wellbeing support, clear career progression, and flexible working to aid recruitment and retention, especially in rural areas.

Concrete steps include incentives for rural postings, longer appointment times for complex cases, protected time for training, and governance that monitors safety alongside digital expansion to ensure improvements don’t widen inequalities.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise targeted pay and incentives, not just generic raises. Regional pay differentials, retention payments for staying in harder-to-staff areas, and relocation packages will help fill shortages in rural towns and high-demand roles such as GPs, mental health specialists, and community nurses. Bursaries and debt relief for students who commit to service in underserved areas, with protected time for study and clear career progression, would build a sustainable pipeline.

Overseas recruitment should be used responsibly: streamlined visa routes, rapid credential recognition, structured welcome and integration support, and safeguards to prevent draining source countries of healthcare professionals. Complement this with local training expansion, apprenticeships, and return-to-practice schemes to fill gaps while maintaining quality.

Crucially, ensure safe staffing levels, adequate backfill, reasonable workloads, supportive supervision, and mental health support for staff. Use real-time workforce data to align supply with patient demand, and offer housing assistance and flexible models to help staff stay in post and deliver timely, appropriate care.

To keep care safe and high quality while improving access, the workforce plan should prioritise sustainable staffing that reflects real patient demand, including capacity for evenings and weekends. This means ensuring enough GPs, GP practice nurses and mental health professionals so appointments aren’t squeezed into tiny windows or cancelled last minute. It also requires stable, predictable funding rather than short-term patches, so teams aren’t constantly playing catch-up. 

I’d support flexible roles and clear career pathways to help recruitment and retention locally: part-time options, job sharing, robust supervision, mentoring, and genuine opportunities for progression into leadership or specialist roles. Staff wellbeing must be embedded—adequate rest between shifts, accessible mental health support, and protected time for training and debriefs after difficult cases. 

Invest in pipelines: strong local training placements, better links with schools and universities, and incentives for those willing to work in under-served areas. Pair this with smarter use of technology and admin support so clinicians spend more time with patients rather than chasing forms. Finally, ensure truly integrated working across primary, community and mental health services so handovers are smooth and safety is safeguarded during busy periods.

I think an NHS workforce plan should prioritise clear funded career pathways and protected CPD for all staff, plus strong mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to hold onto experienced clinicians and to support early-career teams. For instance, guaranteed CPD budgets and structured mentorship for new recruits, combined with funded return-to-practice routes that offer flexible hours, would help people rejoin the workforce after a break and fit caring responsibilities. Apprenticeship routes into nursing, pharmacy support, and allied roles can widen the talent pool without delaying patient care, as our area has shown how staff shortages lengthen waiting times.

Second, reduce bureaucracy that takes time away from patients: fewer targets, less duplicative paperwork, streamlined referrals, and improved IT usability would free clinicians to see more patients safely. Third, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and others—with proper training and supervision to share GP workload. A coordinated hub model can improve continuity and reduce handoffs, protecting quality of care.

As someone living in England, I think any NHS workforce plan must not merely chase headcount but ensure staffing supports safe, high-quality care. It should clearly define the scope of practice and provide robust revalidation and indemnity arrangements, including funded protected clinical supervision for new roles like advanced practitioners or care coordinators. Without this, rapid recruitment risks unsafe practice or professional burnout. In my area, clinics sometimes rely on quickly trained staff with insufficient supervision, which can compromise patient safety. We also need multidisciplinary teams and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to rebalance workloads. For example, better-integrated social care support would reduce avoidable hospital visits and allow GPs to focus on complex cases. Another priority is responsible overseas recruitment: streamlined visas, recognition of overseas credentials, integration support, and safeguards to avoid draining workforce from source countries. Finally, career progression and predictable funding are crucial. Clear routes from nursing or AHP roles into advanced practice, with mentorship and protected supervision, would help retention. Overall, a plan that combines strong professional governance with cross-sector collaboration will deliver safer, more sustainable care rather than short-term staffing bursts.

From what we hear locally, any NHS workforce plan must be designed with local flexibility at its heart. A rigid national blueprint risks leaving gaps in different communities - what a surprise. Priorities should be shaped by real-world experience and tested in pilots before wider rollout. In practice, I think plans should focus on:
- Local talent pipelines: stronger links with schools, colleges and training providers; expanded return-to-practice routes; streamlined onboarding so staff can start delivering care sooner.
- Retention and morale: manageable workloads, protected time for supervision and CPD, clear career paths and mentoring, fair contracts, and reduced reliance on agency staffing.
- Safe care and workforce models: ensuring safe staffing levels and appropriate skill mix; reducing unnecessary admin with better digital tools; ensuring supervision and safe handovers.
- Well-being and flexibility: access to mental health support, flexible shift patterns to fit family life, and supportive management culture.
- Training and development: ongoing upskilling, simulation training, leadership development.
- Data, evaluation and safeguarding: pilots with robust data on vacancies, turnover, patient outcomes, patient safety indicators; learning loops to adapt.
- Cross-service collaboration: aligned recruitment and workforce planning across GP, community, and hospital teams; local feedback informs the scale and pace of implementation.
In sum, let local pilots guide reform, with strong staff support, transparent data, and a clear path to safe, high-quality care for all.

I welcome the direction of an NHS workforce plan that puts patient safety and quality at the heart of access improvements. My experience in England, where demand for GP, community and mental health support often outstrips local capacity, underlines the need for a plan that prioritises safe staffing, continuity of care and rigorous safety monitoring as we expand services. Without those safeguards, pushing for faster access could paradoxically worsen outcomes. So, I’d like the plan to prioritise three practical foundations: safe staffing ratios with continuity, flexible working to retain staff, and targeted pay and incentives to attract staff to hard-to-fill roles and areas.

First, safe staffing ratios must be explicit targets with real-time monitoring across primary, community and mental health teams. This means clear, evidence-based staffing dashboards that show skill mix, patient load, and vacancy rates, updated regularly and publicly reported. It also means continuity-preserving models: small, stable teams where patients consistently see the same clinicians, coupled with robust handovers when changes are unavoidable. In our area, when a clinician is off sick or on leave, the ripple effects are immediate—backlogs grow and patients with ongoing needs fall through the cracks. A workforce plan that funds and enforces protected staffing levels and predictable rosters would help prevent that. I’d like to see fixed minimum ratios for GPs, nurses, health visitors, and mental health clinicians, with flexibility to adapt to local demographics, while avoiding a race to the bottom on waiting times at the expense of safety.

Second, flexible working arrangements and wellbeing supports are essential for retention. A diverse workforce will be retained only if jobs fit real lives and mental health needs. That means more part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, and flexible hours to cover school runs, carers, and other commitments, without penalising career progression. In practice, this could look like expanded GP and nurse rosters that offer stable, predictable patterns, and formal pathways for clinicians to switch between roles or return after a career break with a tailored induction. Proactive mental health services for staff, easy access to confidential wellbeing support, and protected time for CPD and reflective practice will reduce burnout and foster high-quality care. In our town, where stress levels in front-line teams are high, such measures would translate into steadier teams and better patient experiences.

Third, targeted pay, retention payments and relocation packages are sensible levers to attract staff to underserved areas and to high-demand roles within NHS teams. The plan should include bursaries and accelerated progression for clinicians willing to work in high-need settings, relocation support for graduates willing to move to rural or coastal communities, and retention payments that recognise the extra pressures in community and mental health work. Flexible financial packages—coupled with strong career ladders and opportunities for continuing professional development—would help recruit the right people and keep them there long enough to build relationships with patients and local services.

Alongside these core priorities, I’d urge the plan to invest in practical steps that demonstrate how safer staffing supports better access. For example, maintain robust onboarding and supervision for new staff, expand return‑to‑practice programs with tailored competency checks, and fund apprenticeships and career pathways that bring in staff from diverse backgrounds. We also need transparent governance: regular reporting on staffing levels, service quality, and safety incidents, with clear accountability for local areas to meet agreed targets.

Finally, the workforce plan must align with the broader goal of integrated, proactive care. Safe, continuous relationships with GPs, community nursing, and mental health teams help people get the right care sooner and reduce crisis episodes. By combining safe staffing, flexible working, and targeted incentives, we can grow the NHS workforce in a way that keeps patients safe while expanding access and improving outcomes. I’m hopeful that this approach will help families like mine experience faster, reliable care without compromising the quality and safety they rely on.

absolutely the plan should prioritise responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, credential recognition and integration support, plus multi-year ring-fenced funding for training and workforce initiatives; clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation, appropriate indemnity and protected clinical supervision to ensure safety!

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise people and practicality as much as targets and numbers. For me, safe, high‑quality care comes when teams are properly staffed, not when managers chase hour reductions or automation alone. Key priorities would include:
- Clarity and flexibility in roles: durable, well‑supported career paths across primary care, community services and mental health; more part‑time and job‑share roles so people can stay in the NHS while juggling study or family commitments.
- Manageable workloads and reduced admin: better Rostering, simpler IT systems, and less duplicated digital forms so clinicians spend more time with patients and less time chasing paperwork.
- Wellbeing and professional support: protected time for supervision, peer support, and access to mental health services for staff to prevent burnout.
- Compensation and progression: competitive pay, clear progression criteria, and recognition of long hours during surges.
- Training and recruitment: robust schemes for new graduates, return‑to‑practice pathways, and diverse recruitment pipelines to reduce vacancies and bring fresh ideas.
- Data‑driven planning: real‑time staffing data to anticipate peak times and avoid over‑reliance on scarce locums.
If the plan keeps staff supported and the work better organized, patients will experience safer care and shorter waits over time.

absolutely i strongly support an NHS workforce plan that prioritises attracting, retaining and supporting staff while preserving safe, high‑quality care. Key priorities should include targeted competitive pay packages, retention payments, relocation assistance and bursaries to attract clinicians to underserved areas and high‑demand roles such as GPs, district nurses and mental health professionals. Short‑term incentives paired with clear long‑term career prospects will help fill vacancies more quickly and encourage people to stay. 

Alongside pay, we need clear funded career pathways: structured progression routes, protected time for CPD, and visible milestones from entry to senior roles. Protected CPD is essential so staff can stay up to date without feeling they must sacrifice patient care. Mentorship programmes for new graduates and experienced staff, plus formal return‑to‑practice schemes after breaks, will improve retention and safety by transferring tacit knowledge and reducing skill fade. 

In practice, I’ve heard of trusts offering bursaries tied to service obligations and relocation grants that boost applications in rural posts, and colleagues benefiting from mentors and return‑to‑practice pathways. When these elements are funded and coordinated, they support continuity of care, reduce burnout and keep services safe, accessible and local where people need them most!

The NHS workforce plan must cut unnecessary targets and admin, reduce duplicated tasks, and streamline referrals with better IT to free clinicians for patient care, while investing in training and supportive leadership to keep high-quality, safe services.

In Wales, to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe, the plan should start with clear scope-of-practice for every role, including new ones like physician associates and advanced nurse practitioners. This helps teams coordinate tasks and prevents gaps or doorways where responsibility falls through. Revalidation should be straightforward, proportionate, and protected by dedicated time so clinicians can demonstrate ongoing competence without being punished by paperwork or delays. Indemnity is essential: we need clear, affordable, and accessible cover for the broader tasks teams take on, including home visits, digital consultations and non-traditional roles. The plan must fund protected clinical supervision and mentoring—practical, scheduled time for case review, reflective practice, and peer support, so staff can develop safely as their roles evolve.

Also necessary are robust training pipelines, with local supervision networks, clear career progression, and decent working conditions; frontline staff should see real opportunities to grow rather than be burned out. Ensuring safe staffing levels and regular MDT meetings would boost confidence that changes won’t compromise patient safety, and would help preserve the high standard of care we expect.

Agree. Prioritise targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas (rural, urban deprived, coastal) with housing and transport support, plus reduce admin burden, streamline referrals and boost IT usability to keep care safe while attracting and retaining staff.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan should prioritise targeted competitive pay and retention incentives—retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract people to underserved areas and high-demand roles. We’ve seen how vacancies in GP practices spill over into longer waits and overworked teams, so financial incentives tied to service in difficult posts can help stabilise local services. Training bursaries should be aimed at nursing, allied health roles and GP-support positions to build a broader, skilled front line. Flexible working, predictable career progression and dedicated wellbeing support are also essential to keep staff motivated and reduce burnout.

Critically, we must expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams so GP workload can be redistributed safely. That means clearer governance and supervision for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles, with defined scopes of practice and strong training pipelines. For example, nurse-led clinics and pharmacist-led medication reviews, with supervision for prescribing where appropriate, can free GPs for complex cases. In practice this would improve access in local hubs and reduce reliance on urgent care, provided staffing ratios are maintained, CPD is funded, and managers actively support teams. This balanced approach would deliver safer, more resilient care that people can rely on.

absolutely the plan should prioritise steady recruitment of frontline staff—GPs, nurses and therapists—by expanding domestic training pipelines and, where needed, responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, credential recognition and robust integration. Also target housing, transport and incentives for hard-to-fill rural and coastal areas, while safeguarding source health systems!

From my perspective living in England and seeing communities like ours, the plan should prioritise those areas where shortages bite hardest: rural, urban deprived and coastal communities. This means housing support or allowances, transport help, and relocation packages to attract and retain staff in hard-to-fill posts. I would also emphasise flexible shifts and clear progression so people can make a long-term career locally. Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles—with proper training and supervision to safely redistribute GP workload. In practice, this could be GP-led hubs where nurse prescribers, pharmacist reviews, and allied health professionals handle routine follow-ups, triage, and medicines management, with robust supervision and safety checks. In our area, I’ve seen how a well-coordinated district nursing and therapy team lightens GP demand and improves patient experience. Continual professional development, governance, wellbeing support, fair pay, and clear progression paths will help attract and retain staff and keep care safe and high quality.

The workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived, and coastal—plus housing and transport support to recruit and retain staff. It should expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, PAs, paramedics, allied roles) with training and supervision to safely redistribute GP workload and keep high-quality care.

Prioritise reducing admin burden and duplicative targets, streamline referrals, and make IT user-friendly. Invest in flexible staffing, ongoing training, and local support in rural NI so clinicians can focus on safe, high-quality, patient-facing care.

I think the most important priority for an NHS workforce plan is to grow domestic primary care capacity from the ground up. If we want safer, higher‑quality care that people can rely on in the evenings and at weekends as well as during the working day, we need more trained staff entering and staying in primary care. The best way to do that is to massively expand undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university‑practice partnerships that keep learning connected to service needs.

First, increase undergraduate places and hands‑on primary care exposure. Medical, nursing and allied health students should have structured, protected GP and practice placements as a core part of their training. This isn’t simply about more numbers; it’s about high‑quality experiences where students learn alongside experienced clinicians, with dedicated supervision and feedback. When trainees feel confident in a real practice, they’re more likely to stay in the sector after qualification rather than chasing roles abroad or in hospital settings. My own experience in local health services has shown how crucial it is for new graduates to have a clear sense of what it’s like to work in primary care, including the realities of triage, chronic disease management and the day‑to‑day workload.

Second, expand postgraduate training and new primary care roles with protected time. GP training numbers must rise, but so should pathways for physician associates, nurse practitioners, pharmacists with clinical responsibilities, and community paramedics. These roles can relieve GP workloads, improve access to same‑day care, and maintain safety when supported by robust supervision. Protected time for hands‑on learning, formative feedback and mentoring should accompany every recruitment push, so trainees aren’t pulled away by service pressures and can progress with confidence.

Third, broaden apprenticeships and career ladders. Apprenticeships for healthcare support workers, medical assistants and practice administrators can create visible routes into nursing, allied health or GP roles. A clear, funded ladder from HCA/healthcare support to practice nursing or PA training helps people see a future in primary care and strengthens retention. In practice terms, that could look like a two‑to‑three year apprenticeship track that combines on‑the‑job learning with formal assessments and time for theory at college or university.

Fourth, build strong university‑practice partnerships with protected placements. Collaborative hubs that co‑design curricula with practices ensure training aligns with real service needs. These partnerships should guarantee access to practical rotations in urban and rural settings, with shared governance to protect learning time and patient safety. Some areas already benefit from general practice teaching networks where students rotate through several practices in a defined period; expanding and standardising these models would amplify their impact and improve equity of access to high‑quality experiences.

Fifth, target training where shortage and inequity are greatest. Investment must reflect geography and demographic need. Rural and coastal areas often face greater staffing gaps and heavier workloads; providing incentives for trainees to gain experience in these settings, including relocation support, extended placements and remote supervision, will help distribute the workforce more evenly and reduce disparities in access.

Sixth, ensure financing, workload and wellbeing support are part of the package. Multi‑year funding that follows trainees into their early career stages is essential to continuity and retention. Administrative burden should be reduced where possible, so clinicians can concentrate on patient care and teaching. Protected time for supervision, peer support and wellbeing initiatives is equally important to prevent burnout and keep morale high.

Seventh, embed readiness for digital, triage and integrated care. Training must cover the practical use of digital records, NHS 111 and triage pathways, and the coordination between GP, community services and mental health teams. This isn’t a separate skill set; it’s part of everyday primary care. Trainees should learn how to navigate the care navigator platforms that I’ve advocated for previously, so new staff can contribute to safer, faster access for patients from day one.

Finally, build in evaluation and iteration. Each program should have measurable goals on recruitment, retention and patient outcomes, with feedback loops from learners, supervisors and patients. The goal is not just more staff, but better safety, continuity and confidence in primary care.

In plain terms, this is about making primary care a viable, attractive long‑term career path for more people in this country. If we invest in education, protected learning time, and sustainable partnerships between universities and practices, we’ll see more GPs, more nurses and allied health professionals, and a stronger front line that can deliver timely, high‑quality care without risking staff burnout. That’s how we keep people healthy, at work, and supported by a dependable NHS.

Any NHS workforce plan should prioritise interoperable IT and secure, user-friendly systems that frontline teams can rely on, with substantial, ongoing digital training. But it must also safeguard options for patients who are digitally excluded or prefer non-digital routes. From my experience, delays in accessing timely GP or mental healt support strm in part from silos and repeated data entry; a plan that gives clinicians real-time access to a shared record across GP, hospital and community services, plus direct booking and decision support, would reduce duplication and errors and free staff to care. Training must cover privacy, cyber security, and practical use of tools, not just new software rollouts. Paper or phone options should remain robust for those who need them. Regarding recruitment, using overseas staff should be donee responsibly: streamlined visas, rapid credential recognition, structured integration programs, and safeguards to avoid depleting shortages in source countries. Pair this with smart retention: realistic workloads, career progression and protected time for training, and supportive leadership. In practice, a plan that combinrs tech, people, and compassionate care will sustain safety and high quality while gradually easing capacity pressures.

From where I sit, watching the pressures on primary care and community services, any NHS workforce plan must be practical, well-funded and designed to keep care safe and patient-centred. It should not just chase more staff, but ensure the right people with the right training are supported to stay in the system long term. The three threads I’d prioritise are interoperable IT with strong cyber security and staff digital training, transparent local workforce data with clear evaluation, and clearly funded career pathways with real opportunities to learn, mentor and return to practice.

Interoperable, secure IT and digital literacy
- The plan must prioritise interoperable systems that genuinely talk to one another across GP practices, mental health teams, community nursing and social care. Fragmented IT wastes hours, creates errors and slows patient care. We need shared records, common care plans and real-time updates so a patient isn’t handed from one quarter to another with no visibility of what happened previously.
- Security cannot be an afterthought. As technology expands, so do risks. Investment in robust cybersecurity, data governance and privacy protections should be core, not optional upgrades.
- Staff digital training is essential. Digital tools should save time and enable safer, quicker decisions, not add to workload. Training must be protected and practical, with ongoing refreshers and easy access to support for those who aren’t tech-native.
- We must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients. Not everyone has reliable internet or a device, and some prefer face-to-face contact. The plan should fund digital inclusion work, such as training for patients, access to hotlines or offline booking channels, and dedicated staff to help people navigate digital options without being penalised for not going online.

Transparent local data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation
- Localised, transparent workforce data are a must. We need regular dashboards showing staffing levels, vacancy rates, turnover, training uptake and how these relate to patient outcomes and wait times. Data should drive funding decisions, not merely report them.
- Sound modelling and predictive planning are key. Projects should be assessed by whether they reduce avoidable hospital admissions, shorten waits for primary care or mental health support, and improve safety margins. This means building in scenario planning, risk registers and clear triggers for intervention.
- Evaluation frameworks must be built in from the start. We should test what works where, learn quickly from pilot changes, and scale what actually improves access and safety rather than what sounds good on paper.

Clear funded career pathways, CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice
- Sustained funding for protected CPD time matters. Staff need opportunities to keep up-to-date with evidence-based practice without feeling their day job will collapse as a result.
- Mentorship and structured career pathways help retain experienced clinicians and support new entrants. A robust system of mentorship, peer support, and formal recognition of competencies builds confidence and reduces burnout.
- Return-to-practice schemes should be extended and funded, with practical retraining, supervision and gradual re-resourcing for those who have paused their careers. This is particularly important for skilled nurses, GPs, and allied health professionals who have made meaningful contributions in the past but drift away because of unwelcoming or unsupportive return routes.
- Career progression must be visible and achievable locally. Staff should see a ladder that leads to expanded roles, advanced practice, and leadership opportunities, supported by protected time, succession planning, and appropriate pay progression.

From my experience, expansion in numbers won’t fix gaps if the underlying systems aren’t solid. In our area, even when new teams are added, if the IT is fragmented, if staff aren’t trained to use new tools, or if there’s no clear route for career development and return-to-practice, burnout rises and turnover follows. A workforce plan that couples technology and data with tangible staff support and development is the only way to maintain safe, high-quality care while rebuilding confidence and stability in the system.

In short, invest in interoperable, secure IT and comprehensive digital training, ensure digital inclusion for all patients, base planning on transparent local data and robust evaluation, and guarantee funded career pathways with mentoring and return-to-practice routes. If you get those right, recruitment and retention will follow, and care quality will not be compromised as we broaden access across primary and community services.

I think any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe staffing, continuity of care, and robust safety monitoring if we’re to expand access without compromising quality. Safe staffing ratios and a clear system to track safety need to be embedded in every service, with real-time data and escalation if pressures rise. Continuity matters too: smaller multidisciplinary teams, longer appointment blocks, and “team around the patient” approaches help maintain trust and clinical quality as services grow. 

To attract and keep staff, targeted pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries are essential—especially for rural and island areas and for high-demand roles like GPs, district nurses and mental health clinicians. Without these incentives, shortages will choke the improvements we’ve started. 

Growing the pipeline is equally key: increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships so trainees learn in real primary care settings and remain in Scotland. That creates familiar, community-based clinicians who understand local needs. 

In my experience, a rural practice benefited when a relocation grant brought in a skilled nurse practitioner; the team could offer more appointments without compromising safety. A balanced plan that combines safe staffing, targeted incentives, and domestic training capacity will sustain access gains while preserving quality and continuity for patients across Scotland.

To recruit, retain, and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan must prioritise stable, long-term funding and clear career structures. I’d like to see secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements that enable sustained workforce initiatives, expand training capacity and reduce the churn caused by short-term policy changes. When funding is predictable, trusts can recruit with confidence and plan longer-term service models. Key priorities: funded career pathways with visible progression ladders for nurses, therapists, GPs and mental health workers; protected CPD time; robust mentorship and return-to-practice schemes so skilled colleagues can re-enter the service after breaks. In my experience, staff retention rises when there are realistic workloads, flexible hours, and opportunities to specialise without losing a stable base. Invest in training capacity at local colleges and hospitals, plus practical on-the-job mentoring and simulation-based training. Ensure safe staffing levels, with adequate time for home visits and longer appointments for complex cases. Provide housing support or allowances to attract staff to underserviced areas. In short, stable funding plus clear, funded development paths will help the NHS keep experienced staff while training the next generation and maintaining patient safety.

Prioritise secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain recruitment and training capacity, with reduced policy volatility; clarify scope-of-practice, support revalidation and indemnity; protect clinical supervision for new roles; and ensure safe workloads to preserve patient safety and care quality.

An NHS workforce plan must put patient safety at the heart of recruitment and retention. Prioritise safe staffing ratios and real-time workload visibility so that when vacancies arise, rosters don’t compromise care. This means clear minimums for nursing and allied health cover on each shift and robust safety dashboards that flag rising risk and trigger targeted action.

Second, emphasise continuity-preserving models. When patients see a stable team, clinical knowledge stays with the group and errors or delays fall. Long-term GP panels, stable MDTs and reduced churn should be built in as core design principles rather than afterthoughts.

Third, keep rigorous safety monitoring. Regular audits, incident reviews and transparent reporting must translate into staffing decisions and roster design, not sit in a drawer.

Fourth, retention through flexible, inclusive working: offer part-time options, job-share, phased retirement, and strong childcare support plus proactive mental health services. This helps attract people with caring responsibilities, supports those returning after time out, and tackles burnout—important for young staff who want balance.

Fifth, support development without sacrificing care quality: practical training, mentoring and safe progression paths aligned to real-service needs; streamlined admin and better digital tools to cut unnecessary burden on clinicians.

In short, you can only improve access if we safeguard safe, sustainable care. The plan should pair immediate staffing fixes with long-term, people-centered policies.

Fund a workforce plan that expands and regulates multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, PAs, paramedics and allied roles) with clear supervision to safely redistribute GP workload. Provide flexible hours, funded CPD, mentoring and return-to-practice schemes to retain staff and protect quality care.

To be effective, the NHS workforce plan must address both short-term pressures and longer-term capacity. I want funded, clearly defined career pathways with protected CPD time, strong mentorship, and accessible return-to-practice schemes. Too often staff leave because progression and development are unclear or paused by other priorities. A robust framework would map local talent pipelines from nursing, AHPs and pharmacy into primary care roles, with transparent funding tied to milestones. 

Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload: expand nurse practitioners, pharmacists with prescribing rights, physician associates, paramedics, and allied roles, all with structured supervision and defined scopes of practice; deliver integrated clinics and on-call support to reduce avoidable GP demand. 

Third, develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Regularly publish vacancy rates, time-to-fill, retention, training outcomes, and patient-safety indicators so plans can be adjusted promptly.
