Concrete examples from local areas show that mentorship schemes, return-to-practice cohorts, and pharmacist-led minor-ailment services can relieve GP pressure while maintaining quality, but they require sustainable investment.

To recruit, retain and deliver safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan must start with clear scopes of practice, robust revalidation processes and durable indemnity arrangements. When people know what they can safely do and how they are protected, new roles can be introduced without compromising safety. I would support funded, protected clinical supervision for expanding roles—advanced clinical practitioners, physician associates, nurse practitioners and pharmacists in primary care—so supervision is embedded in their timetables rather than added on later. This builds confidence, supports clinical decision‑making and reduces risk as teams grow.

Second, invest in education pipelines to grow domestic supply. Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships to guarantee local access to GPs, nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals. In our area, better uni‑practice rotations and funded GP training posts would help convert students and trainees into stable, long‑term staff, easing shortages.

Finally, address retention through flexible working, wellbeing support, mentoring and clear career progression. Together, these steps would sustain high standards of care while expanding access for patients.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise flexible working, diverse recruitment routes and funding certainty. Flexible hours, part-time options, job-sharing and phased retirement help retain experienced staff who understand local needs and can mentor newer colleagues. Childcare support and carer-friendly policies are essential to widen the pool of applicants and reduce turnover. Proactive mental health services, regular wellbeing checks and accessible counselling can protect staff resilience and prevent burnout. 

Expand training capacity and clear career paths: protect training posts, increase GP registrar places, and develop nursing apprenticeships so people can progress without lengthy gaps. Equally important is multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements enabling sustained workforce initiatives and reducing volatile policy changes that disrupt planning. 

Strong local workforce planning with flexible deployment and continuity of teams will maintain safety and quality, for example longer appointment times for complex cases and nurse-led clinics with stable staffing. In Scotland we’ve seen how these measures support both patients and frontline staff, keeping care compassionate and consistent over time.

From my experience with struggling to get GP slots and hearing about CAMHS delays, I think any NHS workforce plan needs to be flexible and locally informed rather than one-size-fits-all. A plan should prioritise several interlinked things. First, flexible, well-supported staffing models to keep workloads safe: stable rosters, a robust locum/banks system, and clear routes for experienced staff to return after breaks. Second, clear training and progression with funded schemes for nurses, allied health professionals, and mental health workers, plus mentorship and protected time to develop skills. Third, a strong focus on staff wellbeing and safety: reasonable hours, access to mental health support, good supervision, and safe working environments. Fourth, use local pilots and rapid evaluation to test different staffing approaches, measure patient safety and satisfaction, and scale what works. Fifth, recruitment that reaches diverse pipelines and offers incentives for long-term retention in underserved areas. In my area, when staffing and after-hours support improved, patient delays decreased; where it didn’t, they grew. Frontline staff must shape the plan, and we need transparent data on what works so good practices can be rolled out quickly.

As an organisation that works with young people across England, we welcome a workforce plan that prioritises recruiting, retaining and supporting staff while keeping care safe and high quality. Any strategy should recognise the realities of student life, part-time work, and the increasing demand on GP, community health and mental health services. It should also be ready to include international recruitment in a responsible way, so long as it strengthens NHS capacity without undermining health systems elsewhere or compromising safety and standards here. With those principles in mind, our key priorities would be:

- Safe, sustainable staffing with clear supervision and governance
  - Establish evidence-based staffing ratios and workload controls across primary, community and mental health services, with robust supervision for all new and expanding roles (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates, etc.). This must be coupled with transparent metrics on wait times, safety indicators and patient outcomes so teams aren’t stretched beyond reasonable limits.
  - Build predictable rotas, sufficient backfill for leave, and flexible working patterns that reflect the needs of students, early-career staff and those with caregiving responsibilities. Flexible options should not erode continuity of care; instead, they should be designed to sustain long-term engagement.

- Strong training pipelines and career progression
  - Expand high-quality placements and sandwich-style training across general practice, community services and mental health, with clearly defined career ladders and accessible continuing professional development. This should include supervision, mentorship, and opportunities to specialise without losing sight of the generalist skills that underpin safe, joined-up care.
  - Create recognised career pathways for international recruits that include structured induction, language and cultural competence support, and formal credential recognition, so newcomers can contribute quickly and confidently while safeguarding patient care.

- Responsible and ethical international recruitment
  - Use overseas recruitment to fill genuine gaps, but with streamlined visa processing and fast-tracked credential recognition that meet NHS standards. Any approach should be coupled with robust integration support (orientation, peer networks, language training, and local acclimatisation) and safeguards to avoid draining health systems in source countries.
  - Establish periodic reviews to ensure international recruitment does not cause unintended shortages elsewhere and that ethical recruitment practices are consistently followed.

- Multidisciplinary teamwork as a core model
  - Accelerate the expansion of multidisciplinary teams within GP practices and community hubs, with clear roles and referral criteria. Pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics and other professionals can manage routine care safely, freeing GPs to focus on complex conditions, safeguarding, and urgent investigations. This requires transparent governance, shared patient records (with consent) and reliable handovers.

- Focus on retention through wellbeing and culture
  - Prioritise staff wellbeing, mental health support, and a workplace culture that values teamwork, respect, and patient-centred care. Address burnout factors such as workload, complexity, and administrative burden by simplifying processes where possible and providing dedicated administrative support.
  - Recognise and reward frontline staff, with visible pathways to leadership and meaningful involvement in service design. Involve current staff and young people in co-designing workforce strategies to ensure practical, real-world applicability.

- Local, data-driven planning with equity in mind
  - Use local data to tailor workforce plans to community needs, including rural versus urban disparities. Ensure parity of access to high-quality care by supporting recruitment and retention across all settings, not just high-density urban areas.
  - Treat data on staffing, patient experience and outcomes as a core governance tool. Regular reporting to staff, patients and communities will strengthen trust and drive continuous improvement.

- Digital readiness without compromising human care
  - Equip staff with training for digital tools that support triage, scheduling and care pathways, while safeguarding against over-reliance on automation. Ensure there are non-digital options for those who need them and protect privacy and consent across systems.

Overall, the plan should be pragmatic, locally responsive and built on strong governance, transparent metrics and meaningful involvement from young people and frontline staff. If done well, a wisely balanced approach—combining domestic training expansion with ethical overseas recruitment, robust supervision, and a culture of continuous learning—could help deliver timely, safe and high-quality care for today’s students and families while sustaining the NHS into the future.

From our experience of working with patients across urban, rural and coastal communities in England, any NHS workforce plan must be built around three core priorities: targeted recruitment and retention where it is hardest to fill roles, robust local data to steer decisions, and the safe expansion of multidisciplinary teams that can relieve GP workloads without compromising care. Taken together, these elements can help us keep the right staff where the need is greatest while maintaining high-quality, safe services.

First, tailor incentives and support for hard-to-fill areas. We know poverty, distance and housing pressures shape workforce supply as much as salary. A national plan should therefore include bespoke packages for rural, coastal and urban-deprived locations, with practical levers such as housing and transport support, flexible deployment models and clear career progression paths. Examples include housing allowances near practices, relocation subsidies, and targeted recruitment campaigns that partner with local authorities and social care, schools and employers to create a stable, welcoming environment for families. Travel subsidies and easier access to affordable housing are not luxuries but essential ingredients to keep skilled clinicians on the ground where patients need them most. We should also align retention schemes with workload realities—averaging bolt-on shifts or short-term postings can backfire if teams feel overstretched. We need transparent local planning that recognises the specific needs of each community, and governance to prevent inequitable bottlenecks, especially in hard-to-fill sites.

Second, develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. Sustainable, evidence-based planning requires real-time visibility into vacancies, time-to-fill, turnover, sickness absence, staff mix and patient outcomes by site. A shared local data platform with standardised metrics would enable us to forecast demand, test what works (for example, in which settings a nurse practitioner-led clinic reduces GP load or where pharmacists can safely manage stable chronic conditions), and adjust funding and training accordingly. Importantly, data collection should be designed with staff and patients in mind—minimising administrative burden and ensuring privacy. Pilots should be tightly evaluated using patient experience, safety indicators and cost-effectiveness, with findings feeding into a broader, adaptable framework rather than a one-size-fits-all national rollout.

Third, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload while preserving continuity of care. The idea that we can simply deploy more clinicians without proper training or governance is not viable. We should expand teams that include nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied professionals, with clear scopes of practice, robust supervision, shared clinical records and integrated care pathways. This requires standardised protocols, joint training, and strong local supervision so that expanded teams feel confident in decisions and patients experience seamless care. For example, co-located teams in community clinics or primary care hubs—comprising nurse prescribers, mental health nurses, pharmacists and social prescribers—can handle routine follow-ups, medication reviews and early mental health interventions, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases. Any expansion must be accompanied by sustainable workload planning, protected time for professional development, and well-supported supervision to prevent burnout and preserve patient safety. We should also ensure these teams remain anchored in the patient’s ongoing relationship with their preferred clinician whenever possible, so continuity of care is not eroded.

Beyond these three pillars, we should embed well-being and workforce safeguarding into every plan: reasonable workloads, safe staffing levels, access to training and clinical governance, and assurance that digital tools do not replace human judgment where it matters most. Any workforce strategy must be funded with predictable, long-term commitments and tied to local accountability so communities can see tangible improvements in recruitment, retention and care quality.

In summary, a successful NHS workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives for the hardest-to-staff areas, invest in transparent local data and evaluation mechanisms to guide decisions, and responsibly scale multidisciplinary teams with the right training and governance. When implemented with careful planning, strong local leadership and adequate funding, these steps can help deliver timely, high-quality care while supporting staff and protecting patient safety.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan should focus on three linked priorities. First, responsible overseas recruitment. We need streamlined visa routes and quicker credential recognition so skilled clinicians can join the NHS without unnecessary delays. It’s essential to provide thorough integration support—induction, language assistance if needed, mentoring and buddy systems—alongside safeguards to prevent draining health workers from source countries and to monitor impact on those systems. In my circle of friends doing nursing and support roles, smooth onboarding and clear expectations make a huge difference to morale and patient safety.

Second, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding for workforce development. Long-term funding for training capacity, expanded recruitment pipelines, and retention initiatives helps stabilise staffing levels and project planning. It also reduces disruptive policy shifts that leave teams under-resourced just as demand grows.

Third, flexible and supportive working arrangements to retain diverse staff. This includes flexible hours, part-time and job-share options, phased retirement, reliable childcare, and proactive mental health services. Strong supervision, fair workloads, and clear career progression must run alongside these measures to sustain high-quality care.

This approach aligns with the need for steadier staffing and safer, more accessible services that I’ve seen discussed in my community discussions and reflects a practical path to reduce delays in care.

From my experience in Scotland, a successful NHS workforce plan should do two things at once: free clinicians from endless admin and duplicative tasks so they can care for patients, and provide solid, funded career paths that keep staff motivated and skilled over the long term. In practice that means prioritising three areas: reducing unnecessary targets and paperwork, and streamlining referrals and IT; and providing clear, protected development routes, mentoring and return-to-practice opportunities so both experienced staff and early-career colleagues can grow with the service.

First, reduce admin burden and improve IT usability. Targets that chase throughput or tick-box exercises can pull clinicians away from patients and increase stress. We need a plan that cuts duplication and makes referral pathways simpler and faster. In my area, when a nurse practitioner-led clinic took on routine infections and wound care, GP time freed up considerably, but the potential was even bigger if the IT systems spoke to each other and cut duplicate data entry. A streamlined triage and online booking system, with shared care plans across GP practices and community services, would save time, reduce errors and help clinicians focus on care rather than forms. Interoperability is critical—if a patient’s notes, test results and care plans display consistently across settings, there’s far less back-and-forth and fewer unnecessary delays.

Second, fund and protect career development. Staff retention hinges on a clear, funded ladder: protected CPD time, mentorship, and well-structured return-to-practice schemes. Let’s guarantee dedicated time for learning without penalising clinicians for stepping away briefly for family reasons or to upskill. Mentorship should be built into every stage—from newly qualified staff to those returning after a career break—so they have trusted guidance as they take on more responsibility. A real advantage would be dedicated pathways to expand the scope of practice for nurse practitioners, allied health professionals and therapists, with accredited credentials that support progression into senior or leadership roles. It’s not just about keeping experienced clinicians; it’s about giving early-career staff a credible, visible route to lasting careers in NHS Scotland.

Third, make workforce planning responsive to actual service needs, with strong support for rural and semi-rural areas. The recruitment incentives, regional training hubs and transport solutions we discussed earlier should sit alongside reliable workload budgeting and staffing targets that reflect patient demand rather than arbitrary numbers. Return-to-practice schemes could be especially valuable in rural communities where vacancies linger; subsidised CPD and relocation support would help smaller practices attract and keep skilled staff. I’ve seen how a rotating roster of experienced staff across a regional hub can stabilise service levels, and I’d like to see that model expanded with explicit funding and governance to prevent gaps in care.

Fourth, promote team-based care and role expansion with safeguards for safe practice. If more non-physician clinicians can manage minor conditions and triage appropriately, that frees doctors to handle complex cases while maintaining safety. Our community already benefits from a nurse practitioner-led clinic; with proper training, supervision and clear escalation processes, this model could be standard across Scotland. Training must cover not just clinical skills but collaboration, communication and handover protocols so teams work seamlessly and patients do not fall through the cracks.

Finally, invest in staff wellbeing and safety. Adequate staffing levels, predictable rosters, access to mental health support for staff, and safe working environments are essential to retain people who are burnt out by chronic understaffing. A workforce plan that visibly reduces avoidable stressors—while still driving quality and access—will produce steadier, safer care for patients.

In short, the plan should value people as much as patients: cut the admin burden, modernise IT and referrals, fund clear career paths, mentor and support return-to-practice, and tailor recruitment to where it’s most needed while safeguarding wellbeing. If we get this right, Scotland will see safer, higher-quality care and a workforce that stays with the NHS long term, not just for today but for years to come.

I agree that any NHS workforce plan should prioritise secure, long-term funding and stronger training capacity to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care. In my area, the consequences of short-term policy shifts are clear: vacancies drag on, training slots are under pressure, and routine care slips further down the queue. A ring-fenced, multi-year settlement would give NHS organisations the confidence to expand training places across doctors, nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals, while investing in supervision, career progression paths and robust wellbeing support to tackle burnout.

The plan should prioritise: 1) expanding training capacity and recruitment pipelines, including GP training places and local multi-disciplinary training hubs, 2) proven retention measures—competitive pay, flexible working, safe workloads and wellbeing programmes, 3) targeted international recruitment with streamlined onboarding and strong induction, 4) safer staffing levels and task-shifting to skilled professionals (practice nurses, physiotherapists, pharmacists) to free GPs for complex cases, 5) reducing policy volatility so workforce strategy can be sustained, 6) reducing administrative burden through smart tech and support roles.

With such commitments, the long-standing delays in GP appointments (often two to three weeks), mental health referrals taking months, and the general backlog could be tackled more effectively while preserving high standards of safety and care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise stronger links and joint funding across health, social care, mental health and community services. This means expanding multi-disciplinary teams with shared budgets and clear career pathways—care coordinators, nurse prescribers, mental health practitioners and social care workers working side by side to redistribute workload from GPs and reduce duplication. Invest in training, flexible working, protected time for continuing professional development and sustainable staffing models that reflect local demand. Local hubs should have integrated rosters and shared recruitment to stabilise teams, backed by a robust retention package and clear supervision structures to prevent burnout.

Responsible overseas recruitment can help fill gaps, but must be done with safeguards: streamlined visa and credential recognition processes, comprehensive integration support (orientation, language, mentorship), and strict safeguards against depleting source health systems. We should also monitor impact on domestic training pipelines and ensure patient safety is not compromised by rapid onboarding. Use digital tools to cut admin time and align pay, workload and career progression, so nurses, therapists and care coordinators feel valued and stay in posts. With coherent cross-sector funding and responsible recruitment, we’ll build a resilient, person-centred system.

absolutely the workforce plan must fund clear career paths, protected CPD, mentorship, and return-to-practice schemes to keep experienced clinicians and new staff. It must also guarantee safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models, and robust safety monitoring so access improvements don't compromise care!

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality, a workforce plan should place people at the centre and recognise that high‑quality care depends on a well-supported, diverse team. It must be practical, locally responsive and long‑term, not a one‑off recruitment drive. My view is shaped by seeing colleagues burn out under heavy, inflexible schedules and by the real need for care models that work for families and carers as well as patients.

- Flexible, human‑centred working patterns: Prioritise flexible hours, part‑time and job‑sharing options, and phased or staged retirement for experienced staff. These arrangements help retain skilled professionals who might otherwise leave early because of childcare responsibilities or burnout. In a local practice I’ve observed, a nurse wanted to reduce hours to balance family needs, but rigid rotas pushed them away. Allowing flexible schedules, with reliable cover and clear handovers, would keep experienced clinicians in post and maintain continuity for patients. Childcare support and paid care‑leave can make a big difference for staff with dependants, and should be normalised across roles, not treated as a perk.

- Proactive mental health and wellbeing supports for staff: A workforce plan must fund and normalise mental health resources for staff themselves—confidential counselling, peer‑support networks, resilience training and protected time for wellbeing activities. Burnout is not just a staff issue; it directly affects patient safety. I’ve heard from frontline colleagues about exhaustion after long stints in high‑pressure wards; easy access to mental health support and manageable workloads would reduce sick leave and improve morale, which in turn benefits patients.

- Transparent local data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation: Decisions should be informed by transparent, localised workforce data and scenario modelling. This means tracking vacancy rates by role and site, sickness absence, turnover, staff vacancy-to-recovery times, and patient safety indicators. Evaluation frameworks should tie funding and planning to outcomes for staff welfare as well as patient care. In some areas, dashboards help managers spot impending shortages and reallocate training or recruitment efforts accordingly; in others, data is siloed and planning is reactive. A consistent, local approach would enable more proactive, targeted investment.

- Clear training, career development and progression: Provide structured CPD and cross‑skilling opportunities so staff can move into roles that fit their strengths and life stage (e.g., advanced nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists with prescribing rights). Mentoring and protected time for training should be built into rosters. When staff see a visible path forward and receive ongoing development, turnover falls and patient care improves.

- Realistic workload management and safe staffing: Strong governance around safe staffing levels, with staffing models that reflect patient complexity and turnover. Streamline admin and non‑clinical tasks so clinicians spend more time with patients. Where appropriate, expand team models that allow task‑sharing across professions to relieve bottlenecks without compromising safety. A practical plan would tie workload indicators to funding and performance targets, ensuring safe care is not sacrificed for throughput.

- Diverse recruitment and inclusive retention: Actively recruit from a range of backgrounds and develop routes that support flexible entry for people who bring valuable experiences but may need different working patterns. Induction, local onboarding, and buddy systems help new staff settle quickly and stay longer. A diverse workforce enhances patient trust and helps services be more responsive to whole communities.

- Local, visible support networks and infrastructure: Provide on‑site or nearby childcare options, eldercare support, and reasonable transport provisions for shift patterns. Enabling staff to manage family responsibilities reduces absenteeism and improves morale. Flexible shift swapping and predictable scheduling give staff a better work‑life balance and stabilise teams.

- Consistent funding aligned to people, not just numbers: Funding should reward retention, training, and wellbeing, not only new hires. That means longer‑term contracts, retention payments in high‑demand areas, and investment in staff facilities and digital literacy so digital tools support rather than demand more work.

Importantly, the plan should ensure that care access for patients does not depend on a single mode of delivery. Even as digital tools expand, robust non‑digital routes must stay available, well‑staffed and properly funded. Safer, more flexible, more compassionate staffing models will help us keep high‑quality care while supporting the people who deliver it. The overall effect would be lower burnout, better patient safety and stronger, more sustainable services for communities.

A sustainable NHS workforce plan should prioritise cutting unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks to free clinicians for patient-facing care, while continuing to recruit and retain high-quality staff. Key priority areas include: simplifying referrals and care pathways so real clinical time isn’t swallowed by admin; and modernising IT to be truly usable in busy settings—a single, interoperable electronic record with straightforward referral templates, smart auto-fill, and minimal duplicate data entry. Streamlined IT should support front-line teams rather than add complexity, with decision support that respects clinical judgment. 

Beyond digital changes, we need to reduce non-clinical burdens and align targets with patient outcomes. Remove repetitive compliance checks, and ensure dashboards measure safety and quality rather than tick-box activity. Invest in flexible staffing models, strong induction for new international hires, mentoring, protected time for training, and robust wellbeing support to sustain staff and morale. 

Evidence from pilots shows when admin load is reduced and IT systems are more usable, triage improves and same-day slots increase, cutting waiting times by around a third in some practices. With sustained government funding, a clear delivery timetable and accountable local planning, this approach can deliver safe, high-quality care while attracting and retaining the workforce we need.

I think the NHS workforce plan must prioritise three linked strands to keep care safe while improving access. First, safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models. When teams are stretched or the same clinician is not consistently available, the risk of mistakes rises, especially for older patients with multiple conditions. We need enough skilled staff and stable teams, plus robust safety monitoring and regular appraisal of care standards so improvements to access don’t come at the expense of quality. Second, transparent, localised data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks. Local planners must have real-time information on staffing, demand and outcomes to target funding, shape training, and spot issues before they affect patients. Frontline involvement in forecasting and review is essential. Third, investment in interoperable IT and secure systems with ongoing digital training, while ensuring alternatives remain for those who are digitally excluded. Efficient digital tools can speed up care, but we must not lock out people who rely on phones or paper records. In my experience, when staffing is stable and teams communicate well, access improvements work; when that’s lacking, delays and anxiety rise for vulnerable patients like me and my family.

Prioritise reducing admin, duplication, and complicated referrals by improving IT usability, freeing clinician time for patients; plus flexible hours, part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, accessible childcare and proactive mental-health support to recruit, retain and sustain safe, high-quality care.

Agree that the NHS workforce plan should prioritise transparent, localised data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. In practice, this means building real-time dashboards at the local level showing staffing mix, vacancy rates, turnover, training pipelines and projected demand for GPs, nurses, mental health workers and allied professionals. By modelling recruitment and retention scenarios, funds can be directed where they are most needed rather than applying blanket targets that miss rural realities.

Key KPIs could include patient access targets (routine GP appointments within two weeks; same-day mental health triage), urgent care wait times, staff vacancy and sickness rates, burnout indicators, and patient safety metrics. An evaluation framework should assess the impact of mobile clinics, outreach teams and telehealth hubs on access, outcomes and workload distribution across teams. Localised dashboards and evaluation should feed funding and workforce planning decisions in real time.

From living and working in rural Wales, shortages have hit timely care and staff morale. Local data would enable targeted incentives, flexible working, strong career progression and training pipelines that keep skilled staff in communities. Transparent reporting also builds trust with patients and communities while helping ensure safe, high-quality care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams across primary and community care, with clear scopes of practice, robust training and ongoing supervision to safely redistribute GP workload. Invest in a pipeline of competent staff: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals, with funded routes into practice, protected time for supervision, and formal appraisal. This would free GPs to manage complex cases while still maintaining safe, high-quality care. In my experience, when teams are well-supported, patients benefit from quicker access—for example, same-day triage and initial assessments by experienced nurses or PAs, and pharmacist-led medicines reviews that can help prevent admissions. Key measures include standardised governance, access to senior clinical oversight, and safe prescribing protocols. Retention should be strengthened through clear progression ladders, flexible contracts, competitive pay, and a supportive work environment. Additionally, ensure workforce planning aligns with local population needs, with digital decision-support and data sharing to sustain high-quality care as teams grow.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise stable, long-term funding that is ring-fenced for workforce initiatives. Predictable budgets over several years let boards build real training capacity, sustain supervision, and implement effective recruitment and retention schemes without constant policy churn. Specific priorities would include expanding training intake for GPs, nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals, plus dedicated return-to-practice programmes and career development that keep experienced staff in the system. It’s also vital to plan safe staffing levels with evidence-based models, smart rosters and workload management so we can maintain high-quality care without burning people out.

Retention hinges on flexible working options, reasonable caseloads, strong wellbeing support, and clear progression paths—these are essential for the dedicated teams that serve older residents in our communities. In Northern Ireland, targeted recruitment and retention incentives for rural and peri-urban practices, including relocation support where needed, would help sustain local patient care. Finally, align workforce planning with real service needs, ensuring digital tools support staff while keeping non-digital access available for those who need it most.

I would prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload. This means more nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals working in primary and community settings, with strong training, defined scopes of practice and supervision. With robust protocols, these teams can triage, manage chronic conditions, run follow-up clinics and carry out home visits, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases while preserving safety and continuity of care. 

In practice, this requires clear career pathways, protected training time and ongoing supervision, plus reliable IT so shared records travel with patients across services. For example, in our area pharmacist-led medication reviews and nurse-led follow-up slots have reduced GP pressures when adequately funded, but they need consistent funding and integration with primary care records. 

Second, strengthen joint funding and commissioning with social care and mental health and community services. A pooled budget for community teams, home care and early intervention would improve holistic care and patient outcomes, reduce avoidable admissions and ensure smoother transitions. Steps include unified workforce planning, joint recruitment pipelines, and shared performance metrics so teams work as one system for the patient from initial contact to discharge.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable, integrated staffing across health, social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and maintain safe, high-quality care. Strengthening links and joint funding across sectors would enable teams to share skills and manage holistic patient journeys rather than sending people between services. Specific priorities: jointly funded recruitment and training pipelines (apprenticeships, nursing associates, physiotherapy assistants) with clear career ladders; protected time for supervision and CPD; and scalable staffing models that reflect local demand, including multidisciplinary teams in GP practices, care homes, and community hubs. Create more cross-sector secondments and colocated teams so staff can learn from each other and reduce duplication. Invest in digital tools to cut admin burden and support remote triage, while maintaining safe staffing ratios and reasonable caseload limits. In rural areas, fund mobile clinics and integrated care coordinators to bridge gaps. All planning should be underpinned by shared workforce data, regular review, and a funding envelope that supports long-term retention through wellbeing, flexible working, and career development.

Any workforce plan must be clear about how we grow and support the people who actually deliver care, while resisting quick fixes that undermine safety or continuity. In my view, three priorities matter most, and I’d want them to be delivered with proper guardrails and real funding.

First, build a domestic primary care pipeline that can actually fill GP shortages without leaving patients waiting longer or eroding training quality. That means increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, but with protected placements and strong university‑practice partnerships. It can’t just be a numbers game. Placements should be guaranteed in GP practices across regions that reflect local need, with sustainable funding for supervision, practice rotation costs, and protected time for students and trainees to learn in real settings. I’d want clear timelines, milestones and retention requirements tied to those placements so someone who starts in a training pathway isn’t pushed out by poor local support or workload pressure before they qualify. My worry is that without stable, regionally balanced pipelines, we end up with more trained clinicians in some areas and gaps in others, exactly where access to same‑day appointments already feels unpredictable.

Second, expand multidisciplinary teams only with tight regulation and robust supervision, and with a clear understanding of how that affects patient experience and safety. It’s sensible to widen roles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied staff to share routine workload. But it cannot be done by waving in more people without a governance framework that defines scope of practice, escalation rules, and when a GP must be involved. I’ve seen how handoffs can slow things down or fragment care, especially for young people who depend on continuity with a named clinician. Any plan to redistribute GP workload should come with explicit training standards, ongoing supervision, measurable safety indicators, and a shared medical record that makes sense to patients. We also need transparent referral and escalation criteria so patients aren’t bouncing between services or waiting for multiple sign‑offs.

Third, recognise that value comes from strong GP access and reliable triage, with MDTs acting as support rather than a replacement. In practice, this means investing in more same‑day GP slots, simpler online triage that routes people quickly to the right clinician, and clear pathways to escalate to a GP when needed. It also means better IT, record sharing, and systems that reduce administrative burden so clinicians can focus on care rather than paperwork. If we multiply roles, we must guarantee continuity when a patient needs someone who knows their history, and ensure patients retain real choices about who they see from the outset.

Beyond these three pillars, the plan should address working conditions and retention to stop people burning out. Adequate staffing levels, predictable rosters, protected time for professional development, mental health support for staff, and fair pay will matter just as much as the training pipelines themselves. I’d also want local commissioning to enable flexible, sustainable recruitment—recognising that young people like me value stability, clear career progression, and the sense that your GP team is a cohesive unit rather than a carousel of different clinicians.

In short, push for more domestic supply and smarter MDT use, but only with real safeguards: regionally balanced training pipelines, strong supervision and governance for every expanded role, streamlined and safe pathways to GP care, and a focused effort to improve working conditions and retention. Otherwise, there’s a risk we end up with more clinicians, but not safer, faster access for patients who need timely, trustworthy care.

From where I’m standing in England, in my mid‑60s, the NHS workforce plan needs to be practical first and foremost: enable clinicians to spend more time with patients and less time on admin, while rebuilding a steady pipeline of skilled staff who can work across primary care, mental health and social care in a coordinated way. Key priorities I’d expect to see in any NHS workforce plan:

  - Stop layering more reporting on clinicians who already juggle triage, prescriptions, and patient contact. In practice, reducing admin bottlenecks and building a strong training pipeline go hand in hand with a more integrated care system. If the NHS commits to these priorities—cutting needless bureaucracy, expanding practical training opportunities, and funding joint service delivery with social care and community partners—we’ll see more timely access, more confident clinicians, and safer care for patients. Crucially, any plan must preserve clinical judgement and local autonomy, while ensuring that a sustainable, well-supported workforce can deliver the hub‑based, multidisciplinary care that works in real life.

Overall, I’d say I agree with a workforce plan that centres on easing clinicians’ workload, expanding capacity through training, and financing integrated services to share the burden. It’s only by doing all three together that we’ll keep high‑quality care available to those who need it, when they need it.

From where I stand in England, any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff must be practical, well-funded and long‑term. It should not rely on “pilot” schemes or churn-friendly targets that shift work around without actually increasing patient-facing time. My lived experience in a area where appointments can be scarce, interpreters are in short supply and admin tasks swallow precious minutes with patients underlines why a few clear priorities are essential.

Funded career pathways, protected professional development and return‑to‑practice routes are non‑negotiable. We need transparent, well‑funded routes from entry roles into clinically qualified positions, with mentorship baked in from early on. For nurses, allied health professionals and GPs in training, that means paid time for training, funded supervision and a clear ladder that leads to senior roles rather than a cliff edge where people feel it’s safer to move abroad or out of the sector. Return‑to‑practice schemes should be streamlined and well advertised, so people who paused for family or other reasons can re‑join without months of form-filling and uncertainty. In my experience, a nurse who returned after a career break benefited enormously from a structured program and a dedicated mentor; without that, the effort to re‑skill and integrate can be a real deterrent.

Reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks that steal clinician time from patients. A lot of admin burden comes from multiple IT systems that don’t talk to each other, endless data collection for reporting, and referral bottlenecks that require repetitive handoffs. The workforce plan should prioritise simplifying referrals, improving IT usability and standardising processes across primary and secondary care so clinicians can see more patients and spend less time chasing paperwork. In practice, that could mean a unified, user‑friendly EHR with shared referral queues, automated triage where appropriate and protections against prescriptive, one‑size‑fits‑all targets that push clinicians toward checkbox metrics rather than quality care.

Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity of care. It’s not enough to add more appointment slots if the people delivering them are stretched or constantly changing teams. Safe staffing must be defined by evidence and calibrated to local need, with dashboards that flag risks before they materialise. Continuity‑preserving models—small teams, stable supervision, and predictable rostering—build trust with patients, reduce avoidable referrals, and support better outcomes. Where there are gaps, we should supplement with properly managed agency or locum staffing that comes with robust onboarding and supervision, not as a permanent workaround.

Safety monitoring and a culture that values clinician well‑being are essential to any credible plan. Adequate staffing must go hand in hand with decent working hours, access to mental health support for staff, reasonable overtime expectations, and a mechanism to report and learn from safety incidents without blame. When staff feel supported, patient safety and care quality follow.

Investment in training pipelines and local workforce planning is crucial. The plan should fund local courses, apprenticeships, and partnerships with universities to grow a pipeline that reflects the communities served. We should also invest in interpreters and culturally competent staff, and create clear career paths for people from diverse backgrounds. My area still struggles with language barriers and trust gaps in communities with high housing stress and debt—these issues won’t be solved by better clinics alone; you need staff who understand daily realities and can communicate effectively at the point of contact.

Finally, fair pay, good conditions and real recognition for clinical staff are not optional extras. Competitive salaries, pension security, flexible working where possible, and supportive leadership are essential to retain experienced clinicians and to attract newcomers who are otherwise looking elsewhere. The plan must be transparent about funding commitments, with multi‑year horizons so teams aren’t left in limbo after a few quarters of promises.

In short, the NHS workforce plan should create a sustainable ecosystem: clear, funded career progression; liberated time for patient care through streamlined processes and better IT; and staffing models that keep patients safe without compromising quality. To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise growing domestic supply and sustaining current teams. Second, ensure flexible working patterns to retain a diverse workforce: flexible hours, part‑time and job‑share options, phased retirement and accessible childcare, all tied to manageable caseloads. A robust NHS workforce plan must prioritise people first—recruiting, retaining and supporting staff in a way that keeps patients safe and services high‑quality. It should be practical, humane and sustainable, recognising that we cannot keep relying on ever‑larger numbers of overworked staff. In my view, there are three interlocking pillars: immediate stabilisation with responsible recruitment, strong career development and working conditions, and robust safeguards that protect both the NHS and health systems abroad.

First, overseas recruitment must be part of a careful, ethical strategy. Our local NHS cannot function without international talent, but recruitment should be responsible and reciprocal. Streamlined visa routes for qualified healthcare workers, with efficient recognition of international credentials, would help fill shortages without leaving vacancies unfilled for long. A clear pathway for bridging training and rapid language and cultural orientation would help new recruits integrate safely and effectively. Importantly, we must avoid draining source countries of doctors and nurses; any overseas recruitment should be governed by ethical codes and bilateral agreements that support training and capacity building where it is most needed. Training partnerships, joint workforce planning, and investments that bolster health systems in source countries should accompany active recruitment so we do not undermine global health.

Second, credential recognition and integration must be fast, transparent and sensible. A standardised, nationwide process for validating overseas qualifications, with minimal duplication and clear timelines, would reduce months of uncertainty for workers and for employers. Bridging programs should be targeted and flexible—mentoring, peer support, language training, and cultural competence—so new staff can perform safely from day one. Alongside this, robust induction and ongoing professional development must be guaranteed, with protected time for upskilling and supervision to prevent burnout and to maintain patient safety.

Third, we need real commitment to retention and conditions that let staff deliver high‑quality care. That means safe staffing levels, predictable rotas, and manageable workloads—no more reliance on short‑term agency staff to fill chronic gaps. Career progression pathways, funded CPD, and leadership opportunities should be available to all bands of staff, not just clinicians at the top of the pyramid. Flexible working options, supportive wellbeing services, and practical measures such as reduced administrative burden and better IT tooling can make a real difference to morale and retention. Pay fairness, recognition, and clear, consistent performance management are essential to keep skilled staff within the NHS long‑term.

Additionally, the plan must invest in domestic capability to reduce future shortages. Expanding training and apprenticeships for nurses, GPs, allied health professionals and social care workers, and ensuring attractive training placements across regions, will help build a more self‑reliant workforce. We must also align workforce planning with patient pathways—e.g., expanding capacity in mental health and community services to support the integrated hubs I’ve advocated before, so staff can work across teams without endless handoffs and wait times for patients.

Safety and quality must be non‑negotiable. Transparent staffing metrics, robust governance, and strong safeguarding practices are essential, especially in community and mental health settings. Any recruitment strategy should include ongoing evaluation of its impact on patient outcomes and the resilience of local services. Regional and local variations matter; the plan must tailor staffing to community needs and to the demands of 7‑day access without overburdening teams.

In summary, an NHS workforce plan worth having would couple ethical, streamlined international recruitment with rapid credential recognition, solid integration support, and clear protections for both the NHS and health systems abroad. It would be underpinned by robust training pipelines at home, worthy working conditions, and ongoing investment in wellbeing and professional development. If these pieces fit together, we can recruit and retain the people needed to deliver safe, high‑quality care now and in the years ahead, while keeping faith with our global responsibilities.

From my position in Wales, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe, high-quality care by enabling well-supported multidisciplinary teams and clear governance around new roles. I’ve seen how stretched GP and primary care teams can be, especially in rural areas, and I want to see a plan that makes safe redistribution of tasks possible without compromising patient safety. That means three intertwined priorities: strong governance and clarity around scope, robust support and supervision for new roles, and sustainable funding and career pathways that keep staff in post and motivated.

First, there must be explicit clarity on scope of practice and professional boundaries. It is essential to have published role profiles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals working in GP practices or community hubs. These profiles should spell out what tasks can be undertaken autonomously, what requires GP sign-off, and how complex cases are escalated. In my experience, the ambiguity around what a new role can do leads to delays and inconsistent care. A practical example would be a pharmacist-led med-review clinic with fixed referral criteria and GP checks only for high-risk prescriptions or unusual drug interactions. That kind of clarity helps teams work confidently, safely and efficiently.

Second, indemnity arrangements and revalidation must be fit for purpose for these expanded roles. Indemnity should follow the clinician, not be tied to a single employer or site, and there should be a straightforward path to cover new duties as roles evolve. I’d favour a national or well-coordinated regional fund to underwrite liability for newly introduced roles during a transition period, with transparent governance. Revalidation and annual appraisals should be portable when staff move between practices or community hubs, so there isn’t a constant administrative burden that discourages people from taking on extended duties. We need reassurance that patient safety isn’t sacrificed as teams grow.

Third, fund protected clinical supervision and structured ongoing training. New and expanded roles only work if there is protected time for supervision, case reviews and continuous professional development. I’d like to see monthly or bi-monthly supervision clinics where senior clinicians, such as GPs or consultant colleagues, review tricky cases with nurses, pharmacists or PAs. In a rural hub I’ve heard of, a small team gained real confidence once a senior clinician joined for weekly mentorship; patient safety improved and staff morale rose. Guarding supervision time also helps with risk management, incident learning and reducing burnout among already stretched staff.

Alongside this governance backbone, the plan should actively expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with proper training and supervision. We should widen the use of nurse-led chronic disease clinics, pharmacist-led medication reviews, and the growing role of physician associates and paramedics in primary care, all under robust supervision and clear escalation pathways. Training pipelines must be explicit: short-upskilling courses, supervised practice periods, and formal career ladders that offer longer-term progression into senior MDT roles. A practical bonus is to anchor these teams in local hubs where possible, reducing travel for patients in rural Wales and enabling more integrated, timely care.

Crucially, funding must be stable and predictable. Competitive pay, contracted hours that respect work-life balance, and a plan that funds frontline staff rather than short-term agency cover will improve retention. I’ve seen how heavy reliance on locums undermines continuity of care; a workforce plan that funds permanent or longer-term contracts for expanded roles would help retain skilled staff, especially in remote communities. Local recruitment initiatives, supported with mentoring and protected development time, can build a stronger sense of career belonging and reduce turnover.

Finally, governance and data must track safety and quality as teams grow. Regular audits, patient safety indicators, and transparent incident review should be built into the workforce plan so staffing changes translate into real improvements for patients. In rural and semi-rural Wales, where access already presents challenges, these elements could unlock safer, more timely care and less unnecessary travel for patients with chronic conditions or complex needs.

If this plan combines clear scope, robust supervision, portable indemnity and revalidation, and sustainable funding for MDT expansion, we’ll not only ease GP workload but also safeguard high standards of care. That ties directly into improving access and reducing delays, which is what matters most to patients and families across Wales.

In shaping an NHS workforce plan, we believe the foundations must be safety, stability and trust. Improving access to GP, community and mental health services cannot come at the expense of quality. For young people in particular—many with long-term or complex needs—continuity of care and a consistent team behind every appointment are crucial to getting timely, effective help. The plan should prioritise three linked strands: safe staffing, clear scope and support for new roles, and targeted incentives to recruit and retain staff where it’s hardest to fill roles.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models: Set strong, enforceable baselines for staffing across primary care, community services and mental health. But do not chase throughput at the expense of relationships; where possible, patients with chronic or complex needs should have a named clinician or a small stable team that carries their care across GP, nurse and therapist contacts. This means protecting time for longer appointments when needed and avoiding fast, handoff-heavy models that fragment care. In practice, this could mean longer slots for complex cases and a care pathway that follows the patient rather than everyone chasing separate targets. Real-time staffing dashboards should track actual clinician-to-patient loads and allow managers to reallocate without breaking continuity.

- Safety monitoring and quality alongside new roles: Any expansion of roles like physician associates or advanced nurse practitioners must come with robust safety nets. This includes clear scope-of-practice boundaries, formal revalidation pathways, and funding for protected clinical supervision as standard, not add-ons. Indemnity arrangements should be automatic and comprehensive so clinicians can practice safely without defensive barriers. A well-supported workforce is visible through routine safety reviews, incident reporting, and post-appointment audits that feed back into training and staffing decisions rather than just ticking boxes.

- Tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas: Deliver targeted packages for rural, urban-deprived and coastal areas. This should go beyond pay, including housing support, relocation grants, subsidised transport, flexible working patterns, and guaranteed access to continuing professional development. Build local training pipelines that recruit from and stay connected to these communities, so people see a real path to long-term careers nearby. Flexible deployment models can ensure that rotation through different settings does not erode continuity for patients who need a stable team.

- Clear scope, supervision and professional development: The plan must specify how new and extended roles are supported with supervision, mentorship and career progression. Staff who stay in the system often cite predictable supervision and opportunities to upskill as key reasons for staying. Protect time for reflective practice, case reviews, and joint clinical sessions across disciplines—this strengthens safety cultures and reduces the risk of errors when teams are working at scale.

- Localised, data-informed workforce strategies: Use local health demand signals to shape recruitment, including seasonal or fluctuating pressures in coastal towns or urban centres. Data should show not only headcounts but the impact on patient outcomes, wait times, revisit rates and continuity indices. If access improves only when clinicians are spread thin, quality will suffer; the plan must guard against that.

- Patient-centred delivery and involvement: Involve young people and families in workforce planning so the models reflect how care is actually used. For example, patient feedback on continuity and handovers should shape how teams are structured and how supervision is allocated. Where patients experience their care as a “named clinician plus team” rather than a series of handoffs, engagement and attendance improve, which in turn supports timely access.

Overall, the NHS workforce plan should anchor recruitment and retention in continuity and safety. Investment in protected supervision, clear scopes of practice, and safety monitoring must be inseparable from access targets. Then, incentives to recruit in hard-to-fill areas—not just to attract staff but to keep them with sustainable, well-supported career paths—will deliver both faster access and higher quality care for young people and the broader population.
