These pilots should have clear minimum standards for team composition, referral pathways, and data-sharing requirements, while allowing local flexibility to fit community needs. Public information campaigns will help people understand who to contact for which issues and how to escalate if symptoms worsen.

- Put people first: staffing, well-being and development. Retention depends on predictable career pathways, protected time for continuing professional development, and manageable workloads. The plan should ensure supervision, opportunities for rotation across roles, and access to mentoring for less experienced MDT members. This is essential to keeping high standards of care while expanding team-based models.

In practice, these principles map onto concrete steps I’ve seen work in local settings: embedding pharmacists to handle routine med reviews and minor infections; using paramedics and physician associates for triage and some routine consultations; and, importantly, making sure patients still have access to a familiar point of contact if desired. The overarching aim is to free clinicians from unnecessary admin and non-patient-facing tasks so they can focus on high-quality, face-to-face or patient-centred care when it matters most. If the workforce plan keeps data, governance and patient experience front and centre, it can build a more resilient, sustainable NHS that actually delivers timely care for everyone.

Overall, I support a workforce plan that prioritises transparent local data, reduces bureaucratic load, and expands well-supported multidisciplinary teams with strong supervision and interoperable IT. It’s the combination most likely to recruit, retain and sustain high-quality care without compromising safety or continuity for patients.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise interoperable and secure IT systems, with comprehensive staff digital training, while safeguarding options for patients who are digitally excluded. Staff must be able to share records seamlessly across GP practices, community services and hospitals, with robust cyber security and clear accountability. This reduces duplication, supports safer decision-making and frees time for direct patient contact. We must also ensure we don’t leave digitally excluded patients behind: maintain strong phone access, paper records where needed, and accessible face-to-face options in local hubs. 

But technology alone won’t solve workforce pressures. The plan needs clear, funded career pathways, protected continued professional development, structured mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff. In my area, burnout and turnover partly stem from limited progression and time for training; protected CPD time and senior mentoring would make a real difference. There should also be investment in practical roles—nurturing training pipelines for pharmacists, technicians and allied staff with supervised placements and clear progression. A balanced approach—tech-enabled care complemented by people-focused development—will sustain safe, high-quality services across Scotland.

To keep care safe and high quality, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise staffing that actually matches demand, with a focus on stable teams and workable workloads. In practice, that means more frontline staff in GP practices, community nursing and mental health teams so we’re not constantly chasing vacancies or relying on ad hoc agency cover. In my experience, routine checks and care coordination suffer when teams are stretched and admin eats into time with patients. 

Key priorities I’d want to see include:
- Adequate core staffing and predictable rosters to cover peak times and prevent burnout.
- True multi-disciplinary integration, with care navigators who can guide people through GP, community and mental health services, reducing the friction and delays my family and I have faced.
- Clear progression and training opportunities to attract and keep people in local areas, including local apprenticeships and schemes that reflect community needs.
- Reasonable workloads and wellbeing support so staff can provide safe, thorough care without fatigue or quick burnout.
- Admin relief and user-friendly tools that staff actually use, cutting duplication and freeing clinicians to spend more time with patients—incl. home visits where appropriate.
- Competitive pay and conditions to recruit and retain staff locally, rather than losing them to other regions or sectors.

Even with more staff, the plan must ensure sustainable, well-supported teams; otherwise improvements risk being short-lived and fail to address the access and coordination gaps I’ve highlighted.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise practical, targeted incentives for hard-to-fill posts and underserved areas. This includes competitive pay for high-demand roles, retention payments, and relocation packages, supported by bursaries to fund training in nursing, general practice, mental health and allied health across the regions most in need. Flexible working is essential: part-time, job-share, flexible start/finish times and phased retirement should be available to widen the workforce net and reduce burnout. Adequate childcare support is crucial so staff can balance work and family commitments.

Long-term funding and clear career pathways with strong supervision are vital to retain staff and sustain quality care. Invest in proactive mental health support for staff and safe staffing models with manageable rosters, supervision and continuing professional development. Build local recruitment pipelines through schools, colleges and apprenticeships, and align with social care and VCSE partners. Finally, digital tools must support staff without substituting human contact or eroding face-to-face care.

An NHS workforce plan should blend modern digital capability with real-world accessibility and wellbeing. It should prioritise interoperable, secure IT systems and comprehensive staff digital training, but preserve non-digital options for patients who are digitally excluded, such as phone triage, paper reminders, and local access points. In practice this means shared electronic records across primary and community services, clear data protection standards, and ongoing cyber security training for all staff. I’ve seen digital tools streamline referrals and capacity planning, but also witnessed how older or low-income patients can be left behind if we rely too heavily on online channels. Targeted incentives are vital for hard-to-fill areas: rural, coastal and urban deprived settings should receive housing and transport support, plus mentoring and tailored recruitment campaigns to attract clinicians, nurses and allied health professionals. Flexible working matters too: part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement options, and funded childcare can help retain a diverse workforce and reduce burnout. Finally, proactive mental health support, decent supervision, and manageable rosters are essential to sustain safe, compassionate care.

From my experience juggling work and family in England, any NHS workforce plan needs to recognise that recruiting staff is only part of the solution; keeping them supported and safe to practice is equally important. I think priorities should include:
- Building multidisciplinary teams in community hubs where GPs, nurses, mental health clinicians and pharmacists can collaborate, share supervision, and reduce avoidable travel for patients.
- Cutting unnecessary admin and improving digital systems so clinicians can spend more time with patients.
- Ensuring sustainable workloads with transparent safe staffing levels, predictable rosters, and flexible/part-time options to improve retention, especially for those balancing caregiving duties.
- Clear career paths and local recruitment to reflect the communities served, with strong training and mentorship to grow from within.
- A focus on staff wellbeing and early access to mental health and peer-support services, plus realistic rest periods to prevent burnout.
- Monitoring impact with simple metrics, and being prepared to adjust with funding and time.

The main challenge is aligning funding with care quality; the plan should be flexible and evidence-based to avoid compromising patient safety while rebuilding capacity.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the plan must balance three pillars: people, technology and patient access. First, invest in the workforce itself: competitive pay and incentives, flexible working, strong wellbeing support, faster international recruitment routes, and solid admin/back‑office support to cut non‑clinical workload. Second, prioritise interoperable, secure IT that actually works in practice: shared electronic records across primary, community and mental health services; robust data sharing with clear governance; secure systems with single sign‑on to reduce duplication and delays; and dedicated funding for training clinicians and staff to use digital tools, plus ongoing cybersecurity upskilling. This tech backbone should truly reduce admin burden rather than add steps. Third, safeguard alternatives and digital inclusion: ensure easy non‑digital channels (phone, in‑person) remain, while providing devices, local digital hubs and digital literacy support so nobody is left behind.

When these elements are funded upfront and coordinated, clinicians will have time and the right tools to deliver high‑quality care, and staff are more likely to stay long‑term rather than burn out.

Agree. To recruit, retain and safeguard high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan must put people first with clear, funded career pathways, protected CPD time, and strong mentoring and return‑to‑practice routes. Staff need defined progression from early‑career roles into advanced practice, with funded rotations across primary, community and hospital teams so people can build confidence and skills where the need is greatest. Mentoring schemes, supervisor capacity, and funded peer‑to‑peer coaching should be standard, not exceptional. Return‑to‑practice programs after career breaks—complete with supervised placements and phased re‑entry—are essential to retain experienced staff. Protected CPD should be genuinely protected: time off, funded training, and capacity for reflective learning, not just annual credits. In my area, when practices had mentor networks and dedicated CPD windows, morale and retention improved and patient care felt safer. Clear allocation of training to skill mix in multidisciplinary teams reduces burnout and supports safe care. Finally, leadership development and flexible working options help attract and keep staff in Scotland’s NHS as we move toward more integrated, colocated services.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality, I think the NHS workforce plan should rest on three priorities. First, responsible international recruitment: streamline visa routes for healthcare workers, and speed up credential recognition with clear bridging programmes. Regulators and employers should align to support integration, including language and cultural competency training, mentorship, and locally staffed induction. Importantly, there must be safeguards to avoid depleting source countries: set ethical quotas, monitor impact, and invest in education and placements there. 

Second, strengthen domestic pipelines: meaningful career progression, flexible working patterns, competitive pay, and robust wellbeing support to tackle burnout. Third, ensure safe, well‑supported teams: reliable staffing models, transparent rostering, and continued access to ongoing training so staff can maintain high standards.

In my area, a mixed team of local and overseas clinicians—backed by shared IT and a clear onboarding path—reduced delays and improved patient flow without compromising safety. If accompanied by long‑term funding and good governance, this approach should deliver safer, higher‑quality care as demand grows.

There is a strong case that an NHS workforce plan should do more than simply recruit numbers; it must create sustainable, rewarding careers in the places and roles where staff are most needed, so that safe, high‑quality care is consistently possible. Drawing on our experience of areas with high deprivation and workforce pressure, I would prioritise a package of linked measures that make roles attractive, workable and lasting for staff, while also improving patient outcomes.

- Competitive pay and targeted financial incentives
- Ensure base pay remains competitive with other sectors and with regional cost pressures.
- Retention payments for hard-to-fill, high-demand posts, particularly in underserved districts or specialty areas with chronic vacancies.
- Relocation and transition support for staff moving into high-need communities, together with practical assistance (schools for children, housing advice, local integration support).
- Bursaries and student funding tied to service commitments in underserved areas, with clear paths to return on investment for the NHS and the community.

These financial measures should be coupled with a clear commitment to sustainable, long-term staffing rather than short bursts of recruitment. In practice, where relocation support and retention payments are offered, practices in our area have found that people are prepared to move and stay longer, reducing nurse turnover and the need for frequent temporary staffing.

- Safer, more predictable, and flexible staffing models
- Set and routinely monitor safe staffing levels across all disciplines to avoid overwork and burnout, with staffing rotas that protect rest periods and patient safety.
- Build stable skill mixes in teams so that clinicians are not overloaded with tasks outside their scope; empower highly trained support roles and allied health professionals to share responsibility for care pathways.
- Flexible working arrangements to improve retention, including part-time routes, job sharing, and patient‑facing roles that fit diverse life circumstances, while keeping continuity of care for patients.

Flexible working helps keep skilled workers in the NHS longer, especially where family and caring responsibilities are a real barrier to full-time positions.

- Career development, training, and progression
- Clear, funded routes for progression (nursing, midwifery, allied health professionals, physicians associates, etc.) with guaranteed access to continuing professional development and leadership training.
- Return‑to‑practice programmes, refresher courses, and supervisor support so colleagues who left the workforce can rejoin safely and confidently.
- Exposure to different settings (primary care, community teams, mental health) through structured rotations, with mentorship and a disciplined handover process.

A visible ladder of progression helps staff see a future in the NHS, reduces attrition, and supports a culture of excellence. In our area, practices that offered formal CPD and leadership development saw improved morale and fewer resignations, even when workloads remained challenging.

- Recruitment pipelines and international recruitment with robust integration
- Build local pipelines by partnering with schools, colleges, and universities to offer early exposure to healthcare careers and to cultivate talent from the communities most served.
- Apprenticeships and ‘grow your own’ initiatives to widen participation and create pathways into nursing, diagnostics, and allied health roles.
- Thoughtful international recruitment where needed, with clear orientation, mentor support, and a structured integration package to ensure new arrivals can practice safely and feel welcomed.

The goal is not quick fixes but a steady, values-driven pipeline that mirrors the patient population and strengthens local teams.

- Wellbeing, safety, and supportive culture
- Comprehensive occupational health and mental health support, including confidential counselling and peer support, to tackle burnout and long-term stress.
- Regular, constructive supervision and supervision-led quality improvement projects that involve frontline staff in shaping workflows.
- A culture of safety where staff feel empowered to raise concerns and contribute to safer care without fear of repercussions.

- Diversity, inclusion, and language support
- Proactive recruitment from diverse communities and targeted outreach so the workforce better reflects the population served.
- Mandatory cultural competence and trauma-informed care training for frontline staff, plus funded interpreters and language support to ensure access to care is not impeded and that communication remains high quality.

- Data-informed planning and accountability
- Local workforce dashboards that track vacancy rates, turnover, sickness, and patient safety indicators; tie incentives to sustained improvements in safety and patient experience, not just headcount.
- Regular review of what works, shared learning, and scaling up successful, equity-focused initiatives.

In short, an NHS workforce plan should couple financial incentives with real career development, predictable staffing, wellbeing, and a culture that values diversity and patient-centered care. When staff feel supported, adequately trained and fairly compensated, they stay longer, deliver higher-quality care, and patients experience safer, more reliable services. This approach aligns with our broader aim of equitable access and outcomes across communities and is what we should be building into every workforce plan.

I’m not sure there’s a single set of priorities that would fit every area. In our patch, staffing pressures are clear, and while some teams manage well, shortfalls are impacting access and safety. A workforce plan should prioritise keeping care safe and high quality while avoiding staff burnout and reducing backlogs that harm patients. From what I’ve seen, helpful priorities might include:
- Flexible, predictable rosters that cover GP and community clinics without leaving patients waiting for days or weeks.
- Clear career progression and local recruitment, with real opportunities for training and advancement to keep staff in the area.
- Adequate support roles (admin, triage, nursing) so clinicians can focus on direct patient care.
- Mental health and wellbeing support for staff, including supervision and reasonable workloads.
- Real-time monitoring of staffing levels with contingency plans to manage surges.
- Better integration across primary care, community services and mental health so teams can cover gaps quickly, without patients having to travel or wait longer.
I can’t point to a single policy that would fix everything, but any plan that makes staffing more predictable, adequately resourced, and focused on safe care would help our area.

Prioritise joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to share workload and deliver holistic care, plus responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, proper credential recognition, integration support and safeguards against draining source health systems.

I think having a NHS workforce plan is essential, but I’m not sure there is a single set of priorities that will fit every area. What matters most in practice is keeping safe, high‑quality care while genuinely addressing the access problems older people face. In our area, GP appointments can be two weeks away and mental health slots scarce after referral, so any plan should prioritise local staffing that can plug these gaps. That means enough district nurses and therapy staff in community clinics, clear links with social care to stop discharge delays, and mixed teams so patients aren’t pushed from pillar to post. Flexible working patterns, targeted recruitment in rural postings with transport support, and incentives to retain experienced staff would help, alongside training that improves care for older people and digital literacy where needed. I’m cautious about grand targets without local pilots and solid evidence, and I’d want patient choice preserved so new arrangements don’t simply shift bottlenecks elsewhere."

I believe any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe staffing levels and continuity-preserving care models, backed by robust safety monitoring, so improvements in access never compromise quality. In practice, that means ensuring enough GP and nurse appointments are available and not just chasing demand with digital triage, and guaranteeing patients have a named clinician or stable care team who can see patterns over time. For mental health, longer initial assessments and regular, consistent follow-ups should be the norm to reduce crises.

Crucially, we need secure, multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain recruitment, training capacity and retention initiatives, rather than short-term policy shifts that leave teams guessing. In my area, staff turnover spikes when conditions feel uncertain and training slots get squeezed by unpredictable funding cycles. A longer horizon would help—more GP training places, support for international recruits with proper induction, and funding that enables expanded roles for nurses, pharmacists and social prescribers.

Investments should also support flexible working, wellbeing, and robust safety-monitoring dashboards so we can track safe staffing and quality in real time. If these elements are funded and coordinated, access can improve while care remains safe and person-centred.

From my long experience with NHS services, I’d like to sre an NHS workforce plan that prioritises secure multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding to underpin sustained workforce initiatives, training capacity and reduced policy volatility. Without stable funding we chase targets rather than outcomes, and recruitment for GPs, nurses and therapists remains fragile, piling pressure on locums and fragmenting care that older patients notice in continuity and ongoing support. The plan should commit to longer‑term budgets for recruitment and retention, plus protected time for training and supervision so new roles can be integrated safely and patient safety is protected. It should also clarify scope‑of‑practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements, and fund protected clinical supervision to support new roles and maintain high safety standards. Invest in interoperable IT and secure systems and provide staff digital training, but safeguard altrrnatives for those who cannot use digital tools and keepp simple, local non‑digital pathways for booking and urgent care. In my area, constant locum cover means I see different clinicians and worry about gapss in communication for my long‑standing conditions. NHS111 often pushes me toward self‑car when I need prompt assessment, causing delay and anxiety. A workforce plan tha combines stable funding, clear governance, practical digital inclusion and robust supervision would help deliver safer, high‑quality care for people like me.

From my perspective, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise stabilising the workforce as the foundation for safe, high-quality care. In my area, GP vacancies and high turnover break continuity of care I rely on, and this is unsustainable. To address this, we need targeted competitive pay and retention payments that reflect the day-to-day pressures of frontline roles, plus relocation packages to attract clinicians to underserved places. Bursaries and funded training for students and career-changers will grow capacity in high-demand areas like GP, district nursing, mental health and allied health professionals. 

Incentives must go hand in hand with real support: defined career progression, strong supervision, and realistic workloads to prevent burnout. Reassure staff with protected time for ongoing professional development and the chance to work in stable teams with a named clinician overseeing care. Linking pay and location incentives to longer-term posts helps reduce locum reliance, improves continuity, and keeps care safe and patient-focused.

As someone living in Scotland, I’d like to see an NHS workforce plan that puts local need at its heart. It should start with transparent, localised data, modelling and KPIs so funding and performance monitoring reflect what’s really happening in communities and in practice. Evaluation must be ongoing, with feedback loops showing whether staffing changes improve access, safety and quality of care, not just headline targets.

A priority should be expanding domestic supply of primary care and related roles through more undergraduate and postgraduate places and apprenticeships, backed by protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships. In practical terms, this means funded training pipelines with rural placements, backfill for trainees, and portable accreditation so staff can move between practices without losing recognition. This approach reduces reliance on agency staffing and supports continuity of care.

Equally important is a robust focus on retention: manageable workloads, protected time for professional development and outreach, structured mentorship, and clear career progression. Local deployment plans should be linked to transport access and telehealth options in rural and deprived areas to sustain high‑quality care where it’s most needed. These steps together would help recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safety and quality at the forefront.

From my perspective, any NHS workforce plan must be honest about local realities and built on solid, visible data. It should prioritise developing transparent, localised workforce information, with modelling, KPIs and evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. In my area we still see GP and mental health vacancies, more reliance on temporary staff, and longer waits that threaten continuity of care. Clear dashboards that track staffing levels, turnover, sickness, patient wait times, and safety and experience outcomes should be publicly available so communities can understand and trust how funds are being used. 

The plan must also translate data into practical action: targeted recruitment and training pipelines, career ladders for care staff, and flexible working patterns that do not erode long-term relationships with a regular GP. Allocate resources to community-based roles (pharmacists, allied health professionals, wellbeing coaches) to ease pressures on primary care. Provide strong retention incentives, manageable workloads, and reduced administrative burdens to keep skilled staff in post. 

Finally, pilot new models with robust evaluation against patient outcomes, safety metrics and satisfaction, and scale only where proven. Having lived with stretched services, I know transparent data and local learning are essential to recruiting, retaining and delivering safe, high-quality care.

From Scotland, I believe NHS workforce planning must put sustainable recruitment and retention at its core to protect safe, high-quality care. It needs clear, funded career pathways and protected CPD budgets so both seasoned clinicians and early-career staff can grow without fear of funding gaps. Mentorship and structured return-to-practice routes would help keep skilled staff in the system and attract others back after career breaks. Targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages, and bursaries are essential tools to draw people into underserved areas and high-demand roles, including community and mental health teams where vacancies linger. Without this, new teams risk instability and gaps in patient care despite promises of reform. We also need multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements so training capacity, staffing pipelines, and service redesign aren’t derailed by short-term policy shifts. Long-term budgets would support stable training posts, robust supervision, and the capital to expand digital infrastructure. If we invest in sustainable staffing models, we’ll see fewer locum-dependent gaps and real improvements in timely access and care quality across Scotland.

A NHS workforce plan should build long-term resilience by prioritising stable, well-funded recruitment and retention that recognises local realities and the realities of delivering care in diverse settings. From where I sit, the strongest plan would combine targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas with protected, ring-fenced funding for training and development, and a clear strategy to share workload across health and social care and community services. It must be concrete, locally adaptable, and capable of withstanding short-term political or policy changes without collapsing our existing momentum.

Prioritise recruitment and retention in hard-to-fill areas: We absolutely need tailored incentives for rural, coastal, and urban-deprived communities where vacancies persist and turnover is high. Practical measures should include housing and transport support, relocation grants, and flexible rosters that make long shifts feasible for people with caregiving responsibilities. In my area, the shortage of GPs and district nurses means patients wait longer for routine care, and staff burnout can be seen in rising sickness absence. Providing affordable housing near clinics and subsidised public transport for shift work would remove real barriers to volunteering for tough postings and keeping staff in those communities long term. Supporting staff with family-friendly options and safe, predictable working patterns would also help retention.

Ensure multi-year, ring-fenced funding for workforce initiatives: Short funding spells and capricious policy changes make it impossible to plan training pipelines, career progression, and retention schemes. A multi-year settlement would allow trusts to expand training places, establish mentorship and return-to-practice programs, and invest in staffing capacity that mirrors local population needs. This stability is essential to break cycles of temporary fixes and clinician churn. In practice, it would let us commit to expanded multidisciplinary teams (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, psychologists) and to sustaining them with robust supervision and professional development.

Expand and sustain training capacity: We need more training places across nursing, allied health, medicine, and mental health, with real-time access to high-quality CPD and protection for time to learn. Return-to-practice schemes and bridging programs should be streamlined and well-funded so experienced professionals feel welcomed back after career breaks. In my experience, staff who complete a supported return-to-practice pathway are more likely to remain engaged and provide continuity of care, especially in areas where recruitment is most challenging.

Support wellbeing and safe care through workload planning: A workforce plan cannot succeed without addressing workload, morale, and safety. That means funded longer-term recruitment, realistic staffing targets, and safe, predictable rotas, plus access to psychological support and supervision. Flexible working options and well-being initiatives should be embedded as standard, not as afterthoughts. When teams are supported, patients experience shorter waits, better continuity, and safer care.

Strengthen links with social care and community services: Bolder joint funding and governance that enable shared staffing, cross-training, and task-shifting can redistribute loads and prevent bottlenecks. For example, trained care coordinators, community health workers, and well-supported care homes can take on follow-up checks, medication reviews, and basic rehab, freeing up GPs and hospital teams to manage complex cases. In practice, this requires interoperable IT, common records, and joint performance metrics so care is coordinated rather than duplicated or fragmented.

Invest in careers, leadership and pathways: The plan should explicitly fund career pathways—from trainee to senior clinician and into leadership roles—so people can see a long-term future in the NHS. Mentoring, protected time for CPD, and opportunities to specialise or move between roles (for example, primary care to mental health integration) would help retain staff who otherwise look for growth elsewhere.

Data, governance and local autonomy: Local workforce boards should have real influence, with transparent metrics on wait times, staff wellbeing, and patient safety. Central policy should set the direction, but trusts must be trusted to tailor solutions to their communities. That mix of guidance and local control is what keeps the system responsive while maintaining consistency in safety and quality.

Overall, the plan should be realistic, phased and patient-centred. In the short term, invest in targeted incentives and support for hard-to-fill posts; in the medium term, scale multidisciplinary teams and training capacity; in the long term, lock in stable funding, robust supervision, and strong partnerships with social care and community services. When staff feel valued, supported, and able to do their jobs safely, patients benefit from timelier access, better continuity, and higher quality care.

Three priorities should guide an NHS workforce plan, guided by what people like me actually need when juggling study, part‑time work and health concerns. First, develop transparent localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. By mapping capacity and demand for GP, community and mental health services at evenings, weekends, and during term times, leaders can target recruitment and workload planning where it’s most needed, and track whether changes improve access without creating new bottlenecks.

Second, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements. Stable funding would enable sustained workforce initiatives, expand training capacity, and reduce short-term policy volatility that makes it hard to recruit and retain staff. With predictable budgets, local trusts can commit to longer training pipelines, apprenticeships, and flexible working patterns that still uphold safe care.

Third, prioritise safety and continuity as access expands. This means safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving care models, and robust safety monitoring so faster access never comes at the expense of quality. Real‑time dashboards, regular clinical audits, and strong triage protocols are essential to keep both patients and staff confident.

Taken together, I want a plan that ties access improvements to solid data, stable funding, and unwavering attention to patient safety and staff wellbeing.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise safety, continuity and long‑term supply alongside fair, targeted incentives. In practice this means: safe staffing and continuity-preserving models, with real‑time dashboards to monitor nurse and care‑staff levels, and minimal reliance on short‑term agency cover. Teams should be kept together where possible to protect clinical judgment and patient experience, and safety monitoring should be explicit, actionable and transparent. 

Pay and incentives should be targeted to hard‑to‑staff roles and underserved areas: competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries linked to measurable retention and service quality outcomes. 

Training and pipeline must be expanded: more undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university‑practice partnerships to fund GP, district nursing, mental health and allied health pathways. This should include return‑to‑practice routes with appropriate retraining and competency checks. 

Safety and accountability: link workforce expansion to patient outcomes and access metrics, requiring local plans with clear milestones to ensure access improvements do not compromise care quality. In our area, district‑nurse shortages and prolonged mental health waits show why these elements must sit at the heart of any plan.

In my view, an NHS workforce plan should start from people: the staff who deliver care day to day and the patients they serve. To recruit, retain and support a safe, high‑quality service, I’d prioritise three interlinked strands that reflect what I’ve seen and what matters to staff and service users alike.

Flexible, sustainable working: many of us juggle study, part‑time work or caring responsibilities, so offering flexible hours, part‑time positions, job‑share options, and phased retirement can help retain experienced colleagues who would otherwise leave. Practical measures like predictable rotas, reasonable workloads, and childcare support (on‑site provision, subsidies, or access to flexible family leave) would reduce burnout and widen the talent pool. In my circle, colleagues have stayed in nursing and allied roles longer when they could balance home life with work, and that continuity translates into better patient care. Proactively normalising flexible arrangements across bands, with clear career progression, is essential.

Staff wellbeing and mental health support: the job is demanding, and a proactive approach to mental health—for staff and trainees—should be central. That means confidential, easy‑to‑access counselling, mental health days without stigma, peer‑support networks, and targeted wellbeing programmes during busy periods. When staff feel supported, they’re more engaged, make safer decisions, and stay in roles longer. This also includes safe de‑escalation and burnout prevention training, so teams aren’t pushed into deteriorating conditions simply because coverage is thin.

Expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams: to safely distribute GP workload and maintain quality, we need well‑structured teams consisting of nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles with proper supervision and governance. Training pathways and standards must ensure these colleagues can take on appropriate responsibilities with clear accountability. For example, trained PAs or advanced nurse practitioners could manage routine reviews, triage, and follow‑ups, freeing GPs to devote time to complex cases. I’ve seen pilot models where non‑GP clinicians handle chronic disease checks and minor acute issues, with good patient feedback and shorter waiting times; with robust supervision, these models can scale up safely. It’s about ensuring every role has what it needs—supervision, continuing education, and a clear scope of practice—so care is consistent and safe.

Career development and progression: a robust pipeline—from student placements to newly qualified staff and return‑to‑practice routes—helps recruit from local communities and keep people in the workforce. Supportive onboarding, mentorship, and funded CPD opportunities will help staff feel valued and grow within the NHS. Flexible training routes, modular learning, and protected time for development should be standard, not exceptional.

Data‑led planning and accountability: workforce planning must be transparent and evolving. Regular dashboards should show vacancy rates, staff sickness, training completions, and patient safety indicators, with action plans when targets aren’t met. This ensures managers can anticipate gaps—such as a surge in vacancies in a particular specialty—and respond with targeted recruitment, flexible staffing, or expanded MDT capacity before patient care is affected.

In short, a successful plan respects staff as essential partners in care: it enables flexible work lives, supports mental health, builds strong multidisciplinary teams with clear training and governance, and keeps a strong eye on wellbeing and safety. If these elements are funded and measured, NHS services will be more resilient, patients will experience steadier access to high‑quality care, and the workforce will feel valued and less prone to burnout.

From my perspective in Wales, and as someone who’s seen how stretched services can be for young people, any NHS workforce plan should prioritise not just more staff but the right staff with clear roles, strong supervision and solid safety nets. It needs to be practical for rural areas, sensitive to language needs, and designed so staff feel supported enough to stay. In short, I want a plan that clarifies what new and expanding roles can do, protects patients, and provides real, protected time for supervision and development.

Key priorities I’d expect to see:

- Clear scope-of-practice and governance for new roles. If we’re expanding roles like care coordinators, health coaches, or embedded mental health workers in GP hubs, there must be explicit boundaries, well-defined responsibilities, and strong interfaces with GPs, nurses, social care and schools. This helps prevent role creep and patient confusion, and it makes training and supervision more straightforward. It should also ensure Welsh-medium provision and cultural competence so young people feel understood.

- Robust indemnity arrangements and risk management. Staff will be doing more cross‑service work, which is great for patient care but raises questions about liability and protection. The plan should guarantee accessible professional indemnity coverage for all staff, including those in new or blended roles, with clear guidance on who is responsible for costs and how claims would be handled. This reduces anxiety among staff and helps keep people willing to take on innovative roles in hubs or community teams.

- Streamlined revalidation and ongoing professional development. Revalidation should be clear, proportionate and not overly burdensome for clinicians taking on new roles or working across services. Build in protected time for appraisal, CPD, and peer review so quality and safety aren’t compromised when staff take on expanded duties or work flexible patterns to meet demand.

- Funded, protected clinical supervision and onboarding. New roles and expanded teams need structured supervision to maintain safety, confidence, and quality of care. This means dedicated supervision slots, both in person and remotely where necessary, with a focus on clinical decision-making, safeguarding, and culturally appropriate practice. Supervision should be funded and time‑protected to avoid being squeezed by day-to-day workloads.

- Targeted training pipelines and retention incentives, especially in rural Wales. Create clear career pathways that start with placements in schools, primary care, and community services, then progress to advanced practitioner or team-lead roles. Address workforce pipeline gaps with funded training, supported return-to-practice for those who’ve paused their careers, and incentives to work in harder‑to‑staff areas. Include language and cultural training so staff can serve Wales’ diverse communities effectively.

- Focus on wellbeing and safe staffing models. Adequate staffing levels, realistic workloads, and access to mental health support for staff are essential to keeping services safe and preventing burnout. Flexible working, reasonable on‑call expectations, and wellbeing resources should be embedded in the plan.

- Data governance and digital capability. For integrated hubs, we’ll need secure data-sharing arrangements and staff training on privacy. Staff should have access to user-friendly digital systems that enable safe, efficient coordination—without excluding those with limited internet access or private spaces at home. Telehealth and blended models can extend reach, but equity must be part of the design.

- Governance, monitoring and accountability. The plan should establish clear metrics—staff retention, patient wait times, safety incidents, and patient experience—tounded by regular review cycles. Pilots and phased rollouts, with patient and public involvement in design and evaluation, will help refine models before scaling.

- Co-design and local tailoring. Given the diversity of Wales, local workforce plans must be adaptable, with communities and Service users involved in shaping roles, supervision models, and training needs. That alignment with local reality is essential for sustainable recruitment and high-quality care.

In practice, I’ve seen how a well-stuffed hub can improve access and outcomes, but without robust supervision and clear role boundaries, it can become chaotic and unsafe. A plan that foregrounds clarity, protection for staff, and ongoing learning—while keeping care close to people’s homes—feels most likely to deliver the safer, more timely services young people in Wales need. I’d like to see a staged, co-designed rollout that tests approaches in different regions, learns quickly, and scales only what proves safe and effective.

absolutely to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise clear scope of practice, robust revalidation, and appropriate indemnity arrangements. New roles should be introduced with protected clinical supervision funded long‑term to sustain patient safety and consistent standards. Develop explicit competency frameworks, with phased progression and mandatory supervision for expanded roles such as nurse practitioners, physician associates and mental health support workers; without this, practice can drift and safety boundaries blur as teams stretch!

Thinking about an NHS workforce plan that works for patients like me, I would prioritise transparency and local accountability. A plan that sets out transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks would help decide where to recruit, train and fund. For example, knowing in my area how many GPs, practice nurses, and mental health staff are available now and when retirements are likely would allow us to plan ahead rather than scramble when vacancies appear. KPIs should cover vacancy and turnover rates, wait times for appointments, average length of consultations for chronic care, staff burnout indicators, and patient safety metrics. Localised modelling could show how investments in longer appointments or multi-disciplinary teams affect outcomes and costs. Fundamental actions would include sustainable funding linked to local staffing needs, expanded training pipelines, and retention measures: career development, flexible working, safe workloads, and decent pay. Integrating more nurses and psychologists into primary care would support continuity of care and reduce hospital visits. Finally, use technology for smarter triage and remote check-ins to complement in-person care. In short, data-driven, locally tailored planning will help keep high-quality care safe and sustainable.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the plan should prioritise funded career pathways, protected CPD time, robust mentorship and return-to-practice schemes. These measures help both longer-serving clinicians and newer staff feel supported and able to progress.

A second priority is expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles should be trained and supervised to safely redistribute GP workload. With clear competencies and supervision, a pharmacist-led medicines review or a nurse practitioner triage can handle routine problems, leaving GPs to focus on complex cases. In Wales, this would require standardised training, consistent supervision, and governance across practices, plus flexible deployment models to match local demand.
Practical steps include funded CPD and protected time for professional development; formal mentorship for all new starters; return-to-practice pathways; streamlined onboarding; and retained career ladders with transparent progression. Invest in digital supervision tools and shared protocols so teams can work cohesively across settings.

From my experience, where teams have strong mentoring and clear progression, staff stay longer and patient care feels steadier; where opportunities are scarce, turnover increases and continuity suffers.

I’d back an NHS workforce plan that grows our own people, keeps teams well-supported, and preserves safe, high‑quality care. Key priorities should be: first, expand the pipeline of primary care staff by increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university‑practice partnerships. That builds a steady, locally rooted workforce and reduces reliance on external recruitment. Second, align and fund social care, mental health and community services together, so workload is redistributed and care becomes more holistic. Integrated teams and joint funding help clinicians spend less time on admin and more time with patients. Third, make retention practical and fair: offer flexible hours, part‑time and job‑share options, phased retirement, childcare support, and proactive mental health services to prevent burnout. Experience in my area shows that capacity increases work best when continuity of care is preserved, so training, deployment and service design must balance more staff with stable relationships for patients with complex needs. Overall, a plan that builds domestic capacity while strengthening cross‑sector collaboration and staff wellbeing should deliver safe, sustainable care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise several practical, funded steps. First, funded, clearly defined career pathways from training through to specialist roles, with transparent progression and salary milestones so people can see a long-term future with the NHS. Second, protected CPD time and funding: guaranteed time off for development, plus funded courses and access to simulation and digital learning so skills stay current. Third, structured mentorship and sponsorship: formal pairings for new graduates and returning staff, with clear goals and protected supervision time.

Fourth, return-to-practice schemes: accessible routes for those who have paused work, with supervised refreshers and bridging modules to reinstate competence safely. Fifth, flexible working and wellbeing support: flexible shifts, part-time options, and practical wellbeing packages to improve retention, especially for younger staff balancing study or family commitments. Sixth, safe staffing and workload management: appropriate staffing ratios, robust induction, and regular skills checks to maintain quality and safety. Finally, transparent accountability and data: publish retention, CPD uptake and progression metrics to drive continuous improvement.

Investing in these areas helps sustain experienced clinicians and supports early-career staff, delivering safer, higher-quality care for communities.

I think any NHS workforce plan must prioritise attracting, retaining and supporting staff while safeguarding safe, high‑quality care. In practice that means targeted, competitive pay where shortages hit hardest, plus retention payments to discourage churn. A relocation package should be available for staff moving to underserved areas or high‑demand roles, with a clear induction and local support. Bursaries or funded training places for nurses, GPs and allied health professionals, tied to service commitments in hard‑to‑staff locations, would help fill long‑standing gaps. 

But pay and funding alone aren’t enough. Sustainable, long‑term funding is essential, together with safe staffing levels, reasonable workloads, and protected time for CPD and supervision. Flexible working, better wellbeing support, and reduced admin burden would help staff stay engaged. Clear career progression, mentoring and visible local leadership are also key to retention. 

Data‑led planning should identify where new posts and training places are most needed, including pathways for appropriately integrating overseas recruits with proper induction. Any plan must be transparent about expectations, monitor impact on patient safety and outcomes, and ensure fair access to care across communities.

Prioritise stronger links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workloads and deliver holistic patient care, so staff can maintain safe, high‑quality services across sectors.

An NHS workforce plan should be built around safe, high‑quality care delivered by well-supported staff. Key priorities must include clarifying scope-of-practice for expanding roles (advanced clinical practitioners, physician associates, care coordinators) so teams know what is within their remit, and ensuring revalidation remains efficient and predictable, not a hurdle. Indemnity arrangements should be robust and consistent across settings, with transparent funding so staff are protected when working in new or expanded roles.

Funded, protected clinical supervision is essential to developing confidence and maintaining patient safety as roles evolve. This means protected time for mentorship, case reviews and reflective practice, with access to senior clinical oversight, including in remote or rural locations. Combine this with structured induction programmes and clear career progression to improve retention.

Governance should emphasise consistent standards, real-time safety reporting and regular outcomes monitoring. Recruitment should balance domestic talent growth with international recruitment under robust onboarding, language support and integration.

Finally, the plan must promote flexible, sustainable working conditions and wellbeing support, and harness digital tools like digital triage and integrated appointment systems to reduce unnecessary workloads. In our area, these elements would help stabilise services without compromising safety.

I think a practical NHS workforce plan should prioritise what keeps people in the job and keeps patients safe, while expanding access where it’s most needed. That means embracing flexible, diverse working patterns, funding competitive pay and targeted incentives, and building clear training pipelines that grow our own workforce in primary care and community services. It also has to align with the co-located, multidisciplinary hubs I mentioned earlier, so staffing models support seamless, integrated care rather than competing silos.

- Flexibility and wellbeing as a core element: make it easier to balance work with caring responsibilities by offering greater access to flexible hours, part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, and reliable childcare support. In practice, this could mean shift models that cover evenings or weekends without overwhelming individuals, plus proactive mental health services and reduced after-hours burden. A lot of burnout comes from rigid schedules paired with high workloads; protected time for mental health and personal resilience should be built into every role and team, with backfill arrangements that don’t push the same people into constant overtime.

- Pay, incentives and targeted recruitment: to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles, we need targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages, and bursaries. These shouldn’t be one-off; there should be ongoing incentives linked to staying in post or completing certain training milestones. In my community, we’ve seen colleagues move away for better pay or easier commutes; without local incentives, it’s hard to build stable teams that patients can rely on.

- Grow our own workforce through training pipelines: increase undergraduate, postgraduate, and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships. This is essential for ensuring a steady stream of well-prepared clinicians who understand local needs. Practical steps could include formal joint training contracts with protected time for clinical practice, funded placements in GP practices and community services, and incentives for students who commit to working in primary care after qualification.

- Support for staff development and progression: a clear career ladder, mentoring, structured CPD, and opportunities for cross-disciplinary experience keep morale high and reduce turnover. For instance, junior nurses who rotate through primary care, mental health, and community teams with achievable milestones stay engaged and gain the breadth needed for future leadership. Multidisciplinary training tied to shared care plans also supports safer, more consistent care for patients who require complex support.

- Safe, high-quality care through data-informed planning: workforce planning must be linked to service demand and patient safety metrics, ensuring safe staffing ratios and covered rotas in every hub. In practice, that means better data on workload, real-time capacity planning, and reducing reliance on temporary staff by building robust pipelines and flexible hiring terms. Digital scheduling and shared IT systems between NHS teams and VCSE partners will be crucial to maintain continuity when staff numbers fluctuate.

- Local inequities and housing mobility: offer practical relocation assistance and housing support for staff moving to underserved areas, with local partnerships to ease the transition. This helps reduce vacancy periods in hard-to-fill posts and supports families settling into new communities.

In short, the plan should treat people as the core asset—support them with flexibility, fair pay, training, and career growth—while ensuring the staffing architecture is designed to sustain safe, high-quality care in the communities that need it most. That approach will help us keep good people in the NHS, welcome new recruits, and deliver the integrated, responsive care our hubs are designed to provide.

absolutely from my perspective living in England, I’m not sure there is a simple set of priorities for an NHS workforce plan. In practice, safe, high‑quality care depends on enough staff across GP, community, and mental health services. When staffing is stretched, routine GP slots can vanish for weeks, counselling waits drag on for months, and after‑hospital discharge nurse visits get postponed, as I’ve seen in my area. There are some pilots—online booking, weekend clinics, regional hubs—that help a bit, but they only work if there are enough clinicians and support staff to deliver the care people need.

I’m hesitant to pick a single formula that would fit everywhere. I suspect any plan should look at staffing levels and safe ratios, training and career progression, and the conditions under which staff can work flexibly without compromising patient safety. It would help to listen to frontline staff about workload and burnout, and to have good data to measure whether recruitment and retention efforts actually improve access and quality. In short, more staff and better support matter, but I’m not convinced there’s a universal answer!

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safe, high‑quality care, the plan should prioritise stable funding, flexible working and strong development pathways, alongside responsible international recruitment. First, secure multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding specifically for workforce initiatives—recruitment, training, supervision and digital staffing tools—so trusts can plan beyond yearly cycles and avoid disruptive policy shifts. In my area, funding volatility has made long‑term staffing strategies hard to sustain and patient care can suffer as a result. Second, expand flexible working options: part‑time roles, job‑share, phased retirement, accessible childcare support and proactive mental health services for staff. These changes help retain diverse talent and reduce burnout, something I’ve seen when colleagues cut back hours to cope with family life or stress. Third, invest in local training and clear progression routes—apprenticeships, nursing associates, cross‑disciplinary training—to grow the NI workforce and reduce dependence on agency staff. Fourth, overseas recruitment should be used responsibly: streamlined visas and credential recognition with structured integration support, alongside safeguards to avoid depleting source health systems. Finally, ensure safe staffing ratios and robust clinical supervision as you expand the workforce to protect patients.

An NHS workforce plan should focus on four clear priorities to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality. First, targeted pay and incentives: competitive pay, retention payments for hard-to-fill posts, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and high‑demand roles such as district nursing, mental health in the community, and allied health professionals. Practical support for families and flexible career options matter as much as salary. In my area, a few district nurse posts have stagnated for years; relocation packages would help fill them and stabilise teams.

Second, local data, modelling and evaluation: develop transparent, localised workforce data, clear KPIs and evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding decisions and performance monitoring. Regular dashboards on vacancies, turnover, training uptake and patient outcomes would help communities see progress and adjust quickly.

Third, interoperable IT and digital capability while protecting those who are digitally excluded: invest in interoperable, secure systems and provide ongoing staff digital training; maintain strong non-digital access channels (phone triage, in-person care) so no one is left behind.

Fourth, supportive teams and training pipelines: strengthen supervision, safe staffing levels, and workload management; expand multidisciplinary teams; foster clear career progression, apprenticeships and partnerships with colleges to create local pipelines.

These priorities would reduce burnout, stabilise services and improve timely access to care.

I support an NHS workforce plan that prioritises long-term, targeted incentives to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care. In hard-to-fill areas—rural, coastal and urban deprived—tailored packages matter: housing and transport support, relocation or accommodation assistance, flexible shifts and clear career progression, in addition to competitive pay. These measures help attract GPs, nurses, mental health workers and allied professionals who might otherwise be unavailable.

A secure, multi-year funding settlement is essential. Ring-fenced, predictable funding for workforce initiatives, expanding training capacity and sustaining return-to-practice and apprenticeship programmes reduces policy volatility and lets boards plan and build durable pipelines for multi-disciplinary teams.

I’d pair this with proven steps: expanding funded training places across Scotland, supporting return-to-practice, growing apprenticeships for healthcare assistants and nursing associates, and ensuring protected CPD time. Strengthen appointment triage and scheduling to maximise staff effectiveness and patient safety. With stable funding and location-focused incentives, we can recruit where it’s hardest and maintain high-quality care for all.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise targeted incentives to recruit and retain staff where recruitment is hardest—rural and coastal Scotland, urban deprivation pockets—through housing support, affordable transport, flexible contracts, and return‑to‑practice routes. Without addressing distance and cost of living, clinical teams will remain stretched and turnover will stay high. Practical examples include relocation packages for GP partners in remote communities, salary supplements for social care and mental health roles shared across NHS and local authorities, and supported routes into training for people from these areas.

Secondly, strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services via joint funding and integrated workforce plans to spread workload, reduce burnout and improve holistic care. Co‑locating services and multidisciplinary teams can be rolled out in community hubs and GP practices, with clear pathways between sectors.

Thirdly, invest in interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training, while safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients through paper records and telephone triage, community navigators. This combination helps maintain safe, high‑quality care without leaving disadvantaged patients behind.

In Scotland, these steps would align with existing local partnerships and address the language and access barriers I’ve seen firsthand.

From our experience delivering health and wellbeing services across Scotland, recruiting and retaining staff in rural, coastal and urban-deprived areas is the real barrier to timely access. The workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives—local housing support, targeted relocation allowances, and reliable transport subsidies—to recruit and retain GPs, nurses and mental health workers in these harder-to-fill areas. Clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation processes, and funded protected clinical supervision are essential to safely support new roles and maintain patient safety as teams expand.

We also need to grow the workforce pipeline. Increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships would help in the longer term, especially for primary care. In our region, limited training slots and lack of rural rotations contribute to vacancies; dedicated training pathways with guaranteed placements would help.

In practice, a combined approach—place-based incentives, professional support, and expanded training—would align with our shift toward integrated, place-based hubs and reduce delays in access.

As a young person in Wales and part of a youth-focused organisation, I think any NHS workforce plan must put people at the heart of service delivery. It should offer clear, funded career pathways from frontline roles through to senior clinical posts, with transparent timelines and measurable milestones so staff can see a real route for progression. Protected CPD time and dedicated development budgets are essential; staff shouldn’t have to choose between improving their skills and providing safe care today. Structured mentorship and supervision for early‑career colleagues, plus robust return‑to‑practice schemes, would help those who have paused in their careers rejoin with confidence, especially after life or caring responsibilities. Flexible working, wellbeing support and realistic staffing levels are vital to prevent burnout and maintain safety. In Wales, we should target recruitment from local communities and campuses, creating pathways into community hubs that we already promote, with digital skills training to support new models of care. Ultimately, steady workforce planning aligned with hub-based, integrated teams will sustain high‑quality care and keep access timely for people who need it.

The NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving care models and rigorous safety monitoring, while boosting recruitment and retention, training and wellbeing support, and sustainable workloads to ensure access improvements never compromise clinical quality.

From where I stand in Northern Ireland, any NHS workforce plan must be judged by how it translates into safer, quicker, and more consistent care for ordinary people, not just by clever policy language. In my experience, the problem isn’t only about more staff somewhere; it’s about having the right staff where people actually live—often in rural villages—and making sure they can do their jobs without being stretched to breaking point. With older residents in mind, the plan should prioritise practical, on-the-ground improvements that help people stay well at home and avoid long hospital trips when possible.

Priority areas I’d want to see reflected in a workforce plan:

- Strengthen the community-based workforce. We need more district nurses, physiotherapists, and occupational therapists who can visit homes regularly, assess falls risk, support rehabilitation after hospital stays, and coordinate simple but vital tasks without endless referrals. If teams are under pressure, the first casualty is timely and effective care at home, which drives people into hospitals sooner than necessary.

- Safe and sustainable staffing. It’s not enough to recruit more staff; we must keep them. That means realistic workloads, predictable rosters, adequate time for each patient, and reliable supervision. Burnout among nurses and therapists in areas with limited back-up leads to gaps in care that older people notice quickly. A workforce plan should set safe staffing standards and enforce them, even during winter peaks when urgent care needs rise.

- Integrated roles and a care-coordinator approach. For patients with multiple needs, one named coordinator who can pull GP, community health, and mental health services together would save families time and reduce confusion. In practice, that could be a small team or a single point of contact who tracks a care plan and makes sure appointments don’t clash or get missed.

- Flexible, supportive working conditions. We must offer varied hours, job sharing, and easier access to transport or relocation support for staff serving rural communities. When staff can balance work with personal responsibilities and travel challenges, they stay longer and deliver better care.

- Training, progression, and local recruitment. A clear route for ongoing education, specialisms, and career progression—especially for district nursing and allied health professionals—helps retention. Programs that enable return-to-practice after a break, funded CPD, and locally advertised training posts will help attract people to work in Northern Ireland, rather than elsewhere.

- Wellbeing and mental health support for staff. The same compassion we want for patients should apply to those delivering care. Access to mental health supports, reasonable workloads, and strong peer support reduces sickness absence and improves patient safety.

- Responsible use of technology with human contact in mind. Digital tools can help triage and coordinate care, but they should not substitute personal contact. We should ensure non-digital options remain available for those who struggle with online systems, and invest in training so staff can use new tools effectively instead of adding to their burden.

- Rural recruitment incentives. Targeted schemes—such as scholarships, relocation assistance, and time-limited service commitments—could help attract staff to villages and small towns where vacancies hit families hardest.

- Governance, safety, and quality monitoring. The plan must include transparent staffing data, safety dashboards, and robust escalation processes so patients and families know who is responsible for what and when to expect follow-up.

- Honest communication about capacity and expectations. If delays are inevitable, patients deserve timely, clear information about wait times and what can be done in the meantime. That honesty helps families plan and keeps trust in the system.

In short, a workforce plan that works for older people in Northern Ireland is one that prioritises practical, locally based care—well-supported community teams, safe workloads, clear coordination, flexible working for staff, strong training and progression routes, and compassionate leadership. If these elements are in place, the rest—the numbers and the budgets—will matter far less because people will experience timely, competent care closer to home.

Agree. A sustainable primary care workforce hinges on expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams with proper training, supervision and governance to safely redistribute GP workload. By widening roles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied professionals, we can handle routine reviews and triage safely, freeing GPs for complex cases. This must be backed by clear scopes of practice, shared decision-making, and robust clinical governance, plus co-located clinics where patients access physio, mental health support and district nursing in one place. Incentives are essential: targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries should be offered to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles. At the same time, expansion of education and training is critical: more undergraduate places, postgraduate fellowships and apprenticeships, with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships, so we grow the domestic primary care workforce long term. In my area, a nurse practitioner-led clinic and pharmacist-supported medication reviews have already reduced GP load without compromising safety, when there is good supervision and clear protocols. All this must be underpinned by sustained investment in career progression and manageable caseloads to keep staff and patients safe.

I very much support a NHS workforce plan that expands and regulates multidisciplinary teams to share the workload safely and keep high-quality care at the heart of primary care. In Scotland, where many communities are small or spread out and our older population needs careful, continuous care, getting the right mix of staff with appropriate supervision is essential. It isn’t about replacing GPs but about enabling them to focus on the most complex cases while nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals cover routine reviews, medication management and timely triage. The plan should be practical, well funded and overseen by strong clinical governance so that every task sits on a clear, patient-safe pathway.

Key priorities I would want to see in an NHS workforce plan:

- Expand and regulate effective teams within primary care. Create reliable, skill-milled teams that include nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals who can carry out routine reviews, handle chronic disease management, perform safe prescribing checks and deliver urgent triage. Ensure every role has a defined scope of practice, with supervision from GPs where needed and robust escalation routes for uncertain cases.
- Build strong training and career pathways. Invest in longer training pipelines and on-going CPD, with protected time for mentors and supervision. Offer targeted incentives for working in rural or underserved areas, flexible career options (part-time, job-sharing) and clear progression routes so staff can grow within the service and stay in Scotland.
- Prioritise safe delegation and governance. Establish standardised protocols, decision-support tools and evidence-based pathways so that non-GP clinicians can confidently manage common conditions and medication reviews. Ensure there is always a GP, or consultant-level oversight, available for complex decisions, with clear documentation and accountability.
- Invest in the right mix of recruitment and retention measures. Competitive salaries, housing and relocation support where needed, strong occupational health services, and measures to reduce burnout (reducing admin burden, reasonable workloads, protected time for reflective practice) will help attract and keep skilled staff.
- Strengthen digital and data-enabled teamwork where appropriate. Shared patient records, e-prescribing, and remote monitoring can help teams operate more efficiently, but they must be paired with rigorous data governance, privacy protections and user-friendly IT training so older patients and those less comfortable with tech are not left behind.
- Ensure patient-facing accessibility and continuity of care. While expanding the team, keep the patient experience at the forefront: same-day triage when symptoms arise, clear appointment pathways, and always an option to see a clinician in person if needed. The plan should not erode personal contact and should recognise the value of a consistent care relationship, particularly for those managing multiple conditions.
- Focus on safety, quality, and evaluation. Implement real-time workload monitoring, service-level targets, and regular audits of safety and outcomes. Use findings to refine team roles, redistribute tasks if a model isn’t delivering the expected care standards, and share learning across practices.
- Rural and acute care integration. In many parts of Scotland, closer collaboration between GP practices, out-of-hours services, community pharmacies and paramedic-led urgent care can cut unnecessary hospital referrals and bring care closer to home. This requires clear protocols and transport and accessibility considerations for frail, elderly patients.
- Public health and prevention integration. Multidisciplinary teams can extend preventive services, screening and vaccination campaigns, and early health education, contributing to better long-term health outcomes and easing pressure on urgent care and hospital services.

From my own experience in our area, when practices have started to use a pharmacist for medication reviews and a nurse-led long-term condition clinic, responses from patients have been positive: people move more smoothly through care pathways, and GPs have more room to focus on complex cases. But it only works if the workforce is properly trained, supervised, and resourced, with clear governance and consistent access to non-clinical support (administrative back-up, IT help, and transport when needed).

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanded, well-supported multidisciplinary teams with clear scopes, strong supervision, and ongoing development, paired with digital tools and a patient-centred approach. When done right, this will relieve GP workload, shorten waits, improve safety, and keep care compassionate and accessible for Scotland’s aging population.

Prioritise diverse recruitment, including overseas sourcing with streamlined visas, rapid credential recognition, and robust integration support, paired with domestic training and retention; guard against draining source health systems while maintaining safe, high-quality care.

i strongly believe i believe an NHS workforce plan should be grounded in safe, well-supported staffing that can sustain high‑quality care now and in the future. To keep care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams with proper training, supervision and governance. This means giving nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals defined scopes of practice, supported by robust supervision from GPs and senior clinicians so we can redistribute the GP workload without compromising safety. Equally important are targeted recruitment and retention measures for underserved and high‑demand areas: competitive pay, retention bonuses, relocation packages and bursaries tied to service commitments.
