Invest in training pipelines—apprenticeships and funded courses—to build a steady flow of capable staff, with good working conditions, sensible rosters, mental health support and clear opportunities for career progression. This combination should help maintain safety while expanding access to timely care.

Prioritise funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship, and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff, alongside safe staffing and realistic workloads to maintain high-quality care.

absolutely i don’t think there’s a single, universal NHS workforce plan that will fit every part of Scotland and still guarantee safe, high‑quality care. From my experience as a student, the pressures hit GP access and university mental health services, so any plan needs to be flexible and locally informed. Priorities should include safer staffing levels with strong supervision and clear career progression to help retain staff, especially newly qualified nurses and mental health workers who shoulder heavy workloads. It would help to expand multi‑disciplinary teams in local hubs—district nurses, pharmacists and allied staff working together—provided there’s solid training, defined roles, and ongoing CPD. Practical steps I can see as making a difference include offering more flexible shifts (evenings and weekends) so students aren’t squeezed out of care, better supervision and mentoring, and more student and graduate placements to grow the workforce pipeline. Invest in digital triage and smarter rostering to cut admin time and free clinicians for direct care. But I’m uncertain which mix would work best everywhere; decisions should be driven by local data, patient safety and lived experience, not broad promises!

From where I stand, the NHS workforce plan must be guided by two simple truths: you recruit and retain staff where there are gaps, and you keep patients safe by ensuring a strong, stable team is always on duty. With that in mind, I’d prioritise a mix of targeted incentives, safe staffing and continuity, and solid governance—all backed by real investment in training and flexible, humane working models.

First, tailor incentives for the hardest-to-fill places. Rural, urban deprived and coastal areas often struggle to attract and keep staff. We should offer housing and transport support, practical relocation packages, and targeted salary uplifts where there is persistent vacancy pressure. Pair this with local career pathways—such as funded training places, team rotations, and opportunities to specialise in community and multidisciplinary roles—to make staying feel like a clear, long‑term choice rather than a short‑term fix.

Second, prioritise safe staffing and continuity of care. It isn’t enough to have more staff on paper; patients must see the same clinician where possible, and teams should be staffed so that capacity matches demand across GP hubs, community services and mental health. Safe staffing ratios should be a hard metric, not a soft promise, supported by rostering that preserves continuity and minimises unnecessary hand-offs which can erode quality.

Third, strengthen safety monitoring and governance. I’ve seen how quickly a small variance in staffing can translate into delays or errors. A robust safety dashboard, regular audits, near‑miss reporting, and clear accountability help ensure that access improvements don’t come at the expense of clinical quality. Staff wellbeing must be part of that safety net—manageable workloads, access to wellbeing support, and reduced administrative burden so clinicians can focus on patients.

Fourth, invest in multidisciplinary teams and the right scopes of practice. We need pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates and mental health practitioners embedded in primary care, with clear training routes and consistent governance. IT and shared records are essential so teams can coordinate without friction and patients don’t have to repeat their story. Co-location in GP hubs, with digital triage and flexible same‑day slots, can transform access while preserving safety.

Fifth, provide strong training, career development and progression. A plan that works long term must build a pipeline: apprenticeships and upskilling for nurses, physios moving into extended roles, and mental health staff trained to act early in primary care settings. Adequate supervision, standardized accreditation, and protected time for training are not optional extras but core requirements.

Sixth, ensure flexible, humane working practices. Flexi-hours, part-time routes, and return‑to‑practice programmes help recruit and retain a wider pool of staff, including carers and those returning from breaks. Reducing needless bureaucracy and providing administrative support can also make roles more sustainable, which in turn boosts retention.

Finally, finance and delivery must be stable, not episodic. Workforce plans require long‑term funding commitments, predictable salary envelopes, and real-world evaluation so successful pilots can be scaled without eroding patient safety or staff morale.

In short, I want a plan that recognises staffing as the foundation of safer, quicker access to care: targeted place-based incentives, safe and continuous care, rigorous safety governance, expansive MDT models, strong training pipelines, flexible working, and steady, well‑funded investment. When staff feel valued and supported, patients notice the difference in the quality and reliability of the care they receive.

I live in England and I’m writing as an individual who has watched the NHS struggle to staff services while still trying to keep patients safe and cared for. Any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff must be practical, fair and data‑led, with a clear eye on keeping high‑quality care available for older people like me, and for everyone in our diverse communities.

First, international recruitment must be responsible and ethical. We do need skilled staff from overseas, but it must be done with streamlined visas and credible credential recognition, not a shortcut that leaves other health systems strained or drains away essential staff from their own countries. The plan should include robust integration support: language and cultural orientation, mentoring on arrival, and funded wraparound services so new colleagues can settle and work safely and confidently. At the same time, there should be safeguards to prevent depletion of source countries’ health systems and to ensure staffing numbers meet patient need rather than organisational convenience. In practice, this could mean time‑bound visas tied to local workforce planning data, structured return‑to‑practice pathways for those who have stepped away, and ongoing ethical recruitment monitoring with independent review.

Second, the plan must be transparent and locally grounded. I would expect transparent, locally‑focused workforce data, modelling and KPIs that inform funding, staffing levels and performance monitoring. If managers can see vacancy rates, turnover, average time to fill posts, and patient safety indicators in real time, they can plan more effectively and respond before cracks widen. In our area, publicly available dashboards showing missed appointments, clinician workload, and the presence of agency staff helped local teams spot where burnout risk was rising and reallocate resources accordingly. Evaluation frameworks should accompany funding so we can learn what actually improves outcomes—not just what sounds efficient on paper.

Third, flexibility is essential to retain diverse staff and reduce burnout. Offering flexible hours, part‑time options, job‑sharing, phased retirement, accessible childcare and proactive mental health services makes a real difference. I’ve heard from colleagues who would have stayed longer if they could balance family and work better, and I’ve seen how teams stay resilient when staff can stagger shifts or reduce hours without losing professional standing. For older workers especially, phased retirement or twilight roles can transfer crucial experience to newer clinicians while easing the transition. A workforce plan that normalises flexible working across primary care, community services and mental health will help keep skilled people beyond retirement age in the system where they are most needed.

Fourth, training, development and career pathways must be expanded and well funded. It’s clear that we need more training places, better return‑to‑practice routes for those who have left the profession, and stronger continuing professional development across disciplines. Local partnerships with universities, colleges and employers should create routes that suit mature workers’ needs—part‑time study, modular CPD, and on‑the‑job learning supported by protected time. In practice, where teams had clear CPD funding and protected learning time, staff stayed longer and performance improved.

Fifth, safe staffing and high‑quality care must be non‑negotiable. The plan should set minimum staffing levels and ensure robust supervision, clinical governance and peer support. Recruitment is essential, but without sustainable staffing and good working conditions, safety suffers and patient trust ebbs. That means investing in allied roles—practice nurses, social workers, mental health workers—and ensuring teams can function at full capacity without crushing workloads.

Finally, use technology to our advantage, not as a substitute for people. Streamlining admin, adopting user‑friendly digital systems, and employing smart rostering can free clinicians to do more patient‑facing work and reduce burnout. Equally important is engagement with staff and unions to ensure reforms are workable on the ground and that front‑line concerns are heard and acted on.

In short, I’d prioritise ethical international recruitment with solid integration safeguards, transparent local data and KPI systems to inform planning, flexible working arrangements to retain a diverse workforce, expanded training and return‑to‑practice routes, and unwavering attention to safe, high‑quality care alongside staff wellbeing. If these elements are embedded together—with clear accountability and ongoing evaluation—the NHS can recruit wisely, keep excellent staff, and provide the safe care that my generation and future generations deserve.

Agree that the workforce plan should prioritise transparent localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks, to inform planning and funding, while cutting unnecessary targets and admin and improving IT usability so clinicians can focus on patient-facing care.

Without predictable funding, recruitment campaigns falter, teams can't expand training, and morale suffers when short-term shifts force staffing restructures. Key priorities include long-term funding for recruitment and retention with competitive pay progression and targeted incentives for rural and hard-to-staff posts, plus protected career development budgets; expanding training capacity with more clinical placements for students and trainees across nursing, allied health professionals, pharmacists and physician associates, along with expanded apprenticeships and mentorship networks; ensuring safe staffing and wellbeing through guaranteed safe staffing levels, protected time for supervision, CPD and mental health support to reduce burnout; providing flexible career paths with clearly defined progression, cross-disciplinary skills and flexible or fixed-term roles to improve retention; investing in digital and remote support such as scalable telehealth, remote supervision and IT to reduce on-site pressures; and strengthening local planning and quality through data-driven workforce modelling, targeted support where needed, and ring-fenced budgets for service continuity. In our organisation, stable funding has allowed us to run longer clinical placements and sustain a physiotherapist-led pathway; when funding is uncertain, these programs stall.

To recruit, retain and support staff while ensuring safe, high‑quality care, the plan should prioritise reducing unnecessary targets and paperwork, simplifying referrals and making IT easier to use so clinicians can spend more time with patients. A streamlined e-referral process with clear, local handoffs between primary, community and hospital teams would help. Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models matter most; stable teams with experienced clinicians supervising juniors lead to quicker recognition of deteriorations and fewer mistakes. We also need robust safety monitoring and learning from near misses. Localised workforce data, transparent modelling and KPIs should inform planning and funding decisions, with regular public reporting so communities understand how staffing matches demand. Finally, invest in training and flexible working to attract and retain staff, while preserving non-digital access for those who struggle with technology. In short, less red tape, better IT usability, safer staffing and clearer local data will deliver better care for older residents like myself.

A strong NHS workforce plan should balance investment in technology with real people-focused safeguards, and actively support staff to prevent burnout while maintaining safe, high-quality care. First, invest in interoperable, secure IT and ongoing staff training so systems are usable, reliable and integrated across primary, community and mental health services. Crucially, preserve safeguarding and offer alternatives for digitally excluded patients, including ring-fenced phone and in-person pathways that mirror digital options. Second, prioritise flexible working models to recruit and retain a diverse workforce: flexible hours, part-time roles, job-share and phased retirement, alongside childcare support and proactive mental health services. Fourth, expand multidisciplinary teams and supportive leadership to sustain safe care with appropriate staffing ratios and robust CPD. In short, Tech-enabled care must go hand in hand with human-centred roles, flexible cultures and streamlined processes that keep patients at the centre.”

- Training, progression and return‑to‑practice pathways: expand training places for GPs, nurses, mental health professionals and allied roles; develop strong return‑to‑practice schemes with funded retraining so experienced clinicians rejoin the workforce. - Data, funding and scale: invest in durable, long‑term funding rather than short‑term pilots. In summary, a successful NHS workforce plan for rural NI should prioritise: well-governed multidisciplinary teams; flexible and inclusive working conditions; robust training and return‑to‑practice pathways; targeted recruitment with genuine retention incentives; comprehensive staff wellbeing; and scalable digital and mobile care models underpinned by stable funding and real‑time data. If these elements are funded and coordinated, we can deliver safe, high‑quality care close to home for our communities.

The plan must lock in multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain workforce initiatives and training capacity, reduce policy volatility, and ensure safe staffing ratios. It should prioritise continuity of care models and robust safety monitoring to protect quality as access expands.

As someone who has watched rural health services stretch to meet need, I welcome a NHS workforce plan that puts practical recruitment, retention and professional support at its core while staying firmly focused on safe, high‑quality care. - Competitive, role‑specific retention payments and bursaries to keep people in postlonger term
- Clear funded career pathways, with protected CPD, mentorship and return‑to‑practice routes

Targeted pay and relocation support has to be a cornerstone. Rural and high‑demand roles like GPs, district nurses, mental health practitioners and diagnostic staff struggle to compete with urban salaries and the lure of easier commutes. Having a predictable ladder of progression—say, a funded annual CPD budget, formal mentorship contracts, and clearly defined clinical leadership opportunities—helps retain staff who might otherwise move to larger trusts or urban settings.

Interoperable IT and robust digital training are critical, but they must complement, not replace, human care. I’ve seen how digital tools can speed up referrals, give patients faster access to records, and reduce unnecessary trips. Beyond money and IT, the plan should address the realities of rural practice: safe staffing levels, manageable workloads, and good supervision. Continuous quality governance—regular audits of staffing, patient safety indicators, and well‑being metrics for staff—will help keep care safe even as workloads rise.

Examples from practice reinforce these points. A stable team—GPs, nurses, and mental health workers who know the local community—reduces missed appointments, improves chronic‑disease management, and shortens waiting times for mental health support. Telehealth hubs and mobile clinics work best when there is a dependable workforce behind them, plus the digital tools and training to use them confidently. A funded path from training into rural practice, with clear incentives to stay, would make these pilots sustainable rather than temporary experiments.

In short, a workforce plan that prioritises targeted competitive pay and relocation support; explicit, funded career progression and return‑to‑practice routes; and interoperable IT with strong digital training—while preserving multiple access routes for digitally excluded patients—will help recruit, retain and support staff while protecting the safety and quality of care in rural England.

Prioritise reducing unnecessary targets and admin, streamlining referrals and improving IT usability to free clinicians for patient-facing care. Prioritise flexible working options (part-time, job-share, phased retirement), childcare support and proactive mental health services, with safe staffing levels and manageable workloads to recruit, retain and sustain high‑quality care.

Any NHS workforce plan should put people at the heart of safe, high‑quality care. It must prioritise sustainable staffing across GP practices, community nursing, and mental health, with reliable routes to recruit and retain the right mix of skills in the right places. That includes competitive pay, predictable rosters, and manageable workloads to protect wellbeing and prevent burnout. I’d like to see expanded training and clear career paths for nurses, allied health professionals, and support staff so they can up‑skill and stay in local communities rather than moving into locums or leaving the area. Flexible working patterns and part‑time routes are essential, especially in rural areas, alongside shifts that fit family life while keeping patient safety front and centre. Reducing administrative burden and giving clinicians better decision‑making tools could free time for care. Robust supervision, mentoring, safe staffing ratios, and transparent workload management are crucial. Finally, involve patients and frontline staff in co‑designing workforce changes so plans reflect local needs rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all approach. When done this way, we’ll attract, keep and support staff while maintaining high‑quality, safe care for communities.

Thank you for the opportunity to feed in on NHS workforce planning. From my perspective living in England and engaging with local primary and community services, the most effective plan to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality is one that is predictable, well-funded and people‑centred. It should reduce short‑term policy volatility and invest in sustainable growth across the whole workforce, with a clear, practical pathway from training through to retirement. In particular, I would prioritise the following areas:

- Secure multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding for workforce initiatives
  - Lock in stable, long‑term funding specifically for training capacity, recruitment campaigns, workforce planning analytics and staff wellbeing. This would reduce churn caused by policy shifts and allow trusts and practices to plan multi‑year staffing needs, undertake meaningful recruitment drives and invest in retention programs without constant stop‑start funding changes.
  - Use these funds to expand multidisciplinary teams in primary care, integrating GPs, nurses, pharmacists, mental health practitioners and allied health professionals so patients can be seen by the most appropriate clinician without inappropriate handoffs or delays.

- Increase domestic training capacity for the NHS workforce
  - Expand undergraduate medical, nursing, pharmacy and allied health professional places, and grow apprenticeship routes with protected placements that are embedded in university‑practice partnerships. This would help build a robust, domestic pipeline for primary care and community services, where staffing shortages are most acutely felt.
  - Guarantee protected training placements and funded rotations in community settings so trainees gain experience where most of the care happens for people with long-term conditions, mental health needs, and complex social circumstances.
  - Strengthen local and regional partnerships to ensure training capacity grows alongside service demand, rather than chasing vacancies after the fact.

- Use overseas recruitment responsibly and ethically
  - A targeted, needs‑led approach to international recruitment can help fill gaps quickly, but it must be done responsibly. Streamlined visas and faster credential recognition should be paired with robust integration support, including language, cultural orientation, and mentoring, so new staff can work safely and effectively from day one.
  - Put safeguards in place to protect health systems in source countries, with quotas tied to reciprocal agreements and ongoing monitoring of impact. This approach should be transparent and guided by published workforce data so communities can see how international recruitment fits into longer‑term domestic capacity building.

- Focus on retention, wellbeing and safe, sustainable workloads
  - Improve working conditions by ensuring safe staffing ratios, reasonable caseloads and predictable rosters. Staff wellbeing supports—access to mental health resources, peer support, and time for CPD—are essential to keep skilled clinicians in the NHS.
  - Invest in career development and clear progression pathways, including mentorship and leadership opportunities within primary care and community services. When staff see a future with opportunities, turnover slows and continuity of care improves.
  - Deliver flexible working options where possible to help staff balance caring responsibilities and professional duties, especially in rural areas where recruitment challenges are greatest.

- Strengthen data, governance and accountability
  - Build robust workforce planning systems that use up‑to‑date data to forecast demand, track vacancies, and monitor patient safety indicators. Regular public reporting on staffing levels, recruitment success, and patient outcomes will help identify gaps quickly and support targeted fixes.
  - Ensure governance and patient safety protections accompany all expansion plans, with clear standards for supervision, appraisal, and continuing education.

- Prioritise primary care and community care
  - Given the central role of general practice in delivering timely access, any workforce plan should prioritise GP and practice nurse capacity, with supported access to mental health professionals and social care colleagues. Local strategies that couple training capacity with practice placements and university partnerships will deliver a stronger, more resilient primary care workforce.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan should be stable, long‑term and people‑centred. By combining ring‑fenced funding, expanded domestic training, responsible international recruitment, strong retention measures and robust governance, we can grow a capable, diverse workforce able to deliver safe, high‑quality care now and into the future. This aligns with the aim of improving timely access to GP, community and mental health services I described earlier, because a well‑staffed, well‑supported system is the backbone of reliable, equitable care for everyone.

Prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, PAs, paramedics and allied roles) with clear scope, funded protected supervision, and robust revalidation/indemnity. This supports safe GP workload redistribution while preserving high-quality patient care.

From where I stand as a student in England, I’m not sure there’s a single ‘right’ priority for an NHS workforce plan. What matters most to me is that staff have the capacity to deliver safe, high‑quality care without burnout, and that includes primary care and mental health teams. First, there needs to be enough staff and the right mix of roles, with realistic workloads. I’ve seen GP slots vanish two weeks ahead and talking therapies take months to start; this signals staffing and capacity gaps that a plan should address with sustainable recruitment, better retention, mentoring, and flexible working options to suit people at different life stages. Second, training and progression must be clear. Let junior clinicians see a clear path to skill development without being kept in bottleneck posts. Third, wellbeing and safety must be baked in: protected time for supervision, reasonable hours, and safe staffing levels so patient care isn’t compromised. Digital tools should support, not substitute, care: secure messaging, triage, and video assessments can help reduce delays, provided staff are trained and supported to use them well. Finally, links between NHS services and universities should be strengthened so students can move smoothly from campus wellbeing to NHS care, with joint planning on staffing and weekend/after‑hours coverage. I’m cautious about overpromising on quick fixes, but a plan that combines staffing, training, wellbeing, digital thinking, and campus links feels plausible.

I believe the NHS workforce plan must prioritise a strong, practical approach to recruiting, retaining and supporting staff, while safeguarding the safety and quality of care that patients rely on. From my perspective as an older resident in a rural area, I see every day how staffing gaps can delay appointments and complicate access to help. The plan should therefore address both where staff are needed most and how to keep them motivated, satisfied and safe in demanding roles.

- Tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas: Keep a focused push on recruiting to rural, urban deprived and coastal communities. This includes housing support close to clinics, affordable accommodation schemes, relocation grants and housing subsidies, as well as transport assistance for those who must travel long distances. Flexible or extended hours, and practical supports like safer, easier parking and good local transport links, can make a real difference. I’ve heard neighbours explain that even when a clinician is available, the lack of nearby housing or a long commute puts people off taking a post. Targeted incentives in these areas should be part of a sustained plan rather than a one-off effort, and ought to include pathways for retired clinicians to return or work part-time without bureaucratic delays.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models: Plans must prioritise safe staffing levels across general practice, district nursing, mental health and urgent care so that access improvements don’t compromise quality. This means clear, binding targets for nurse and GP-to-patient ratios, plus mechanisms to protect continuity of care where possible. Stable teams help patients, particularly the elderly and those with multiple conditions, build trust and avoid repeated recounting of symptoms. Safety monitoring should be real-time and transparent—regular safety audits, dashboards showing staffing levels, wait times and incident trends, and compulsory safety huddles in busy services—to spot problems before they affect patients.

- Career development, supervision and wellbeing: A robust pipeline for training, mentoring and career progression is essential. This includes supported return-to-practice routes, flexible working options for senior staff, and multidisciplinary team development so nurses, physios and pharmacists can work at full scope where appropriate. Wellbeing and mental health support for NHS staff themselves matter as much as patient care, so access to confidential counselling, reasonable rostering, and accommodating personal circumstances should be standard.

- Local recruitment pipelines and community integration: Build relationships with local education and training providers to grow a workforce from the community itself. Scholarships or paid placements for students from local areas, partnerships with schools and colleges, and local-resident bursaries can help create a sustainable, locally rooted workforce. In blocking vacancies, use a staged, transparent recruitment process that keeps the patient’s needs in focus and reduces unnecessary vacancies.

- Technology that aids, not replaces, staff: Telehealth and digital booking tools can extend reach and convenience, but must be implemented with adequate training, adequate staffing to support them, and safeguards to prevent extra workload. For example, remote supervision and digital decision-support tools should reduce administrative burden and free clinicians to spend more time with patients, especially those with complex needs.

- Co-design and measurement: I would like to see pilots designed with input from patients and carers in hard-to-fill areas, with clear metrics on access, safety, patient experience and staff workload. If a model works locally, scale it; if it doesn’t, learn quickly and adjust.

In short, the plan should couple targeted recruitment and housing/transport supports with strong safety and continuity standards, and robust staff development and wellbeing. When people feel supported, valued and able to work without compromising safety, they stay longer, and patients benefit with faster, more reliable, high-quality care. I’m optimistic that with careful design and local testing, we can build a workforce that truly serves every community, including our more remote and challenged areas.

Prioritise targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas; back this with transparent local workforce data, KPIs and evaluation; secure multi-year ring-fenced funding to sustain training and reduce volatility.

Representing older residents across England, I welcome a NHS workforce plan that keeps frail, older people at the centre and recognises how staffing levels drive access to care. If we want more outreach clinics, home visits and safe, timely help, there must be enough staff in primary, community and mental health teams, with the right mix to cover rural villages and bustling towns alike. Priorities: sufficient multidisciplinary teams (GPs, district nurses, therapists, pharmacists, social care workers) with clear roles and strong collaboration; improved recruitment and retention in underserved areas, including flexible hours and clear routes for career progression; funded training in geriatrics, dementia, palliative care and safe prescribing; reduced admin burden so clinicians can spend more time with patients; robust supervision and wellbeing support to prevent burnout; and safe staffing ratios with continuity of care to build trust among older residents. The plan should also support outreach and home-based care through stable teams rather than ad hoc arrangements, especially in winter when gaps widen. All of this needs long-term funding and commitment; otherwise, promising policies won’t translate into safer, high-quality care for those who rely on it most.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining high-quality, safe care, the workforce plan must build sustainable, cross-sector capacity and clear governance. This means streamlined recruitment across sectors, shared career pathways and flexible roles that can rotate between primary care, community services and social care without creating gaps in safety.

Clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation, and clarified indemnity arrangements are essential, alongside protected clinical supervision for new and expanded roles. Regular, high-quality supervision and accessible CPD should be funded to support safe innovation. Invest in leadership and wellbeing—flexible working patterns, manageable caseloads, and structured mentorship to improve retention.

Data-driven workforce planning is vital: deploy staff where demand is highest and ensure interpreters and culturally competent teams are embedded so access and safety aren’t compromised. To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise long-term, ring-fenced funding and predictable budgets. Support multidisciplinary teams and digital capability, ensuring technology supports clinicians rather than adding complexity. Overall, I think an NHS workforce plan should prioritise three linked strands: attracting and keeping staff in the system through targeted pay and incentives; equipping teams with the digital and physical tools they need; and addressing the realities of different places with tailored housing, transport and local support. My experience in England shows that without meaningful incentives and good working conditions, the best hires move on to other areas or sectors, which then creates safety risks and a poorer patient experience. A successful plan must therefore be practical, place-aware and people-centred.

- Targeted pay and retention incentives: We need real competitive pay to reflect the demand and the pressures staff face, not just across-organisation parity. Retention payments for hard‑to‑fill roles and high-demand locations should be piloted and expanded where they prove effective. Relocation packages and bursaries for training, plus robust return‑to‑practice schemes, will help recruit from outside traditional pools and bring people back after career breaks. Clear career ladders and recognition for multidisciplinary work would help reduce turnover and improve continuity of care.

- Tailored housing and transport support: Not all areas face the same challenges, but rural, coastal and urban deprived localities often suffer the most from staffing gaps. Housing allowances or secure staff housing options near workplaces, together with reliable transport subsidies or flexible rosters to align with local commuting realities, can make roles in hard‑to‑fill places far more attractive. These incentives must be part of a long-term local strategy, not a one‑off perk.

- Interoperable IT and safe digital practice: A fully integrated IT ecosystem is essential to reduce admin burden and enable clinicians to spend more time with patients. Investment in secure, interoperable electronic records, common care plans and real‑time workforce dashboards will help with planning, workload distribution and patient safety. Staff need ongoing digital training, and systems must be accessible to digitally excluded patients—offering non‑digital routes and language supports where needed. Strong data governance and clear consent processes are non‑negotiable to maintain public trust.

- Pipeline development and flexible career paths: From student placements and apprenticeships to graduate rotations across primary and community care, there should be a clear pipeline into every role. Return‑to‑practice routes must be safe and straightforward, with mentorship and protected time for upskilling. Cross‑disciplinary training—nurses, GPs, therapists, social care workers learning together—will support teams to work more flexibly and safely.

- Safe staffing, workload management and wellbeing: Real-time staffing tools, evidence‑based safe‑staffing ratios, and limits on excessive overtime are essential for high‑quality care. Adequate time for handovers, supervision, and supervision for junior staff reduces errors and improves morale. A proactive wellbeing program—transparent occupational health support, de‑stressing resources, and protected breaks—matters as much as salary.

- Local governance and community partnership: Workforce planning should be co‑designed with staff and patient representatives, local authorities, VCSE organisations and unions. Regular evaluation of retention, sickness, patient safety indicators and experience metrics will help identify which incentives work where. Local pilots followed by scalable rollout, with independent evaluation, will make the plan credible and affordable.

- Complementary pathways for public health and social care integration: Given the integrated hubs I’ve suggested, the workforce plan should recognise the close links between care sectors. Joint recruitment drives, shared induction programs, and common standards for safety and privacy will help create stable teams that can deliver high‑quality, person‑centred care across settings.

In practice, this means a plan that combines money with meaningful structural change: better pay and relocation help to attract people, robust digital infrastructure to reduce waste and support frontline staff, and place‑specific incentives to build teams where they’re most needed. With these elements, and with the right governance and patient involvement, we can move toward a NHS workforce that is stable, capable and able to deliver the safe, high‑quality care people deserve.

A workforce plan must not just recruit; it needs stable, long-term funding, manageable workloads, and strong digital systems to support staff. Priorities should include consistent funding cycles, integration of records, and protected time for training and wellbeing to sustain safe care.

Ongoing monitoring of impact on both domestic supply and international partners will guide expansion.

Local examples show integrated teams and co-located training pipelines improve safety and patient experience; these must be scaled with sustained investment to preserve care quality.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise a stable, well-supported team able to deliver safe, high‑quality care now and in the years ahead. It needs clear funded career pathways for all clinical staff—from nurses and GPs to allied health professionals—with defined steps, time for training, and progression opportunities so people can see a future in the NHS locally. Protected continuing professional development and formal mentorship are essential, including structured return‑to‑practice schemes to draw staff back after career breaks and to guide early‑career clinicians as they advance.

Crucially, we must secure multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding settlements. Short‑term funding cycles fuel volatility and hinder long‑term workforce planning, training capacity expansion and fair, manageable workloads. A stable investment framework would also support flexible working options, wellbeing, and competitive pay to retain experienced clinicians and attract new entrants.

Local trusts should be able to plan staffing levels with confidence, expanding training capacity and recruitment where needed rather than resorting to ad hoc fixes. In practice, that means dedicated budgets for mentorship, protected CPD time, and targeted return‑to‑practice programmes, alongside safe staffing standards that safeguard patient care. I believe these measures would help reduce gaps seen in winter and sustain high‑quality care for everyone.

Prioritise targeted recruitment and retention: competitive pay, retention bonuses, relocation support and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas; reduce unnecessary targets and paperwork; streamline referrals and improve IT usability; expand training places with protected placements through uni-practice partnerships to grow domestically.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the plan should prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding decisions and performance monitoring. Real‑time dashboards on vacancies, turnover, skill mix and patient demand at trust and local level would let us target resource where it’s most needed and test what staffing models work, including extended hours and outreach clinics. 

Overseas recruitment should be used responsibly: streamlined visas, clear credential recognition, structured integration support (language, induction, mentorship) and safeguards so source health systems aren’t depleted. When well designed, it can fill short‑term gaps without eroding long‑term capacity, but it must be paired with strong local training and career pathways so benefits aren’t temporary. In my area, temporary staff helped stabilise services during short gaps, yet the real win comes from combining recruitment with ongoing development and retention strategies.

Invest in local training pipelines and wellbeing, with funded return‑to‑practice routes, flexible career paths and protected supervision time to maintain safe staffing levels. Overall, data‑led planning plus responsible recruitment and robust retention measures will keep care safe, timely and sustainable for communities.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise targeted, place-based incentives to recruit, retain and support staff where shortages are most acute—rural, urban deprived and coastal areas. Practical measures include housing assistance near clinics and hospitals, affordable transport subsidies or reliable public transport routes, and relocation grants to reduce the burden of moving for work. Combine these with career development, offering funded training, structured mentorship, and clear progression pathways that include culturally competent care and language skills where needed (to reflect the diverse communities we serve). Flexible working options, part-time routes and robust wellbeing support are essential to retain staff who face high workloads. I’d also back expanded return-to-practice schemes and local placement pipelines, plus targeted international recruitment with strong induction and safeguarding. Ensuring adequate staffing levels, safe patient ratios and multidisciplinary teams will help maintain safety and quality while easing burnout. In our area, better housing and transport links would make a real difference in keeping experienced staff on the ground.

From where I sit, any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff must put people and safety at its heart. In my experience of navigating NHS services as a patient and as a neighbour relying on clinic teams, stability in staffing and genuine support for those delivering care translates directly into better, safer care for patients. The plan should therefore prioritise flexible, sustainable working patterns, strong professional development, clear scope and protection around new roles, and concrete measures to prevent burnout and workforce exits.

First, flexible and diverse working arrangements are essential. Offering more flexible hours, part-time roles, job-sharing and phased retirement would help retain experienced clinicians who might otherwise step back. Childcare support, affordable and accessible, can make a real difference for nurses, reception staff and allied health professionals who want to stay in frontline roles while managing family commitments. Where services have trialled staggered shifts or community-based clinics with flexible timing, staff retention has improved and patient access has not been compromised. I’d like to see guaranteed options for flexible career paths that allow people to move between scalability of clinical work and mentoring or advisory roles as they approach retirement.

Second, proactively supporting staff mental health is not a luxury but a necessity. Healthy teams deliver safer care. The plan should fund protected time for mental health support, easy access to confidential counselling, and robust peer and supervisory support. This needs to be available across all roles—from GP trainees to social prescribers and reception colleagues—so that burnout is prevented rather than treated after the event. An organisation-wide culture that normalises asking for help, with managers trained to spot early signs of strain, will improve morale and patient safety alike.

Third, clarity around scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity is vital as teams expand their roles. When new roles are introduced—care coordinators, health champions, pharmacists taking on extended clinical tasks—there must be clear, formal guidance about what they can and cannot do, what supervision is required, and how indemnity works in practice. I’d also fund protected clinical supervision so clinicians can discuss difficult cases, reflect on practice, and continuously improve patient safety. This is precisely how newer roles are integrated without creating gaps or risks for patients.

Fourth, invest in career development and governance that helps people stay and grow. Structured induction, ongoing professional development, access to mentors, and transparent appraisal systems matter. A plan that includes leadership development for mid-career staff and opportunities for longer-term progression—without forcing people to leave clinical work to stay in the same role—will help retain talent. In my area, teams that paired clinical supervision with clear training pathways saw fewer resignations and faster onboarding for new staff.

Fifth, plan for a diverse workforce that reflects local communities. Flexible pathways should be equally available to people from different backgrounds, ages and life stages. That means considering and funding language support, culturally competent practice, and roles that fit into people’s lives at various stages. A workforce that can relate to patients in the communities it serves will deliver care more effectively and with higher patient satisfaction.

Lastly, the plan should be evidence-led and locally adaptable. Pilot initiatives with robust evaluation—looking at patient safety indicators, staff turnover, sickness absence and patient access—will tell us what works in different settings and where to scale up. It should include simpler administrative processes, better IT support to cut down on paper-heavy tasks, and governance mechanisms that truly protect patients while allowing teams to innovate.

If these elements are funded for the long term and developed with input from frontline staff and unions, we can maintain high-quality care even as demand grows. It’s about keeping our NHS staffed with capable, cared-for people who want to stay in the service and keep helping others.

An NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe, high‑quality care by building capable multidisciplinary teams, backed by robust information systems, governance, and ongoing professional development. Interoperable IT is essential: invest in a single, secure patient record across primary and community care, with reliable data sharing; provide staff with protected digital training and digital champions. But safeguard alternatives for those who are digitally excluded by ensuring strong non-digital access channels and practical help with online booking and triage. 

Clear scope‑of‑practice, revalidation, indemnity arrangements and funded, protected clinical supervision are critical to support new roles and maintain safety. Define what PAs, pharmacist prescribers and extended‑scope nurses can do, with consistent national standards, and guarantee indemnity and supervision hours for those roles. 

Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: formally grow MDTs—nurses, pharmacists, PAs, paramedics and allied health professionals—through shared training, capacity to supervise, and clear decision rights. This helps redistribute GP workload without compromising safety, as seen when pharmacist med reviews or paramedics undertake home visits, under proper supervision. 

Recruitment and retention supports matter too: streamlined registration and language support for international staff, competitive pay, flexible working, well‑being resources, and clear career progression. In our area such measures would stabilise services, protect continuity of care and reduce over‑reliance on locums.

To recruit, retain and support staff without compromising care, the NHS workforce plan must put safe staffing at the core. This means clear, enforceable staffing ratios that reflect patient need and acuity, not optimistic headcounts. In rural and outer-town areas, there is a real risk that access improvements will stretch teams unless continuity is preserved; therefore, prioritize fixed small teams or longer, reliable rosters so patients see the same clinicians and avoid avoidable handovers.

Safety monitoring should be embedded: real-time dashboards on staffing, patient outcomes, and escalation pathways; independent reviews of near misses; structured debriefs after high-risk shifts. Support roles that ease workload—more practice nurses, physician associates, and pharmacists integrated into care teams—plus protected time for supervision, training and quality improvement.

Recruitment and retention must be locally grounded: local training pipelines, apprenticeships, funded onward training, and fair pay with predictable hours, plus guarantees around cover for leave. Flexible working should be offered in a way that maintains continuity of care.

In short, access gains must go hand in hand with robust staffing, predictable workloads and strong safety oversight to protect quality while improving access.

Any NHS workforce plan that truly helps recruit, retain and support staff, while preserving safe, high‑quality care, must be built on three interlocking priorities: tight, safe staffing ratios; models that protect continuity of care; and rigorous safety monitoring. These safeguards ensure access improvements don’t come at the expense of patient safety or clinical outcomes.

First, safe staffing ratios have to be the baseline. It isn’t enough to simply add more appointment slots; we need consistent, verifiable staffing levels across GP, community and mental health teams. That means clear minimums for core teams and real‑time oversight so shifts aren’t covered by stretched staff juggling multiple roles. In practice, this could mean mandated protected time for supervision and handovers, a cap on patient loads for key roles, and regular, transparent reporting on staffing levels and safe staffing breaches at practice and network level. When staffing is stable and predictable, clinicians can focus on quality care rather than firefighting workflow, and patients see the benefit in shorter waits and better continuity.

Second, continuity of care must be central to any reform. Our experience in the last few years shows that when patients see the same clinician or stable teams, outcomes improve, mistakes fall, and patients feel more reassured. A workforce plan should prioritise continuity-preserving models—such as team clusters with consistent staffing, longer placements for trainees to develop relationship capital, and robust handover systems that keep the patient journey coherent even as staff rotate. We should aim for longer attachments in community and primary care where possible and reduce unnecessary churn caused by short-term postings. This is particularly important for people with chronic conditions or mental health needs, where ongoing relationships and trust drive better management and timely escalation when care is needed.

Third, we must strengthen safety monitoring and governance. Plan‑level dashboards that track not only access metrics (like same‑day slots and wait times) but also safety indicators (adverse events, prescribing safety, incident reports, and timeliness of safeguarding referrals) are essential. Regular clinical supervision, independent reviews of significant safety concerns, and rapid learning cycles so teams can adapt practice when problems are found all contribute to a culture where safety is the default, not an afterthought. In my experience, when teams have clear safety metrics and a mechanism to learn from near misses, patient confidence naturally grows and burnout is less likely because clinicians know issues are taken seriously and addressed.

Fourth, tailor incentives to hard‑to‑fill places. The private geography of England—rural, urban deprivation and coastal areas—demands flexible, targeted approaches. A workforce plan should include housing and transport support, relocation packages, and local incentives that help attract and retain staff where recruitment is hardest. This means practical support like affordable housing near sites, subsidised travel, and flexible rosters that recognise long commutes or family responsibilities. In tandem, provide accelerated training pathways and regional career progression, so people can see a future in their community rather than feeling forced to move elsewhere for development opportunities.

Fifth, invest in the conditions that sustain staff: development, wellbeing and manageable workloads. High‑quality care depends on staff who are well supported: protected time for professional development, dedicated wellbeing resources, mentoring networks, and realistic workloads that leave space for reflective practice and safe, thorough care. Flexible working, job sharing and the option of safe, supported part‑time roles should be standard to help clinicians stay in practice without compromising patient access.

Finally, implement evidence through pilots with clear targets. Test staffing models and continuity strategies in stretched areas, collect data month by month on access and safety, and publish results so communities can judge whether care is improving. Involve patients and frontline staff in the design and evaluation so the plan reflects real local needs rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all approach.

From my own experience, when a same‑day slot exists, it stabilises people’s confidence in the system, and continuity of care matters more than we sometimes admit. A workforce plan that robustly protects safety, keeps patients with the same clinicians where possible, and makes housing and transport a practical reality for those in hard‑to‑fill areas is the right way to deliver timely access without compromising quality. If we get these components right, we’ll see safer care, happier staff and better outcomes for patients across GP, community and mental health services.

Prioritise funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and early-career staff, ensuring safe, high-quality care; but these need sustained funding and manageable workloads.

From my perspective, any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff must prioritise stability, simplicity and genuine investment in people. In our villages and small towns, where services are already stretched and staff frequently commute long distances, the biggest risk to high‑quality care is uncertainty and burnout driven by short‑term funding and heavy admin load. A clear, multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding settlement would make a real difference to patient care by enabling sustained workforce initiatives, expanded training capacity and predictable hiring pipelines, rather than constant cycles of pilots that fade away.

Key priorities I would like to see in an NHS workforce plan include:

- Long‑term, ring‑fenced funding for workforce development: commit to multi‑year budgets that cover recruitment drives, training places for nurses, allied health professionals, and pharmacists, and protected time for upskilling and supervision. In rural areas, targeted schemes to attract staff—such as relocation support, hardship allowances and clear progression paths—are essential. This stability would reduce churn, help retain experienced clinicians, and make it easier to plan services around patient needs.

- Training capacity and flexible career pathways: expand local training and return‑to‑practice routes, with funding for clinical placements and mentorship. A practical example from our area is the success of local mentor schemes and practice nurse training days that have eased GP workloads; with longer‑term funding, these could be scaled up to cover more practices and specialties, including mental health in primary care.

- Reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplication: staff time spent on admin is time not spent with patients. The plan should simplify referrals, streamline pathways, and improve IT usability. For instance, a common triage system and fewer handoffs could cut delays and reduce duplicative data entry. Better IT design—intuitive electronic records, single sign‑on, and interoperable systems across primary, community and mental health services—would free clinicians to focus on care rather than chasing forms.

- Integrated IT that actually supports clinicians: usable, secure technology is not optional; it’s essential to patient safety. Interoperability between GP systems, community health records and hospital discharge summaries would enable safer, faster decision‑making and smoother patient journeys. Co‑designing these tools with frontline staff and older patients would help ensure they are practical in everyday workloads.

- Safe staffing and wellbeing as core components of workforce planning: set clear staffing thresholds and ensure there is protected time for supervision, peer support, and mental health resources for staff. A sustainable workforce is impossible without attention to morale, rest periods, and reasonable hours. Flexible working arrangements, job sharing and longer annualised hours with built‑in training and wellbeing blocks would help attract and retain staff who have caring responsibilities at home.

- Local recruitment and retention, with a clear pipeline: proactive, regionally tailored recruitment campaigns, including international recruitment where appropriate and ethically managed, plus clear pathways to progression, will help fill vacancies in rural areas. Relocation packages and local, visible career ladders give people confidence that staying in the same area is worthwhile.

- Clear governance and measurement: establish robust metrics on staff vacancies, staff wellbeing, patient experience, wait times and outcomes. Regular feedback from patients and carers should shape workforce planning, and pilots should lead to scalable, cost‑effective expansion with demonstrated value for money.

In practice, when staff feel supported and processes are streamlined, care improves. I’ve seen under strain how admin bottlenecks delay reminders for vaccinations or follow‑ups after hospital discharge, which then leads to avoidable attendances and anxiety for families. Conversely, where there is a stable team, decent training opportunities, and a well‑designed telehealth or triage system in place, patients get timely care with less upheaval.

Ultimately, the NHS workforce plan must give staff stability, remove needless friction, and invest in long‑term capacity. With multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding and a commitment to simpler, more user‑friendly IT and referral systems, we can sustain safer, high‑quality care for people like me who rely on local, accessible services.

An NHS workforce plann should prioritise clear, funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain both experienced clinicians and early-career staff. Crucially, guarantee protected time and funding for CPD each year, with nationally recognisedd credits so staff don’t have to choose between learning and patient care. A structured mentorship programme and robust induction across teams would build confidence, reduce early-career turnover and support safer, higher-quality care. Return-to-practice routes must be straightforward, with timelyy re-registration and any necessary retraining provided without punitive delays. Finally, safe staffing ratios, sustainable workloads and accessible wellbeing and supervision support are non-negotiable if we are to protect patient safety and staff morale over the long term.

Prioritise secure multi-year ring-fenced funding to sustain workforce initiatives, expand training, and protect CPD; combine funded career pathways with mentorship and return-to-practice, plus safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models to safeguard quality.

PRIORITIES MUST INCLUDE CLEARLY FUNDED CAREER PATHWAYS, PROTECTED CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT, ROBUST MENTORSHIP, AND ACCESSIBLE RETURN-TO-PRACTICE SCHEMES, ALONGSIDE SUSTAINABLE FUNDING TO RETAIN EXPERIENCED STAFF AND SUPPORT EARLY-CAREER CLINICIANS WITHOUT COMPROMISING PATIENT SAFETY.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise stronger links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and deliver more holistic care. Joint funding and commissioning can support home-visit teams and community hubs, so older residents and carers get timely help without always travelling to town.

We also need streamlined revalidation processes and mentoring schemes to keep staff confident and up-to-date. Flexible, regionally coordinated training hubs across Wales can attract and retain staff by offering clear career progression in primary care and community settings. This approach keeps high-quality care safe as our population ages and reduces unnecessary hospital visits through better early intervention and better coordinated care across sectors.

i really think i think any NHS workforce plan must prioritise making sure there are enough staff across primary care, community services and mental health to deliver safe, high‑quality care without overburdening those delivering it. In practice that means predictable, reasonable workloads, protected admin time and teams that can cover early mornings, evenings and weekends so patients aren’t stuck waiting or slipping into crisis due to gaps. From my experience, same‑day access hinges on having enough clinicians, not just a clever booking system. 

Invest in integrated, multi‑disciplinary teams in community hubs: one appointment that involves a GP, a nurse, a counsellor and a social care link only works if there are sufficient staff in each role and clear pathways between NHS 111, urgent care and mental health teams. From my experience in Northern Ireland, any NHS workforce plan must keep patient safety and high-quality care at its core, while building a resilient, well-supported staff system. It should prioritise interoperable IT and secure systems so GPs, community teams and hospitals can share information smoothly, reducing duplication and delays. That helps with retention as people see a clear path and feel valued. In practice, that means funded multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics—embedded in primary and community settings, supported by stable funding rather than short-lived pilots.

A focus on workload, wellbeing, mentoring and career progression will keep staff well and able to provide safe care. Long-term planning and funding should follow teams rather than faddish projects, ensuring continuity for patients and a steady, capable workforce across Northern Ireland, including older patients who benefit from straightforward, person-centred contact when needed.

From my perspective in Scotland, any NHS workforce plan must not just chase more staff but keep them safe, supported and where they matter most for patients. In practice, that means ensuring sustainable staffing levels across GP, community and mental health teams so services aren’t repeatedly pulled away to hospital wards, leaving clinics cancelled or delays in triage. Practical measures include offering flexible, locally tailored working patterns and protected backfill so weekend or urgent slots aren’t sacrificed; creating clear career pathways with supervision and professional development for nurses, allied health professionals and social care partners; and investing in wellbeing support to prevent burnout. I’d also prioritise multi-disciplinary teams and cross-training so clinicians can manage on‑the‑day triage and short‑notice demand without compromising safety. Rural recruitment requires targeted incentives, strong links with local training providers, and supported relocation or rotation schemes. Digital tools should support care but not replace human contact, with training and governance to keep data secure and workflows reliable. Finally, real-time workload data and safe staffing dashboards will help managers make decisions that protect quality of care and patient experience, like keeping essential services running rather than cancelling them.

i strongly believe an NHS workforce plan should prioritise recruiting, retaining and supporting staff while ensuring safe, high‑quality care. From rural experience, when a GP or nurse leaves, queues grow and patients can be left waiting too long. From where I stand in England, responding as an individual and drawing on what I’ve seen in local services, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise people-friendly, flexible working that helps recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high-quality. Burnout is real, caring responsibilities are real, and the demand for services won’t slow down, so the plan has to build resilience into the system from the ground up.

Key priorities I’d expect to see, with practical reasoning and real-life examples, include:

- Flexible, varied working patterns across the board. This isn’t a “nice to have” but a core need if we want more people to stay in roles or come back after time away. Part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, and adaptable start/finish times for GPs, nurses, mental health workers and technicians would make shifts more predictable for people with childcare, eldercare or health needs. In my area I’ve spoken with clinic staff who’ve left partially because the schedules didn’t fit their lives, and I’ve seen colleagues step back to manage caring responsibilities. If flexible patterns were standard, we’d improve continuity of care and reduce gaps in service.

- Strong childcare and family-friendly policies. On-site or subsidised childcare, clear policies for parental leave, and protected breaks can make a huge difference to retention. I’d also like to see extended hours where needed, with safe staffing still guaranteed, so families aren’t forced to choose between essential care and paying for options outside work hours. A few staff I know would have remained in nursing if there had been reliable childcare support or more predictable shift patterns during school drop-offs and pick-ups.

- Proactive mental health and wellbeing support for staff. If the NHS is serious about high-quality care, it must treat staff wellbeing as essential, not optional. Easy access to confidential counselling, peer-support networks, regular wellbeing check-ins, and time allocated for supervision and rest breaks during busy periods would help prevent burnout and maintain empathy in patient care. This aligns with my concern that mental health services in the community should be well-supported so staff aren’t jumping between high-stress crises and administrative overload.

- Clear training, development and return-to-work pathways. A strong plan would fund ongoing professional development, apprenticeships for new entrants, and robust return-to-practice routes for those who’ve paused their careers. Allowing staff to upskill without prohibitive costs or time pressures supports retention and helps cover shortages in specialties that suffer the most when demand spikes.

- Safe staffing and workload management. The plan must set realistic staffing levels that keep patient safety at the forefront. That means better rostering, fewer non-clinical bottlenecks, and investment in skilled support staff who free clinicians to focus on direct patient care. I’ve seen how heavy non-clinical workloads contribute to errors and fatigue; addressing this is essential if the workforce is to deliver consistently high standards.

- Reducing administrative burden through better systems. Time spent on paperwork and repeated data entry drains clinical capacity and mood. Modern, user-friendly IT platforms, joined-up records, and effective administrative support should be core parts of the workforce strategy, not afterthoughts. This would also help with continuity of care, which I strongly support.

- Leadership, culture and inclusion. Staff need empowering line management, regular supervision, mentoring, and a culture that prioritises psychological safety. The plan should explicitly promote diverse recruitment and inclusive progression to ensure the services reflect the communities they serve, which in turn supports collaboration across GP practices, community health teams, and mental health services.

- Local flexibility and multisector collaboration. Workforce strategies should recognise local needs and enable partnerships across hospital, primary care and community services. This includes shared training, joint backfills, and flexible deployment models that can respond quickly to local pressures while maintaining safe care.

Taken together, these priorities would help recruit and retain a broader mix of staff, support their wellbeing, and keep care safe and high quality for patients. If the NHS can offer flexible hours, dependable childcare, proactive mental health support, and fair development opportunities, we’ll see more people staying in roles and more communities benefiting from stable, accessible care over the long term.

Based on my experience, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving care models and robust safety monitoring to ensure access improvements do not undermine quality. It also means designing teams around continuity: a named GP or stable multidisciplinary team, supported by experienced nurses, therapists and care coordinators who share the same care plan and handovers. This approach reduces avoidable misunderstandings and repeated tests.

Investing in governance and safety culture is essential: regular clinical audits, incident reporting, and real-time safety dashboards to flag risks as workloads fluctuate. Training and career progression, better flexible working to retain skilled staff, and targeted recruitment to fill shortages must accompany governance. Finally, embed practical supports like longer appointments for complex patients, protected time for team case reviews, and interoperable information sharing so that access improvements never compromise quality.

Agree - what a surprise. Prioritise targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract and retain staff in underserved areas and high-demand roles, so safe, high-quality care is sustained across all services.

Prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, robust modelling and clear KPIs with evaluation frameworks to guide planning, funding and performance monitoring; ensure staffing decisions protect continuity of care, reasonable workloads and sustained safe, high-quality services.

From my vantage as an older person living in England, I want an NHS workforce plan that actually delivers safer, higher‑quality care by investing in people who stay, grow, and feel valued. It isn’t enough to recruit more staff if we don’t give them real reasons to stay or to take on new roles safely. A robust plan should prioritise clear, funded career paths, protected professional development, and dependable support that reaches every corner of the country, including rural and coastal areas where recruitment is hardest. Here is how I think it should work in practice:

- Funded, clear career pathways: Create and fund structured routes from entry to advanced practitioner across GPs, nurses, pharmacists, and allied health professionals. This means paid apprenticeships, funded specialty training, and obvious progression steps so experienced clinicians don’t feel trapped or pushed out to the margins. My experience in a busy practice shows that young clinicians who see a future in primary care are more likely to stay; lack of progression is a real turn‑off.

- Protected CPD and time for learning: Give clinicians protected time and funding for ongoing training, with access across urban and rural sites. CPD must be practical, relevant, and equitable, so staff in deprived or remote areas aren’t advantaged elsewhere. When people feel they can develop without sacrificing patient care, retention improves and safety improves too.

- Mentorship and return‑to‑practice schemes: Establish robust mentorship for new graduates and return‑to‑practice programs for those who paused their careers. A dedicated mentor can help someone navigate the complexities of a patient’s history and local pathways, which is especially important for continuity and safety with older patients where you don’t want to start from scratch every time.

- Defined scope‑of‑practice, revalidation and indemnity: Provide crystal‑clear scope‑of‑practice for new and evolving roles, with straightforward revalidation processes. Indemnity arrangements should be aligned with these roles so clinicians aren’t deterred by cost or complexity when they broaden their responsibilities. This is essential to keep patient safety at the forefront as teams expand.

- Protected supervision and oversight: Fund structured, protected clinical supervision, particularly for those taking on advanced or new responsibilities. Small teams and mixed‑skill groups benefit from regular supervision to course‑correct and reinforce safety practices. In practice, supervision is often squeezed or rheostated by workload; guaranteeing it is a safety net for patients and a confidence boost for staff.

- Tailored incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas: Deliver targeted packages for rural, urban deprived, and coastal locations—housing support, transport assistance, relocation grants, and local climate or housing incentives. These should be paired with local career opportunities and family support so staff don’t feel they must uproot entirely to work in different communities.

- Local workforce planning and data transparency: Use accurate, local data to forecast demand and plan training pipelines accordingly. Health boards should publish forward plans so communities understand why vacancies exist and what is being done to fill them, helping to build public trust.

- Wellbeing and safe staffing as a feature, not an afterthought: Address workload, staffing ratios, staff burnout, and access to occupational health and mental health support. A plan that ignores wellbeing will fail; you cannot deliver safe care with exhausted teams.

- Multidisciplinary and team‑based care: Expand roles for pharmacists, physiotherapists, and other professionals within primary care teams, with joint training so teams function smoothly and patients experience continuity. This also supports safer prescribing and better chronic disease management for older patients.

- Practical models for training delivery: Invest in simulation, digital competence, and flexible training delivery to reach remote communities. Online mentoring and regional training hubs can reduce disincentives to stay in or move to under‑served areas.

In short, the plan must connect workforce investment to real patient safety and continuity benefits. It should reward long‑term commitment to primary care, provide tangible means to develop and stay, and remove bottlenecks caused by indecision or patchy support in hard‑to‑fill places. Only with funded career pathways, protected CPD, meaningful mentorship, clear scope and indemnity, and targeted regional incentives can we build a stable, high‑quality NHS workforce that keeps pace with the needs of older residents and the wider community.
