The plan should balance tech‑enabled care with strong human support, aging‑friendly approaches, and culturally competent practice to preserve safety and quality for all patients.

Agree. To recruit, retain and support staff while preserving safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise stronger, jointly funded links across NHS, social care, mental health and community services. This will redistribute workload, reduce duplication, and enable holistic care at home and in community hubs. Key moves should include expanding undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and robust university–practice partnerships so domestic primary care capacity grows where it’s most needed. Practical steps could be pooled budgets for community teams, joint workforce planning forums with local authorities, and cross-sector recruitment drives that create clear career ladders for GPs, nurses, paramedics and mental health workers.

From our experience in rural areas, joint out‑of‑hours and outreach teams, backed by social care capacity and telehealth links, cut unnecessary hospital visits and support families. We need secondments between hospitals and social care, flexible staffing models, and wellbeing and professional development packages to retain staff.

Ultimately, safe care hinges on enough trained staff, protected time for CPD, and data‑driven rostering to match demand. This integrated approach is the best way to sustain services now and into the future.

From our experience representing older residents in England, a NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe, high‑quality care through well‑supported multidisciplinary teams and robust IT. Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals—so they can share routine GP workload under clear supervision and defined decision‑making boundaries. With age‑related conditions, polypharmacy and frailty, staff across professions can manage reviews, vaccinations, falls risk assessment and chronic disease monitoring, freeing GPs to concentrate on the most complex cases. Provide standardised training, ongoing supervision and clear career progression to recruit and retain staff, plus flexible rostering aligned to patient needs and continuity of care.

Invest in interoperable, secure IT so clinicians can access up‑to‑date records, share care plans and coordinate across GP practices, community teams and hospitals. Couple staff digital training with robust non‑digital options to safeguard digitally excluded patients. Maintain strong non‑digital access channels—telephone triage, same‑day telephone or in‑person appointments, and community hubs where staff can help patients navigate digital tools.

Introduce governance and monitoring to ensure safety and outcomes, and collect data on MDT impact on wait times, patient experience and equity. In our experience, where teams operate with clear protocols and supervision, older residents receive timelier, safer care while retaining options that suit those who are not digital‑enabled.

In my view, an NHS workforce plan should be anchored in three priorities to recruit, retain and support staff while safeguarding safe, high‑quality care: sustained funding that enables realistic, long-term planning; targeted incentives and practical support for those working in hard‑to‑fill places; and a workforce design that values wellbeing, development and workable workloads as much as it does recruitment numbers.

- Secure multi-year, ring‑fenced funding: Short-term funding cycles drive churn and undermine training capacity. A stable funding settlement would enable sustained recruitment drives, expanded training places (medical, nursing, allied health professionals, and support roles), and predictable workforce development. In practice, this would mean confirmed budgets for a minimum period of five years, with annual refreshers tied to clear milestones on training slots, supervision capacity, and service expansion. It would also reduce policy volatility that currently disrupts local recruitment plans and commissioning decisions.

- Tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas: Recruitment and retention aren’t one‑size‑fits‑all. We should deliver targeted packages for rural, urban deprived, and coastal communities that reflect the realities on the ground. This could include housing and relocation assistance, affordable transport options, and improved access to local schooling or childcare. In my area, where GP vacancies have stretched services, housing support and subsidised travel for staff commuting from nearby towns could make roles genuinely liveable and sustainable and help shift the balance between demand and capacity.

- Expand and diversify the training and career ladder: A credible plan must grow training capacity across the whole workforce and provide clear, attractive progression routes. That means more placements for medical students, nursing students, paramedics, pharmacists, therapists, and first‑contact clinicians, plus robust supervision and protected time for professional development. For international recruits, streamlined induction and a structured integration path with mentors can speed up safe upskilling while safeguarding patient safety. In practice, I’ve seen how GPs and practice teams benefit when nurse practitioners and physiotherapists share the workload and bring different skills to the front line; expanding these roles should be a deliberate priority in workforce planning.

- Smart workforce design and deployment: Teams working at the top of their licence, with flexible skill mixes, can relieve bottlenecks and improve access. A plan should promote integrated care teams, with general practice supported by first‑contact physiotherapists, prescribing pharmacists, and digitally-enabled triage where appropriate. Effective rostering and real‑time staffing data are essential so we can match demand with the right mix of staff, not just people to fill slots.

- Focus on wellbeing, workload and safety: Recruitment alone won’t sustain services if staff burn out. The plan must fund wellbeing programmes, access to supervision and peer support, reduced administrative burdens, and protected time for reflection and learning. A safer, more humane working environment translates into better patient care and lower staff turnover.

- Local accountability and community voices: Local workforce plans should involve clinicians, support staff, patients and carers in setting what good recruitment and retention look like in their area. Regular evaluation against waiting times, safety metrics, equity of access and staff satisfaction will help ensure the plan translates into tangible improvements on the ground, not just glossy targets.

- IT and integration as enablers: A strong digital backbone supports safe care and efficient staffing. Shared care plans, real‑time access to patient data, and interoperable IT systems reduce duplication, streamline referrals, and help teams coordinate more effectively across primary, community and hospital settings.

I’m cautiously optimistic that a well‑designed NHS workforce plan can deliver the expansion we need without compromising quality or clinician wellbeing. For this to work, it must pair credible, long‑term funding with tailored, place‑based approaches and real opportunities for staff to grow, develop and stay in the NHS. Only then can we move toward parity between physical and mental health services in access, quality and experience for both patients and staff.

I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three core threads: reducing admin burden and duplications; flexible and supportive working arrangements; and secure, long-term funding to grow and sustain skills. On workload, we need to remove unnecessary targets and paperwork that pull clinicians away from patients; simplify referrals; and ensure user-friendly IT and interoperable records so a GP can see what’s happened elsewhere in seconds. In my experience at a small co-located hub, streamlined IT and a shared calendar freed time for real patient contact and quicker follow-ups. 

On people, offer flexible hours, job-share options, phased retirement and childcare support; invest in proactive staff mental health services; protect time for supervision and peer support to prevent burnout. Flexible hours and diverse arrangements help retain a wider range of talent and keep teams resilient. 

On funding, lock in multi-year, ring-fenced funding for training capacity, recruitment campaigns and workforce modernization to avoid short-term policy volatility derailing long-term plans. This stability supports longer apprenticeships, training places and staff development.

Finally, ensure safe, high-quality care with clear staffing norms and ongoing training alongside robust supervision. A durable, well-funded plan like this would help recruit, retain and support staff while delivering consistently good care, even in busy periods.

Prioritise reducing unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, streamline referrals and improve IT usability to free clinicians for patient-facing care; plus targeted pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles.

A robust NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe, high‑quality care by building sustainable teams, expanding domestic training, and using international recruitment responsibly, all aligned to the needs of underserved communities.

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: integrate nurses, physician associates, pharmacists, paramedics and allied health professionals into primary care with clear scopes of practice, strong supervision, governance, and escalation pathways. In practice, when these roles support triage and same‑day care with appropriate oversight, GP workload is reduced without compromising safety.

- Grow domestic supply with protected training: increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, backed by university–practice partnerships and protected placements, including in deprived and ethnically diverse areas to support equity and retention.

- Use overseas recruitment responsibly: welcome skilled staff as a supplementary resource with streamlined visas, rigorous credential recognition, comprehensive integration and language support, and safeguards to prevent undermining health systems in source countries. It should complement, not replace, local training and development.

- Focus on retention, wellbeing and equity: ensure safe staffing levels, adequate time for supervision and mentoring, fair pay, access to interpreters and culturally competent support, and transparent monitoring of outcomes and retention to address disparities.

These priorities together can deliver safer care, steadier workloads for clinicians and better access for patients in all communities.

From where I stand in England, I’ve seen how staffing pressures ripple through every part of the health service, from GP practices to community and mental health teams. A useful NHS workforce plan should be realistic, long-term and focused on safety, development and stability. It must support people who are already on the front line while making room for new roles and different career paths. In short, it should combine clear expectations with the resources to meet them, so we don’t end up with quick fixes that erode care quality over time.

Key priorities I’d expect the plan to prioritise include:

- Clear scope of practice and robust professional development: when new roles are introduced, such as nurse practitioners or physician associates, there must be explicit scope trees, supported by accessible training and straightforward revalidation. This reduces ambiguity for staff and patients alike and keeps care safe as roles expand. It helps junior clinicians grow into more responsible positions without undermining patient safety.

- Indemnity arrangements and predictable risk protection: staff and employers need clarity and stability about indemnity costs. Unpredictable or sky‑high indemnity can deter skilled people from choosing primary care or mental health roles, especially at the practice level. A plan that locks in reasonable, predictable protections will support recruitment and retention.

- Protected clinical supervision and mentorship for new roles: alongside more flexible responsibilities, there must be guaranteed time for supervision. Protected supervision helps maintain safety when teams are expanding, and it supports staff wellbeing by offering a clear route for professional oversight, feedback and growth. In my experience, where supervision is thin or pressured, junior staff burn out and patient safety can suffer.

- Secured, multi-year, ring-fenced funding: long-term funding settlements are essential to plan workforce development, expand training capacity and reduce policy volatility. Short-term grants or annual funding swings make it difficult to commit to longer programmes (such as allied health professional training or practice nurse development) and to sustain recruitment pipelines. A predictable settlement would enable trusts and practices to hire, train and retain more effectively.

- Expanded and protected training capacity: the plan should fund more training placements across general practice, community services and mental health, with clear pipelines from training into sustainable roles. In practice, one area I know has struggled is filling training posts because of funding gaps and limited placements; addressing this with ring-fenced funds would let local providers plan more confidently and improve service continuity.

- Flexible, resilient workforce models: we need a workforce that can work flexibly across settings and time to meet patient needs, including part-time routes, return‑to‑practice schemes, and routes for international-trained clinicians who meet high NHS standards. Flexible models help with retention and broaden the candidate pool, but they must go hand in hand with consistent induction and supervision to protect safety and quality.

- Safe staffing, governance and wellbeing: safe ratios and robust governance structures should be embedded in the plan. Recognising staff wellbeing as a core safety issue—mental health support, reasonable workloads, protected break times and access to peer support—helps reduce burnout and improves patient outcomes.

- Data-driven, locally responsive planning: the plan should require transparent workforce data and allow regions to tailor recruitment and development to local needs. Regular reviews and public reporting on staffing levels, turnover, wait times and training outcomes will help keep services aligned with what patients actually experience.

- Alignment with digital care trajectories without sacrificing human touch: as we expand training in digital tools and remote care, we must ensure staff are well-supported and protected by supervision, so patients still receive safe, person-centred care when digital channels aren’t suitable.

Experience in my area shows the risk of relying too much on short-term staffing or ad hoc training. When locum cover becomes the norm, patients experience gaps in continuity and clinicians can feel overstretched. A strong, well-funded plan that prioritises defined roles, predictable costs and protected supervision would enable teams to recruit with confidence, train thoroughly and stay with the NHS for longer, delivering consistently high-quality care.

If these priorities are embedded in a durable, well‑funded strategy, we’ll have a better chance of recruiting the right people, keeping them motivated and ensuring patients get timely, safe and high‑quality care across GP, community and mental health services.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise growing the domestic primary care supply and strengthening multi-disciplinary teams. I support increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships so students train in GP practices and community teams here in Scotland and pursue sustainable careers locally. This would address shortages more reliably than relying on international recruitment and help us build teams that understand local needs. 

We also need transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks. By mapping vacancies, turnover, training capacity and workload across NHS boards and social care, we can forecast needs, target funding and monitor progress effectively, rather than guessing what’s needed years down the line. In my area there have been GP vacancies and high workloads for district nurses, and placements often require students to travel between services; local data and planned investment would improve scheduling and outcomes.

Finally, strengthen links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and deliver holistic patient care. Co-located, well-supported teams in community hubs, with clear career progression and staff wellbeing protections, would reduce burnout and improve continuity. Community collaboration and local intelligence make real improvements possible.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise deeper integration across health and social care with joint funding and shared outcomes. When pressure is highest, especially in mental health, community and primary care, we need to fund collaborations with social care and community services to redistribute workload and support holistic patient care. Practical steps include creating shared posts between primary care, social care and mental health teams; establishing co-located multidisciplinary hubs; and providing back‑office and data-sharing support so clinicians can focus on patients.

We also need clear, funded career pathways, protected CPD time, structured mentorship and robust return-to-practice routes to retain experienced clinicians and support early‑career staff. This should include funded buddy schemes, protected supervision hours, leadership development opportunities, and bridging programmes for those returning after career breaks. In addition, we must guarantee safe staffing levels, predictable rosters and timely workload monitoring to safeguard quality.

In our area, CAMHS waiting times remain lengthy and out-of-hours support is inconsistent; these issues show the need for cross-sector alignment and sustained investment in people. A sustainable plan must tie workforce development directly to integrated, patient‑centred care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving care, with active safety monitoring to ensure access improvements do not compromise quality. It must also cut unnecessary targets, reduce paperwork and eliminate duplicated tasks, and streamline referrals with user-friendly, integrated IT. Clinicians need time for patients, not admin. In Wales, where GP and mental health access is still challenging for students juggling study and part-time work, this matters for frontline experience. For example, a single digital records system with automated triage and real-time updates across primary care, community health and CAMHS would save hours each week and cut avoidable delays. To recruit and retain staff, fund long-term career progression, stable rosters and flexible working, plus protected time for training. Continuity—patients seeing the same clinician when possible—improves outcomes, supported by reliable staffing and ongoing safety checks with regular audits. In short: fewer admin burdens, better IT, safe staffing and continuity, plus robust safety monitoring, so access improves without sacrificing care quality.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan should be built on three connected pillars. First, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams across primary care and community services. This means investing in nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles with clear scopes of practice, robust training and supervision, and well‑defined pathways to share GP workloads where appropriate. In practice, where pharmacists and nurse prescribers take on medication reviews and chronic disease follow‑ups, GP time is freed for complex cases and patients experience smoother care journeys. Second, prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity‑preserving models, coupled with strong safety monitoring. That includes named clinicians or stable team assignments, real‑time workload data, regular audits and a culture of incident reporting, so access improvements do not erode quality. Third, tailor incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas—rural, coastal and urban deprived settings—with housing and transport support, flexible rosters, and clear career development. I’ve seen how targeted support in staffing and location incentives can make roles more attractive and sustainable. Taken together, these measures would help expand access without compromising safety or patient experience.

A robust NHS workforce plan must be built on practical, patient-centred change that frees clinicians to care for people, while giving staff the stability, development and support they need to stay safely and effectively in post. From our experience in the community, reducing unnecessary targets and admin burden is not soft policy; it directly improves quality and safety by freeing time for face-to-face care and timely decision-making. The plan should prioritise three overarching areas: practical workforce sustainability, streamlined systems that cut duplication, and stable funding that underpins long-term capability.

- Reduce admin load and streamline referrals to free clinician time for patients. Too many targets, dashboards and duplicated data entry pull clinicians into busywork rather than patient-facing care. A practical approach would be to simplify reporting, align performance measures across primary and mental health services, and create a single, interoperable referral and patient record system. For example, standardised referral criteria between GP, community services and mental health teams, plus a unified triage pathway, would cut delays and errors. Enhancing IT usability—clear workflows, intuitive interfaces, offline capabilities where connectivity is patchy, and better integration with hospital systems—would markedly shorten waiting times and improve safety because decisions are evidence-based and timely.

- Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding for sustained workforce initiatives. Short-term policy volatility and quarterly funding cycles erode planning and morale. We need long-term commitments that enable recruitment, scale-up of training, expanded supervision and wellbeing support, and targeted retention strategies. This includes funded programmes for GP and nurse pipelines, mental health professionals, and allied health staff, with protected budgets for supervision, professional development and extending working hours when needed. In our area, stable funding would prevent recurrent gaps in rosters and enable sustainable recruitment plans rather than stop-start campaigns that leave services stretched.

- Expand training capacity and career development to attract and retain staff. A clear, well-funded progression ladder reduces turnover and builds confidence in the workforce. Priorities should include: expanded local training hubs for GPs, nurses, therapists and technicians; fast-tracked registration where appropriate with rigorous quality safeguards; protected time for study, supervision and reflective practice; and leadership development at all levels. Practical steps could involve multi-professional training collaborations, apprenticeships for allied roles, and dedicated time for mentors to support junior staff. This investment translates into better continuity of care, improved safety, and a more resilient service overall.

- Build workforce planning around safe, high-quality care. The plan must define safe staffing levels and ensure sufficient cover across shifts, with particular attention to out-of-hours and crisis response capacity. This includes a dependable on-call and crisis workforce, as well as robust supervision and wellbeing packages to prevent burnout. A safer care culture comes from predictable rosters, adequate time for complex cases, and the ability to escalate when thresholds are reached without fear of punitive targets.

- Drive efficiency through smarter, user-friendly IT and integrated pathways. We should prioritise electronic health records that talk to each other, real-time referral tracking, and patient-accessible appointment information. Simple things—auto-filled forms, pre-visit checks, and triage-enabled call centres—save time and reduce patient risk. Training on these tools should be part of the standard onboarding and ongoing professional development, not a one-off exercise.

- Focus on equity and local needs. Workforce planning must reflect urban and rural realities, with flexible staffing models to cover gaps in doctors, nurses and therapists where they are most needed. Equitable access to high-quality care requires that recruitment, training and retention strategies are tailored to diverse communities and that technology supports, not hinders, access for all patients.

- Promote cross-service collaboration and staff wellbeing as core enablers of safety. Integrated teams spanning GP practices, community health, and mental health services require joint planning, shared governance, and common quality standards. Equally important is patient-centred wellbeing support for staff—mental health resources, supervision, reasonable workloads, and recognition of workload spikes during crises.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan should reduce bureaucratic burden, ensure stable, long-term funding for staffing and training, and invest in user-friendly IT and integrated referral pathways. This combination will help maintain safe, high-quality care now and into the future, while giving health staff a clear, supported career path within a stable, predictable system. We stand ready to collaborate with NHS England, regional bodies and local authorities to turn these priorities into tangible, funded programmes that deliver real benefits to patients and staff alike.
I'm cautious. A workforce plan should first confirm funding, safe staffing levels, and local capacity before defining recruitment targets or special programs.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high-quality, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise durable, funded career pathways, protected CPD time and budgets, mentorship for all new entrants, and effective return-to-practice schemes. These measures help retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff to build confidence and skills. In my area, a local practice that allocated protected CPD days and paired junior GPs with experienced mentors saw improved morale and steadier patient care over two years. 

We also need to recognise the role of digital systems. Invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, with comprehensive staff training, but ensure robust alternatives for digitally excluded patients—maintaining telephone triage, in-person clinics and paper records where needed. Practical steps include multi-year workforce planning aligned to service design, transparent workload dashboards, flexible rostering and strong cross-disciplinary teams to spread demand. A well-supported workforce will deliver safer, higher-quality care and reduce burnout for everyone.

Agree. In Scotland, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise a credible, long‑term strategy underpinned by secure, ring‑fenced funding that allows sustained recruitment, training capacity expansion and robust staff wellbeing. Multi‑year funding reduces policy churn and enables predictable career progression, supervision, and competency development across GPs, nurses, AHPs and social care roles. Key priorities include building capacity for training pipelines, expanding apprenticeships, and creating flexible working models that improve retention in rural and high‑need areas while safeguarding patient safety and supervision. Cross‑professional teams, supported by co‑located community hubs that integrate primary care, community health, mental health and social care with VCSE partners, should be prioritised, with shared records, same‑day GP triage and streamlined referrals to cut waits and avoid unnecessary handoffs for older patients and carers. 

Overseas recruitment can play a part, but it must be responsible: streamlined visas, efficient credential recognition, structured integration support and mentorship, with safeguards to avoid undermining health systems in source countries. It should supplement domestic capacity, not replace it. From where I stand, any NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things that go hand in hand: keeping patients safe with high-quality care, giving staff the time and tools to do their jobs well, and making sure people who aren’t comfortable with digital systems aren’t left behind. In practice that means a strong focus on interoperable IT, secure systems, and staff digital training, backed by targeted pay and practical incentives to attract people to areas and roles where the need is greatest. 

First, invest in interoperable IT and robust data security. A single, real-time set of records across primary care, community services, and mental health teams would dramatically reduce duplication, paperwork and repeated histories. It would make it easier for clinicians to see a patient’s full journey, coordinate care, and keep up with urgent needs without forcing people to re-explain themselves to every new clinician. Real-time rostering and cross-provider triage tools would help ensure staffing levels match demand and reduce last-minute cancellations that disrupt patient safety. But technology must be secure and designed with clinicians, not just IT specialists, in mind. 

Second, train staff effectively and keep them supported in using digital tools. That means practical, ongoing digital literacy training, protected time for upskilling, and champions across teams who can help colleagues adapt to new systems without creating extra workload. It also means building in safeguards for those who can’t or won’t use digital channels. My experience of trying to book care online shows how quickly things can stall if there isn’t a clear option for someone who’s less comfortable with tech. So alongside digital channels, there must be reliable non-digital routes—phone lines, local access points, and help desks—so no one is excluded from timely care.

Third, recruit and retain people where needed with tangible incentives and career pathways. This should include targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and to high-demand roles such as GPs, nurses, mental health professionals and allied health professionals. In addition, longer-term strategies matter: clear career progression, mentoring, flexible working options, safe staffing ratios, and workload management that prevents burnout. A workforce plan that ties these incentives to visible career ladders and recognised roles will be more attractive to students and existing staff alike—and more likely to hold onto them once they’re trained.

I’ve seen how gaps in staffing affect not just waiting times but the quality of care. When there are enough trained hands to balance primary care, community visits, and mental health support, patients get quicker access and better outcomes. And when digital tools are well implemented but not exclusive, clinics can be more efficient without leaving anyone behind. 

To deliver what patients need, the plan must be data-led with measurable targets: digital adoption rates across pathways, patient-received alternatives for those with limited digital access, turnover and vacancy rates in high-demand roles, and the impact on safety indicators and patient experience. If the NHS can align interoperable IT, staff skills, and fair, location-sensitive incentives, we’ll have a workforce that can deliver safer, higher-quality care while keeping young people and families hopeful about getting help when they need it most.

Prioritise targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles; secure multi-year ring-fenced funding for sustained training and capacity; reduce admin burden and streamline IT and referrals to free clinicians for patient care.

Prioritise long-term funding for retention, training, and smart local commissioning, plus interoperable, secure IT infrastructure and staff digital training, with safeguard for digitally excluded patients to ensure safe, high-quality care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise clear scope-of-practice and robust professional development. I’ve seen new roles emerge in primary care, like nurse practitioners and physician associates, but without clear scope and affordable indemnity, staff hesitate to take on extended duties. The plan should fund protected clinical supervision and regular mentoring to sustain patient safety and help staff adapt to evolving responsibilities. Indemnity and revalidation processes need to be streamlined and predictable, so clinicians can focus on patient care rather than administrative hurdles. A transparent career ladder with protected time for training would also boost retention and morale.

Investing in interoperable IT and secure systems is essential: shared records, safer e-referrals and decision support reduce errors and free up time for patients. But we must preserve non‑digital routes and ensure digital training is accessible for everyone, including those less confident with technology.

Crucially, the plan should embed safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models, with consistent safety monitoring to catch strain early. For me, a named clinician who follows patients across services, supported by stable teams and good handovers, remains the cornerstone of safe, accessible care and helps prevent pressure on urgent services.

Any NHS workforce plan should be grounded in transparent, locally specific data. That means publishing up‑to‑date modelling, KPIs and evaluation frameworks at the local level so funding, recruitment targets and performance measures reflect real patient need and staffing realities rather than generic targets. In practice, this would help explain persistent delays and staff burnout when demand outstrips supply. 

We also need solid investment in interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training, but with safeguards for patients who are digitally excluded. If digital triage replaces quick human contact, there must still be robust, visible alternatives and clear escalation routes, plus ongoing in‑person support in the community. 

Crucially, we must reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. Streamlining referrals and improving IT usability would free clinicians to see patients directly. For example, simpler cross‑service referral paths between GP, mental health and social care, and reducing repetitive data entry would save hours each week and cut waiting times. A plan that aligns staffing with actual demand, provides better tech, and protects non‑digital access is essential to recruiting and retaining capable staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality.

Any NHS workforce plan must ensure we can recruit, retain and support staff without compromising safety or quality. I think the plan should prioritise safe staffing ratios across GP practices, district nursing, community mental health teams and hospital discharge pathways, with clear targets and public reporting. It should also promote continuity-preserving models—stable, small teams and longer clinician-patient relationships—so people see the same clinicians and handovers don’t undermine safety or satisfaction.

A core element is joint funding and integrated workforce planning with social care, mental health and community services. By sharing posts and pooling budgets, workloads can be redistributed, helping avoid bottlenecks and enabling care in local hubs. Co-located teams, shared digital records and aligned management would reduce duplication and improve patient flow.

Safety monitoring must be built in: real-time dashboards on staffing, wait times, adverse events, and safety concerns, with independent reviews when thresholds are breached. Invest in career pathways, flexible working, wellbeing support, and robust induction for international recruits to sustain morale and quality.

In our area, a linked hub could ease dementia care and support carers, but only if there is joint funding and strong safety oversight to protect quality as access expands.

From my experience in England, any NHS workforce plan should be rooted in predictable staffing and real support for the people on the frontline, not just targets. Priorities should include: safe, sustainable staffing levels across GP, nursing, admin and mental health teams; better recruitment and retention in hard-to-staff areas through local incentives and clear career progression; flexible rosters and affordable childcare near hubs to help working families stay in the job; protected time for training, supervision and mental health support to avoid burnout; improved admin and triage capacity so clinicians can spend time with patients rather than chasing paperwork; investment in cross-disciplinary teams at integrated care hubs so physio, counsellor and GP can share records and coordinate care; robust workforce planning using real-time data to match demand with staffing; easier full-time and part-time routes, return-to-practice schemes, and stable long-term contracts to reduce turnover; invest in digital tools to reduce duplication and streamline scheduling; and focus on safety by maintaining safe ratios, reasonable workloads, and strong safeguarding procedures. In short: staff supported, valued, and well-equipped to deliver high-quality care locally.

From my perspective as a young person living in England, any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality needs to be practical, better funded and people-centred. In my experience, timel recruitment is only part of the problem—retention and supportive integration are what make the difference in patien care, especially for people like me who might need consistent, long-term access to services. Second, there must be clear, publicly funded career pathways that enable both new entrants and exprrienced clinicians to progress. That means protected funding for continuous professional development, formal mentorship schemes for graduates and return-to-practice routes for those who’ve taken a break, perhaps for caring responsibilities or study. A well-structured preceptorship for newly qualified staff in their first two years, with regular supervision and manageable caseloads, would help reduc early burnout and improve retention. For those already in the system, targeted CPD opportunities aligned to local service needs and cross-disciplinary training to support multi-disciplinary teams would boost confidence in delivering high-quality care. Third, retention must be a core designn feature. This includes safe staffing levels, sensible andd predictablee rosters that accommodate training and study, and strong supervision.
