Flexible working arrangements, better recognition and reward for experienced clinicians, and practical measures to support career longevity (such as phased retirement options and opportunities to move between clinical practice and education) would go a long way. In my own circle,, burnout and inconsistent staffing contribute to delays in getting timely help, which only amplifies the problems during exam periods or peak service times. Finally, the plan should tie workforce growth to service design, not just numbers. That means investing in roles that support care pathways—carr coordinators, digital-enabled triage, and joint training across primary, community and hospital settings—so teams can work more efficiently and patients experience seamless access to trratment and advice. It should also be underpinned by transparent local implementation, with strong governance, patient and staff input, and clear metrics on wait times, vacancy rates and patient safety outcomes. In short, recruit where it makes sense and is sustainable, invest in people through funded CPD and mentoring, protrct staff wellbeing and safe working conditions, andd align workforce growth with joined-up service design. If policy makers get that balance right, we’lll be closer to parity with physical health in both urgency and quality of care, which is especially important for young adults like me who rely on timely support.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining high-quality, safe care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise reducing unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and focus on improving IT and referral systems so clinicians can spend more time with patients. This means setting realistic, outcome-focused targets rather than heavy tick-box quotas, and ensuring non-clinical admin time is protected with dedicated support staff. Streamlined, standardised referral pathways across GP, community and mental health services, powered by an interoperable IT system and a single patient record, would cut duplications and delays. Invest in care coordinators and administrative roles to handle scheduling, triage and follow-ups, freeing clinicians for front-line care (as if that will ever happen). Expand multidisciplinary teams and ensure safe staffing levels with predictable rosters, workable workloads, and time for supervision and professional development to prevent burnout. Offer flexible working patterns and robust recruitment incentives to attract and retain staff. In my experience, when admin burden is reduced and IT is user-friendly, clinicians have more patient-facing time, and care quality and continuity improve for patients and their families.

Prioritise responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, clear credential recognition and strong integration support, to widen capability without draining source health systems. Also target hard-to-fill areas with housing and transport incentives. Finally, clarify scope-of-practice, revalidation, indemnity and fund protected clinical supervision to sustain safety.

i really think funded career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain staff; interoperable, secure IT with ongoing digital training while safeguarding options for digitally excluded patients; and targeted incentives including housing and transport for hard-to-fill rural and urban areas, ensuring safety and quality!

Prioritise tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas (housing, transport) to recruit and retain staff; invest in interoperable IT and digital training with protections for digitally excluded patients; and develop transparent local workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation to guide planning and funding, plus sustained support for interpreters and multidisciplinary teams.

An NHS workforce plan should build a robust domestic pipeline, ensure flexible, compassionate working arrangements, and govern safe staffing. Priorities: expand undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships so more clinicians train and stay in primary care. This will reduce dependence on agency staff and improve continuity of care. For retention, offer flexible hours, job-sharing, phased retirement and robust childcare support, backed by proactive mental health services for staff to prevent burnout. Create clear, supported career pathways with modern supervision and abundant CPD, and ensure return-to-practice routes so experienced colleagues can rejoin after a break.

Workforce planning must be demand-led and data-driven, with investment in multidisciplinary teams—pharmacists for repeat prescriptions, physiotherapists for musculoskeletal care, mental health practitioners—so workloads are manageable and high-quality care is maintained. Improve rostering, safe staffing levels and quality standards, and provide digital/remote options to widen coverage without compromising safety. In my area, partnerships between universities and GP practices have shown how trainees can support clinics while training; expanding these models would help recruit and retain staff across the system.

Living in England, I want a workforce plan that both grows the domestic supply of skilled primary care staff and looks after people who already work in the system. In practice, that means three interlocking priorities: building the pipeline of homegrown clinicians, making roles and pathways clear and safe, and protecting staff wellbeing so we can keep good people doing high‑quality care for the long term.

- Grow domestic supply with protected training and strong university‑practice links. I’d prioritise expanding places for undergraduate and postgraduate training, plus funded apprenticeships in primary care roles. Protected placements at the point of study—where students or trainees work in real GP and community settings with mentoring rather than being pulled into unrelated admin duties—should be standard. University‑practice partnerships can help ensure training matches what teams actually need in practice, from prescribing safely to team‑based care delivery. In my area, when training places were aligned with local clinics, I saw more trainees stay on as locums or staff after qualifying, which helped with continuity and safety.

- Clarify scope, support new roles and protect safety. Clear scope‑of‑practice boundaries, robust revalidation processes and appropriate indemnity arrangements are essential when we introduce more non‑GP clinicians (pharmacists, physiotherapists, physician associates, nurse prescribers, etc.). Fund protected clinical supervision for these roles so junior colleagues have reliable mentors and senior oversight. This isn’t about replacing GPs; it’s about expanding safe, appropriate tasks at the right level so patients are seen sooner and care is more coordinated. A practical example is a pharmacist embedded in a practice to review medicines for people on multiple drugs; with proper supervision and clear protocols, that reduces errors and frees GPs to focus on the most complex cases.

- Retain diverse staff through flexible working and supportive practices. We know burnout is a real issue, and retention hinges on more than pay. Flexible hours, part‑time options, job shares and phased retirement can broaden who stays in the workforce without compromising patient safety. Childcare support, predictable rostering, and proactive mental health services are not optional extras—they’re essential to keeping trained staff engaged and able to deliver high‑quality care consistently. In line with this, offering flexible career trajectories helps retain experienced nurses, therapists and other clinicians who might otherwise leave early.

- Invest in teams and practical measures that improve safety and access. The evidence from multidisciplinary teams is clear: when roles are well defined and supported by supervision, patient safety improves and waiting times reduce. My experiences in local clinics show how a pharmacist review can cut medication errors, and a physiotherapist lead on early musculoskeletal consults can shorten the path to treatment. To scale this, the workforce plan should fund protected supervision, clear team roles, and practical steps like shared training modules and joint appraisal systems so everyone knows how they contribute to safe care.

- Accountability, milestones and local implementation. A national plan needs local accountability: milestones for new training places, protected placements achieved, supervision capacity, and measurable improvements in wait times and safety indicators. Trusts should be encouraged to run pilots—testing flexible rosters, new scopes of practice, and supervision models—and share learning so successful approaches can be rolled out where they fit best.

Overall, I support an NHS workforce plan that grows the domestic supply of primary care staff through targeted training with protected placements and strong university‑practice partnerships, clarifies roles while protecting patient safety, and makes flexible working and wellbeing support a core part of retention. If these pieces are put together, we’ll not only recruit more people into primary care but also keep them delivering high‑quality, safe care for patients and their families over the long term.

I think any NHS workforce plan must do two things at once: grow the supply of skilled staff and protect their working conditions so patients receive safe, high-quality care. Prioritise expanding training pipelines across primary care: increase undergraduate medical and nursing places with guaranteed GP/primary-care placements, broaden postgraduate training in general practice, and create robust apprenticeship routes for healthcare assistants, AHPs and pharmacists. University–practice partnerships should fund protected placements and co-design curricula with frontline service needs, so new staff transition to confident, capable clinicians rather than chasing short-term slots.

Make planning transparent and localised. Develop robust workforce data, modelling and KPIs at regional and local levels, with clear evaluation frameworks. Use real‑time vacancy rates, turnover, patient wait times and safety indicators to guide funding, recruitment and retention strategies, and publish dashboards so practices and commissioners can anticipate shortages and intervene early.

Retention and wellbeing must be integral: protected supervision time, manageable workloads, clear career progression, mentoring, and reduced reliance on agency staff. Invest in non-digital access through adequate staffing for phone lines, reception, and community hubs so improvements aren’t undone when tech changes. In my area, stronger uni–practice links could help fill GP vacancies while keeping patient experience central.

A Brexit-era reality and the pressures of an aging population tell me we must plan our NHS workforce with care, balance and a long view. A workforce plan that recruits, retains and supports staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care should rest on several interlocking priorities, all tested against how they land on patients and communities.

- Grow the supply in a sustainable, people‑centred way. Expand training places across nursing, medicine, allied health and mental health; back return‑to‑practice routes and ongoing CPD so staff feel they can build a career here and stay. We’ve seen how a steady team, with members who have grown into their roles, delivers better continuity and confidence for patients. Practical steps include funded mentoring, structured career ladders, and decent facilities to prevent burnout.

- Ensure safe, high‑quality care through safe staffing and the right skill mix. This means clear staffing targets, reasonable workloads, protected time for complex cases, and strong clinical leadership at all levels. My own experience shows that shorter appointments and overworked teams undermine trust and the ability to manage chronic conditions well. A workforce plan should link staffing standards to patient outcomes and to the aim of longer first consultations for complex cases where needed.

- Recruit responsibly from overseas, with well‑designed integration. International recruitment can fill real gaps—especially in rural and coastal areas—if handled with safeguards. Streamlined visas and faster recognition of qualifications should be part of the package, but they must be paired with robust integration support: language assistance if needed, structured induction, mentoring, and access to local professional networks. It’s crucial that such recruitment does not deplete health systems in source countries. That might mean caps aligned to domestic training capacity, reciprocal arrangements, and investments that help those systems train their own staff.

- Make integration practical and lasting. New staff should have a clear path to accreditation and revalidation, not a revolving door of short postings. A buddy system, culturally aware supervision, and cross‑disciplinary team introductions can help with trust, safety and patient‑facing confidence. Integrated digital records and consent processes are essential so newcomers can see a patient’s history quickly without repeating work, thereby supporting continuity of care.

- Focus on retention through culture and conditions. Flexible rosters that protect rest, improved workspace and facilities, fair pay, and access to wellbeing and mental health support for staff are not luxuries—they’re the backbone of high-quality care. When staff feel valued, workloads are more manageable and training can be sustained. I’ve heard too many stories of talented clinicians leaving because the working environment becomes untenable; a plan that prioritises morale and professional development will pay dividends in patient outcomes.

- Target rural and community care with tailored packages. Recruitment should be matched with incentives for rural posts—relocation support, housing assistance, longer blocks of primary care provision, and the use of mobile clinics or telehealth hubs to bring services closer to people who struggle to travel. My own town benefited from a nurse‑led outreach clinic that reduced unnecessary trips and kept people out of hospital by offering regular checks locally; such models should be scaled and evaluated.

- Leverage technology to support staff and patients. Digital records, telemedicine, and robust triage pathways can reduce avoidable demand on scarce staff, freeing clinicians to focus on those who need hands‑on care. But technology must complement, not replace, humane, face‑to‑face care; training in digital competence should be part of onboarding for every new recruit.

- Measure, learn and adapt. A credible plan should pilot new staffing models in different settings, tracking patient outcomes, staff satisfaction and turnover. Feedback from patients—especially older adults and those with chronic conditions—must inform tuning of staffing levels, appointment lengths, and multidisciplinary pathways.

In short, the NHS workforce plan should balance expansion with protection of standards: more staff, but better support; more overseas recruitment, but with safeguards for source countries; longer, higher‑quality consultations where appropriate, enabled by adequate staffing; and a strong emphasis on retention through decent conditions, leadership, and professional fulfilment. If these elements work together, we can preserve the continuity and empathy that older patients value while delivering timely, safe, high‑quality care for everyone.

i strongly believe to ensure NHS recruitment, retention and high-quality care, the workforce plan must place people’s lives and wellbeing at the centre. Flexible and humane working patterns should be a cornerstone: more job-sharing, part-time roles, set-up of phased retirement, and better access to childcare support. When staff can balance family or caring responsibilities, burnout falls and turnover drops. In my experience, practices that offered flexible hours and supportive induction for international staff saw fewer vacancies and better morale. We must extend these options across all roles, with safe rosters and protected time for training.

Mental health and wellbeing cannot be an afterthought. Proactive services—on-site counselling, resilient-workshops, easy access to confidential support, and guaranteed time for peer supervision—help staff stay resilient and deliver safe care.

On recruitment, overseas hiring should be done responsibly: streamlined visas and recognition of qualifications, language and cultural induction, mentoring on arrival, and clear career pathways. This should be paired with safeguards to avoid draining health systems in source countries, including bilateral commitments and investing in training capacity abroad.

Finally, invest in development and leadership: robust induction, mentoring for all new staff, and targeted funding for CPD to keep skills sharp and leaders visible at the front line!

From my point of view as an older resident in England, a NHS workforce plan should do two things in tandem: actively attract staff to hard‑to‑staff areas and high‑demand roles, and make sure those staff can work safely, with the right support so the quality of care isn’t sacrificed in the rush to see more people. I’m not against competitive pay or incentives, but they must be part of a longer‑term, safety‑driven strategy that really changes how teams are built, supported and deployed.

Key priorities I would want to see:
- Targeted recruitment and relocation incentives that genuinely reach underserved areas
  - Competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to recruit GPs, district nurses, mental health professionals and first‑contact clinicians where shortages are real
  - Robust induction and mentorship so newcomers feel confident in local guidelines, cultures and the way teams actually work on the ground
  - A clear link between incentives and staying in post long enough to build stability and continuity for patients
- Safe staffing and continuity of care as core safeguards
  - Ensure safe staffing ratios and predictable rosters so patients aren’t short‑changed while trying to squeeze in more appointments
  - Continuity‑preserving models that reduce churn, with longer placements in teams where possible so patients see familiar staff and a consistent care plan
  - Ongoing safety monitoring and quality checks to ensure that access gains aren’t achieved at the expense of clinical standards
- Strong training, supervision and wellbeing support
  - Regular supervision, protected time for professional development and practical on‑the‑job training, especially for newly recruited staff from abroad or from other sectors
  - Wellbeing support, manageable workloads and flexible working where appropriate, so staff can maintain high standards without burning out
  - Clear career pathways and leadership development to help retain capable clinicians within the system
- Better workforce deployment and collaboration
  - Use primary care networks and integrated teams to deploy floating staff, urgent‑care slots and extended hours in a predictable way, so patients know where to go for same‑day problems
  - Faster onboarding for international recruits, with standardised induction and local governance checks, so they can contribute quickly without compromising safety
- Local accountability and transparent data
  - Local leaders should publish monthly data on wait times, staffing levels, and patient outcomes, with a clear plan to close gaps in underserved areas
  - Involve frontline staff in planning and governance so the plan reflects real day‑to‑day challenges and practical solutions

In practice, I’ve seen how gaps in staffing echo through the system. A neighbour needed a same‑day GP appointment for a chest infection, but the earliest slot was two weeks away. NHS111 sent him home to self‑care, which didn’t feel safe, and the later nurse assessment produced a fragmented care plan between primary care and community teams. A workforce plan that guarantees safer staffing levels and a reliable triage pathway could have redirected him sooner to the right clinician, with less stress and fewer handoffs.

Similarly, delays in talking therapies for mental health illustrate how access depends on robust, well‑staffed teams and clear handoffs. If we want to improve access without compromising quality, the plan must couple recruitment incentives with strong safety nets, supervision and monitoring that keep care at the standard patients expect.

So, in short: prioritise targeted, well‑funded recruitment and retention to address regional and specialty shortages, but couple that with a rigorous focus on safe staffing, continuity of care, staff wellbeing and transparent local accountability Obviously.... If the system can deliver both the people and the safety framework, we’ll see real improvements in timely access and quality care for all, including those of us who rely on it most.

A workforce plan should prioritise three things that align with how care is actually delivered and what reduces clinician burnout. First, cut unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. Streamline referrals and invest in user-friendly IT that shows real-time capacity and patient history so clinicians spend more time with patients, not chasing forms or chasing data. In my area, admin overload clearly eats into consultation time and delays care. Second, strengthen links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and enable holistic care. Shared care pathways and integrated dashboards would help co-ordinate appointments and avoid fragmented care. Third, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied staff—with clear supervision and governance. This would safely shift routine tasks away from GPs, freeing them for complex cases, while ensuring quality and safety. Around training, provide protected time for upskilling, structured mentorship and clear career progression, plus flexible working options to improve retention. Local examples show that when admin is reduced and teams collaborate across sectors, patients get timely, safe care and staff feel supported rather than overwhelmed.

From where I sit, an NHS workforce plan that prioritises real flexibility, strong training pipelines, and better integration with social care and community services will do the most to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality.

First, flexibility and humane working patterns are essential. My generation is increasingly juggling careers with family responsibilities, and rigid, traditional hours simply aren’t sustainable. The plan should promote flexible hours, part‑time arrangements, job‑shares and even phased retirement for highly experienced clinicians who want to reduce hours rather than leave altogether. Providing predictable, well‑designed rotas that still preserve continuity of care matters far more than the occasional extended shift. Practical examples I’d like to see include protected hours for family‑friendly shifts, on‑site or subsidised childcare, and access to flexible start and finish times. When staff can organise their schedules around life pressures, burnout falls and retention rises.

Second, a stronger emphasis on training and development will grow the domestic workforce and keep care local. We need more undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and genuine university‑practice partnerships. This isn’t about quick fixes; it’s about creating real career ladders in primary care, mental health and community settings. I’d like to see funded training pathways that allow student clinicians to work in primary care across all stages, with guaranteed practice placements in local networks. My impression is that where training posts are co‑funded by universities and practices, there’s a clearer line of sight from study to job, and new entrants feel valued from day one.

Third, we must move workload where it belongs and strengthen integration with social care, mental health and community services. Better joint funding and governance can reduce pressure on GPs and hospital services by distributing complex care more evenly. For example, if social care teams have access to the same shared care plans and digital tools as primary care, a lot of care coordination—such as discharge planning and home‑based support—can be handled out in the community. This not only improves patient experience, it also frees clinicians to focus on those cases that truly require medical expertise. In practice, I’ve seen smarter MDT working in local pilots where district nurses, social workers and GPs share access to the same client records and care milestones; it makes a real difference to timely interventions and avoids duplicated effort.

Fourth, wellbeing and mental health support for staff must be embedded into the plan. Proactive mental health services—counselling, resilience training, staff wellbeing days and rapid access to peer support—should be funded and normalised, not treated as an add‑on. If teams feel cared for and know help is readily available, the turnover caused by burnout falls and morale rises. This isn’t just about staff; it’s about safer, more compassionate patient care when someone in a team is struggling.

Fifth, safety and quality must be built into every change. Flexible staffing should come with robust workforce planning to avoid gaps and ensure safe ratios. I’d want to see transparent targets for staffing levels, clearer escalation routes when workloads spike, and strong governance so redesigned roles don’t dilute patient safety. Digital tools that help with rota planning, workload forecasting and cross‑site coverage could be part of the solution, as long as they are user‑friendly and protect time with patients, not just managers.

Finally, there should be a clear expectation that funding follows the patient, not the department. Sustainable workforce reform requires long‑term funding commitments—permanent training posts, shared funding for community services, and incentives for practices in areas with the greatest workforce pressure. In our local area, a few extra training posts or a joint fund for social care integration would have a tangible impact on whether a practice can offer extended hours without compromising safety or workload.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan should combine flexibility for staff, expanded homegrown training pipelines, and stronger, better‑funded links with social care and community services. If done right, we’ll retain our experienced clinicians, welcome a more diverse workforce, and deliver safer, more integrated care for patients. That would build resilience across the system and reduce reliance on urgent crisis responses, which benefits everyone involved.

I live in England and, as someone in my early 60s, I see that a stable NHS workforce is essential to safe, high‑quality care. The plan should prioritise multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding so trusts can recruit, train and retain staff without constant policy risk. This means adequate slots for regular supervision, CPD, and clear career pathways that reward long‑term service rather than short‑term contracts. 

Interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training must be central. A common, protected record so GPs, community teams and mental health services can share up‑to‑date information reduces duplication, supports early intervention and helps maintain continuity of care. However, we must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients—more phone and in‑person options so nobody is left behind. 

Workforce planning should address workload and wellbeing: safe staffing levels, protected admin time, manageable caseloads, and robust supervision. Practical examples I’ve seen include longer appointments for complex cases and joint care planning that travels with the patient. Finally, invest in crisis teams, talking therapies and community nurses in a way that keeps local teams stable and capable of delivering timely care.

I would like the NHS workforce plan to prioritise sustainable, long‑term funding and solid training pipelines, alongside modern, secure IT that staff actually find user‑friendly. Interoperable systems across GP practices, hospitals and community teams are essential, but they must come with proper staff training and strong protections for patients who are digitally excluded—phone and face‑to‑face options must stay available. A ring‑fenced, multi‑year funding settlement is crucial to avoid constant policy churn and to fund recruitment, training capacity and retention initiatives with real continuity.

From my experience of waiting for timely GP support, visible, ongoing investment in workforce development pays off in steadier, safer care: longer placements, better supervision, and the chance for clinicians to build lasting relationships with patients. We need more undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places in primary care, with protected placements and university‑practice partnerships to grow domestic supply.

Overall, invest in people, invest in reliable, secure systems, and guarantee a stable funding horizon so staffing can improve without compromising safety or care quality.

it's outrageous that i think an NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams to safely share GP workload, while keeping patient safety and high‑quality care at the core. This mirrors what I’ve observed locally and what would make services more accessible for young people like me who juggle study, work, and family commitments.

Key priorities I would support:

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: Let nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals play more active, well‑defined roles in primary care. For example, a nurse practitioner or PA could run same‑day triage, manage routine illnesses, review chronic conditions, and handle medication reviews in collaboration with a GP. A pharmacist embedded in a practice could lead med reconciliation and safety checks, reducing inappropriate prescriptions or drug interactions. Paramedics could do home visits for urgent but non‑life‑threatening issues, freeing up GPs for more complex cases. All roles would work within clear scopes of practice with robust supervision to ensure patient safety.

- Training, supervision and safety nets: These teams must be built with strong training pipelines, ongoing CPD, and protected supervision from GPs and senior clinicians. Clearly defined escalation pathways are essential so complex cases are promptly handed to the right clinician. Regular case reviews, joint clinics, and shared care plans would help maintain continuity, which I know from experience matters a lot for mental health and long‑term conditions.

- Localised recruitment and retention strategies: Develop local, practical routes into primary care roles—link universities and healthcare apprenticeships with GP practices, offer flexible working, affordable training, and clear progression. Supporting staff wellbeing and manageable workloads will be crucial to retaining talent in these new roles, so people aren’t pulled away by burnout or inadequate support.

- Transparent data, modelling and KPIs: Build and publish local workforce data with real‑time modelling and key performance indicators. This should cover vacancy rates, time to fill, turnover, and team composition, plus patient‑facing metrics like wait times, continuity of care, and safety indicators (medication safety, missed referrals). Evaluation frameworks would show what works, justify funding, and guide adjustments as needs shift in different communities.

- Integration and information sharing: MDTs must be able to share information securely and smoothly, so patients don’t experience fragmented care. Consistent documentation, joint care plans, and routine MDT reviews will support better decision‑making and reduce duplicated tests.

- Focus on access and equity: For me, the most important gain from MDT expansion is easier access for all, including those with language or transport barriers. An embedded team with multilingual staff and interpreters, plus a predictable schedule of same‑day slots, would help young people stay in education or work rather than missing appointments or waiting weeks for a referral.

Concrete examples would help validate these ideas: in a couple of local practices, introducing on‑site pharmacist and nurse‑led triage reduced GP appointment demand and improved safety checks on medications. A physician associate workforce pilot enabled faster triage and allowed GPs to concentrate on complex cases, with positive feedback from patients about quicker access and clearer information. When data dashboards were used to adjust staffing to peak times and patient cohorts, wait times and missed follow‑ups decreased.

Overall, I’d like to see a plan that clearly expands safe, supervised multidisciplinary teams, supported by local data and evaluation to fund what works and revise what doesn’t. If done well, this approach would preserve the quality and continuity of care I value, improve access for young people, and help keep GP workloads sustainable for the long term.

To recruit, retain and support staff while preserving safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan should balance three linked priorities: people, technology and inclusive access. First, invest in stable staffing with realistic workloads, clear career paths, flexible working options and robust wellbeing support, plus leadership development and multidisciplinary teams that can sustain local GP practices and community services. Second, build interoperable, secure IT as the backbone of care: real‑time access to shared records across primary, community, mental health and hospital services; consistent data standards and cybersecurity; and protected time for staff to train on these systems and adopt new workflows. In my view, training must be practical, ongoing and accompanied by change management so new tools actually save time and reduce errors, not add burden. Third, safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients: maintain non‑digital booking and triage channels, provide digital skills support and ready access to staff who can guide patients through new systems, and offer devices or offline options where needed. In practice, IT improvements must serve reliable, locally anchored services with clear care pathways; without that, tech upgrades can fragment care. This balanced approach supports retention and safe care.

I believe the NHS workforce plan must prioritise growing our own workforce through increased training places—undergrad, postgrad and apprenticeships—with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships. This is the most reliable way to increase local primary care capacity and reduce reliance on temporary staff. Practical steps include ring-fenced funding for GP and district nursing placements, extended placement durations, and collaboration campuses that place students in mixed primary and community teams. To keep people in the service, provide clear funded career pathways, protected CPD time, structured mentorship and return-to-practice schemes. Experienced clinicians should see real progression and recognition, while new staff get robust support to build confidence and competence. Also essential is better integration with social care, mental health and community services. Joint funding and aligned training can redistribute workload, support proactive care, and deliver a more holistic patient experience, especially in rural areas where staffing gaps bite. A plan that combines growth in training with cross-system collaboration will sustain safe, high-quality care.

I broadly support a NHS workforce plan that puts patient safety and high-quality care at its core, while making sure staff are recruited, retained and well supported. From what I’ve seen locally, it isn’t enough to add more bodies; we need clarity, safeguards and sustainable funding to stop a revolving door of locums, burnout and fragmented care. The plan should prioritise the following, anchored in real-world practice and ongoing evaluation.

- Clear scope-of-practice and governance for new and expanding roles: As we bring in roles like physician associates, pharmacists in primary care, physiotherapists and paramedics taking on more front-line work, there must be explicit, nationally aligned boundaries. When a clinician’s scope is ambiguous, miscommunication and delays creep in. Define what tasks can be done independently, what must be escalated to a GP, and what conditions require back-referral. Establish standardised referral pathways and risk thresholds so the patient’s journey is coherent regardless of who they see.

- Robust revalidation and protected CPD time: Continual competence matters as roles expand. Staff need protected time for annual appraisals, training and refresher courses. Revalidation processes should be streamlined and sympathetic to workload pressures, not add administrative burden that slows recruitment.

- Indemnity arrangements that don’t hinder recruitment or continuity: A clear, affordable indemnity framework is essential. If clinicians fear personal liability or high premiums, they’ll hesitate to embrace new responsibilities or stay in roles long enough to develop expertise. This needs to be system-wide and predictable, not negotiated case by case.

- Funded, protected clinical supervision for new roles: New and changing roles work best when there is ongoing supervision and mentoring from experienced clinicians. Fund regular, protected supervision time (1:1 or small groups), with supervisors who are appropriately trained. This supports patient safety, helps integrate new staff into teams, and reduces the risk of errors or silos.

- Safe staffing, workload management and burnout prevention: Plans should be driven by data on demand, predictability of peaks, and realistic job planning. Avoid relying on unpaid overtime or excessive hours. Build in return-to-practice schemes and flexible staffing that can respond to local fluctuations without compromising care quality.

- Clear career pathways and strong retention initiatives: Staff are more likely to stay if there are visible progression routes, opportunities to specialise, and recognition of experience. Local career ladders, mentorship, and rotation opportunities help spread expertise and prevent skills from stagnating.

- Integrated training pipelines with strong governance: Forge closer links with universities and primary-care training hubs to ensure new entrants are job-ready. Think apprenticeships and short placement rotations that embed safe practice from day one, with clear handoffs to GP leadership where needed.

- Digital literacy and governance: As care becomes more digital, ensure frontline teams are trained to use systems safely, share records securely, and follow standardised referral and escalation protocols. This reduces errors and improves patient experience.

- Wellbeing and psychologically safe culture: A workforce plan that also funds mental-health and wellbeing support, peer networks, and leadership development will help staff stay resilient and engaged, which in turn sustains care quality.

In practice, when a practice is understaffed or overreliant on locums, continuity of care and patient safety suffer. A well-funded plan that fixes scope, supervision, indemnity, and wellbeing—while providing robust training and clear career paths—would deliver safer, higher-quality care and improve staff morale. Relying on short-term fixes isn’t enough; we need durable structures and predictable investment so clinicians can focus on patients rather than navigating governance gaps.

For example, pathways for nurse practitioners, physician associates, and pharmacists to take on more responsibility in primary and community care would hel us free up GPs for complex cases. An NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable staffing alongside ensuring safe, high-quality care. I think the NHS workforce plan should be ambitious but balanced, prioritising both responsible overseas recruitment and stronger domestic training to keep care safe and high quality. Retention and wellbeing cannot be afterthoughts: supportive leadership, sustainable workloads, flexible scheduling where possible, meaningful CPD, and access to mental health support. Invest in training and clear career pathways to grow allied roles (nurse associates, advanced practitioners) so the workforce can share workload safely. Ensure staffing models are responsive to demand, with real-time workload data guiding staffing and safe patient loads.

From our work with young people across England, the NHS workforce plan should be seen as a long-term, joined-up strategy that keeps patients safe while building a resilient, motivated workforce. It isn’t just about filling posts; it’s about distributing workload more fairly across health and social care, mental health and community services so that every young person receives timely, high-quality care in the right setting.

Priorities we think matter most:
- Integrate and co-fund a whole-system workforce model. Strengthen links with social care, mental health services and community teams to share tasks that currently sit in NHS settings alone. Joint funding for blended posts, shared roles and common recruitment milestones can reduce bottlenecks and create smoother care pathways for families and schools. This should be backed by joint commissioning arrangements and clear referral routes so a young person isn’t bounced between services.
- Build and sustain long-term pipelines. Increase training places in medical, nursing and psychology/therapy training; expand return-to-practice packages with supervised placements; grow apprenticeships that combine on-the-job learning with study. Robust mentorship, protected CPD funding, and clear career progression help staff stay in the system and keep up-to-date with best practice.
- Tailored, place-based recruitment and retention. Deliver affordable housing and accessible transport support and targeted incentives for staff in hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities. Pair these with local recruitment drives, school and college partnerships, and clear pathways into lifelong careers to improve retention.
- Safe, high-quality care through sustainable staffing. Set and monitor safe staffing levels across all roles, avoid excessive workloads, provide strong supervision, and ensure manageable teams so staff can deliver compassionate care. Invest in extended-scope roles for nurses and allied health professionals, with robust governance and supervision frameworks.
- Multidisciplinary, colocated teams. Create multidisciplinary primary care and community teams that include GPs, nurses, pharmacists and mental health practitioners. When teams share back-office tasks and follow-up care, it frees clinicians to focus on urgent or complex cases and improves continuity for young people.
- Strong mental health and early-intervention capacity. Integrate mental health support within schools, colleges and community hubs, with rapid access to talking therapies and crisis response that can operate beyond standard hours where needed. This reduces escalation and keeps young people engaged with support that suits their daily lives.
- Smart use of technology, with a people-centred balance. Use online booking, triage tools and telehealth to reduce delays and reach hard-to-access groups, but preserve in-person assessments where contact matters. Data-driven scheduling can cut admin burden and free clinicians to see more patients, while maintaining safety and personalised care.
- Staff wellbeing and culture. Prioritise supportive leadership, manageable hours, safe environments and anti-bullying policies. Regular supervision, peer support, and recognition help retain staff, which in turn protects patient safety.
- Transparent data and learning loops. Build workforce dashboards showing vacancies, turnover, training uptake and patient outcomes. Publish targets and progress so trusts can learn from each other and scale what works.
- Co-design with young people. Involve patients and service users in planning appointment models, digital interfaces and crisis pathways. Real-world feedback will improve both access and the relevance of care.
- Clear delivery plans with evaluation. Start with scalable pilots that have explicit milestones, independent evaluation and a plan to roll out successful models. Local flexibility should be allowed to respond to demographic shifts without losing core standards.

In practice, a plan that aligns workforce growth with stronger cross-sector collaboration, predictable funding, and genuine involvement of young people will deliver safer, higher-quality care. It will also help us prevent burnout and retain the staff we need to keep pace with rising demand.

We recognise a need for any incentives to be carefully designed so they support staff who serve in the most challenging areas while ensuring quality and equality in care. Overall, the enduring message is simple: invest in people, invest in training and progression, and invest in partnerships that share the load so that care remains safe, modern and accessible for all young people.

i really think i think any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care has to be practical, well funded and clearly linked to how care is actually delivered in communities. Based on what I’m seeing locally and what colleagues tell me, there are three priorities that should be at the heart of any credible plan.

A jointly funded model—shared commissioning, aligned targets, and pooled budgets—would let teams work more holistically and keep people safe at home or in the right setting. We also need investment in digital supports—shared records, triage tools, and decision aids—so the right professional sees the patient first time. Finally, the plan must be data-driven and transparent. National targets should sit alongside local delivery plans with clear milestones and regular public reporting on progress and disparities between urban and rural settings and among different deprivation gaps. If we couple more integrated care with robust training pipelines, protected placements, and well-regulated MDTs, we can recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safety and high-quality care at the forefront.

I’m firmly in favour of a NHS workforce plan that prioritises three things that matter to me as a student and someone who wants to see faster, safer care: expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams, using clear local data to plan and fund services, and ensuring safe staffing ratios with continuity of care. These elements feel practical and aligned with what actually helps patients get timely help without compromising quality.

First, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams. I’ve seen in practice how much GP workloads can slow things down when a clinician is juggling too many roles. If we can properly train and supervise a broader mix of staff—nurses, nurse prescribers, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics, and other allied health professionals—and clearly define what they can and cannot do, it would let GPs focus on the most complex cases. This isn’t “more bodies” for the sake of it; it’s about safe redistribution of tasks so people can book same-day or next-day slots and get seen by the right professional first time. In campus and local clinics, where students often struggle to fit appointments around lectures and shifts, having a nurse practitioner for triage, a pharmacist co-managing stable medicines, and a PA handling minor acute issues can cut queue times dramatically. That also needs robust supervision and ongoing training—so these roles can grow, renew skills, and feel valued rather than treated as stopgaps. I’d like to see clear career pathways and apprenticeship routes into these roles, with shared training standards across trusts to avoid regional patchiness.

Second, develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs. If we don’t know where vacancies or bottlenecks are, we can’t fix them. Local dashboards should track staff mix, vacancy and turnover rates, training vacancies, patient wait times by pathway, and outcomes tied to specific teams (for example, same-day access in GP, CAMHS responsiveness, and pharmacist-led chronic-disease management). Importantly, these metrics should be reported publicly and used to shape investment—so communities can see progress and areas still needing attention. I’d want universities and health boards to collaborate on data collection—partnering with student welfare services and local VCSEs to capture demand patterns (evenings, weekends, term-time peaks) and model staffing accordingly. When the plan is transparent and well-evaluated, it’s easier to justify sustainable funding and to adjust approaches if something isn’t working.

Third, prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models with safety monitoring. It’s not enough to add more people if they’re not deployed safely or are constantly moved between sites. Safe staffing means predictable rosters, adequate nurse and support staff levels, protected time for training, and backfill that doesn’t erode care quality. Continuity—seeing the same clinician where possible—builds trust and reduces errors; it also makes it easier to manage long-term conditions, mental health follow-ups, and safeguarding. If a practice uses stable teams, with shared IT systems and joint care plans, patients are less likely to have to retell their story and more likely to receive timely, integrated care. I’ve witnessed how staff burnout and high vacancy rates ripple into longer waits and lower morale; a workforce plan that safeguards staffing levels and supports career development would help recruit and retain people, particularly in hard-to-staff specialties and in community settings.

Practical steps I’d like to see include: regular, local workforce modelling to anticipate demand; ring-fenced, long-term funding for expanded teams and for hubs that bring GP, nursing, mental health and pharmacy services under one roof; governance that enables shared appointment systems and joint care plans; and public reporting of workforce metrics alongside patient outcomes. It’s also vital that the plan is co-designed with frontline staff, trainees and, where possible, students so it fits what actually works in real life, not just in theory.

Taken together, these priorities would help deliver timely, high-quality care without burning out staff or compromising safety. In short: empower and regulate a broader, well-supported multidisciplinary workforce; base decisions on transparent local data; and protect staffing levels and continuity to keep care safe and effective as access improves.

This approach supports our goals of extended access and reducing GP workload, while keeping care safe and person‑centred.

For example, when a patient is at risk of escalation, a jointly funded care coordinator could mobilise home support, reducing hospital admissions and freeing up GPs to focus on complex cases.

- Expanded, well-supported roles and clear progression. Increasing the number of GPs is important, but we also need more nurses with advanced scope of practice, physician associates, pharmacists in primary care, and allied health professionals who can run short yet effective clinics for common conditions. Providing protected time for training, mentorship and accredited CPD ensures staff feel valued and stay in the system rather than leaving for private sector or burnout.

- Safer staffing, with predictable, sustainable rosters. Flexible patterns that align with real-life needs – early starts, evenings and some weekend work – are essential, but must come with safe patient-to-staff ratios, adequate admin time, and robust supervision. - Local flexibility with long-term funding. Staffing needs differ by place: rural areas, coastal towns, and urban neighbourhoods all have distinct pressures. - Wellbeing, safety and culture. Burnout is a real driver of turnover. Plan should include accessible mental health support for staff, safe working environments, reasonable workloads, and a culture that values team well-being as much as clinical outcomes.

- Equity in staffing. The plan should explicitly address barriers that deter people from entering or staying in NHS roles, including flexible working for carers, language and cultural awareness training for teams, and recruitment from diverse communities to reflect the patient base.

In my own area, I’ve seen how a more integrated approach could ease pressures. When a patient’s social needs are met by a care worker or district nurse coordinating with a GP, it frees clinicians to concentrate on complex conditions. It also reduces repeated visits and the churn of short-term fixes. If these workforce principles are embedded in policy and funded for the long term, we’ll move closer to safe, high-quality care that treats people holistically rather than as separate parts of the system.

Patient and carer voices should shape workforce decisions, particularly around working hours, transport, and community services that influence access to timely care.

In short, a sustainable NHS workforce plan should recruit and retain staff through supportive leadership, clear roles, and continuous learning; use ethical, well-managed overseas recruitment where appropriate; unlock productivity with interoperable technology while protecting access for digitally excluded patients; and fund supervised practice to keep care safe as we introduce new roles. I’d favour long‑term rosters where a small group of GPs, nurses, and allied health professionals share responsibility for a patient cohort, with clear handover processes and shared records. Where staff are redeployed or cover is needed, that should be managed to protect continuity rather than fragment care.

Safety monitoring must underpin every expansion. Real‑time data on safety indicators, timely incident reporting, audits of triage decisions, and patient feedback should be standard. For mental health and urgent non‑emergency needs managed by telehealth or mobile teams, we need dashboards to flag trends, near misses, and gaps in access that could compromise safety. Regular clinical governance reviews should be paired with patient experience data to ensure that newly introduced roles or sites are not just accessible, but safe for all users.

Scope of practice, revalidation, and indemnity matter. As roles broaden, we need clear, published scopes of practice so staff know what they can do, who supervises them, and how decisions are escalated. Revalidation must keep pace with new tasks—especially for nurse prescribers, physiotherapist independent prescribers, pharmacists in GP hubs—and be supported by protected time. Indemnity arrangements should be explicit and affordable, including for staff in mobile or community settings. Too often, fear about liability limits timely care; a predictable indemnity framework will encourage clinicians to take on flexible, locally responsive roles without compromising patient safety.

Funded protected clinical supervision is critical to support new and expanding roles, particularly in rural or underserved areas. Regular supervision, mentoring, and case discussions—whether in person or remotely—help clinicians translate training into safe practice and reduce the risk of errors. If a pharmacist starts prescribing in a rural clinic or a nurse takes on extended nursing roles, there should be scheduled supervision with an experienced clinician, with follow‑up review of prescribing decisions and patient outcomes.

In addition, invest in training and career pathways that keep people in the workforce rather than driving them away. Local training hubs, supported supervision, and clear progression routes (including return‑to‑practice schemes for those who’ve stepped back) will help attract and retain staff in rural settings, where shortages are most acute.

Putting these elements together means access improvements don’t come at the expense of safety or quality. A workforce plan that prioritises safe staffing, continuity of care, and rigorous safety monitoring—coupled with clear scopes, reliable indemnity, and funded supervision—would give communities confidence that expanded access is real, sustainable and patient‑centred.

Overall, I’m in favour of prudent expansion that treats staffing and safety as inseparable from service design. If we get the people side right, the benefits for timely, local and high‑quality care will follow.

A robust NHS workforce plan must prioritise stability, clarity and targeted incentives so staff can deliver safe, high‑quality care now and in the longer term. From our experience supporting rural and underserved communities, the following priorities are essential.

- Long‑term, ring‑fenced funding and workforce planning capacity. Stability at scale is needed to grow training places, run return‑to‑practice schemes, and fund ongoing workforce development without shifting policy direction every year. Multi‑year settlements for primary care, mental health and community teams enable sensible service design, longer‑term recruitment targets and the retention of skilled staff in hard‑to‑fill roles.

- Clear scope of practice, revalidation and protected clinical supervision. To support new and expanding roles (such as nursing associates, physician associates, and advanced nurse practitioners), we need well defined boundaries, consistent revalidation timelines, and funded, protected supervision. This helps maintain patient safety while allowing teams to evolve with local needs. Indemnity arrangements must be clarified and funded so clinicians can work with confidence across settings.

- Targeted, competitive pay and progression incentives for underserved areas. To attract and retain staff in rural or high‑demand specialties, offer relocation packages, retention payments, bursaries for students from those areas, return‑to‑practice incentives, and flexible career pathways. These should be time‑bound but tied to longer‑term career development so staff can commit to staying in place.

- Expanded training capacity and local pipelines. Increase local training placements in general practice, community health, mental health, and district‑level care, with strong links to universities and research partners. Invest in multi‑disciplinary training hubs, simulation facilities, and early exposure to integrated care so graduates are ready for the realities of teamworking in co‑located hubs.

- Flexible, sustainable workforce models with strong multi‑disciplinary teams. Encourage flexible staffing, cross‑training, and clear role boundaries within teams (GPs, nurses, pharmacists, social care workers, VCSE staff) to optimise capacity. Allocate protected time for supervision, quality improvement, and continuing professional development so high standards are maintained even in busy periods.

- Focus on staffing safety and wellbeing. Set safe staffing targets, monitor workload, provide confidential wellbeing support, and implement mechanisms to reduce burnout. Adequate rest periods, access to mental health support, and reasonable on‑call expectations are essential for quality care and staff retention.

- Data‑driven, localised workforce planning. Use real‑time, locality‑level data to forecast demand, track vacancy and turnover rates, and evaluate the impact of recruitment incentives. Regularly review metrics like time‑to‑fill, staff vacancies by role, and patient safety indicators to adjust plans quickly.

- Housing, transport and practical supports. For rural areas, link workforce planning to housing, transport, and local infrastructure so staff can relocate or commute reliably. Targeted packages can reduce one of the biggest barriers to recruitment in these areas.

- Clear career pathways and inclusive progression. Provide transparent pathways from entry roles through to senior clinical positions, with support for upskilling, mentoring and opportunities to work across settings. This strengthens retention and builds a resilient local workforce.

In practice, a plan that combines these elements—with co‑located multi‑disciplinary teams, supported by robust supervision and stable funding—will better sustain safe, high‑quality care. For example, a rural hub staffed by GPs, nurse prescribers, mental health professionals and social care staff could rely on a ring‑fenced training fund and a relocation package to attract clinicians, while a formal supervision framework and indemnity backing ensure patient safety. By aligning funding, governance and career development with local need, we can reduce turnover, improve staff morale and, ultimately, deliver more timely and integrated care for patients.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving care models, with ongoing safety monitoring to ensure access improvements do not erode clinical quality. This means explicit limits on workloads, transparent staffing dashboards, and protected time for supervision and training. It also requires robust mechanisms to maintain care continuity—stable teams, effective handover protocols and local decision-making to avoid churn that harms outcomes. 

We should strengthen links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and support holistic patient care. This would include integrated discharge planning, shared back-office functions and pooled recruitment funds so teams can be built where they are most needed, rather than in silos. 

Targeted recruitment incentives are essential: competitive pay, retention bonuses, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles (specialists, mental health nurses and allied health professionals). While offering these, ensure clear career progression and supportive supervision to retain staff long term. 

From experience in my area: a relative waited several weeks for CBT; extended-hours GP slots and crisis teams would reduce escalation. Transition to community hubs and digital tools must be paired with options for those without digital access. Transparent milestones will help maintain trust.

From a rural Scotland viewpoint, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise stable, multi-year funding and ring-fenced allocations that enable sustained workforce initiatives, expanded training capacity and reduced policy volatility. Short-term budgets drive dependence on agency staff and make long‑term planning untenable for small practices. A credible plan would fund more nursing, GP and allied health training places, expand placements in rural areas, and provide predictable career pathways so people stay rather than move away. 

Overseas recruitment should be used responsibly: streamlined visa routes for essential roles, rapid credential recognition, structured integration support (induction, language training, mentoring) and robust safeguards to avoid depleting health systems in other countries. In practice, this means clear return-on-investment timelines, ethical recruitment codes, and shared capacity-building with source countries. 

Retention must be at the heart of any plan: improved staffing-to-patient ratios, safer workloads, flexible working arrangements, and strong professional development and supervision, especially in remote communities. We also need investment in digital workflow tools and telehealth where appropriate, so scarce staff can care for more patients without compromising safety. In my experience, stable funding and clear career pipelines would transform local access and care quality, reducing reliance on short‑term fixes.

I support a NHS workforce plan that recognises the realities of rural Scotland and the pressures on GPs, community and mental health teams. It should prioritise interoperable IT and secure systems paired with comprehensive staff digital training, while safeguarding non-digital channels for digitally excluded patients. This means shared patient records across primary and community care, robust cyber-security, and regular refreshers so staff can use telehealth, e-prescribing and triage safely. Practical setups like telehealth hubs in villages, plus strong back-up options (phone triage, home visits) are essential as a safety net.

Flexible working patterns are also critical: more part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, and proactive childcare and mental health support to reduce burnout and keep a diverse workforce. In rural areas, rigid hours drive staff away; adaptable schedules help retain experienced clinicians while welcoming new talent.

Clear, funded career pathways matter too: protected CPD time, formal mentorship, return‑to‑practice schemes, and structured progression for nurses, therapists and doctors. These create a credible route for both experienced clinicians and early‑career staff, improving retention and care quality.

Finally, targeted recruitment incentives for rural areas, sustainable training budgets, and proactive succession planning are necessary to sustain safe, high-quality care during workforce pressures. The combination of tech, flexibility and clear development pathways aligns with better patient access and outcomes in my experience.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe, high‑quality care by ensuring there are enough staff in GP, community and mental‑health services to reduce delays and avoid burnout. Overseas recruitment can help, but it must be responsible. Use streamlined visas and fast‑track credential recognition, but couple this with strong integration support: language preparation, local induction, mentoring, and protected time for onboarding. Put safeguards in place to avoid draining source countries’ health systems, for example ethical recruitment caps, regular impact reviews and adherence to international codes.

At the same time, invest in domestic capacity: longer‑term training pipelines, expanded numbers on medical and nursing degree routes, better careers development and progression, and improved retention through fair pay, flexible and predictable rostering, and staff wellbeing. On‑boarding and supervision should be robust, with clear career paths and access to continuing professional development so new staff can work in integrated care pathways and with shared medical records.

From my experience, shortages in my area mean longer waits, higher stress for existing teams, and inconsistent care. Bridging programmes for internationally trained staff and easy routes to practice in primary care would help, but only if paired with real workforce planning, adequate funding, and safe staffing targets.

Prioritise stronger links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and sustain holistic patient care - what a surprise. Also target competitive pay, retention bonuses, relocation packages and bursaries to attract and retain staff in underserved and high-demand areas.

Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models, with robust safety monitoring, so expanding access never sacrifices quality. Focus on sustainable workforce planning, targeted recruitment with real workload limits, and ongoing support for staff well-being to sustain high standards of care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan should prioritise stronger links with social care, mental health and community services, funded jointly so workload is redistributed and patients get holistic care closer to home. Practical steps: a single, shared IT platform and streamlined referral routes to cut duplication; multi-disciplinary teams with a care coordinator to navigate patients through services; more community and practice-based roles (nurse practitioners, physiotherapists, pharmacy support) integrated with GPs; targeted training and clear career progression; fair, predictable workloads; flexible staffing to cover sickness and maternity without compromising access; improved supervision and mentoring for junior clinicians to reduce burnout; recruitment incentives in undersupplied areas; long-term funding for back-office support to reduce admin burden. Also: remove unnecessary targets and paperwork that pull clinicians from patients; better IT usability and decision support to speed up safe, appropriate decisions. With these in place, clinicians can focus on continuity of care, longer appointments for complex cases, and better outcomes.

From my perspective as a resident in Scotland, any NHS workforce plan must start by securing safe, stable staffing levels across primary care, community health and mental health, with practical incentives that actually help people choose to work and stay in hard-to-fill places. In rural, coastal and urban deprived areas, the recruitment and retention challenge is not just about wages; it’s about housing, transport, predictable rotas and genuine career progression. Here’s what should be prioritised to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining high-quality care.

- Prioritise safe, sustainable staffing as the foundation. Develop demand-led workforce models that set realistic targets for GP teams, district nursing, mental health professionals and allied roles, with funded, long-term posts rather than reliance on short-term locums. In my area, vacancies and stretched rotas push staff to breaking point and push patients to emergency care; predictable staffing reduces that pressure and improves safety.

- Tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas. Create targeted packages for rural, coastal and urban deprived communities that address the realities people face when moving to work there. This should include housing support (e.g., affordable housing, relocation allowances or housing priority for NHS staff), transport assistance (travel subsidies, reliable public transport schemes, and safe car-sharing options), and flexible working arrangements (job shares, predictable rotas, part-time options) to accommodate family and caring responsibilities.

- Build and sustain local training pipelines. Invest in local training and apprenticeships that bring students into the communities where they’ll work. Expand multidisciplinary roles within primary care (pharmacists conducting medication reviews, physiotherapists managing common musculoskeletal issues, paramedics or physician associates handling triage). Provide funded placements for medical and nursing students in rural/coastal practices, robust return-to-practice pathways, and protected time for CPD so staff can progress rather than stagnate.

- Strengthen multidisciplinary teams with clear governance. MDTs should be the norm, not the exception, with well-defined scopes of practice, supervision, and protocols so patients are seen quickly by the right professional. Where pharmacist-led reviews or nurse-led clinics have been introduced, patient outcomes improved and GP workloads fell; these models need wider rollout with proper training and oversight.

- Protect and promote wellbeing. Workloads must be manageable, with safe staffing levels, access to mental health support, and supportive leadership. Provide regular well-being check-ins, debrief opportunities after difficult cases, and recognition for frontline staff. Burnout is a real risk and undermines both safety and morale.

- Ensure digital tools complement, not replace, human care. Digital scheduling, triage and remote consultations can help, but must be paired with non-digital routes for those who are digitally excluded. Invest in community hubs with digital access, staff to assist navigation, and flexible in-person slots for those who need them. Practical examples include public helpdesks, mobile clinics and transport support to keep services accessible.

- Foster strong links with local communities and authorities. Align NHS workforce planning with housing, transport, schooling and local economic development so staff can settle long-term. Local recruitment festivals, “grow-your-own” schemes through schools and universities, and clear integration support for international hires will improve retention if the living environment is viable.

- Transparent targets and accountability. Publish clear progress against staffing KPIs, involve patients and frontline staff in design, and maintain ring-fenced funding for staffing and training initiatives. If money is released without guardrails, improvements won’t last.

In practice, a plan built on these priorities would begin correcting the root causes of vacancies and turnover rather than merely mitigating their symptoms. In my area, a small package of housing support, a relocated nurse to a coastal clinic, and a pharmacist-led review service could together transform access and safety. This is not about resisting technology; it’s about ensuring that digital tools are deployed where they’ll actually help, while the human infrastructure is strong enough to sustain safe, compassionate care.

From years living in rural Scotland, I know the NHS workforce plan must do more than promise short-term fixes. It should secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding specifically for recruitment, training and retention so teams can grow together and stay stable. That means expanding GP registrar places and practice nurse training, but also investing in mental health professionals, pharmacists and allied health professionals who can work in primary care. Homes, relocation grants and flexible working arrangements are essential so staff aren’t pushed away by the barriers of rural posts.

The plan should fund practical measures: protected clinical supervision, clear career pathways and interdisciplinary teams with robust wellbeing and workload management to prevent burnout. Training capacity must be expanded so we can train the next generation locally rather than relying on short-term allocations. Telehealth and digital support should complement, not replace, staff, with clear governance and adequate admin support.

Crucially, funding must be long-term and predictable to allow local services to design sustainable models—whether mobile clinics, hub services or co-located teams—while safeguarding patient safety and choice.

From what I’ve seen in our area, a NHS workforce plan that genuinely works will focus on three big things: making it easier for staff to do their jobs well, expanding and supporting multidisciplinary teams so care isn’t bottlenecked at the GP, and making digital systems reliable while still being inclusive for patients who can’t use online channels.

- Interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training: We need a single, secure digital backbone that all primary care teams can use so notes, tests and care plans flow smoothly between GPs, pharmacists, physiotherapists, nurses, and paramedics. When a pharmacist can see the patient’s latest red‑flag symptoms, or a nurse can review a patient’s meds at the same time as a GP, the patient gets a safer, faster service. It’s vital that this works for everyone, including people who aren’t digitally savvy or don’t have good internet access. That means protected non‑digital pathways and staff who can help patients navigate online channels. Ongoing digital training for all staff should be funded and built into roles, not treated as an extra task.

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: I’ve seen the benefits when practices bring in pharmacists for medication reviews, physiotherapists for back pain, and physician associates to handle routine tasks. It helps reduce GP workload so complex cases get the attention they deserve. Any workforce plan should set clear standards for MDT roles, supervision, and career progression, plus safe staffing levels so no one is overloaded. We also need structured return‑to‑practice routes and ongoing CPD so new and returning staff feel confident taking on more responsibility over time. International recruitment can help, but it must include robust language training and integration support.

- Streamline admin, reduce unproductive workload: A lot of time is eaten up by duplicative admin, redundant paperwork and convoluted referrals. The plan should prioritise simpler referral pathways, better IT usability, and less clerical burden for clinicians, so more time is available for patients. That doesn’t mean lowering safety or accountability; it means making the system easier to navigate and ensuring front‑line staff aren’t blocked by needless processes.

- Training, pipelines and career development: Expand training numbers across general practice and allied roles, with funded placements in local surgeries and protected time for supervision. Return‑to‑practice schemes should be well funded because bringing people back into the workforce is cheaper and quicker than starting from scratch. Apprenticeships and mid‑career CPD help refresh skills and bring fresh perspectives. When staff can see a clear route for progression, more people stay long‑term rather than moving to other sectors.

- Flexible working, wellbeing and safe staffing: Flexible patterns, job sharing and part‑time routes with clear progression help attract a broader workforce and reduce burnout. Strong wellbeing support—supervision, mental health resources, reasonable workloads—must be built into every team. Ensuring safe staffing levels, with real‑time data to monitor workload, will protect care quality even when demand spikes.

- Local leadership and patient involvement: The plan should support local leaders to innovate—pilot new MDT configurations, measure what works, and scale successful models. Patients should have a say in how services are staffed and scheduled; visible improvements in timeliness and continuity will reinforce trust in the system.

In short, a workforce plan that prioritises interoperable IT and staff training, expands well‑supported multidisciplinary teams, and removes needless admin while protecting flexible working and wellbeing is the best way to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality. The examples we’ve started to see in our area—pharmacists handling reviews, physiotherapists front‑lining musculoskeletal care, and extended hours—show this approach can work. It will take steady funding, strong governance and national backing, but with sensible pilots and robust evaluation, we can make primary care responsive to both staff and patients.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while safeguarding high-quality care, the workforce plan should prioritise a few linked, practical priorities. First, safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models so experienced clinicians lead care as access expands, minimising risky handoffs. Second, flexible working options—part-time roles, job-shares, phased retirement—and practical supports like childcare and proactive mental health services for staff to reduce burnout and attract a more diverse workforce, including those balancing study or caring responsibilities.
