Third, secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements that fund recruitment pipelines, ongoing training capacity and staff development, and dampen policy volatility that erodes morale and planning confidence. Fourth, robust training, mentorship and supervision with clear progression pathways, so staff can grow within local hubs and communities we already work with. Fifth, strong safety monitoring and data-driven workforce analytics to ensure access gains don’t compromise quality, with frontline feedback and patient voices informing adjustments. Finally, prioritise local recruitment and alignment with co-located hub models, digital access and privacy protections.

From our experience with engaging young people, flexible, well-supported staffing is key to stability; long-term funding is essential to sustain improvements without sacrificing safety and standards.

absolutely i support a plan that prioritises fair pay and retention payments, relocation assistance, and bursaries to attract staff to underserved areas; responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas and credential recognition; and expansion and regulation of multidisciplinary teams to safely share GP workload with proper training and supervision!

Prioritise clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation and indemnity, and fundedd protected clinical supervision for new roles to safeguar patient safety. Deliver tailored incentives for rural, urban-deprived and coastal areas, plus housing and transport support; fund transparent career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes.

From my position as a resident in England, with experience watching how the system responds to rising demand and growing workforce pressures, I think an NHS workforce plan must prioritise three core strands: robust, interoperable digital infrastructure with sensible safeguards; flexible, wellbeing-centered working patterns to attract and retain staff; and strong, well-supported training pipelines that grow the domestic primary care workforce. All of this needs to be delivered in a way that keeps patients safe, preserves high-quality care, and recognises that not everyone can or wants to engage with digital solutions.

First, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, underpinned by comprehensive staff digital training. Staff should be able to share information quickly and securely across GP practices, community teams, and mental health services so care is continuous rather than fragmented. In practice, that means unified patient records with clear consent processes and robust data governance, so people don’t have to repeat their story to every clinician. It also means user-friendly systems that actually support clinicians rather than add to their workload. At the same time, we must safeguard alternatives for those who are digitally excluded—older residents, those with limited internet access, or patients who are uncomfortable with online portals. Paper-based options or telephone triage must remain available, with clear pathways to digital access when and where appropriate. I’ve seen national rollouts of online booking and triage work well in some places, but in others they create new barriers for particular groups; a one-size-fits-all approach would be a mistake.

Second, prioritise flexible hours, part-time and job-share roles, phased retirement, and strong mental health and childcare support to help retain a diverse workforce and reduce burnout. Burnout isn’t just about long days; it’s about predictable workloads, decent time off, and the capacity to balance personal life with professional duties. Flexible working patterns also help attract a broader range of candidates, including those who may want to continue contributing after retirement or those with caring responsibilities. I’ve spoken to local staff who valued childcare support and mental health services on site or through employer arrangements, which made a real difference to retention. A plan that offers flexible rotas, protected staffing levels, and accessible mental health supports will help keep experienced nurses, GPs, and allied health professionals in the service instead of choosing earlier retirement or leaving the NHS altogether.

Third, expand training opportunities—undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeships—with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships. Building a sustainable pipeline for primary care work means more domestic students entering training, with guaranteed hands-on placements that align with real community needs. I would like to see extended use of apprenticeship routes into nursing, physician associate roles, and clinical pharmacist positions, all with clear progression routes. Protected placements help learners gain confidence in community settings and in cross-disciplinary teamwork, which aligns with the goal of integrated, co-located hubs I’ve advocated for previously. A well-funded strategy here would reduce reliance on international recruitment in the long term and build a workforce that understands local communities.

Beyond these three strands, the plan must emphasise safe staffing levels and realistic workload planning, with strong leadership development and supportive line management. A culture that values staff wellbeing, gives teams autonomy within safe guardrails, and offers constructive professional development will improve care quality and patient safety. It also needs to address recruitment and retention from a regional perspective—rural areas, small towns, and urban neighbourhoods each have distinct workforce challenges; solutions must be tailored and funded accordingly.

In practice, this means clear milestones, long-term funding streams, and governance that doesn’t rinse and repeat pilots every couple of years. It also means involving patients and carers in workforce design so that care remains personal and continuous, not merely process-driven. My experience suggests that when IT works alongside strong human support, when staff can flex to meet demand, and when training pipelines feed the system with capable, motivated people, safer and higher-quality care follows.

Overall, I would endorse a workforce plan that is technologically smart but human-centered, flexible yet stable, and forward-looking in training and development while protecting those who still rely on non-digital routes to access care.

Prioritise funded career paths with protected CPD, structured mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain staff; combine this with targeted competitive pay, retention bonuses, relocation packages and bursaries to attract people to underserved areas, ensuring safe, high-quality care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise three linked aims to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care. First, free clinicians to spend time with patients by cutting unnecessary targets, reducing duplicated paperwork, and streamlining referrals. IT must be intuitive and interoperable across primary, secondary and social care, with practical on‑the‑ground support to help older staff use new systems. In rural areas, where admin time can swallow hours, simplifying workflows is essential. Second, secure multi‑year, ring‑fenced funding for training and recruitment. This means expanded GP, nursing and allied health professional training posts, longer‑term pipelines with universities, and protected time for supervision and professional development to avoid sudden policy shifts derailing progress. Third, strengthen integrated care by aligning social care, mental health and community services through joint funding and shared roles, such as discharge coordinators and multidisciplinary teams that share responsibility for caseloads and outcome measures. Fourth, improve working conditions and wellbeing: safe staffing levels, flexible rosters, supervision, decent rest periods and clear career progression to reduce burnout. Fifth, tailor local delivery: develop rural and underserved area career ladders with supported outreach and digital tools to widen recruitment and retention. This holistic approach reflects our experience that reducing admin, ensuring stable investment and enabling cross‑sector collaboration deliver safer, higher‑quality care for patients.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding training capacity across undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship routes, with protected placements and robust university-practice partnerships to grow domestic primary care supply. Training must run alongside service delivery, not in isolation—this means funded, protected time for supervision, appraisal and mentorship, and clear career progression paths. Practical steps include increasing funded places in medical, nursing and allied-health professional programmes, with guaranteed practice placements, including in underserved areas; expanding apprenticeship routes that combine on-the-job learning with academic study; and creating regional pipelines linking schools, colleges and universities to local GP practices. Equally important are investments in workforce support: flexible working, good staffing ratios, ongoing professional development, and access to wellbeing and supervision resources; language and cultural competency training; and targeted incentives to retain staff in areas with higher needs. This should be backed by transparent workforce planning data to ensure quality is not sacrificed for numbers.

From my experience in our area, a successful NHS workforce plan has to do more than just promising more staff. It needs to set out practical, people-centred foundations that actually keep patients safe while enabling clinicians to work effectively. With that in mind, I’d prioritise the following:

- Clear scope-of-practice and governance for new and expanded roles. When we introduce roles like physician associates, clinical pharmacists, or nurse practitioners into primary care, we must define exactly what they can and cannot do, how they work within teams, and how supervision and escalation work. Ambiguity creates risk, delays, and poor patient experience. A transparent framework helps staff feel confident and patients receive consistent care.

- Robust revalidation tied to patient safety. Revalidation processes must be practical and proportionate, so capable staff aren’t pushed into bureaucracy for bureaucracy’s sake. We should fund protected time for ongoing appraisal and learning, with clear links to measurable quality and safety outcomes. Where revalidation acts as a barrier, it undermines morale and retention.

- Indemnity arrangements that are clear and affordable. The cost and complexity of indemnity can deter new roles and deter experienced staff from taking on broader responsibilities. A plan should guarantee affordable, predictable indemnity cover linked to role requirements, with clear guidance on when additional coverage is needed for complex procedures or new scopes of practice.

- Funded, protected clinical supervision for new and existing roles. Introducing new roles or expanding duties must be supported by supervision that protects patients and supports staff development. This means protected time for supervisors, formal triage and escalation pathways, and a governance framework that monitors safety, not just activity. In practice, pilots fail when supervision is patchy or inconsistent across sites.

- A strong education and training pipeline with protected placements. If we want more domestic primary care staff, we must expand undergraduate, postgraduate, and apprenticeship places and guarantee protected clinical placements in primary care. Universities and NHS bodies should be required to partner in long-term placements, with funding that recognises the cost of supervision, placement supervision, and real-world practice experience. This should include wider access for local recruits to improve geographic balance and retention.

- Structured career pathways and retention incentives. A plan should outline clear routes for progression within primary care, with predictable CPD opportunities, leadership training, and options to move between roles without losing seniority or pay. Adequate staffing must accompany career development to avoid trained staff leaving after short stints in new roles.

- Workforce planning that addresses distribution and workload. We need to balance expansion with sustainable workload and safe staffing ratios, ensuring rural and deprived areas aren’t left behind. This includes flexible training models and supportive arrangements for staff wellbeing, including reasonable hours, access to onsite childcare where possible, and practical transport solutions for those in remote locations.

- Integration of non-clinical roles to free up clinicians for complex cases. Pharmacists, social prescribers, and allied health professionals should be integrated into primary care teams with defined scopes, supported by supervision and governance rather than used as stopgaps. This helps maintain safety while expanding access.

In short, a credible NHS workforce plan should couple ambitious expansion with solid protections: clear scopes, dependable revalidation, affordable indemnity, protected supervision, and a robust training pipeline. These elements are essential to recruit and retain staff without compromising high-quality, safe care. Without them, more bodies in the system won’t translate into better care for patients, and we’ll just see burnout and higher turnover among already stretched teams.

I support a NHS workforce plan that both expands capacity and protects safe, high‑quality care. It should prioritise responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, rapid recognition of international qualifications and strong integration support, while safeguarding health systems in source countries and avoiding depopulation elsewhere. Practical steps include a smooth visa route for skilled clinicians, culturally attuned induction and mentoring, and robust safeguards to prevent exploitation or fatigue. 

Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload. We need more nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals, working to the top of their training, with clear scopes, supervision and strong clinical governance. In my practice, nurse‑led triage and pharmacist medicines reviews cut waiting times for routine concerns and allowed GPs to focus on complex cases, improving safety and continuity for patients with multiple conditions. 

Third, address pay and incentives to attract staff to underserved areas and high‑demand roles: targeted competitive pay, retention bonuses, relocation packages and bursaries for training. Coupled with local training pipelines and mentoring, this helps staff settle, stay and provide consistent care for families who rely on stable teams. 

Finally, ensure digital records and flexible staffing models support continuity of care as the workforce expands, so patients see the same clinicians and experience safer, more seamless services.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan must prioritise safe staffing levels across all services and strengthen links with social care and community teams so workloads are shared rather than dumped on already stretched colleagues. Joint funding and pooled planning with social care can help create truly holistic pathways and reduce avoidable demand on NHS services. Invest in continuity-preserving models—stable teams with longer placements, named leads and robust handovers—to safeguard clinical quality as demand grows, instead of relying on short-term agency cover. Embed safety monitoring in workforce planning: real‑time staffing dashboards, regular safety risk assessments and linked patient safety reviews to catch issues before they affect care.

Practical steps I’ve seen work include multi‑disciplinary, co‑located teams with shared admin and back‑office support; care coordinators to navigate complex journeys; protected time for professional development and supervision; flexible working patterns and clear career ladders to retain experienced staff and enable mentoring of newer recruits. Strengthening joint work with social care in crisis response and with mental health teams is crucial to prevent bottlenecks that compromise quality while improving access. A plan that keeps people safe, supported and well-led will underpin the access improvements our area needs.

I would urge the NHS workforce plan to place funding and structure behind clear career paths, protected continuing professional development, and robust return-to-practice routes to retain both experienced clinicians and newer staff. Key priorities should include funded, transparent career ladders that connect clinical roles with progression—nurses, GPs, practice staff, and allied health professionals—so people can see a long-term future in the NHS. Protected CPD time and dedicated budgets are essential; training opportunities must be planned and guaranteed rather than dependent on short-term funding whims. Mentorship schemes linking senior clinicians with trainees and early-career staff help build confidence, safety culture and reduce turnover. Return-to-practice programs, supported by supervised onboarding, allow experienced workers returning after a break to reintegrate safely. In my experience, apprenticeship and internship routes bring local people into the workforce and improve retention over time. We also need flexible working options, wellbeing support, safe staffing targets, and reliable recruitment pipelines with solid induction and digital training. A coherent plan that pairs immediate actions with sustainable development will sustain high-quality, safe care, especially in underserved communities.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise flexible, people‑centred working patterns to recruit and retain staff while keeping safety at the forefront. This means more flexible hours, part‑time roles, job‑sharing and phased retirement options, along with childcare support and proactive mental health services to reduce burnout and widen the experienced workforce.

To safely redistribute GP workload, we must expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied roles, all with clear training, supervision and governance. For example, a nurse‑led chronic disease clinic can manage stable patients, a pharmacist can triage minor infections and review medicines, and physician associates or paramedics can carry out routine reviews and home visits under supervision. Proper IT links and shared records are essential so care is continuous and safe across teams.

Prioritise safe staffing ratios, continuity‑preserving models and ongoing safety monitoring to ensure access improvements do not compromise quality. In practice, I’ve seen neighbours wait weeks for counselling; embedding mental health staff in local clinics can offer timely help.

With robust supervision, training, and governance, and flexible working arrangements, we can build teams that support both patients and staff, improving access without sacrificing safety or quality.

Prioritise a joined-up NHS workforce plan with social care and community services, sharing funding to redistribute workload and deliver holistic care; targeted incentives for rural, coastal and deprived urban areas, including housing and transport support; plus flexible working, wellbeing and multidisciplinary teams to retain safety and quality.

I would prioritise a workforce plan that recognises the reality of overloaded services and seeks to rebalance workload through closer collaboration with social care, mental health and community networks. This means joint funding streams, shared recruitment and retention strategies, and role redesign so staff operate at the top of their capability while patients receive timely, safe, holistic care. It should be supported by transparent, localised data—clear dashboards on vacancies, turnover, sickness, wait times, and patient outcomes—driven by accessible modelling and KPIs with regular evaluation to steer funding and performance. Concrete steps include: allocate targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, coastal, urban deprived—including housing, transport, and relocation support; create local career pathways with training, supervision, flexible working, and wellbeing resources; expand multidisciplinary teams and cross-sector rotations; use co-located hubs with shared records and governance to streamline on-boarding and redeployment. Finally, establish long-term funding and governance for a learning-into-practice cycle, with pilots to test what works in local context.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise funded, clearly defined career pathways from entry to leadership, with protected continuing professional development and formal mentorship. Return-to-practice schemes should be robust, offering supervised re-entry and refreshing training so experienced clinicians aren’t lost to gaps in care. Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams by actively funding and overseeing roles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates and paramedics, with clear scopes of practice and strong supervision so GP workload can be redistributed without compromising safety. Build stronger training pipelines—longer apprenticeships, undergraduate placements, and clinical fellowships—paired with guaranteed funded CPD days and competency frameworks. Focus retention on flexible working options, manageable workloads, wellbeing support and visible progression into senior or leadership roles. In my area, introducing more pharmacists and nurses in primary care with solid supervision has eased GP pressure and improved safety; a staged rollout nationwide with similar support would help maintain high-quality care while expanding access.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise expanding domestic training pipelines and targeted location-based incentives. Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements in primary care, backed by university-practice partnerships that enable training near home and clear progression into NHS roles. This approach builds a steady, locally rooted workforce and reduces dependence on long-term international recruitment.

Deliver tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal—to attract and keep staff. Include housing and transport support, relocation assistance, and accelerated career pathways that reward long-term service in those communities. Pair these with wellbeing and safe-staffing commitments: manageable workloads, continued CPD funding, strong supervision, and flexible working options to sustain safety and job satisfaction.

Evidence from a small local pilot placing trainees in surgeries briefly improved access, but gains faded as trainees moved on. A scaled, well-supported programme of protected placements and regional university-practice hubs could convert that into lasting service improvements.

To recruit, retain and support staff while preserving safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise safe staffing ratios across all settings, with predictable rosters and the ability to cover peak times without compromising patient safety. From my experience in local clinics, when teams stay the same and patients see the same clinician, wait times and safety concerns tend to improve. Continuity-preserving models are essential: teams that consistently see the same patients, with robust handover processes and multidisciplinary collaboration, reduce avoidable delays and sustain trust in urgent access improvements. Safety monitoring must be built in: real-time staffing dashboards, regular review of wait times, safety incidents and near-misses, with rapid corrective actions and transparent reporting. Staff wellbeing and reasonable workloads are non-negotiable: protected rest, mental health support, manageable caseloads, and opportunities for professional growth. Strong recruitment and retention pipelines—local recruitment, apprenticeships, and clear career pathways—will help reflect the communities served. Invest in training and supervision to maintain quality as roles expand, while digital tools should support clinicians, not replace human contact. Importantly, funding and governance must be stable to sustain integrated hubs and new models of care without fragmenting teams.

Prioritise interoperable, secure IT and comprehensive staff digital training, while safeguarding non-digital options for those digitally excluded. Strengthen joint funding and links with social care, mental health and community services to share workload and protect safe, high-quality care.

From living in rural England and watching how the health service operates on the ground, any NHS workforce plan must start with stability and local capability. You can pour money into new digital systems or centralised models, but if there aren’t enough clinicians and support staff in the villages and towns, patients simply can’t be helped quickly or safely. I’d urge a workforce plan that prioritises sustainable funding, practical flexibility, and a clear link to local access improvements—so that the front line isn’t pulled back by short-term policy shifts.

Key priorities I’d want to see reflected in any plan:

- Secure, multi-year and ring-fenced funding for workforce initiatives. Short funding cycles create recruitment uncertainty, disrupt training capacity, and make it harder to sustain retention schemes in rural areas. A three- to five-year horizon would let practices plan locally—hire and train GPs, nurse practitioners and practice nurses, support staff, and carers, and invest in the necessary infrastructure. In our village, a mobile clinic and a small on-site team could work only if the funding remains reliable year after year; otherwise, the service is all promise and no delivery.

- Flexible working to recruit and retain diverse staff and reduce burnout. Rural roles benefit from varied schedules: part-time positions, job-sharing, phased retirement for experienced clinicians, and robust childcare and mental health support for staff. I’ve seen colleagues slow to retire because they want to mentor younger colleagues and keep local access steady, rather than pushing the workload entirely onto a younger cohort. Offering flexible hours and supportive policies would help keep skilled people in our community without sacrificing care quality.

- Protect and grow training capacity and local pipelines. A steady supply of trained professionals is the backbone of timely access. This means expanding GP training slots in rural-friendly settings, increasing nurse practitioner and allied health professional training, and ensuring meaningful rural placements. Long-term planning should include funded apprenticeship routes, mentorship schemes, and opportunities for mid-career professionals to retrain for local roles when they wish to relocate or extend their contribution.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity of care. It’s crucial that as we expand access through new models, we don’t dilute safety. Plan for safe staffing levels, but also prioritise continuity—stable teams where patients see familiar clinicians, and a system to monitor and respond quickly when staffing drops below safe thresholds. I’ve observed how familiar, continuous care reduces hospital admissions and keeps chronic conditions stable; disruption to teams often negates any short-term efficiency gains from centralisation.

- Practical retention and wellbeing measures. In rural settings, burnout isn’t just a buzzword—it translates into longer waits, missed follow-ups, and reduced access for vulnerable residents. Policies should include regular clinical supervision, protected time for professional development, access to mental health support for staff, and practical supports like housing assistance or travel allowances where travel is a barrier. These small but meaningful steps help maintain a dedicated workforce in dispersed communities.

- Anchoring workforce planning in local capacity and infrastructure. Beyond people, we need the right premises, parking, and digital tools that staff can actually use without adding to their burden. For example, if a mobile clinic is to work, it needs coordinators, drivers, and local reception support; if telehealth is used, there must be on-site help so patients and staff aren’t left navigating tech alone.

- Collaboration with voluntary and community sectors. Local partnerships for transport, volunteer drivers, and community-facing health champions can unlock access without overburdening core clinical teams. A well-coordinated approach to workforce that includes these partners strengthens the whole system in rural areas.

In short, I believe the plan should shield and grow the workforce in a way that makes rural access improvements possible without compromising safety or quality. Sustainable funding, flexible working, training pipelines, safe staffing, and strong local partnerships are not luxuries; they are the prerequisites for real, long-term improvements in timely, high-quality care for older residents and others with mobility challenges.

If the government can embed these priorities in an NHS workforce plan, we would start to see the promised improvements in access without sacrificing the standards that keep people well.

From what I see locally, and what I’ve heard from family and friends who rely on GP and community services, any NHS workforce plan needs to be stable, practical and future-facing. It should prioritise three things: long-term, ring-fenced funding; robust investment in interoperable IT with real support for those who can’t access digital services; and a relentless focus on cutting admin burden so clinicians can spend more time with patients. These aren’t quick fixes, but they’re the elements that will keep the system safe and high quality over time.

- Secure, multi-year funding for workforce initiatives. We need funding that survives political cycles and isn’t subject to sudden cuts or reallocate-and-cut decisions. Ring-fenced allocations for training capacity (medical, nursing, mental health), return-to-practice routes, and targeted retention schemes in underserved areas would allow trusts and practices to plan ahead rather than juggling short-term firefighting. This should also cover apprenticeships and funded career progression pathways so people can move into more autonomous roles without losing financial security.

- Invest in training capacity and local pipelines. Expand regional training places, GP specialty training slots, nursing and allied health training, and CPD opportunities. Practical steps I’d like to see include more placements in local bases, better access to supervision, and loan forgiveness or targeted bursaries for those who commit to working in areas with higher need. Councils and hospitals could also develop mentorship and clinical supervision programmes that help retain staff after early career years.

- Interoperable, secure IT plus inclusive digital training. A big portion of the pressure comes from systems that don’t talk to each other, slow interfaces, and cyber-security concerns that force extra checks. An NHS-wide push for interoperable electronic records, standard data formats, user-friendly IT, and reliable technical support would save clinicians hours each week. At the same time, staff must be trained to use these tools effectively. Importantly, we must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients: maintain robust phone triage, in-person clinics, and simple, clear routes to access care so nobody falls through the cracks.

- Reduce administrative burden and streamline referrals. Clinicians are spending too much time on paperwork, duplications, and unnecessary targets. We should simplify referral pathways, remove duplicated steps, and improve IT usability so workflows are smoother and more predictable. This will free up time for patient-facing care and reduce burnout. In practice, many GPs report that even minor IT inefficiencies create bottlenecks that delay treatment; better-designed pathways and fewer clicks can have a real, tangible impact on care quality.

- Flexible working and wellbeing as core components. A sustainable workforce hinges on reasonable workloads, predictable contracts, and access to confidential wellbeing support. Job-sharing, flexible rostering, protected admin time, and strong supervision should be embedded in the plan so staff can balance work with life, reduce turnover, and provide safer care.

- A clear, locally responsive retention strategy. Alongside national funding, trusts should have locally tailored retention programmes—clear career ladders, mentorship for early-career clinicians, opportunities for progression in district nursing and community mental health posts, and targeted financial incentives where demand is highest. That combination helps keep skilled staff where they’re most needed and reduces repeated churn.

In short, a successful NHS workforce plan must be long-sighted and practically funded, make technology work for clinicians without leaving digitally excluded patients behind, and free clinicians from bureaucratic burdens so they can focus on safe, high-quality patient care. If we get these right, the NHS in our area can both meet today’s pressures and build resilience for the years ahead.

I strongly support a NHS workforce plan that prioritises recruiting, retaining and supporting staff while ensuring safe, high-quality care. Central to this should be transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. When leaders can see local vacancies, turnover, training capacity and workload pressures in real time, they can target resources where they are most needed and prevent bottlenecks before they arise. In my area, GP, district nursing and mental health posts often stay unfilled for months. A local dashboard showing vacancy rates, fill times, staff sickness and patient wait times would help shape recruitment campaigns, flexible working options and career progression paths. KPIs should include staff wellbeing, safe staffing levels, patient safety indicators and continuity of care, linked to funding triggers so improvements translate into action. Support for retention—mentoring, manageable rosters, supervision, and clear progression—matters as much as new recruitment. We also need pilots with rigorous evaluations before scaling up, and transparent reporting so communities can see whether the plan actually shortens waits and improves outcomes.

Any NHS workforce plan must put safe, high‑quality care at the centre while expanding teams. In practice this means clear scope‑of‑practice boundaries and governance for new roles, with protected clinical supervision funded and built into every implementation plan. Revalidation and ongoing professional development should be streamlined, with dedicated time, reasonable admin support and funded reflective practice; otherwise we risk delays, drift and burnout. Indemnity arrangements must be clarified and affordable. Uncertainty about liability costs can deter skilled staff from extending their scope or taking on new roles, such as physician associates or nurse prescribers. The plan should offer subsidised indemnity or guaranteed cover for pilots and for cross‑organisation work in primary, community and mental health settings. To recruit and retain, provide structured career paths, flexible working and protected supervision. Our area already experiences vacancies and turnover among GPs and therapists; for new roles, protected supervision slots and backfill for supervision time are essential. Also drive targeted recruitment in high‑need communities and ensure safe staffing ratios, workload governance and robust induction. In short, align scope, indemnity, supervision and development with clear funding to attract, retain and protect patients.

A workforce plan for the NHS must prioritise enabling clinicians to spend more time with patients, not more time chasing forms. In practice this means reducing unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks, and making referrals and care navigation as streamlined and digital as possible, so the focus stays on safe, high-quality patient care. The plan should also recognise that staffing pressures won’t be solved by targets alone; it needs to protect clinician time and wellbeing while building sustainable teams.

Key priorities I’d like to see prioritised include:

- Cut the admin burden and simplify targets: remove or consolidate non-clinical targets that pull clinicians into dashboards rather than patient care. Standardise admin processes across primary and community care so staff aren’t repeatedly entering the same data into different systems. In my practice, doctors and nurse prescribers routinely juggle multiple forms and reminders; reducing this duplication would free significant time for patient-facing work and reduce burnout.

- Streamline referrals and care pathways: create a single, clear referral route with minimal hand-offs between GP, hospital services, and community teams. A unified triage point, with shared care plans, would cut delays when patients need physio, mental health support, or social care. For example, a patient with coexisting physical and mental health needs currently experiences two or three separate referral queues; a streamlined pathway would shorten the time to appropriate intervention.

- Improve IT usability and interoperability: invest in user-friendly IT that talks to other systems (GP records, hospital patient portals, community services) so clinicians don’t waste time locating or re-entering information. Features like single sign-on, intuitive dashboards, and real-time access to up-to-date patient data across settings would make a tangible difference. I’ve seen colleagues spend hours chasing missing notes because records aren’t readily accessible in the community; a system that presents a coherent, current snapshot would alleviate this bottleneck.

- Support recruitment and retention with better working conditions: improving IT and processes must go hand-in-hand with staffing plans. That includes clear career progression, mentoring and training that fits alongside clinical duties, flexible working where possible, and sufficient protected time for CPD and quality improvement. When admin is reduced and staffing ratios are safer, staff turnover falls and patients receive more consistent care.

- Prioritise safe and high-quality care: any improvements to reduce burden must be matched with training, supervision and governance so safety isn’t compromised. Build in regular audits of new processes to verify that reducing admin doesn’t inadvertently delay critical decisions or care escalation.

- Embed continuous improvement and measurement: the plan should include metrics on admin time saved per clinician, wait times for referrals, patient flow through primary and community services, and staff wellbeing indicators. Early pilots in selected areas can be evaluated and scaled if they show real, sustained improvement.

From my experience, when practices consolidate booking and referral workflows and adopt more interoperable digital tools, clinicians reclaim time for patient-facing activities. NHS111 triage improved booking, and care navigation became clearer when the IT backbone supported those flows rather than hindered them. In mental health and community services, shared records and simpler referral pathways would stop patients bouncing between services and experiencing avoidable delays.

Ultimately, a robust workforce plan should recognise that better care comes from smarter systems and people empowered to do their jobs well. Reducing administrative friction, streamlining referrals, and investing in practical IT upgrades will help recruit and retain skilled staff while safeguarding the quality and safety of care patients rely on.

An NHS workforce plan must balance the urgent need to fill vacancies with the long-term goal of safe, high-quality care for patients and fair, sustainable conditions for staff. International recruitment can play a constructive part, but only if it is responsible and integrated with strong domestic development and safeguarding measures. With that in mind, I think the plan should prioritise the following areas:

- Ethical, streamlined international recruitment alongside domestic pipelines. A managed approach to overseas recruitment should make visa processes faster for suitably qualified healthcare workers, while maintaining rigorous but fair credential checks. This isn’t about shortcuts; it’s about reducing needless delays that force teams to work short-staffed and overburdened. In practice, that means faster visa decisions, clearer timelines, and predictable routes for registration and deployment, with protections to ensure workers are treated fairly on arrival and in the workplace.

- Robust credential recognition and bridging support. Recognition of overseas qualifications must be credible, consistent, and efficient. Where gaps exist, provide structured bridging programs, supervised practice posts, and language support tailored to clinical needs. For example, a nurse trained abroad may need some additional clinical updates or language familiarity with NHS pathways; a clear, funded pathway to full registration shortens vacancy periods without compromising patient safety.

- Comprehensive integration and ongoing professional development. Integration shouldn’t end at onboarding; it must be a supported, ongoing process. This includes pre-arrival orientation, language and cultural competence training, mentoring or buddy schemes, and access to career progression opportunities. A well-supported overseas recruit can quickly contribute more effectively, while staff from all backgrounds feel valued and able to grow within the system.

- Safeguards against depleting source health systems. We should recruit responsibly from overseas and actively avoid hurting health systems in source countries. That means monitoring where staff are coming from, limiting recruitment where critical gaps exist, and contributing to global health capacity-building—such as funding training in partner countries or offering scholarships that strengthen domestic health workforces there. Ethical recruitment should be a partnership, not a one-way drain.

- Investment in domestic training and retention. To reduce long-term dependence on international talent, the plan must expand domestic training slots for nurses, GPs, and allied health professionals; support return-to-practice routes; and ensure that apprenticeships and career progression are accessible to people from diverse backgrounds. Retention requires manageable workloads, safe staffing levels, supportive leadership, opportunities for development, fair pay, and strong wellbeing and mental health support.

- Safe staffing and strong clinical governance. High-quality care depends on appropriate skill-m mix and staffing ratios across all services. The plan should fund flexible staffing models, reduce reliance on temporary agency staff, and include robust induction, supervision, and continuing professional development. Where international staff are involved, clearly defined supervision and peer support help maintain standards and patient safety.

- Fair, transparent, and inclusive culture. Recruitment should go hand in hand with efforts to build diverse teams that reflect the communities they serve. This includes language support, interpreters where needed, culturally competent leadership, and a workplace where concerns about safety, workload, or discrimination can be raised without fear of retaliation.

In my experience, smart recruitment must walk a line: it should welcome skilled workers from elsewhere to fill genuine gaps, while committing to the long-term health of the NHS and the health systems that supply staff. A practical example would be a healthcare trust that uses a fast-track credential recognition pathway with robust bridging support, paired with targeted NHS-funded training slots for local graduates and returners. That kind of mixed, ethical approach makes it possible to keep patient safety at the forefront while responsibly addressing workforce shortages.

Ultimately, overseas recruitment should be part of a broader workforce strategy that strengthens domestic capacity, safeguards global health, and treats all staff with dignity and fairness. If the plan can deliver that, we’ll avoid the pitfalls of short-term fixations and build a NHS workforce capable of delivering high-quality care for years to come.

From where I sit, a NHS workforce plan that genuinely protects patients while expanding access needs to be built on three steady foundations: safe staffing ratios, workforce continuity, and robust safety monitoring. As our population ages, with more long‑term conditions and complex needs, it is not enough to simply recruit more staff; we must ensure those staff can work safely, stay engaged, and deliver care without risking quality down the line.

First, prioritise safe staffing ratios across all settings. That means ensuring there are enough GPs, practice nurses, allied health professionals, mental health workers and social care links to match patient demand in each locality. Too often I’ve heard of appointments being squeezed because the system is stretched, and that is exactly what undermines trust and safety. A plan that cements safe ratios in routine practice—rather than chasing national targets alone—will help clinicians take the time needed for proper assessments, care planning, and follow‑ups, which in turn reduces hospital admissions and A&E visits.

Second, keep continuity at the heart of care. Continuity-preserving models—named clinicians, stable multidisciplinary teams, and predictable rosters—are crucial for older patients with several conditions. When patients see the same GP or nurse and know their care plan is coordinated across primary, community and mental health services, outcomes improve and patient satisfaction grows. My experience confirms that even small changes in the team can disrupt care and create anxiety for families who rely on trusted professionals. A workforce plan should reward and protect team stability, including protected time for multidisciplinary case reviews and care coordination.

Third, solid safety monitoring must accompany any growth. Establish clear governance, regular clinical audits, and real‑time safety dashboards so we can spot bottlenecks, near misses and unsafe practices before they affect people. If new roles or expanded scopes are introduced, we need transparent reporting that shows how patient safety is being safeguarded, with rapid learning loops to share what works and what doesn’t across hubs and providers.

On expanding roles, it’s vital to clarify scope‑of‑practice and ensure revalidation processes support safe innovation. When new roles emerge—such as nurse or pharmacist prescribers, advanced practitioners, or care coordinators—the plan should fund indemnity arrangements and provide protected clinical supervision. Staff need confident oversight as they take on new responsibilities, and those supervisory arrangements must be funded as a core part of any workforce expansion, not treated as an afterthought.

Investing in education pipelines is also essential. Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university‑practice partnerships. Local, well‑supported placements help grow the domestic primary care workforce where it is most needed and fosters long‑term commitment by trainees who understand the realities of day‑to‑day practice in our communities. I’ve seen how a local partnership between a university and a GP practice can bring talented students into the practice, with proper supervision and a sense that their work is valued. Some then stay on into roles in primary care, which is exactly what we need to reduce long‑term shortages.

Finally, any plan should be designed with input from older residents and people who rely on long‑term care (as if that will ever happen). Co‑design ensures workforce changes fit local transport, accessibility needs and cultural expectations, and it helps protect the relationships that are the backbone of good care.

In short, we should recruit smarter, not just more. A successful NHS workforce plan will prioritise safe staffing, continuity of care, and rigorous safety monitoring; clarify and protect scopes of practice with funded supervision and indemnity; and grow domestic supply through protected placements and strong academic partnerships. If these elements sit at the core of the strategy, we can maintain high‑quality care while expanding access, meeting today’s needs and future challenges alike.

it's outrageous that to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan must place interoperable IT and secure systems at the heart of delivery, supported by thorough staff digital training. When systems can talk to each other and data flows smoothly, clinicians spend less time on admin and more with patients, improving triage, referrals and outcomes. But we must not abandon those who can’t or won’t use online tools; robust non‑digital routes—telephone triage, walk‑in slots, and clear face‑to‑face pathways—must be protected as part of a genuinely hybrid model. 

Crucially, the plan should rely on transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks to inform planning, funding and performance monitoring. Real‑world metrics on vacancies, retention, training uptake and patient safety must guide where to expand or redeploy staff, and how to structure shifts and supervision. In my experience, uncoordinated data leads to gaps and queueing; a unified data approach would enable targeted recruitment and safer staffing levels. 

Additionally, invest in practical training and career progression, with protected time for professional development, mentorship and flexible arrangements to improve retention. Strong governance around cyber security and patient privacy must accompany any digital expansion. A balanced plan that blends robust IT with people, and keeps non‑digital access visible, will sustain safe, high‑quality care for everyone!

it's outrageous that from where I live in Scotland, I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise deeper collaboration across health and social care, with joint funding and planning that recognises the way workloads flow between primary care, mental health, and community services. We won’t solve staffing shortages by siloed recruitment alone; we need a shared pipeline and a workforce that can flex across settings to deliver safe, high-quality care where people actually receive it—in their communities and homes.

Key priorities I’d like to see: 
- Integrated, jointly funded workforce planning: Create a five-year, cross-sector plan between NHS Scotland and local authorities that pools budget for community and social care alongside health. This would support discharge planning, reduce avoidable hospital stays, and fund care coordinators who can steer patients through GP, hospital and community services. When social care is under-resourced, hospital beds fill and GP workloads spike; pooling funding would distribute tasks more evenly and prevent bottlenecks.
- Multidisciplinary teams in local hubs: Expand co-located, multidisciplinary teams in community hubs—GPs, district nurses, health visitors, mental health workers, social workers, pharmacists, physios and occupational therapists, plus social care staff—so people see a familiar group who share the same plan. In practice this could look like a village-based hub with a named contact person, integrated care plans, and same-day triage for urgent needs. We’ve seen how a temporary village hall outreach clinic can keep people out of A&E during refurbishments; with consistent, funded teams, such local solutions could become standard.
- Clear workforce pathways and support to rural areas: There must be targeted recruitment and retention packages for rural roles, including flexible working, housing support, guaranteed rural placements for students, and incentives tied to service in underserved areas. My concern is that rural residents face longer waits and more travel for basic care; a workforce plan that explicitly targets these gaps would help ensure sustainable local services.
- Shared training, supervision and culture: Create joint training across health and social care so staff understand each other’s roles, share best practices on safeguarding and early intervention, and can supervise and mentor new staff across sectors. Leadership and professional development should be available in every sector, not just hospital settings, to build confidence for staff moving between services.
- Task shifting and technology-enabled care: Use skill-mreframing and role flexibility to relieve pressure on doctors and nurses by widening the scope of practice for allied health professionals and trained care workers, under clear governance. Put robust digital tools in place—shared electronic records, real-time staffing dashboards, and telehealth-enabled triage—to reduce duplication and enable quicker decision-making.
- Mental health as a core part of the plan: Ensure that workforce planning for mental health mirrors physical health, with integrated CMHTs, crisis response teams, and access to talking therapies within community settings. When mental health staffing is limited, patients end up waiting longer and relying on GP contacts rather than receiving early intervention.
- Safe staffing, wellbeing and retention: The plan must set explicit safe staffing norms and provide wellbeing support, adequate supervision, and reasonable rosters to prevent burnout. In rural areas in particular, a sustainable mix of professional roles and predictable schedules is crucial to keep skilled staff from leaving.
- Community-facing roles and care navigation: Fund and formalise roles such as care navigators or patient pathway coordinators who can guide people through the system, book appointments, and ensure continuity of care across GP, hospital and social care. This reduces the cognitive load on patients and helps prevent missed follow-ups.

What this would look like in practice is a more predictable, patient-centred system. A patient wouldn’t have to chase multiple agencies when they need support; instead, there would be a single, named contact who can pull in the right team, whatever time the person needs. It would also help with the real-world issue I’ve seen in my community: when one part of the system is stretched, the whole thing strains. A genuinely joint, adequately funded workforce plan would distribute that load more fairly and keep high-quality care within reach.

Ultimately, the plan should be judged on how well it enables timely access, safety and continuity of care at the local level, with staffing and funding aligned to the needs of communities rather than to numerical targets alone. If we invest in integrated teams, shared leadership, and sustained funding for social care alongside health, we’ll stabilise services, improve workforce morale, and, crucially, deliver better outcomes for patients across Scotland.

I support a workforce plan that keeps patients safe and the quality of care high by giving teams clear roles, robust supervision, and real career progression. Specifically:
- Clarify scope of practice and ensure robust revalidation and indemnity arrangements, with funding for protected clinical supervision to support new roles and maintain patient safety.
- Invest in interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training, while safeguarding alternatives and support for those who are digitally excluded.
- Provide funded career pathways, protected continuing professional development, mentorship, and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and support early-career staff.

In my experience, when junior staff have dedicated supervision and explicit CPD opportunities, medication reviews are safer and patients feel heard. Yet uncertainty around indemnity and unclear career paths can deter colleagues from taking on expanded roles, which undermines continuity of care. - Support postgraduate and CPD activity with funding, time, and accessible online options. Accessible, local CPD that fits shift patterns helps prevent professional burnout and promotes retention.
- Implement data‑driven governance with transparent metrics on safety, patient experience, and wait times. Local accountability should be matched with national standards so improvements are measurable and comparable.

In short, an NHS workforce plan should grow domestic supply through protected training and strong partnerships, offer tailored incentives to hard‑to‑fill areas, and expand multidisciplinary teams with robust supervision to redistribute GP workload safely. These elements must sit within multi‑year funding, place‑based planning and clear career ladders so people can see a future in the communities they serve. We stand ready to work with Government and local partners to design pilots that test these approaches, share learning, and embed them in everyday practice so people get timely, high‑quality care wherever they live.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping safety and quality high, the workforce plan must prioritise flexible, sustainable careers and strong cross-system collaboration. Offering more flexible hours, part-time posts, job-sharing and phased retirement would help keep experienced clinicians in the workforce, reduce burnout and widen the pool of applicants, especially in rural Scotland where shortages bite. Support with childcare and predictable rosters makes long-term NHS careers viable and less stressful for families. 

Crucially, we should strengthen links with social care, mental health and community services through joint funding and integrated teams. Shared rotas, co-located teams and blended funding can redistribute workload, cut duplication and enable holistic patient care across settings, rather than passing patients between separate systems. When teams are connected, staff can cover gaps more smoothly and patients experience continuity of care.

Investing in staff wellbeing and development is essential: protected time for training and supervision, proactive mental health support, and reducing administrative burden with adequate back-office support and better digital tools. Clear career pathways and supportive leadership help retain staff long-term. From my experience, people stay where they feel heard, workload is manageable and there are real opportunities to progress.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the workforce plan should prioritise long-term stability, capacity-building and a streamlined admin environment. Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements so trusts can plan, recruit and train without constant policy shocks. This should underpin dedicated training capacity – more GP, nurse, allied health professional, and mental health trainee places, plus expansion of nurse associates, clinical pharmacists and social prescribing workers – with clear progression routes to retain staff locally. Reducing turnover will also rely on sustainable workloads, protected time for professional development, mentoring and safe staffing levels, so morale improves and vacancies don’t reappear.

Crucially, cut unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. Streamline referrals and modernise IT so clinicians spend less time on admin and more time with patients. Invest in user-friendly IT systems, interoperable records and automated reminders that cut duplication. Practical steps include integrated triage pathways, simplified referral forms and better scheduling tools.

Finally, empower flexible deployment to meet community needs (telehealth hubs, outreach clinics, extended hours) and reward teams that deliver high-quality care with manageable workloads. A well-funded, friction-free workforce plan will attract talent and sustain excellent care.

Agree: prioritize targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved and high-demand areas; secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding for sustainable workforce initiatives and training; and use overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, credential recognition, integration support, with safeguards to protect source health systems.

From my perspective in Scotland, a NHS workforce plan that truly keeps patients safe while delivering high-quality care needs to be practical, fair and locally responsive. Three overarching priorities stand out: responsible, well-supported recruitment (including international staff when needed), robust digital and information systems that improve care without leaving digitally excluded people behind, and a carefully expanded multidisciplinary workforce that can share the workload safely and effectively.

Overseas recruitment as a part of a broader strategy
- It can help plug genuine shortfalls, but it must be done responsibly. Streamlined visa processes and clear credential recognition pathways are essential, but they must be paired with solid integration support. That means language and cultural orientation, mentoring, peer networks, and protected routes to professional development so internationally trained staff can deliver safe, high-quality care from day one.
- There should be safeguards to avoid depleting health systems in source countries. This could involve agreements that support health workforce strengthening in other countries, time-bound service commitments, and careful caps so recruitment doesn’t undermine local training pipelines. In practice, I’d want to see transparent reporting on where international staff are coming from, how long they stay, and what onward training or retention support is in place.
- Examples from the front line show why this matters: when a skilled nurse from abroad joins a practice, patient care improves, but if visa delays or credential friction hold people up, it disrupts continuity and increases reliance on temporary staff. Streamlined processes need to go hand in hand with robust induction and a clear retention plan.

Interoperable IT, secure systems and digital inclusion
- We must invest in interoperable, user-friendly IT that lets GPs, nurses, pharmacists and other clinicians access complete, up-to-date information across settings. Secure systems are non-negotiable, with strong data protection and cyber-security.
- Staff need ongoing digital training embedded in career development, not one-off workshops. This includes decision-support tools, remote monitoring, and safe e-prescribing practices, all integrated into workflows so care isn’t slowed down by tech hurdles.
- Crucially, we must safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients. Relying solely on online bookings or portals can widen health inequalities. Paper-based options, telephone triage, in-person signposting and community outreach should be retained and funded so nobody is pushed out of timely care because they don’t use digital channels.
- In practice, the risk is real even in urban Scotland: patients with limited digital access often miss appointments or misunderstand self-management plans unless staff take the time to offer non-digital routes. IT must enable better care, not create new barriers.

Expanded, well-governed multidisciplinary teams
- Multidisciplinary teams should be expanded and regulated so professionals such as nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals can safely take on more routine, high-volume work. With proper supervision and clear governance, this can relieve GP workloads and improve access without compromising safety.
- This means formal scopes of practice, standardised training, and robust supervision structures, plus pathways for rapid escalation when patient risk is identified. For example, trained clinical pharmacists managing long-term medication reviews and early-care triage by advanced practice nurses can free up GPs to deal with more complex cases.
- I’d like to see practical pilots that test team-based models in different settings—urban practices, rural clinics, and community hubs—so we can learn what works where. Data from these pilots should feed national guidance, with accountability and safeguarding measures to prevent uneven quality of care.

Beyond these three pillars, there needs to be a strong focus on sustainable working conditions and career development
- Fair pay, reasonable hours, safe staffing ratios, access to mental health support, and clear career ladders are essential for retention. Flexible working, local training pipelines, and opportunities to specialise help staff stay loyal to the NHS and deliver consistent care.
- Local planning must align with community needs: rural and deprived areas often bear the heaviest burden, so workforce plans should include targeted recruitment, retention packages, and support for local training and apprenticeships to build a home-grown workforce.
- Finally, workforce planning must be transparent. Regular public reporting on staffing levels, retention by role, patient outcomes, and the impact of international recruitment is key to maintaining trust and ensuring the plan remains accountable.

In short, a responsible NHS workforce plan should balance international recruitment with strong integration safeguards, invest in digital infrastructure while protecting those without digital access, and expand multidisciplinary teams with solid training and supervision. If these elements are paired with fair working conditions and local, data-driven delivery, we can recruit, retain and support staff while keeping high-quality, safe care at the heart of the service.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan should prioritise secure, multi-year ring-fenced funding for sustained workforce initiatives, training capacity and long-term planning. A stable settlement would enable local systems to expand training places for GPs, nurses, mental health professionals and allied health staff; fund practice-based education; and create clear career ladders in urgent care, community services and hub-based care. Thank you for the opportunity to respond. In Wales, with an ageing population and many communities spread across rural and urban areas, any NHS workforce plan must focus on expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams, with solid training and supervision, so tasks can be safely redistributed from GPs without compromising safety or quality. To make this work, I’d prioritise several practical steps:

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: bring in more nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals to share routine and ongoing care tasks. For example, a nurse prescriber can manage regular chronic disease reviews, a pharmacist can handle medicines reconciliation and medication reviews, and a physician associate or paramedic can conduct short urgent consultations or follow-ups. When roles are clearly defined and-supported by supervision, this redistribution helps free up GPs to concentrate on complex cases while preserving safety and continuity of care.

- Strengthen training, supervision and progression: create robust training pipelines with protected time for CPD, structured mentorship and formal competency assessments before new tasks are taken on. Regional training hubs could link GP practices with practical placements and classroom learning, ensuring staff move smoothly into expanded roles. In practice, I’ve seen how a well-supported nurse practitioner working alongside a pharmacist in a small community clinic can resolve issues efficiently and prevent unnecessary GP visits.

- Governance, safety and quality: establish explicit scopes of practice, clear escalation protocols and regular audits to safeguard patient safety. Use decision-support tools and ensure supervision in the early stages of shifting responsibilities. This will help patients feel confident in the new models of care.

- Equitable workforce distribution: design models that reach rural and deprived communities where access is hardest. Flexible arrangements, including community hubs, home visits and outreach clinics, should be part of the plan so no one loses timely access because of location or transport issues.

- Retention, progression and funding stability: avoid relying on short-term pilots. Provide clear career ladders, return-to-practice pathways and ongoing, relevant CPD. A stable, long-term funding stream is essential so practices can invest in supervision, supervision and supervision again—because supervision is what makes expanded teams work safely.

In my experience, even small changes can have big benefits. For instance, when a pharmacist within a practice undertook medicines reviews and reminders for those on multiple medicines, there were fewer medication problems and fewer urgent GP appointments. A nurse prescriber taking on routine follow-ups for chronic conditions freed the GP to focus on diagnoses and complex care planning. And when a paramedic or physician associate can see a follow-up or triage a non‑urgent issue, patients gain quicker access and GPs preserve time for the most complex cases.

Overall, a workforce plan that expands and regulates multidisciplinary teams, coupled with strong training, supervision, governance and sustainable funding, will help maintain safe, high-quality care across Wales. It aligns with the goal of improving timely access while protecting patients and supporting staff in challenging times.
