Implementing period‑specific staffing plans (e.g., for flu season) and ensuring ther are enough support staff to handle non‑clinical tasks will let clinicians focus on direct patient care. Accessible wellbeing services for NHS staff must be visible and destigmatized. - Digital tools that actually reduce burden: Invest in integrated IT systems and scheduling platforms that support saf staffing decisions, allow appropriate data sharing, and reduce duplicative data entry. Any digital rollout should include staff input, training, and ongoing support to avoid creating new bottlenecks. - Local partnership and governance: Workforce planning should be co‑designed with local health boards, primary care networks, social care, VCSE partners, and of course patients. Co‑production ensures staff are supported in the community environments they serve and that plans reflect rural realities and transport considerations in places across Wales. - Alignment with the hub and extended‑hours approach: Bringing services closer together is great in principle, but it relies on a stable, well‑supported workforce. That means clear recruitment pathways, rotational models that protect clinician wellbeing, and consistent funding cycles so teams aren’t constantly reorganised mid‑project. In my own experience in Wales, the fragmentary planning I’ve observed can leave staff feeling unsupported and patients waiting longer for care. If we want to offer evening and weekend slots and guaranteed urgent access, we need to back it with transparent data and a plan that actually delivers the staff to staff those times safely. Local health boards should publish regular workforce reports and invite frontline clinicians and patients to review them. A well‑designed evaluation framework will show what works, what doesn’t, and why, and then funding can be redirected quickly to where it makes the biggest difference. Ultimately, a workforce plan that foregrounds local data, practical modelling, and rigorous evaluation will help us maintain safety and high quality acrosss GP practices, community and mental health services, and the evolving hub model. It will also reassure staff that their workloads are manageable and that leadership is listening to the people who deliver care every day.

Prioritise fair overseas recruitment to fill shortages while preserving safety and quality. Streamline visas, recognise overseas credentials quickly, and provide robust integration support. Put safeguards to prevent draining source health systems and ensure ongoing training, mentorship, and retention within the NHS.

To keep safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise two core aims: expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams and creating flexible working patterns to retain staff. First, expand multidisciplinary teams that include nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals who can safely share routine GP tasks under clear training, protocols and supervision. Give these roles defined scopes of practice, investment in supervision time, and robust governance so tasks are redistributed without compromising safety. In rural practices I’m aware of, a well-supported nurse and pharmacist handling stable chronic-disease follow-ups under GP oversight reduced hospital visits and freed GPs to focus on complex cases; it only worked where supervision, evidence-based pathways and good data sharing were in place. Second, make careers sustainable: funded training, clear progression, protected time for CPD, and reliable mentoring so staff feel confident in expanding their remit. Third, offer flexible hours, part-time, job-share, phased retirement, childcare support and proactive mental-health services to reduce burnout and attract a diverse workforce. Fourth, tailor staffing models to local needs, ensuring a mix of on-site and remote support so longer, patient-centred consultations can happen for those who need them most. Taken together, these priorities should recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safety and quality of care.

From an England-based organisation perspective, the workforce plan should prioritise enabling clinicians to care for patients, not chase targets or drown in admin. Key steps: reduce unnecessary targets, streamline referrals and standardise care pathways to cut duplications; invest in user-friendly IT and integrated referral portals to speed decisions and reduce handoffs.

Support new and expanded roles through clear scope-of-practice, updated revalidation, and funded, protected supervision to maintain patient safety. Ensure robust indemnity arrangements aligned to any role expansion.

Retention and wellbeing: offer flexible hours, part-time, job-share, phased retirement, and accessible childcare plus proactive mental health support. These measures help retain a diverse workforce and stave off burnout; our experience shows flexible scheduling and reduced administrative burden correlate with higher job satisfaction and staff retention. Example: a local pilot with co-located admin support and streamlined triage reduced unnecessary GP contacts and freed clinicians for patient-facing work.

Recruitment: targeted pipelines, return-to-practice schemes, and equitable distribution between rural and urban areas, supported by funded supervision and mentorship.

IT implications: single interoperable systems, decision support, and clear governance. If implemented with safeguards, such a plan will sustain high-quality care while attracting and keeping the right mix of staff.

Prioritise responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visas, clear credential recognition, and strong integration support, while safeguarding source health systems. At the same time, offer tailored incentives, housing and transport, especially in rural, coastal and urban-deprived areas to attract and keep staff.

The plan should prioritise clear scope‑of‑practice, robust revalidation and indemnity, and protected clinical supervision to support new roles and patient safety. It must also fund interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training, with safeguards for digitally excluded patients.

I think an NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams to safely redistribute GP workload while protecting patient safety. Key steps: 1) Build clear, governed teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied professionals—capable of leading triage, minor-illness clinics and chronic-disease management, with strong supervision and defined scopes. 2) Safeguard patient safety with transparent scope-of-practice rules, funded indemnity arrangements and protected clinical supervision for new roles so mistakes are caught early. 3) Invest in training and career development—more funded training places, robust return-to-practice schemes, CPD, apprenticeships and protected time for supervision—so clinicians can progress without leaving local services. 4) Local, data-driven deployment—use practice-level data to place teams where they’re most needed; examples include pharmacist-led medicines reviews in smaller surgeries and paramedics in urgent-care roles to ease GP workload. 5) Support and retention—fair pay, flexible contracts, manageable workloads, and support for caring responsibilities to reduce burnout. 6) Infrastructure and digital support—telehealth hubs, digital triage tools and cross-site IT to improve handovers while safeguarding privacy. In short, expand and standardise teams with proper supervision, backed by training and indemnity, while optimising local deployment and well-being to sustain high-quality care.

Prioritising education and training capacity is essential. The plan should focus on increasing domestic supply by expanding undergraduate places, postgraduate programmes, and apprenticeships with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships. This helps recruit into primary care locally and retain staff who understand our communities. It should be complemented by structured career pathways, supervision and funding for extended roles in primary care so teams can work at the top of their skills. 

In practice, ring-fenced GP, nursing and allied health professional training slots in local practices, with funded supervision, would reduce reliance on international recruitment and cut delays for patients. For example, GP registrar schemes in partnership with nearby universities, nursing degree apprenticeships with primary care rotations, and pharmacist or physiotherapist training pathways embedded in general practice would grow capacity without compromising safety. I’ve seen local recruitment pressures lead to longer waits; robust training pipelines would help new clinicians settle and stay, improving continuity of care and patient outcomes. 

Finally, ensure wellbeing and workload planning keep pace with growth: protected CPD time, reasonable supervision, and predictable working patterns so staff remain engaged and safe to deliver high-quality care.

From my perspective as someone living in England and aged over 65, a NHS workforce plan must prioritise stability and long-term capacity as much as fresh targets. Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding for workforce initiatives is essential, including training capacity and protections against short-term policy volatility that disrupt recruitment and retention. Without predictable funding, practices can’t commit to longer training posts or return-to-practice schemes, which I’ve seen cause gaps in care and continuity. The plan should prioritize expanding undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements and strong university-practice partnerships to grow domestic primary care supply. In my area, shortages of practice nurses and mental health staff show how fragile throughput and triage can be when teams turn over. Practical supports like CPD, mentoring, and clear career progression help retain staff and improve patient experience. Overseas recruitment can play a part if managed responsibly: streamlined visas, robust credential recognition, integration support, and safeguards to prevent draining health systems in source countries. Taken together, a stable, well-resourced plan will improve continuity of care, reduce unnecessary hospital visits, and keep high-quality services safe for older patients like me.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise creating a system that supports staff across primary and community care while ensuring safe, high-quality care. In practice, that means stronger links and joint funding with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and provide holistic patient care. When teams share tasks across settings, patients get quicker access and staff avoid being overwhelmed. In our local area, staff are often stretched and appointments cancelled; better coordination between services would help, and mobile clinics visiting village halls and college campuses would cut travel times and speed access.

To retain diverse staff and reduce burnout, we need flexible working patterns: accessible part-time roles, job-shares, phased retirement for older colleagues, and high-quality childcare support. Proactive mental health services for staff themselves are essential so people feel supported to continue in demanding jobs.

Finally, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals should work under clear supervision and with defined roles to safely spread GP workload. That could include joint training hubs, shared electronic records, and mobile or telehealth clinics so patients never lose access when a GP is unavailable. These steps align with my experience juggling study, work, and family and keeping patient care at the center.

From where I stand, any NHS workforce plan has to prioritise safe, high-quality care while taking the pressure off GPs without breaking the thread of continuity that patients rely on. The three pillars below reflect what I’ve seen work well in practice and what worries me if we rely on one-off staffing boosts without proper structure.

First, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with clear training, supervision and governance. It’s not about replacing GPs with more bodies, but redistributing tasks in a way that keeps the patient at the centre. A well-supported role for pharmacists, nurses, physician associates, paramedics and other allied staff can take on long-running, well-defined tasks such as medication reviews, chronic disease monitoring and triage. But this must be done with proper supervision, shared care plans, and robust escalation routes so a clinician who knows the patient’s history remains at the core of decisions. In my experience, where a practice has a pharmacist running medication reviews under agreed protocols and a nurse practitioner leading low-risk chronic care clinics, GP time is freed for complex cases, while safety and continuity aren’t sacrificed. The key is governance: clear scope of practice, mandatory handovers, ongoing training, and regular case reviews to prevent fragmentation. If we get the supervision and integration right, we can extend access without forcing patients to switch clinicians or lose context between visits.

Second, build transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. We need reliable, local evidence to plan, fund and monitor performance—on patient outcomes as much as on throughput. That means dashboards that track staffing mix, vacancy rates, patient wait times, continuity of care indices, hospital admissions for chronic conditions, medication safety events and patient experience. With good data, planning can shift quickly: if a neighbourhood shows high turnover in a particular role or persistent delays in follow-up reviews, the plan can reallocate clinicians or fund targeted training. In practice, our area could benefit from a standardised approach to measuring continuity and outcomes in parallel with activity metrics. It’s not enough to count slots filled; we need to see whether patients with long-term conditions achieve better control, fewer crises, and fewer unscheduled admissions—and adjust funding and training accordingly.

Third, deliver tailored incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal—covering housing and transport, plus flexible working and career development. Recruitment and retention in these places has always been tougher, and the climate for staff wellbeing is real. Incentives must be sustainable and linked to local needs: affordable housing near practices, relocation support, transport subsidies, and flexible or part-time routes that don’t derail skills development. Importantly, these incentives should come with clear pathways for career progression and ongoing professional support, including access to CPD and supervision. If we can demonstrate a real, long-term benefit to lives in those communities and ensure staff aren’t left isolated, we’ll see better retention and more stable services. In practice, I’ve seen coastal and rural services struggle when turnover is high or housing is unaffordable; targeted packages that pair financial support with professional development tend to yield more consistent teams and better patient trust.

All of this must align with the broader goal I’ve described before: keep timely access without compromising continuity and culturally sensitive care. A team-based model should be designed so a patient who walks into a practice meets clinicians who know their history, with the right people available for follow-up. That means not only expanding roles but embedding robust supervision, shared information systems, and transparent local planning.

In short, prioritise: (1) expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams with proper training and governance; (2) transparent local data and evaluation frameworks to drive funding and performance; and (3) targeted, sustainable incentives for staff in hard-to-fill places. When done thoughtfully, these elements support high-quality care, protect patient continuity, and relieve GP workload without creating new gaps in the system.

I think any NHS workforce plan must acknowledge that recruiting and retaining staff is not an end in itself, but a means to keep care safe, continuous and person-centred. My previous concerns about rushing throughput apply here too: you can’t improve access by filling seats if the quality of care and the patient-clinician relationship deteriorate. The plan should therefore balance ambitious recruitment with strong safeguards for staffing safety, training capacity and the integrity of care continuity.

Key priorities I’d expect to see:
- Responsible overseas recruitment with clear safeguards
  - Streamlined visas and quicker credential recognition, but only as part of a responsible, well-supported system. We need to recognise and credit overseas qualifications without creating a flood of short-term fixes that leave NHS teams unstable.
  - Integration support that helps newcomers settle: comprehensive induction, language and communication training, mentorship and structured supervision. A supportive on-ramp matters as much as faster licensing.
  - Safeguards against draining source health systems. This means quotas, transparent reporting on where staff are recruited from, and investments in home-country health workforce development to prevent a net loss elsewhere. It also means fair distribution within the country so rural and underserved areas aren’t left without essential staff.
  - Practical measures to maintain continuity for patients: language and cultural orientation paired with a robust buddy/colleague network so new staff can quickly become part of a stable care team rather than passing through the system.

- Secure, multi-year funding to sustain workforce initiatives
  - Ring-fenced funding for training capacity, apprenticeships, professional development and career progression. Short-term pilots are useful, but long-term stability is what actually changes workforce planning and patient experience.
  - Funding that recognises the full cycle of workforce needs: undergraduate placements, nurse and allied-health student intake, return-to-practice routes, and ongoing upskilling for existing staff. This reduces churn and gives staff a clear career ladder.
  - Protection against policy volatility: if budgets swing with political cycles, clinics never get the time they need to embed new models of care. A predictable funding envelope helps hospitals invest in supervision, simulation training and recruitment pipelines that actually translate into safer care.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving care models
  - Set safe, evidence-based staffing ratios that consider patient acuity, hospital setting and the complexity of care. Widen the lens beyond headcount to include skill mix, task delegation and support staff who keep clinicians doing what matters most.
  - Continuity of care as a governing principle. Use team-based rosters with named clinicians or small, stable teams to preserve the relational element of care. Avoid over-reliance on ad-hoc shifts or high turnover that undermines trust and accuracy of patient records.
  - Safety monitoring as a daily discipline. Require transparent dashboards tracking staffing levels, patient safety incidents, near-misses, clinician burnout and patient satisfaction. If a staffing change improves access but worsens safety, the plan must recalibrate.

- Practical, real-world implementation
  - Invest in local training pipelines and partnerships with schools, colleges and universities to grow the domestic workforce where possible. Encourage flexible routes into nursing, allied health and primary care, including return-to-practice schemes for those who left the workforce.
  - Improve working conditions and retention incentives: reasonable hours, safe workloads, mentoring for new staff, supportive management, and fair pay progression that recognises experience and skill. Flexible working patterns can help retain good clinicians who start families or have care responsibilities.
  - Support for overseas recruits that keeps patients safe without eroding the care you want to protect. This includes language and cultural training, clinical supervision, and clear integration pathways so staff become part of stable teams rather than temporary fixes.

Personal reflections from my own circle reinforce why continuity and staffing quality matter. When a local clinic used short-term agency staff to cover shortages, we saw more missed details, repeated questions, and longer overall pathways to get basic issues resolved. That translated into higher anxiety for families and, ultimately, avoidable hospital visits. If the workforce plan can deliver safe ratios, stable teams and proper training—alongside ethical international recruitment—it can deliver the timely access we want without sacrificing the quality of care.

In short, prioritising sustainable funding, responsible international recruitment with solid integration and safeguards, plus robust safe-staffing standards and continuity-focused care models, is the only way to both recruit and retain staff and maintain the high quality of care patients deserve. If these elements aren’t secured, aiming to increase headcount alone will simply push the system toward the same problems we’re already seeing: staff burnout, inconsistent care and worse patient outcomes.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise three linked areas to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality. First, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, plus thorough digital training for all staff. This must be paired with safeguarding for digitally excluded patients, ensuring strong non-digital pathways (phone or paper notes) remain available. In my experience, clinicians access to a patient’s history quickly makes a real difference to safety and outcomes, and that relies on reliable, well-used digital tools.

Second, develop transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with ongoing evaluation. Local areas know where gaps exist in GP, nurse and therapy capacity, turnover and rostering. Clear dashboards and regular reviews help target funding and drive improvements where they’re most needed.

Third, secure stable funding and local recruitment with clear career progression, flexible working options and predictable rosters so teams can build relationships with patients, including older residents. Supportive supervision, multidisciplinary collaboration, and robust contingency plans for staff absences are essential to preserve continuity of care.

These steps align with keeping access and quality high while ensuring the workforce is valued, well-supported and resilient.

From my view, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation, sensible indemnity arrangements and funded, protected clinical supervision to support new roles and keep patient safety at the heart of care. Where practice nurses, pharmacists, social prescribers or mental health workers take on more triage or extended follow-up, there should be explicit scope documents and joint governance to prevent gaps or duplication. Revalidation processes should be streamlined and adequately funded so staff can stay up to date without excessive bureaucracy.

Indemnity arrangements must cover expanded activities and be funded by employers, with consistency across professions so staff feel protected when working at the top of their licence. Protected supervision is essential when introducing new roles: regular, quality supervision and case discussion help staff grow safely and sustain good care. 

In addition, clear career pathways and flexible, sustainable working patterns will aid recruitment and retention. Safe staffing targets, smarter rosters and sufficient support staff reduce burnout and improve patient safety in GP practices and community teams. In my experience, where supervision is strong and boundaries are clear, care is more reliable and waiting times improve for older patients with complex needs.

Prioritise a balanced workforce plan: invest in interoperable IT and ongoing staff digital training; support overseas recruitment with robust credential checks, integration help and safeguards for source health systems; offer targeted pay, retention incentives, relocation bursaries to underserved areas while maintaining safe, high-quality care.

In line with my ongoing support for locally sensible reform and patient-centred care, I think the NHS workforce plan should prioritise three things. First, tailored incentives to recruit and retain staff in hard-to-fill places—rural, coastal and urban deprived areas. This should include affordable housing, relocation and travel support, flexible working patterns, and clear progression opportunities, so experienced staff stay and newcomers are attracted. In my coastal town, housing and transport barriers are real barriers to building stable teams. Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles—with robust supervision and safe delegation so GP workload can be redistributed without risking safety or quality. This needs common training and shared access to records to function smoothly. Third, couple workforce expansion with strong safety measures: safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models and ongoing safety monitoring. Regular audits, real-time dashboards and triggers if staffing falls short will help ensure access improvements don’t undermine care quality. Added training, return-to-practice schemes and CPD should run in parallel, reinforcing the hub-based, patient-centred approach I’ve supported through local pilots.

I would urge the NHS to base its workforce plan on patient safety first: clearly define scope of practice for staff taking on expanded roles, ensure robust revalidation, and put indemnity arrangements on a stable footing. Fund protected clinical supervision to guide and assess new duties, so patient safety is not sacrificed in the rush to fill vacancies. The plan should also expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied roles—with proper training and supervision to redistribute GP workload safely. In practice, when GP capacity is stretched, having practice nurses and pharmacists carry out medication reviews and minor urgent care helped our local surgeries, but without clear governance and ongoing supervision the risk of errors grows. Long-term retention will depend on clear career paths, flexible working options, and access to continuing education. For an ageing population, ensure teams can deliver home visits and integrate with district nurses, with shared records that keep continuity. A stable, adequately funded plan for supervision and indemnity is essential to sustain safe, high-quality care.

Prioritise interoperable IT, secure systems and ongoing digital training for staff, with protected non-digital options for digitally excluded patients, so care remains safe and high-quality while simplifying workflows and supporting retention.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the workforce plan should balance domestic development with responsible overseas recruitment used as a supplement, not a substitute for training at home. Equitable distribution also matters—provide incentives to work in underserved areas and flexible career pathways that suit different life stages. This approach aligns with the need for more capacity while upholding high standards and responsible, ethical recruitment.

I think the NHS workforce plan must focus on three linked priorities to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping high‑quality care safe. Flexible working, strong wellbeing support and clear progression pathways are essential to keep people in the system rather than burning out or moving abroad Second, places and practical supports: invest in sustainable staffing models and make relocation easier so vacancies in rural or deprived areas can be filled with continuity of care. Third, technology and training: interoperable, secure IT that lets patient records move smoothly between GP,, hospital and community services, with thorough staff digital training. Crucially, safeguard non‑digital options for digitally excluded patients—phone triage and paper records where needed—so no one is left behind. In my area, fragmentation of IT and staffing shortages have driven delays and reduced safety. A plan that combines pay and retention with integrated IT and inclusive access woul improve both safety and quality of care.

A NHS workforce plan should be built around the twin aims of keeping people safe and maintaining the continuity of care that patients rely on, while also attracting and keeping a diverse, motivated workforce. In practice, that means prioritising safe staffing levels, continuity-preserving delivery models and robust safety monitoring, even as we offer flexible, supportive working arrangements to retain experienced staff and bring in new talent.

First, safe staffing ratios must be a foundation, not a afterthought. We need reliable, locally informed benchmarks for every setting—GP practices, district nursing, community teams, and hospital wards—that are tied to patient risk, case complexity and peak times. Too often we’ve seen vacancies become absences in effect, with teams stretched thin and appointment quality suffering. A plan should include real-time staffing dashboards, explicit triggers for recruitment and escalation, and a funded reserve to cover illness and surge periods. This is not about bureaucratic targets; it’s about ensuring a safe standard of care so that longer appointments for complex needs remain feasible and effective, not a sign of overworked clinicians.

Second, continuity-preserving workforce models deserve protected investment. The continuity of a named clinician or small, stable care teams is central to managing chronic conditions and reducing unnecessary hospital visits. The plan should promote rosters and funding that support long-standing clinician–patient relationships—GPs, nurses, and pharmacists who know the patient’s history, medications and social circumstances. This might mean protected slots for ongoing reviews, and structured handovers that preserve a patient’s trusted clinician even as other team members rotate in. In rural and coastal Scotland, where people can travel long distances, continuity becomes even more important for outcomes and patient confidence.

Safety monitoring must be rigorous and transparent. Regular safety reviews, incident learning, and patient feedback should be built into workforce planning. If a plan signals that a staffing change will affect care quality, there must be a rapid, evidence-based mitigation: temporary team reconfiguration, telehealth support, or targeted recruitment. Sharing these safety metrics with frontline staff helps everyone understand why certain staffing decisions are made and reassures patients that quality remains the priority.

From a practical standpoint, flexible working patterns are essential for recruitment and retention. Offering part-time roles, job-sharing, phased retirement, and flexible hours helps us keep experienced clinicians in the service for longer and makes nursing and allied-health roles more attractive to a broader pool of people, including those caring responsibilities or those returning after a break. In my area I’ve seen colleagues scale back their hours to manage family commitments, and when done right, this reduces burnout and keeps skilled staff available instead of losing them entirely. Providing accessible childcare and dependable mental health support for staff would also make a real difference in retention, especially given the pressures of winter surges and rising demand.

Clear, funded career pathways are essential too. The workforce plan should guarantee protected CPD budgets, structured mentorship, and accessible return-to-practice schemes. It’s important to celebrate both experienced clinicians and those earlier in their careers. For instance, a mentorship model where seasoned GPs or district nurses mentor newer colleagues—not just for clinical skills but for triage decision-making and patient communication—helps sustain quality and confidence across cohorts. Return-to-practice programmes, with tailored retraining for those who paused for family or health reasons, should be funded and streamlined so talent isn’t lost.

Practical examples of how this could work involve both teams and patients. In a community team, a named clinician with a small, stable group—supported by a pharmacist, physiotherapist and social worker—could manage a patient with long-term diabetes and heart risk factors, coordinating bloods, meds and lifestyle advice in a 30-minute slot. If a staff member is temporarily unavailable, the safety monitoring system would trigger a structured handover plan rather than an abrupt gaps in care. For rural areas, mobile clinics and telehealth can supplement in-person visits, with rotas designed to reduce travel burden on patients while preserving the continuity of relationships with familiar clinicians.

Finally, the plan must address the pipeline of recruitment in a practical way. Attractive career ladders, targeted recruitment incentives for hard-to-fill posts and regions, and deliberate succession planning will help; but they must be paired with a clear, funded strategy for retention. We can’t chase quick fixes for access without embedding safeguards that maintain clinical quality and safety.

In short, I’d want the NHS workforce plan to treat safe staffing, continuity of care, and safety monitoring as non-negotiables, while offering flexible work options, robust CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice routes to keep a diverse, capable workforce. That combination feels most likely to improve access without compromising the high standard of care our communities deserve.

I welcome the direction of an NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care. With the system under so much pressure, the plan must be practical, evidence‑based and focused on both expanding supply and making it sustainable in daily practice. I’d prioritise three linked strands: growing domestic workforce through education, offering targeted incentives where recruitment is hardest, and clarifying roles in a way that protects patients and supports staff development.

First, we need to grow supply through robust training pipelines. That means increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected placements and strong university–practice partnerships so students experience primary care and community services early and repeatedly. It should be ordinary for medical and nursing students to spend extended blocks in GP practices and community teams, with clear pathways into jobs at the end of training. It’s not enough to add cohorts; we must guarantee funded, high‑quality placements that are respected in both academic and clinical settings.
