In our area, shortages across GPs, district nursing and mental health teams mean delays and rushed appointments for older residents like me. The plan should prioritise: 
- Targeted competitive pay and retention payments to reward frontline staff and reduce turnover, especially in high‑demand roles and underserved locations. 
- Relocation packages and bursaries to attract people to move to or train in our communities. 
- More funded training places and clear career progression, with mentorship and specialist pathways in geriatrics, mental health, and chronic disease. 
- Flexible, supportive working patterns, adequate admin support, reasonable hours and wellbeing resources to prevent burnout. 
- Strong local recruitment pipelines with schools, colleges and community organisations, so we build a workforce from the area. 
- Investment in safe staffing norms and decent working environments, including both digital and non‑digital ways of delivering care. 
When practices can recruit and retain staff with these incentives, my neighbours will get timely, respectful care and organisations will maintain high standards without constant firefighting.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise building and regulating multidisciplinary teams to share GP workload safely. This means expanding roles for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals working alongside GPs in integrated primary care teams, with clear supervision, defined scopes of practice and ongoing training. In practice, when a practice has a pharmacist and a nurse practitioner supporting triage and medication reviews, patients get quicker, safer replies and GP time is freed for more complex cases. For routinely managed conditions this can cut unnecessary referrals and reduce waiting times.

Securing multi-year, ring-fenced funding is essential so we can grow training capacity, stabilise recruitment, and implement retention schemes without constant policy upheaval. Funding should cover clinical placements, mentorship and digital literacy so teams can work seamlessly across online and in-person routes.

Responsible overseas recruitment can help plug gaps, but with streamlined visas, robust credential recognition, structured integration support and safeguards to protect source-country health systems. This requires clear career pathways and local retention incentives to ensure long-term benefits for patients and staff alike.

Any NHS workforce plan should start by reducing non-clinical burden on clinicians: fewer targets, less duplication, streamlined referrals, and simpler IT systems. In my experience, admin tasks eat into time that should be spent with patients; better electronic records that are intuitive and interoperable would save hours and cut delays in referral pathways. The plan should then prioritise safe redistribution of tasks through expanded multidisciplinary teams: senior nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals working under clear supervision and with defined scopes of practice. This would free GPs to focus on complex cases, while routine reviews, prescribing support, and case management could be shared.

Key investments: scalable training pipelines with protected time, robust supervision, consistent professional standards, and career progression routes; reliable recruitment and retention packages including flexible working, wellbeing support, and safe staffing ratios; and strong governance to ensure safety during role-sharing and triage. Finally, ensure IT improvements: user-friendly platforms, integrated messaging within primary care, and reliable referral handoffs to avoid delays. A workforce plan that balances frontline capacity with good admin and digital tools will maintain high-quality care while addressing burnout.

Prioritise three pillars: invest in interoperable IT and staff digital training while safeguarding digitally excluded; grow domestic supply via undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship placements with strong uni-practice links and wellbeing measures; expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with oversight to safely redistribute GP workload and maintain high care quality.

An NHS workforce plan should be transparent, locally informed and outcome‑driven, balancing recruitment with safe, high‑quality care. It must prioritise safe staffing, continuity of care and robust safety monitoring while expanding access. Central to this is developing localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks so funding and performance monitoring reflect reality on the ground. Real‑time dashboards for vacancies, fill rates, sickness absence and turnover help target interventions quickly and prevent service deterioration. In our area, for example, persistent vacancies impact appointment availability; timely data would enable targeted, local action.

To attract and keep staff, we need targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries for underserved areas and high‑demand roles such as mental health, district nurses and allied health professionals. Funding should follow staff to challenging posts, with mentoring and clear career progression to stabilise teams.

Equally important is safe staffing ratios and continuity‑preserving models—teams where patients see the same clinicians where possible, backed by multidisciplinary groups (pharmacists, physiotherapists, paramedics, physician associates) and clear escalation paths. Safety monitoring should include regular audits, incident reporting and robust wellbeing safeguards to prevent burnout. Finally, plans must couple local delivery and training with national support to scale up where needed, ensuring equity across Wales.

Agree. Any NHS workforce plan that truly aims to recruit, retain and support staff while safeguarding high‑quality care has to put people and their working lives at the centre. From my lived experience in England, the bottlenecks aren’t only about the number of bodies but about how we design roles, support wellbeing, and ensure teams can work safely and predictably. Here are the priorities I’d want to see reflected in a robust plan:

- Flexible, sustainable working patterns. Staff stay when they have options that fit their lives—part‑time and job‑share arrangements, phased retirement, predictable rotas, and reliable back‑fill. Childcare support and strong mental health services for staff are essential to prevent burnout. For many, the difference between leaving and staying is a workable blend of hours, manageable caseloads, and real time for rest and family.

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams. Rebalancing GP workload through MDTs that include nurses, nurse practitioners, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied health professionals is not a luxury—it’s a safety issue. These teams must have clear scopes of practice, robust supervision, appropriate training, and defined pathways so responsibilities are redistributed safely and patients still see a clinician quickly when urgent or complex needs arise.

- Systematic training, career progression and return‑to‑practice routes. There needs to be more training places for GPs, nurses, and mental health professionals, plus high‑quality CPD and leadership development. Return‑to‑practice schemes, apprenticeships, and support for those changing career paths can widen the talent pool and help retain skilled staff who might otherwise leave. Career ladders should exist across primary, community and mental health settings, with funded mentoring and supervision.

- A reliable recruitment pipeline, locally and from overseas. A plan should streamline recruitment, reduce bureaucratic barriers, and provide welcome packages that help with relocation and integration. Sustainable funding is essential to avoid a heavy reliance on agency staff who don’t have the long‑term stake in a community and can burn out quickly.

- Safer, more predictable staffing levels. Staffing ratios and workload forecasting need to be data‑driven so practices aren’t routinely stretched beyond safe limits. That means budgeting for both clinical time and back‑office support, minimising unnecessary administrative burdens, and ensuring sufficient coverage for safe shift patterns so clinicians can deliver quality care without compromising their own safety.

- Strong integration with mental health and community services. Training and supervision should reflect the reality that physical and mental health are intertwined. MDTs should be able to coordinate a single care plan across primary care, community nursing, IAPT, and crisis services, reducing multiple points of contact and repeated assessments for patients.

- Invest in technology that saves time, not creates work. Digital tools should streamline booking, referrals, and information transfer, while leaving clinicians time to actually see patients. Interoperable records and shared dashboards help teams coordinate care without duplicating work or losing critical information.

- Safe, transparent governance and culture. Staff need honest feedback loops, measurable targets, and accountability when targets aren’t met. Regular wellbeing surveys, accessible confidential support, and leadership that prioritises realistic workloads over perceived efficiency gains are essential for retention.

Examples from the ground matter. In my area, consistent GP slots are a rarity and I’ve seen community teams stretched thin; extended hours and walk‑in urgent care hubs could alleviate pressure if staffed with a true MDT approach rather than a single clinician backed by a long waiting list. Flexible hours, stronger child‑care options, and protected time for professional development would not only help recruitment but also keep capable clinicians in the system long enough to build trust with patients.

In short, a successful workforce plan must recognise that safe, high‑quality care depends on diverse, well-supported teams working within a sustainable model. It needs practical, funded measures that improve retention, empower multidisciplinary practice, and deliver timely care for patients without burning people out. That is how we’ll see real progress beyond just tinkering with processes.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality, the NHS workforce plan should: 1) set clear scopes of practice for new roles, with protected time for supervision and robust indemnity and revalidation arrangements, so patient safety is not compromised; 2) expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams in primary care—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals—with structured training and supervision to redistribute GP workload; 3) provide practical examples: practice nurses leading chronic disease reviews and triage, pharmacists conducting medicines reviews and personalised care plans, PAs with defined responsibilities, and paramedics delivering home visits and urgent care in the community; 4) ensure joint funding and planning with social care, mental health and community services to realise holistic care and shared staffing where appropriate; 5) invest in career progression, CPD, wellbeing, reasonable workloads and fair pay to improve retention. In my experience, safer supervision and clearer roles reduce errors and keep patients safe while expanding capacity.

I’m supportive of a workforce plan that recognises that you can’t improve access without ensuring safety and high-quality care every step of the way. In practice, that means four interlocking priorities: safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving care models, rigorous safety monitoring, and multi-year, ring-fenced funding for training and workforce development. Without these, expanding access could simply shift bottlenecks around or risk worse outcomes for patients.

First, safe staffing ratios across every setting. It isn’t enough to recruit more clinicians if teams are still stretched or the workload is not matched to patient need. The plan should set clear, evidence-based staffing standards for general practice, community nursing, and mental health teams, with real-time rostering that can flex in response to demand. Where possible, avoid over-reliance on agency staff whose continuity and familiarity with local pathways are limited. I’ve seen how gaps in staffing can extend appointment wait times, increase no-shows, and fragment care. A safer baseline should be complemented by surge capacity for crises or flu seasons so that urgent access improvements don’t come at the expense of safety and quality.

Second, continuity-preserving models. Patients benefit when a consistent team or a small, named group of clinicians follow them over time. This reduces repetitive retelling of a problem, lowers the risk of miscommunication, and supports better clinical judgments. For example, if a patient with chronic anxiety or a long-term physical condition sees the same GP, nurse, and mental health worker who understand their history, escalation pathways become faster and more predictable. To support this, the workforce plan should incentivise multi-disciplinary teams that retain core staff, introduce stable scheduling, and limit arbitrary churn during service expansions. In rural or suburban areas where staffing can be volatile, guaranteed continuity is especially crucial to prevent gaps in care.

Third, robust safety monitoring. As services expand, real-time safety signals must be available to managers and frontline teams. That includes dashboards showing staffing levels, wait times, clinical risk indicators, and incident trends. Clear escalation protocols, with timely access to senior clinical review when risk thresholds are met, are essential. This is not about blame but about learning and rapid improvement. In practice, a safety-net approach – where data prompts immediate local reviews and targeted support – helps ensure that when access improves, it doesn’t come at the cost of care quality.

Fourth, long-term, ring-fenced funding for training and workforce development. A multi-year settlement that protects and grows training capacity, supports career progression, and reduces policy volatility is essential. The NHS must be able to plan cohorts of GPs, nurses, mental health professionals, pharmacists, and allied health workers over several years, not just months. Ring-fenced funding would pay for accredited training, supervision, and mentorship; expand undergraduate and postgraduate training places; support flexible routes into practice in areas with shortages; and fund retention measures such as wellbeing programmes, reasonable workloads, and safe hours. In my area, policy shifts have repeatedly disrupted recruitment pipelines and training slots; a stable funding stream would help build a workforce that can deliver longer-term improvements to access and quality.

Concrete examples of how this could work include: protected training slots for new mental health practitioners tied to local service expansion, joint recruitment paired with the opening of multi-disciplinary hubs, and fixed funding to develop telehealth and digital literacy for both staff and patients so that access is not limited by transport or geography. Retention initiatives—mentoring for early-career clinicians, career progression pathways, and supportive leadership—would help keep experienced staff in place, reducing turnover and sustaining quality.

Overall, I want an NHS workforce plan that grows the right kinds of staff in the right places, with the right level of experience, and under stable funding. If we get safe staffing, continuity of care, robust safety monitoring, and secure multi-year funding aligned to service expansion, we’ll deliver faster, safer access that reflects the same seriousness we give to physical health care. That’s how we move toward real parity between mental and physical health services and, most importantly, how patients like me experience care that is timely, respectful and effective.

Patient safety and care quality must be the foundation for any NHS workforce plan. Prioritising safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving care models is essential so improving access does not come at the expense of outcomes. This means enough skilled staff across GP, community, and urgent services, and teams that stay together long enough to know patients’ histories. Real-time safety monitoring and transparent workforce metrics are needed so managers can spot shortages before they harm patients. 

We also need flexible working options to recruit and retain staff: varied hours, part-time roles, job sharing, phased retirement, and strong support for childcare and mental health. These measures help reduce burnout and widen the workforce to include more diverse voices. 

Investment in interoperable IT and secure systems is critical, with thorough training for staff. Yet we must safeguard non digital routes for patients who are digitally excluded, including paper records, local hubs, and clear signposting (as if that will ever happen). In my area, moves toward digital only have stressed staff and left some patients behind; a balanced plan would align tech with human care.

I think any NHS workforce plan should put robust, localised data at its core, backed by clear modelling and achievable KPIs, with evaluation built in from the start. Too often national targets feel detached from what’s happening in individual communities, and that makes planning and funding less effective. In practice, we need real-time vacancy data, patient demand patterns, and workforce mix visible at a practice, PCN or local authority level so plans reflect actual need rather than projections alone.

A practical approach would be to set up transparent dashboards that track key indicators for every locality: vacancy rates by role and practice, average wait times for routine and urgent appointments, mix of clinicians (GP partners, salaried GPs, nurse practitioners, physician associates, practice nurses), annual training numbers completed, and staff turnover. It would help to model demand under different scenarios—winter pressures, flu surges, or a rise in complex care needs among older residents—and then measure how changes in recruitment, training capacity or flexible working affect access and safety.

Where I live, you can see how gaps in staffing translate into delays for routine checks or mental health follow-ups. If we had transparent, local modelling that shows how many clinicians we need to recruit by site, and how many training places must be created to meet that demand in three to five years, that would enable more realistic budgeting and hiring. KPIs should cover both access (time to appointment, same-day triage rate, digital channel effectiveness) and safety (medication reviews completed, continuity of care metrics) while keeping patient experience central.

To make this work, we need secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding. Short-term policy shifts make it very hard for practices to plan recruitment campaigns, expand training capacity, or implement flexible working that actually sticks. A multi-year settlement would give time to scale up GP training numbers, support nursing associates and pharmacists in primary care, and fund dedicated admin and care-navigation roles that reduce clinician burnout. In our area, a three-year funding horizon, with reserved funds for language and integration support for international hires and for protected training time, would enable meaningful, sustainable change.

This kind of funding should come with capacity-building around training and supervision, not just pay. Practical investments—protected admin time, clinical supervision, and structured wellbeing support—help staff stay in frontline roles longer, which in turn improves patient safety and continuity of care. And because the system is interconnected, the workforce plan must align with community health teams and mental health services so patients experience smoother pathways and fewer unnecessary referrals.

I’ve seen the contrast: when a practice can offer flexible hours, good staff development, and reliable supervision, morale improves, burnout drops, and retention rises. When funding or planning is flakey, recruitment stalls, and waiting times creep up. A workforce plan that combines transparent local data, solid evaluation frameworks, and stable, long-term funding would give clinicians the backing they need to deliver safe, high-quality care day in, day out.

Overall, the aim should be fewer bottlenecks in primary care, better support for staff, and a system that can adapt to changing needs without constant upheaval. That’s how we protect safety and the quality of care for patients now and in the years ahead.

The plan should prioritise stability, capacity and true integration across health and care. Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding is essential so NHS bodies can plan long-term workforce initiatives, expand training capacity, and offer coherent career pathways without being undermined by short-term policy changes. This budget certainty supports recruitment and retention of nurses, GPs, allied health professionals, mental health staff and social care workers, with flexible working and progression that reflect the realities of ageing populations and complex needs seen in Wales. 

Equally important is strengthening joint funding and links with social care, mental health and community services to redistribute workload and deliver holistic patient care. Shared roles, co-funded posts and integrated teams can reduce bottlenecks, cut duplication, and keep people out of hospital by catching issues earlier in the community. 

Investing in interoperable IT and secure systems, alongside staff digital training, is vital for safer, more coordinated care. But we must safeguard alternatives for those who are digitally excluded, ensuring non-digital avenues remain available for booking, information and support. In my experience, a district-nurse/GP/pharmacist collaborative model anchored by stable funding would make longer, safer appointments possible and relieve stress across local teams, benefiting patients and carers alike.

I strongly believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives for rural, urban deprived and coastal areas to recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care. Practical steps include housing and transport packages: affordable housing near practices, relocation grants, and subsidies for travel or improved local transport links to reduce burnout from long commutes. Targeted recruitment bonuses and longer-term retention bursaries, plus salary supplements where living costs are higher, would help attract clinicians to hard-to-fill posts. 

But financial incentives must be paired with real local support: flexible, predictable rotas; protected time for training and mentorship; and clear career progression paths for allied health professionals, nurses, pharmacists and GPs. Expanding multidisciplinary teams based in community hubs or mobile units can better reach dispersed populations, especially in rural and coastal areas. In my area, mobile clinics and outreach visits improve access, yet turnover remains a key issue; stable staffing comes from consistent incentives and opportunities for professional growth. 

The plan should align with digital care, ensuring staff have time and training to use telehealth safely, so we don’t transfer workload unsustainably.

From my long experience of NHS services, any workforce plan must recognise that shortages are not uniform and that recruitment and retention depend on real local conditions. It should prioritise targeted incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas—rural communities, coastal towns and urban deprived neighborhoods—so staff will see a clear local need and a reasonable pathway to development. This includes housing and transport support: affordable staff accommodation near clinics, relocation assistance, and housing allowances where prices are high; plus reliable transport options such as subsidised bus passes or staff parking near hubs and flexible rosters that reduce long commutes.

Retaining staff needs more than pay. Funding should back safe, well-supported teams with protected CPD time, mentorship and clear career progression, plus minimum staffing ratios to maintain quality and safety. Invest in local training pipelines—placements in community hubs and roles across nursing, allied health and mental health—so people can build a career where they live. And ensure digital infrastructure and robust safeguarding practices so multi‑disciplinary teams can collaborate safely with patients.

From my perspective in England, a NHS workforce plan will only succeed if it creates funded, visible career pathways and robust support for staff throughout their careers. The priorities must include clear, funded ladders across clinical roles with transparent progression criteria and time built in for advancement. Protected CPD is essential: guaranteed weekly time for learning, dedicated funding for courses and revalidation, and access to high-quality modular learning. Structured mentorship and supervision for all staff, plus formal return-to-practice schemes that provide refresher training, supervised practice, and financial support for those rejoining after time away. Retention must be addressed with targeted packages for experienced clinicians and flexible routes into leadership, education and advisory roles to prevent leakage from the system. We also need practical cross-disciplinary pathways—pharmacists to review meds, physiotherapists to share workload—so teams can function safely when shortages bite. Finally, ensure wellbeing and workload controls with access to support services, sensible rosters, and data-driven planning to prevent gaps. These measures must be funded and monitored; without them, expanding services will outpace recruitment and risk safety.

From where I sit in England, any NHS workforce plan must prioritise safe, high‑quality care while modernising how we work—not at the expense of patients who can’t or won’t use digital channels. I’ve seen frontline staff stretched thin by incompatible systems and endless training on new tools, while patients watch and wait. A sensible plan should combine ambitious IT improvement with practical, people‑centred protections for those who are digitally excluded.

Key priorities I’d want to see:
- Interoperable, secure IT with real‑time data sharing
  - A single, shared patient record across primary care, community services and mental health teams, with robust privacy controls and clear governance.
  - Consistent data standards so information can move safely between settings, providers can learn from each other, and clinicians aren’t duplicating work.
  - Strong cyber security and disaster recovery; reliable access even in less‑than‑perfect broadband settings.
  - Realistic rollout with plenty of user testing; avoid forcing changes that disrupt continuity of care.
- Comprehensive staff digital training and support
  - Mandatory, ongoing digital literacy and system–specific training for all clinical and admin staff, with protected time to learn.
  - On‑site digital champions, 24/7 IT help desks, and easy access to user‑friendly interfaces so tech saves time, not creates chaos.
  - Practical guidance on data sharing, privacy, consent and patient choice, so clinicians can use digital tools without compromising trust.
- Safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients
  - Maintain traditional routes: phone access, walk‑in scheduling where possible, and in‑person triage with human support.
  - Fund accessible digital inclusion measures: subsidised devices or data plans for patients, private spaces for telehealth in community hubs, and translation/interpretation support during digital encounters.
- Staffing levels, wellbeing and professional development
  - Clear, funded workforce plans that reflect local needs: safe vacancy targets, sustainable rosters, and predictable patterns so staff can plan and recover.
  - Strong supervision, mentoring and career progression across disciplines; make appealing career paths for nurses, allied health professionals, pharmacists, and mental health specialists.
  - Investment in staff wellbeing, reasonable workloads, and adequate time for reflective practice; reduce burnout by avoiding perpetual change without support.
- Multidisciplinary, locally rooted teams
  - Expand integrated teams that include GPs, nurses, pharmacists, social care colleagues and CMHTs, with shared care pathways and joint training to improve continuity.
  - Flexible deployment that matches patient needs in the community, not just in hospital settings.
- Recruitment, retention and local recruitment pipelines
  - Targeted recruitment from local communities; incentives, bursaries and flexible working to reflect local demographics.
  - Competitive pay, clear career ladders, safe and supportive supervision, and opportunities for rotation to build skills and loyalty.
- Governance, safety and quality
  - Use workforce planning to safeguard patient safety: appropriate staffing levels, regular competency assessments, and robust incident reporting.
  - Ensure digital changes do not erode clinical judgment; keep clinicians in the loop about when to rely on technology and when to rely on human contact.
- Equity, language and inclusion
  - Build interpreters and culturally competent care into every part of the plan; ensure IT tools include accessible language options and patient‑facing materials in multiple formats.

In practice, the best results come from a balanced approach. Interoperable IT and staff digital training can unlock efficiency and safer care, but not if they leave behind patients who lack devices, digital skills or private spaces for consultations. The plan should set milestones, measure real outcomes (wait times, safety indicators, patient satisfaction, equity metrics) and align with local investments in premises, transport and community access points so care remains reachable for everyone.

If these priorities are integrated with sensible staffing models and well‑funded training, we can recruit and retain capable teams while preserving the personal, humane care at the heart of the NHS.

The plan should prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams in primary and community care, with clear scope-of-practice and protected supervision to keep safety and quality high while redistributing workload from GPs. This means investing in training and certified supervision for nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied roles, linked to strong governance and shared records so patient care remains seamless.

Key actions include: formalising scope-of-practice, revalidation processes, and indemnity arrangements that reflect expanded roles; funding protected time for supervision and professional development; and creating transparent career ladders with mentoring and peer review to support retention. Practical examples: a pharmacist-led triage service for common infections, PA-led chronic-disease reviews, and paramedics conducting home visits when appropriate, all under robust supervision and clear referral pathways; nurses delivering mental-health support through community hubs alongside GP teams. These changes would help deliver timely, safe care and reduce unnecessary GP attendances without compromising safety.

Additionally, ensure staff have flexible hours, access to digital triage, and reliable access to training and supervision; integrate workforce planning with digital records so staff can work across sites. Reassurance on indemnity and ongoing professional development will encourage recruitment and retention and sustain high-quality care for patients in England.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safe, high‑quality care, the plan must be measured and multi‑dimensional. It should welcome overseas recruitment where needed, but with strong safeguards: streamlined visas and rapid credential recognition paired with solid integration support (induction, mentoring, language help) and explicit protections so we do not deplete health systems in other countries or erode training pipelines at home.

Transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs are essential. Real‑time dashboards on vacancy rates, turnover, skill mix and safe staffing levels should drive funding, deployment and improvement plans, with independent evaluation to show what works and what doesn’t.

Strengthened links with social care, mental health and community services are crucial to redistribute workload and deliver holistic care. Joint funding and shared care pathways, plus community hubs and cross‑disciplinary training, can extend capacity in practical, locally tailored ways.

Investing in staff wellbeing and development matters too: protected time for training, reasonable workloads, robust supervision and clear career progression. In rural Wales, this means multi‑disciplinary teams, cross‑skilling and flexible staffing that can cover peaks without burning people out. Any plan should also support digital health tools while keeping non‑digital routes available for patients and staff who need them.

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that puts patients first and keeps care safe as we improve access. This means safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models and real safety monitoring guiding every recruitment decision. Practically, set minimum staffing levels per shift for GPs, nurses and allied roles, and ensure teams keep a named clinician so people aren’t passed around at each visit. Robust supervision and clear, secure handovers supported by interoperable IT are essential to maintain quality.

Overseas recruitment should be used responsibly: streamlined visas and rapid credential recognition, plus proper integration support, language training and local mentorship, with safeguards so we do not deplete health systems in other countries. It should add to our workforce, not merely relocate shortages abroad.

Tailored incentives for hard-to-fill places matter: housing near clinics, affordable transport, flexible working patterns and clear progression within local teams. In my district, a housing voucher or reliable bus service would help attract and retain staff in coastal and urban deprived areas.

Funding must follow these priorities; otherwise longer waits or poorer continuity could creep back in. We need both access and safety—together they protect quality of care.

I think any NHS workforce plan should protect safe, high-quality care first, even as we push for faster access. The priorities must include safe staffing ratios across GPs, nurses, therapists and other frontline roles, with clear minimums and flexible rostering so shifts aren’t stretched to breaking point. If workloads aren’t kept in check, longer appointments for complex cases won’t be sustainable and mistakes may rise. 

Continuity-preserving models matter too: give patients a regular clinician for ongoing needs, supported by care navigators and multidisciplinary teams. From my experience, a longer, well-planned consultation helps set a real plan, but it relies on having a stable clinician who can follow through rather than a string of hand-offs that erode trust and lead to rerefers.

Robust safety monitoring is essential: real-time safety data, consistent incident reporting, and governance that identifies staffing risks before patient harm occurs. Use this to adjust rosters, training and supervision rather than simply justify cuts. Pair this with fair pay, career development, and incentives that help retention and morale, including for unsociable hours.

Finally, back this with digital and operational tools that reduce avoidable workload (efficient triage, real-time booking, targeted telehealth) while keeping the human continuity and high-quality care patients expect.

From our perspective, any NHS workforce plan must be built on sustainable funding and long-term commitments, not just quick recruitment drives. It should prioritise clear, funded carrer pathways across all roles, with transparent criteria, progression routes and protected CPD time so staff can develop without compromising patient safety. Structured mentorship andd return-to-practice schemes are essential to keep experienced clinicians and to support early‑career staff back into work with confidence. Flexible working options are also crucial to retain a diverse workforce and reduce burnout—more part-time and job-sharr posts, phased retirement possibilities, reliable childcare support, and proactive mental health services that are easy to access. Staffing models should be data-driven, ensuring safe ratio and skilled rollovers across GP, community and hospital teams, with scope to deploy wider skills where appropriate. Embed wellbeing into daily practice, wit confidential support and reduced stigma around seeking help. Finally, ensure long-term commitment that aligns with service needs beyond political cycles,, with regula reviews of staffing levels, skill mix and patient safety outcomes to drive continuous improvement.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should prioritise tailored incentives for the hardest-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal—to recruit, retain and support staff while delivering safe, high-quality care. In practice, that means housing and transport support, flexible training and progression routes, and targeted recruitment bonuses that acknowledge the extra costs of working in these locations. In my coastal town, GP and district nurse vacancies can hold for months; staff turnover is higher, and patients face longer waits. A housing allowance or subsidised accommodation, plus subsidised public transport or car use, would make these posts viable for graduates who otherwise wouldn’t relocate. We should also back flexible, long-term pipelines with local universities and applied clinical apprenticeships, so people can train where they live and see a career in the NHS. Finally, combine incentives with safe staffing levels, mental health support for staff, and access to modern digital tools to reduce burnout. A plan like this would help keep services consistent and reduce inequalities in access.

I think any NHS workforce plan must place safe staffing at its core. Expanding access to services is pointless if the care isn’t safely delivered. Priorities should include safe staffing ratios across hospitals, GP practices and mental health teams, with regular audits and clear, public reporting on staffing and patient outcomes so communities can see the link between numbers and quality. In our area, when teams are stretched, people wait longer for basic assessment and follow‑up, and decisions risk being rushed. Continuity of care is vital, especially for older residents with multiple conditions: keeping patients with the same clinician or small, dedicated teams reduces errors and unnecessary hospital admissions. This requires recruiting from local communities, offering flexible, well-supported roles, and providing predictable career pathways to retain experienced staff. Robust safety monitoring is essential—strong clinical governance, regular supervision, manageable caseloads, and rapid escalation for risk. Any new capacity must come with proper training and integration into existing teams rather than being deployed in a way that fragments care. If we fund and structure staffing to protect quality, we’ll improve access without compromising safety or experience for patients.

I believe the NHS workforce plan should focus on three intertwined priorities: recruitment, retention and safe care. To attract skilled staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles, there should be targeted pay competitiveness, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries tied to service commitments. In my area, GP shortages mean persistent waits; offering a relocation incentive could bring clinicians into the community without compromising access elsewhere. To keep staff long-term, flexible hours, part-time and job-share options, phased retirement, and supported childcare would help a more diverse workforce stay in the NHS and avoid burnout. Proactive mental-health support for staff is essential, including confidential counselling and reasonable workloads. Finally, safety must come first: safe staffing ratios, continuity-preserving models (same GP or small teams) and ongoing safety monitoring and governance. That combination ensures we don’t improve access at the expense of quality. For example, if clinics can keep a stable team and monitor workloads, more sustainable longer first assessments become feasible rather than piling up backlogs. A workforce plan that blends financial incentives, flexible working and strong safety metrics would help recruit, retain and deliver high-quality care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while preserving safety and quality, the plan should prioritise targeted incentives for hard-to-fill areas—rural, coastal and urban deprived communities—paired with housing, transport and flexible working options. This includes affordable housing near practices, relocation or housing vouchers, and dedicated transport schemes or travel subsidies so staff can reach remote clinics without sacrificing time with patients. Tailored recruitment packages, including sign-on payments, longer service commitments, and support for return-to-practice, would help fill vacancies in district nursing, mental health teams and general practice.

Retention should hinge on safe, structured workloads and continuous professional development. Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models: named clinicians, small teams, and cross-disciplinary champions to limit handoffs and maintain relationships. Regular safety monitoring, open governance, and real-time workload dashboards to prevent burnout and protect patient care. Invest in digital tools that support triage and booking, reducing admin burdens on frontline staff.

From experience, when mobile clinics and extended hours were supported by stable teams, patients accessed care more reliably and safety concerns decreased. The plan must couple access improvements with stable staffing, clear career pathways, and ample safeguarding and quality assurance.

Agree: prioritise localised workforce data and KPIs, increase domestic training pipelines with protected placements and university-practice partnerships, and strengthen joint funding with social care and community services to share workload and keep care safe.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safe, high‑quality care, a NHS workforce plan must focus on three priorities. First, tailor incentives for hard‑to‑fill areas—rural, coastal and urban deprived communities—with housing subsidies, transport support and flexible working to make roles sustainable and appealing, plus clear career progression. In my area, vacancies persist because there isn’t affordable housing or viable commuting options, so staff turnover remains high. Second, cut admin burden and simplify processes. Reduce unnecessary targets, remove duplicated tasks, and improve IT usability and interoperability so clinicians spend more time with patients and less time on referrals or chasing paperwork. A user‑friendly system would help protect continuity of care and reduce burnout. Third, expand training pipelines with protected placements. Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship posts, backed by strong university‑practice partnerships, so new recruits gain real community experience and remain in primary care. Ensure placements in hard‑to‑fill areas, to encourage long‑term practice locally. When combined with stable teams and named clinicians, these measures will support continuity, safer care and better workforce wellbeing, aligning with the approach I’ve advocated for in patient care.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, a plan must start with transparent, localised data, modelling and KPIs paired with a robust evaluation framework. Trusts should publish annual dashboards on vacancies, turnover, workload, waiting times and patient safety so planning funding is targeted and accountable, not rolled out as generic targets. 

Second, provide clear funded career pathways with protected CPD time, structured mentorship and return‑to‑practice schemes. This helps retain experienced clinicians and supports new entrants. Practical steps include funded mentorship posts, short‑term fellowships for early‑career staff, guaranteed CPD allocations, and smoothing pathways back into practice after breaks. My own experience suggests these schemes work best when combined with up‑to‑date onboarding and supervision.

Third, secure multi‑year, ring-fenced funding settlements to sustain training capacity and long‑term workforce initiatives, reducing policy volatility. Adequate funding is essential for recruiting in rural and peri‑urban areas, expanding GP and mental health training places, and standing up apprenticeship routes. 

Other priorities include targeted investment in digital workforce planning tools, and clear deployment rules to ensure trained staff are available where most needed. In my area, steady investment and detailed planning would cut delays in mental health referrals and improve continuity of care across primary and community services.

From my perspective as an older resident in rural England, the NHS workforce plan should do more than simply fill vacancies; it must safeguard safe, compassionate care for vulnerable patients. Priorities I’d expect to see: adequate, stable staffing in general practice and community nursing, with flexible, sustainable working patterns to reduce burnout; multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, therapists, social care link workers) that can share workload and provide home visits for those with chronic conditions; stronger recruitment and retention in rural areas, including local recruitment, housing support, and incentives to attract staff to small communities. Better training and supervision in geriatrics and mental health, plus meaningful career progression and reduced admin burden so clinicians can spend real time with patients. Real investment in social and voluntary networks, transport, and easier access for carers to coordinate care. Safe, user-friendly access to care through both digital systems and telephone booking, ensuring those without internet aren’t left behind. Clear safety standards and robust staff well-being provisions would also be essential. In our village I’ve seen how transport and volunteers keep people connected to appointments; a workforce plan that respects these local realities would help maintain high-quality care for us all.

From my perspective, any NHS workforce plan that aims to recruit, retain and support staff must prioritise safety, quality and sustainable workloads as the foundations of reform. My past experiences in primary and community settings show that simply increasing headcount won’t fix access or outcomes unless we make roles clear, support new ways of working, and genuinely share the burden with social care and community services. With that in mind, the plan should focus on the following priorities, with practical mechanisms to back them up.

- Clear scope-of-practice, governance and revalidation paths: We need explicit, locally applicable scope-of-practice for every new or expanded role (nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists delivering extended services, community paramedics, mental health support workers, etc.). That means agreed competencies, multidisciplinary handover protocols, standard operating procedures, and predictable lines of accountability. Revalidation and continuing competence must be streamlined and affordable, with protected time for annual appraisal, supervised practice, and access to high-quality continuing professional development. Without this clarity, staff will be hesitant to take on broader duties for fear of stepping outside safe boundaries.

- Robust indemnity arrangements and risk management: Indemnity costs and arrangements should not deter teams from expanding roles or from wrapping care around the patient. The plan should guarantee affordable, comprehensive professional indemnity for all extended duties, with simplified claims processes and consistent coverage across primary, community and social care settings. It should also promote shared learning from near-misses and incidents so patient safety improves rather than being used as a barrier to innovation.

- Funded protected clinical supervision and mentorship: New roles and expanded duties must come with safeguarded supervision time, paid mentorship, and peer-review mechanisms. Protected supervision helps maintain patient safety while enabling staff to grow into more complex tasks. Investment should cover clinical supervision networks, remote supervision where needed, and stepping-stone progression pathways that keep staff engaged and less likely to leave the service.

- Integrated workforce planning with social care and mental health: A sustainable workforce must be built with strong links to social care and community services. This means joint funding, joint commissioning where appropriate, and cross-sector secondments to redistribute workload and build holistic care pathways. For example, if a district can share trained community health workers between GP practices and social care teams, we reduce duplicated visits, shorten waiting times for non-medical support, and free up clinicians to focus on clinically complex cases.

- Safe, manageable workloads and staffing ratios: An evidence-based approach to staffing is essential. This includes dynamic rostering, ward- and clinic-level safe staffing, and reliable backups so teams aren’t stretched by sudden surges. The goal is to prevent burnout and retain experienced staff while still enabling career progression for newer colleagues. Where possible, flexible or part-time routes should be supported with appropriate supervision and handover processes.

- Training, career development and returns-to-practice: We should expand training places and offer structured return-to-practice schemes, CPD that aligns with local service needs, and clear career ladders so staff can progress without leaving the system to pursue opportunities elsewhere. In practice, this means protected training time, funded courses, and realistic timescales for upskilling that reflect local demand.

- Data-led governance and accountability: Workforce plans should be underpinned by transparent dashboards on staffing, safety metrics, and patient outcomes at local and network levels. Regular reporting to trusts, CCGs and, where appropriate, patient groups will help identify hotspots and escalate issues before they become crises. Public dashboards showing skill mix, wait times for different services, and supervision coverage would help manage expectations and drive improvements.

- Local collaboration and patient-centred models of care: Finally, the plan must drive practical changes that support patients where they are. This means better integration in community hubs, co-located teams, and shared digital records to reduce duplication and miscommunication. In my experience, when a GP practice, a district nurse team and a social-care assessor sit together for a caseload, patients move through services more quickly and with fewer handoffs that go wrong.

In short, the workforce plan should not be about more bodies alone. It must deliver clear roles, safe practice, protected supervision, fair indemnity, and joined-up funding with social care and mental health. If we pair these core elements with credible local delivery plans, robust governance and transparent measurement, we’ll see safer care, better staff morale and, ultimately, faster, more reliable access for patients.

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that recognises staffing as the backbone of timely, high-quality care. It must enable real capacity growth while safeguarding patient safety, so that more appointments and faster access do not come at the expense of clinical quality. With my own experience juggling study and part-time work, I’ve seen how access can improve when teams are stable and well-supported, but I’ve also seen how care can suffer if staffing is rushed or overloaded. So my view is practical and safety-focused: expand roles where appropriate, but with strong protections and clear professional standards.

- Clarify scope-of-practice and provide robust supervision for new and expanded roles. We should clearly define what tasks can be done by nurse practitioners, physician associates, physiotherapists, mental health practitioners and other allied health professionals in primary and community care, with evidence-based care pathways. This includes patient handovers, triage, chronic disease management, and mental health support. When new roles are introduced, they must be supported by structured induction and ongoing clinical supervision to ensure patient safety and confidence in the team. Fund protected supervision time within job plans, not as an afterthought.

- Align revalidation and indemnity arrangements with the pace of workforce evolution. Revalidation processes should be streamlined so clinicians can complete requirements without endless administrative burden. Allocating protected time for appraisals and professional development is essential, especially for those taking on expanded scopes of practice. Clear, affordable indemnity arrangements are vital so clinicians can practice with confidence, particularly when performing new or shared-care tasks in multidisciplinary teams. Where possible, standardise indemnity terms across settings to reduce confusion and delays.

- Invest in protected clinical supervision and career development. A modern workforce plan must fund sustained clinical supervision for early-career clinicians and those adopting new roles. Regular supervision supports reflective practice, learning from near-misses, and maintaining high safety standards. It also helps with staff wellbeing and retention, which in turn supports continuity of care for patients.

- Prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models. Access improvements must be matched by safe staffing levels: acuity-adjusted ratios, appropriate skill mix, and reliable staffing pipelines. Where possible, teams should maintain continuity by keeping stable rosters and predictable skill-matches, so patients see the same clinician or small, known teams. A continuity model reduces avoidable miscommunication and improves patient experiences, especially for those with chronic conditions or mental health needs.

- Ensure safety monitoring is built into the plan. Implement real-time dashboards on staffing, workload, wait times, and patient outcomes. Use incident reporting and root-cause analyses to identify safety risks related to staffing gaps or new roles, and adjust resource allocation accordingly. Transparent, local data on staffing and safety should be publicly accessible to communities, so gaps are visible and addressed rapidly.

- Build a strong pipeline and retention package. The plan should include clear career progression, funded training places, and flexible working options to attract and keep clinicians in the NHS. Mentoring, peer support networks, and wellbeing initiatives are essential to prevent burnout in demanding roles. Where possible, offer rotations between primary care, community services, and mental health teams to broaden experience while maintaining patient continuity.

- Tie workforce planning to patient access and quality metrics. Staffing decisions should be guided by protected appointment capacity, wait-time targets, and patient experience data. If a strategy to increase GP and therapist slots is pursued, it must be matched by corresponding investments in supervision, risk management, and safety culture so observed improvements in access are not undermined by variability in care quality.

In short, I want a plan that lets people work to their full, safe potential—clarified roles and solid supervision for new models, clear and fair revalidation and indemnity, safe staffing with continuity, and rigorous safety monitoring. If these elements are funded and embedded in daily practice, we can deliver faster access to high-quality care for everyone, including students and young adults like me who rely on timely support to stay well and in education or work.

I think an NHS workforce plan should be built on three core priorities, all of which need to work together to recruit, retain and support staff while keeping high-quality care safe and sustainable.

1) Invest in interoperable, secure IT and give staff real digital capability
- Prioritise interoperable IT systems across primary and community care so patient information flows smoothly between GPs, pharmacists, nurses and therapists. Secure, user-friendly systems with strong cyber security are essential, but they must be matched by practical staff training and ongoing digital support. This means protected time for training, clear guidance on data sharing, and simple workflows that reduce admin burden rather than add to it.
- Safeguard alternatives for digitally excluded patients. My experience shows digital tools speed things up, but we must ensure non-digital routes are just as fast and reliable. That means well-staffed phone lines, in-person reception support, and paper forms where needed, with staff who can help people use digital options when that’s appropriate.
- Use pilots and data to refine tools. Start with local pilots focused on real-world usability and equity of access, then scale what works while tracking patient experience, wait times, and clinician workload.

2) Flexible, humane working arrangements to reduce burnout and attract diverse staff
- Embrace flexible hours, part-time and job-share models, and phased retirement to retain experienced staff who might otherwise leave. Childcare support, family-friendly scheduling, and predictable rosters can make roles more sustainable for younger workers and those juggling caregiving.
- Prioritise proactive mental health and wellbeing support. Quick access to confidential mental health services, supervision, mentoring, and peer support should be built into every role, with management training to recognise and respond to burnout risks early.
- Create a culture of sustained learning and career development. Clear pathways for progression, opportunities for upskilling, and recognition of transferable skills across MDTs help staff feel valued and stay in care.

3) Strong training pipelines and partnerships to grow domestic primary care capacity
- Increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with protected placements. More funded places, bursaries, and structured exposure to general practice in early years can demystify primary care for students and graduates.
- Build university-practice partnerships and collaborative training hubs. Co-designed curricula, joint research opportunities, and local practicum rotations help align skills with needs on the ground and support a smoother transition to independent roles.
- Ensure careers in primary care are attractive and viable long-term. Competitive pay, clear career ladders, and opportunities to specialise in areas like extended-scope practice, mental health in primary care, or chronic disease management will help retain talent.

4) Safe, high-quality care as a constant priority
- Maintain safe staffing ratios and robust governance. Use data to forecast demand, shape team configurations (MDTs with pharmacists, physiotherapists, and allied professionals), and ensure all patient-facing roles have adequate support.
- Invest in leadership and supervision. Strong line management, regular clinical supervision and access to mentors help staff feel supported and confident in decision-making.
- Local leadership empowered to tailor solutions. Workforce planning needs to reflect local demographics, disease burden and service delivery models, rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe.

From my perspective, this combination—robust interoperable IT with training, flexible working to protect staff wellbeing, and a strong education/training pipeline—will help build a resilient NHS workforce. It should also keep care safe for patients who don’t or can’t use digital tools, which is essential for equity.

In practice, I’ve seen clinics where pharmacists or physiotherapists triage routine issues, freeing GPs to focus on complex cases. Flexible shifts have helped some colleagues balance study or childcare. If these elements are supported by well-designed training and governance, I’m confident we can recruit more people, keep them engaged, and maintain high standards of care across communities.

From my perspective as a young person living in England, I want an NHS workforce plan that prioritises transparent, localised data, robust modelling and clear evaluation so we can plan, fund and monitor performance effectively while keeping care safe and high quality. The overall aim should be to recruit, retain and support staff in the right places, without compromising patient safety or the experience of care.

First, localised, transparent data should be the backbone of every workforce plan. Trusts, GP practices and community teams should publish real-time dashboards on staffing levels, vacancies, sickness absence, staff turnover, training activity and patient access metrics. For example, being able to see which areas have persistent GP shortfalls or longer-than-expected wait times would help target training places, return-to-practice initiatives and flexible staffing more efficiently. It isn’t about shouting about problems; it’s about providing an honest picture so local managers can respond quickly and public health teams can coordinate resources.

Second, robust modelling and scenario planning are essential. We need forward-looking projections that factor in population growth, aging, regional health needs, the impact of digital tools on demand, and Brexit-related changes in staffing. A plan should include multi-year funding proposals that reflect these models, with clearly defined triggers for expanding or tightening recruitment as conditions change. In practice, this means local authorities and NHS bodies working with universities and training providers to map out where new nurses, GPs, physiotherapists and mental health professionals will come from and how long it will take to train them.

Third, explicit KPIs and evaluation frameworks.” These should cover access and safety—for example, wait times for GP and mental health appointments, patient safety indicators, and the rate of avoidable hospital admissions—as well as workforce wellbeing. Regular independent reviews would verify whether the plan is delivering the promised reductions in waiting times and improvements in care quality. If a region misses targets, there should be transparent action plans showing what changes will be made and why.

Fourth, planning should be strongly locally led but connected across the system. Local workforce plans must reflect community needs and work in tandem with schools, universities and clinical placement providers. Apprenticeships, return-to-practice routes and clear career ladders should be embedded in local pipelines so people see a viable future in their own area. In my area, I’ve seen how local partnerships between NHS trusts and universities could be more effective if backed by shared data and joint KPIs that are publicly reported.

Fifth, recruitment, retention and wellbeing must be core priorities. That means creating predictable career paths, protected supervision time, mentoring, and flexible working options to reduce burnout. Funding should be tied to delivering these people-centred supports, not just to headcount growth. A good plan would include incentives for staff to stay in the locality and for experienced clinicians to take on leadership roles in their teams.

Sixth, digital infrastructure and data interoperability are not luxuries; they are essential. A workforce plan should fund scheduling systems, digital learning platforms, and secure data flows so teams can share information about staffing needs and patient load across Primary Care Networks, hospital departments and community services. Good data makes better decisions and keeps patients safe.

Finally, accountability to the public matters. Local annual reports showing progress against dashboards, KPIs and milestones would enable patients and staff to see improvements and challenge areas openly. When people can see that the plan is grounded in real data and honest evaluation, trust in the NHS grows and the system can adjust quickly to changing needs.

Overall, I’d like the plan to feel practical and responsive: a living blueprint that uses transparent local data, robust modelling, and clear evaluation to drive recruitment, retention and support while safeguarding the quality and safety of care.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise three linked strands. First, invest in interoperable, secure IT and robust staff training, but guard against digital-only care. In rural areas, digital platforms must be accompanied by alternatives—mobile clinics, outreach teams, and telehealth hubs in accessible venues—to prevent exclusion of older patients who struggle with tech. Second, develop transparent local data, modelling and KPIs with clear evaluation frameworks to guide planning, funding and performance monitoring. That means monthly workforce dashboards at district level, with indicators on retention, vacancies, safe staffing levels and patient outcomes, fed into local decisions. Third, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams—nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and allied roles—under defined supervision and oversight to safely redistribute GP workload. Provide clear scopes of practice, ongoing training, and protected time for professional development. Also prioritise flexible hours, wellbeing support, and targeted recruitment to rural areas, plus international recruitment where needed, but with robust induction and mentoring. Finally, ensure strong governance, risk management and patient safety metrics accompany every expansion to keep care safe while relieving GP pressure.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan should focus on three linked priorities. Prioritise secure, multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain workforce initiatives, expand training capacity and recruitment, and reduce policy volatility. i really think the plan should prioritise building a sustainable, well-supported NHS workforce that can deliver safe, high‑quality care now and in the future. In practice, that means a balanced mix of expanding training pipelines, clear professional roles, robust supervision, and workable supports to keep staff motivated and patients safe. Our experience matches what many communities are experiencing: you can’t recruit your way out of burnout or under‑resourcing without changing how people are trained, supported and deployed. A workforce plan that is locally informed, data driven and aligned to service models will be most effective.

- Expand and fix training pipelines with protected placements: Commit to increasing undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places, with protected, funded placements in primary care and community settings. University–practice partnerships should be strengthened to ensure students gain meaningful, real-world experience in primary care teams, community nursing and mental health services. Where pilots have existed, practices that can shield trainees from administrative overload while offering structured learning report better early‑career retention and smoother transition to independent practice. The emphasis should be on long‑term supply: students taught in real clinics and supported by mentors are more likely to stay long enough to make a difference.

- Clarify scope of practice, revalidation, indemnity and supervision: The plan must provide clarity around scope of practice for new roles (e.g., physician associates, advanced nurse practitioners, paramedics stepping into extended roles) and how revalidation and indemnity will work across organisations. Fund protected clinical supervision so staff in new or expanded roles have regular, high‑quality supervision that maintains patient safety while enabling skill development. This reduces fear and uncertainty for staff choosing to diversify into new roles and supports safer delegation of tasks.

- Fund and standardise protected supervision and mentoring: Clinically supervised induction for all new roles should be a baseline, backed by protected time in rosters. Practical mentoring helps junior colleagues, enhances confidence, and improves patient safety. This is especially important in primary care and community services where complex decision‑making and risk management are daily features.

- Align recruitment with service design and workload: Workforce planning must be closely tied to how services are delivered. If we know that more extended primary care access, home visiting or community nursing will be required, the plan should backfill those needs with tailored recruitment campaigns, flexible working options and realistic workload expectations. Reducing administrative burden and streamlining digital tools can make roles more attractive and sustainable, not just longer hours.

- Retention, wellbeing and career progression: Retention depends on more than pay. We need sustainable working patterns, predictable rosters, adequate break coverage and genuine opportunities for progression. Flexible scheduling, part‑time and job‑share options, and safe staffing levels should be baked into every staffing plan. Regular wellbeing support, peer networks and leadership development for managers at all levels help prevent burnout and improve team morale.

- Support for extended teams and new care models: Invest in roles that extend capacity in primary and community care—practice‑based pharmacists, advanced nurse practitioners, health‑care assistants with defined career ladders, and digital health coordinators. Ensure these teams are integrated with traditional GP and nurse workflows through clear referral pathways, shared information systems and multidisciplinary training.

- Diversity, inclusion and outreach in recruitment: Proactively widen the applicant pool through partnerships with local education providers, schools, and community groups. Ensure recruitment materials and assessment processes reflect diverse communities and remove unintended barriers to entry for underrepresented groups.

- Data, governance and accountability: Build robust workforce data dashboards at regional and local levels to track vacancies, turnover, capacity, and training outcomes. Share lessons learned publicly and involve frontline clinicians and patients in redesign to ensure that workforce changes translate into better access and safer care.

- Practical delivery examples: In several areas, university–practice hubs that offer 6–12‑month protected placements for GP registrars and nursing students have correlated with improved retention after qualification, particularly when these placements are paired with mentored supervision and clear progression paths. Where indemnity costs and administrative burdens are reduced through aligned contracts and standardised processes, practices report smoother onboarding of new staff and less time diverted to navigating complex approvals.

Ultimately, a successful NHS workforce plan won’t be about endless hiring alone. It will be about growing capability in a controlled, patient‑safety‑first way, so new roles are clearly defined, well supervised and adequately supported. It will connect education, practice, and community services in a coherent pipeline, with local flexibility to reflect demographics, geography and local demand. This alignment is the surest route to safer care, shorter waits and a more resilient NHS workforce.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high-quality, the plan should prioritise flexibility, not simply more hours. To recruit, retain and support staff while safeguarding high‑quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise people‑centred, flexible and fair policies alongside clear professional safeguards. Prioritise targeted pay, retention bonuses, relocation bursaries and funded training; expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, PAs, paramedics) with supervision to share GP workloads and maintain high-quality care.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high-quality, the plan should prioritise targeted competitive pay and retention payments to attract people into hard-to-fill roles and underserved areas, plus relocation packages and bursaries to support training where it’s most needed. Flexible working is essential—offer flexible hours, part-time options, job-share arrangements, and phased retirement, alongside strong childcare support and proactive mental health services so staff can manage burnout and stay longer in the service. To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the workforce plan should prioritise funded career pathways, protected continuing professional development (CPD), robust mentorship and return-to-practice schemes, and, crucially, safe staffing and continuous safety monitoring. In my experience, such a plan would make it easier to stay in the profession through exams and busy periods and would improve access and safety at the same time.

I think the plan should prioritise safe staffing, fair pay and wellbeing support; invest in training and supervision with realistic workloads, within budget constraints. Also tackle housing and energy pressures that worsen ill health, so staff aren’t stretched thin.

I strongly support an NHS workforce plan that places funded, clearly defined career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes at the heart of recruitment and retention, alongside transparent local data, modelling and KPIs with robust evaluation. Key priorities I’d like to see prioritised are:

Local placements in rural districts would help would-be recruits feel a sense of belonging and reduce recruitment lag once qualified. In our area, persistent GP vacancies show why a funded, aspirational pathway matters so much for retention.

- Protected CPD and structured mentorship: Professionals need guaranteed time for CPD without piling administrative burden on top. Mentorship schemes, paired with experienced clinicians, help newer staff develop confidence and competence, while reduce burnout. Return-to-practice support should be explicit, with staged re-entry programs, supervised practice, and competency checks so those who paused their careers—perhaps for caring responsibilities or burnout—can rejoin safely and smoothly.

- Return-to-practice and retraining: Streamlined routes for those who left the profession or took time out are essential. Short, targeted refresher courses and flexible re-entry pathways would help maintain a high standard of care and widen the talent pool, especially in areas that struggle to attract staff.

- Localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs: Create transparent dashboards at a local level that track vacancies, time-to-fill, turnover, staff well-being, patient safety indicators and training completions. Data should inform funding and workforce planning, not just report outcomes. For instance, linking vacancy duration and clinician turnover to patient appointment access would help us tailor recruitment incentives and retention schemes to real local need.

- Wellbeing, flexible working and safe staffing: Flexible contracts, job sharing, and smart rostering can improve work–life balance and retention, particularly in small teams. Robust wellbeing support and realistic administrative loads are crucial so staff can focus on delivering high‑quality patient care without burnout.

- Training capacity aligned with service design: Ensure universities, teaching trusts and primary care training hubs can scale up to meet projected demand. Rural placements and longer-term collaborations between NHS organisations should be standard, with incentives to keep trainees in local areas after qualification.

- Digital capability and integration: Embed digital literacy and telehealth training within CPD so staff can confidently use remote monitoring, virtual consultations and online triage. This supports access without compromising safety or the patient–clinician relationship.

- Cross-system and local leadership: Workforce planning must be place-based, with local health and social care leaders collaborating on multi-year funding, governance and accountability. Strong leadership, clear expectations and ongoing evaluation will help translate workforce plans into safer, higher‑quality care on the ground.

In practice, these elements would support the broader changes I’ve advocated for—for example, multi‑discipline hubs and mobile services—by ensuring there are enough skilled, supported staff to deliver them safely. A funded, evidence-based approach with local co-design and accountable evaluation will help us stabilise care in rural communities while improving access and continuity for patients. I’d welcome pilots in rural districts that test these career pathways, mentorship schemes, and local data dashboards, with clear metrics on recruitment, retention, patient outcomes and staff wellbeing.

Overall, a thoughtfully funded, locally informed workforce plan—backed by protected development time, mentorship, return-to-practice routes, and robust data—will translate into safer, more reliable care and a more resilient NHS team across England.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan must prioritise joined-up, long-term workforce planning across the NHS, social care, mental health and community services. Prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, PAs, paramedics) with clear training and supervision to safely redistribute GP workload. Strengthen joint funding with social care and community services to sustain holistic care across Scotland.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the plan must prioritise three things. Prioritise safe staffing levels and continuity of care with strong safety monitoring; cut undue targets and admin burden; streamline referrals and improve IT usability to free clinicians for patients; and secure joint funding and collaboration with social care and community mental health to sustain holistic, high-quality care.

Agree. An NHS workforce plan should prioritise sustainable recruitment, retention and support for staff while ensuring consistently safe, high‑quality care. The workforce plan must prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models, with robust safety monitoring to protect care quality as access expands. i really think from my perspective as an older resident who relies on a stable, patient‑facing care team, the NHS workforce plan must prioritise staffing levels and wellbeing alongside practical changes that free clinicians from unnecessary administration.
