- Reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks: Simplify the annual cycle of audits and forms that pull clinicians away from patients. - Streamline referrals and improve IT usability: Create fast, predictable referral routes with shared decision‑making between primary and secondary care. - Protect time for patient-facing care: The plan should explicitly guarantee protected time for complex reviews, care coordination and home visits where needed. In short, an NHS workforce plan that reduces admin burden, streamlines referrals, and brings together user‑friendly IT with well‑supported, stable teams will directly support the kind of care I value: continuity with a known clinician, longer, more thorough appointments, and a focus on the whole person rather than disparate tests and repeated histories. To keep NHS services safe, high‑quality and sustainable, I think the workforce plan should focus on three linked priorities: people, technology and governance that adapts to new roles. As someone balancing studies and work, I’ve seen how staffing pressures ripple through care quality and waiting times. A plan that backs the people delivering care, while modernising the tools they use and clarifying safety nets, would make a real difference.

First, targeted pay and location incentives to attract and keep staff in underserved areas and in high‑demand roles. This would include competitive base pay, retention payments after a period of service, relocation packages for postings in rural or coastal localities, and bursaries to train in those communities. In practice, that could mean a district with GP shortages offering a three‑year retention prize for clinicians who settle there, or a nursing student bursary tied to a service commitment in a community hospital. I’ve seen friends move away from local area posts because recruitment pressures meant frequent short‑term contracts and long commutes, which harms continuity of care. A more predictable, regionally balanced workforce would stabilise teams and reduce avoidable vacancies that drive longer waits for patients.

Second, invest in interoperable IT, secure systems and staff digital training, while safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients. A connected digital spine—linking GP records, hospital systems, community teams and mental health services—would let a nurse, pharmacist or GP see a patient’s full history, recent tests and current medications in one place. That reduces duplication, errors and repeat explanations of the same symptoms. It would be essential to couple this with rigorous cyber security and strong version control, so patients’ data remains safe. For staff, regular, practical training in how to use new tools—without overwhelming already busy rosters—would be critical. And we must maintain non‑digital routes for those who aren’t online or who struggle with tech: phone triage, in‑person signposting, and clear printed guidance. In campus life and local clinics, I’ve noticed how digital hurdles can widen gaps for students who don’t have reliable internet access between lectures, part‑time work and study. A robust but flexible approach would keep everyone in the system—especially the most vulnerable.

Third, clarify scope‑of‑practice, revalidation, indemnity arrangements and fund protected clinical supervision to support new roles and patient safety. We’re still seeing the introduction of roles like clinician associates or advanced allied health professionals in some areas, but without consistent scope and supervision, patient safety could be jeopardised. A workforce plan should set out clear ladders for progression, with funded, protected supervision for a defined period when clinicians transition into new roles. Revalidation processes must be streamlined to avoid unnecessary friction that makes people leave the NHS or switch to the private sector. Indemnity arrangements should be straightforward and predictable, with shared risk models that reflect modern team care. In practice, this means every new post has a structured supervision plan, a defined scope of practice, and access to indemnity that grows with responsibility. This would reassure staff that their professional development is supported, not hindered by bureaucratic barriers.

In addition, I’d like to see workforce planning that recognises the reality of student life and flexible working. Rotas that allow weekend or after‑hours coverage without burning out staff, and protected time for training and reflective practice, would help retention. It would also help if trusts and local systems piloted flexible multi‑disciplinary units where nurses, pharmacists, mental health workers and GPs share clinics in community hubs. If people can see a clear path—training, supervision, recognition, and a real sense of being part of a stable team—the NHS will attract and keep the number of hands needed to deliver safe care.

Overall, a plan that pays people fairly, rewards loyalty, brings the right technology into everyday use, and guarantees safety through clear roles and strong supervision will make care safer and more reliable. It would also align with the urgent‑care improvements I described earlier: better triage, smarter booking and local access. When staff feel supported and patients aren’t left behind by digital or geographic barriers, high‑quality care becomes feasible everywhere—not just in city centres. That balance matters for me as a young person starting out in adulthood, and for my peers who rely on timely, safe health services in communities across England.

Prioritise interoperable, secure IT and staff digital training, with protected supervision for new roles and clear indemnity arrangements. At the same time cut unnecessary targets and admin, streamline referrals and boost IT usability to free clinicians for patient care, while safeguarding digitally excluded patients.

Focus on fewer targets and paperwork, streamlined referrals, and better IT to free clinicians for patients; offer targeted pay and retention incentives, relocation packages and bursaries; and secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain training and stability.

absolutely i think any NHS workforce plan must aim to keep care safe and personal, not just hit abstract targets. In practice that means enough staff so appointments aren’t rushed and clinicians have time to listen. From my experience in England, when practice teams are stretched, patients miss follow-ups or end up waiting days for a call-back. I’d value locally based care and would support more incentives to recruit and retain staff in smaller communities—nurse prescribers, practice nurses, and reception teams all keep things moving. Flexible working and proper rest for staff are essential to avoid burnout, which I’ve noticed can affect the kindness and attentiveness people receive. Ongoing training, good peer support, and simpler admin processes would help GP practices run more predictably, especially for those of us who aren’t comfortable with digital systems. I’m not sure about a one-size-fits-all approach; any plan should reflect local needs and keep human contact at the heart of care while ensuring safety and quality aren’t sacrificed for convenience!

it's outrageous that prioritise secure, multi-year ring-fenced funding to sustain workforce training and capacity, cutting policy volatility. Combine targeted competitive pay, retention payments, relocation packages and bursaries to attract staff to underserved and high-demand areas, plus housing and transport support in hard-to-fill rural/coastal zones!

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise a balanced, multi-pronged approach. First, build sustainable domestic capacity: expand GP training numbers and early-career pathways, increase funded general practice placements, and reduce non-clinical admin load so clinicians can focus on patient care. Regional planning must ensure predictable staffing, with safe rosters and incentives to work in underserved areas, plus well-funded retention schemes and wellbeing support.

Second, expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams to redistribute GP workload safely. This means larger roles for nurses, nurse practitioners, physician associates, pharmacists, paramedics, physiotherapists and other allied professionals, with clear scopes of practice, robust supervision, defined accountability, and career progression. Such teams should handle routine and follow-up care, supported by digital triage and decision-support tools, with pathways to escalate when needed. In practice, I’d like to see more on-site pharmacists and PAs in GP practices and urgent care hubs to free GPs for complex cases.

Third, responsible international recruitment: use overseas recruitment to plug gaps but with streamlined visas, rapid credential recognition, structured integration support and safeguards to avoid draining source countries’ health systems. Pair this with strong induction, language and cultural training, and explicit return-to-service or partnership commitments where appropriate.

Finally, invest in data-driven planning, reduce burnout through workload management, and expand community services to take pressure off primary care. A workforce plan that combines domestic growth, safe multidisciplinary roles, and careful international recruitment is essential for sustainable, safe care.

I believe a NHS workforce plan must place recruitment, retention and staff support at its core if we’re to keep care safe, high quality and accessible in the long term. In England, where demand is growing and vacancies bite across GP practices, hospitals and community services, a coherent, well-funded plan is essential. Below are priorities I think would make a real difference, drawing on what I’ve seen locally and what would work in practice.

Overseas recruitment done responsibly, with streamlined processes, is part of the answer—not a quick fix. We should welcome skilled clinicians from overseas, but with robust credential recognition, language and adaptation support, and careful safeguarding to avoid depleting health systems elsewhere. Practical steps would include: faster, transparent visa pathways for essential roles; clear, consistent recognition of overseas qualifications; structured induction and bilingual mentorship where needed; and integration support that helps new staff settle into our NHS culture and patient expectations without compromising safety. Experience shows overseas recruits can strengthen services, but we must guard against a drain on source countries and ensure ongoing professional development is funded and accessible. We should also ensure return-to-practice opportunities for clinicians who have stepped away, so the pool remains deep and diverse.

Targeted competitive pay and incentives are crucial to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles. Retention payments, relocation packages, and bursaries for training can tilt the balance in favour of staying in the NHS rather than seeking terms elsewhere. For example, a nurse or GP willing to relocate to a rural or deprived urban area, where vacancies are chronic, needs a package that recognises the extra burden and commute. In my experience, well-designed financial incentives paired with clear career progression can stabilise teams, reduce agency reliance, and protect patient safety as workloads rise (as if that will ever happen). These payments must be predictable, time-bound where appropriate, and tied to service commitments, ongoing training, and high-quality supervision.

Clear funded career pathways and protected CPD are vital for retention of both early-career staff and those with years of service. We need transparent ladders from student and junior roles through to consultant and leadership positions, with protected time for continued professional development. Mentorship schemes, formal return-to-practice programs, and flexible on-ramps will help people rejoin the workforce after a break, or shift careers into high-demand areas. In practice, this means funded mentorship, paid study leave, access to regional or national CPD events, and digital platforms that enable learning without excessive travel. Such supports reduce burnout, improve confidence in clinical decision-making, and enable teams to evolve with new guidelines and technologies. 

A workforce plan must also recognise the value of several well-defined roles and expanded scopes that improve care delivery when properly trained and supervised. Physician associates, advanced nurse practitioners, and allied health professionals can take on important tasks in diagnostic and care coordination pathways, freeing doctors’ time for complex cases while maintaining safety standards. Any expansion should be accompanied by robust governance, clear scopes of practice, and access to supervision and continuing education so patient safety isn’t compromised.

Local and regional tailoring matters. A plan that works in a city hospital won’t automatically work in a coastal or rural village. I’d like to see horizon-scanning, regional workforce dashboards, and flexible pipeline funding that responds to local needs—paired with workforce planning that aligns with extended-hours access, improved urgent care pathways, and strengthened community health services. Protecting patient safety means staffing levels that reflect patient acuity, with real-time data to guide staffing decisions and escalation protocols when pressures rise.

Wellbeing and safe working environments must be embedded in every element of the plan. This includes reasonable rosters, protected time for rest and reflection, access to mental health and occupational health support, and safe induction processes for new staff and returnees. A healthy workforce is a safer, more compassionate one, and it’s essential to public confidence in the NHS.

Finally, the plan should set clear milestones, with independent evaluation and public reporting so taxpayers can see progress and lessons learned. We should scale successful models, avoid endless pilots, and share best practice across regions. In my view, a robust, morally grounded workforce plan—combining responsible international recruitment, strong financial incentives, clear career pathways, practical mentorship, and well-led local implementation—will deliver timely, high-quality care while stabilising the NHS for the communities that rely on it.

i strongly believe to recruit, retain and sustain safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan must put people at its core with tangible, funded career pathways. Clear routes from entry to senior clinical roles help both experienced staff and new entrants see a future in the NHS, reducing avoidable turnover. 

Key priorities:
- Protected CPD time and funding: guarantee paid time for continuing training, supervision and specialisms, not just annual quotas. This supports high standards and helps staff manage workload without sacrificing development.
- Mentorship and buddy schemes: formal mentoring for early-career clinicians and returnees, with experienced colleagues guiding clinical decisions and workload management.
- Return-to-practice schemes: funded retraining, supervised practice and refreshed competencies for those who have paused their careers, so talent isn’t lost and confidence in care remains high.

- Leadership and succession planning: structured opportunities to rotate through primary, community and hospital settings, with leadership development to sustain service design and oversight.
- Monitoring and accountability: publish data on CPD uptake, retention, vacancies and progression, with adjustments to funding where gaps persist.
- Local tailoring and co-design: involve local providers to reflect patient needs, ensuring the plan supports continuity of care across services.

From discussions with frontline staff, protected development and clear career progression are repeatedly cited as crucial to keeping skilled clinicians serving our communities!

From my point of view as someone living in England who uses local GP, community and mental health services, any NHS workforce plan should prioritise transparency, localised data and clear benchmarks. There needs to be open, practical workforce data, modelling and KPIs at practice and regional levels, with an evaluation framework that ties funding to real improvements in wait times, safety and patient experience. Without good data, planning can drift and staff feel left unsupported.

Links with social care, mental health and community services must be strengthened to redistribute workload and deliver holistic care. Shared recruitment initiatives, joint training and pooled budget streams would help smaller practices stay staffed and prevent bottlenecks that push people into hospital settings.

Clarity on scope-of-practice, revalidation and indemnity arrangements is essential, along with dedicated funding for protected clinical supervision to support new roles and safeguard patient safety. For example, nurse prescribers and other positive role-persons can take on expanded duties if governance and supervision are solidly in place.

Finally, invest in staff welfare and flexible working models—extended hours, wellbeing time, better admin support and administrative flexibility—to retain experienced staff. In areas where teams collaborate across primary care and community services, patients experience quicker, smoother access and safer care.

From my experience in England, any NHS workforce plan must put safe, patient-facing care first while cutting waste that diverts clinicians from people who need them. First, reduce unnecessary targets, paperwork and duplicated tasks. Streamline referrals and make IT more usable so clinicians spend less time chasing forms and more time with patients—for example, easier cross-system referrals and integrated digital records so a routine check or chronic-care review isn’t halted by admin bottlenecks. Second, prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models. When teams are unstable or patients see a different clinician every visit, care quality and safety suffer, especially for older patients with complex needs. Ensure sufficient staffing, stable rosters, longer appointments for chronic conditions, and robust out-of-hours cover. Third, implement clear safety monitoring. Establish simple, independent oversight of staffing, wait times, and escalation pathways to ensure access gains don’t undermine quality. Fourth, develop transparent, localised data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks. Local dashboards on vacancies, turnover, clinical outcome measures and funding needs should inform planning and accountability. With these in place, we’ll see safer care and better access without sacrificing the quality my neighbours and I rely on.

Prioritise transparent, localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation to guide planning, funding and performance; offer flexible hours, childcare, phased retirement and proactive mental health support to retain diverse staff; invest in interoperable IT and staff digital training while safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients.

Prioritisr safe staffing ratios, continuity-focused care models and robust safety monitoring to protect quality as access expands. Fund clear career pathways, protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes, and increase undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship places with strong university-practice partnerships.

I think an NHS workforce plan must start from safe staffing levels, continuity of care, and staff wellbeing. Investment in interoperable IT, reliable triage pathways and well-defined MDT processes will reduce confusion and errors.

Ultimately, recruitment must be matched by retention: fair pay, manageable workloads, and visible career progression, all under strong leadership focused on safety and wellbeing. A plan built around people first will sustain high-quality, safe care now and in the future.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise long-term funding stability, safe staffing, and supportive working models that protect care quality. We must also prioritise safe staffing ratios and continuity-preserving models, with safety monitoring built in. Expand training pipelines and career progression, with mentoring and peer-support networks. In my practice, wellbeing programmes and mentoring boosted morale and patient care, showing that well-supported staff deliver safer, timelier access to services.

To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise long-term, ring-fenced funding and robust workforce development. This should include expanding training capacity—more medical places, nursing training and allied health professionals—so we can grow our own staff and reduce dependence on short-term agency staff. To recruit, retain and support staff while keeping care safe and high quality, the workforce plan must tackle burnout and inflexibility head on, and offer realistic, long‑term incentives. To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping high-quality care, the workforce plan must place flexibility and wellbeing at its core. An NHS workforce plan should prioritise long-term stability as much as immediate recruitment. This reduces volatility that currently disrupts recruitment and morale. Specific priorities: expand training and supervision pathways for GPs, nurses and allied health professionals; fund extended rotations, apprenticeships and digital learning; ensure sustainable pipelines in primary care and community services; provide protected time for ongoing professional development; create clear career ladders and leadership training to boost retention; invest in flexible, student-friendly patterns (evenings/weekends, part-time routes) to attract younger staff. Align workforce planning with service demand so hubs and triage pathways are not undermined by staffing gaps. In short, long-term, ring-fenced funding combined with robust training and flexible careers will help deliver safe, high-quality care now and in the future.

Prioritise expanding and stabilising the workforce through competitive pay, robust training, and flexible roles, including responsible overseas recruitment with streamlined visa routes, clear credential recognition, strong integration support, and safeguards to avoid draining source countries, ensuring safe, high-quality care.

Yes, I think an NHS workforce plan should prioritise expanding training and stabilising funding, but with practical safeguards to deliver real local capacity. A predictable, long‑term budget would let practices invest confidently in training capacity, digital triage support, and multidisciplinary roles such as pharmacists and care coordinators working in the community. From my experience of waiting weeks for a GP last winter, we need capacity now and in the months ahead. Training increases must translate into immediate, practical gains in local staffing and rota coverage, especially in rural areas where access is the biggest issue. A plan that pairs expanded training with stabl funding and clear pipelines into local, well‑supervised roles would help maintainn safe, high‑quality care across the board.

Prioritise place-based incentives for rural, coastal and deprived areas, including housing and transport, to attract staff; expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams with proper training and supervision to ease GP load; boost undergraduate, postgraduate and apprenticeship placements through strong university-practice links to grow domestic primary care capacity while maintaining safety.

We should prioritise streamlined visas and quick recognition of overseas qualifications, with good integration support and safeguards so we don't drain source countries; plus fair pay, flexible hours, wellbeing and strong induction to keep safety and quality.

Thank you for asking. From where we sit in our community, a workforce plan that genuinely supports staff is essential to delivering the timely, compassionate care older residents rely on. The plan should be human-centred for workers as well as patients, recognising that stable, motivated teams are the backbone of safe, high-quality services. With that in mind, I’d prioritise the following areas:

- Flexible, humane working patterns to attract and retain a diverse workforce. We know many carers, parents and older staff would stay in the NHS if jobs could fit life stages and family needs. Practical steps include offering flexible hours, part-time roles, job-share schemes, phased retirement, and robust back‑to‑work pathways. In our area, experienced district nurses and community clinicians often reduce hours or leave due to burnout or rigid schedules; allowing job-sharing across shifts and enabling gradual retirement would keep valuable skills in the system and reduce gaps in patient care.

- Proactive mental health and wellbeing support for staff. Burnout isn’t just a risk for patients; it threatens system safety. A plan that funds confidential wellbeing services, easier access to counselling, rested rosters, and reasonable caseloads will pay dividends in safer care. Where staff feel supported, they’re more likely to stay, build relationships with communities, and provide the continuity that older patients need.

- Childcare and practical supports to widen the workforce pool. Childcare costs and availability can be a barrier to recruitment and retention, especially for those returning from maternity leave or joining later career stages. Consider on-site or nearby childcare options where feasible, targeted subsidies, and scheduling that recognises school hours. Small, practical measures—like supervisory support during school holidays or predictable rosters—can make a big difference to staff retention.

- Localised workforce data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation. A plan must be informed by transparent, local data. We need dashboards that track vacancies by role, turnover, time-to-fill, and training capacity, with disaggregated data by age, ethnicity, geography and specialty. Regular reviews using clear KPIs and evaluation frameworks will show what’s working, what isn’t, and where to adjust targeted investments. This helps ensure money goes to things that actually improve staffing and patient outcomes, not just to headlines.

- Multi-year, ring-fenced funding to sustain workforce initiatives. Short funding cycles breed instability, which undermines recruitment and long-term planning. A predictable, multi-year settlement would allow trusts and local systems to grow training capacity, expand multidisciplinary teams, and implement workforce reforms with confidence. It would also reduce the churn that comes when projects start and stop with a new government line or another strategic review.

- Investment in training and progression within local systems. Expanding training capacity—clinical apprenticeships, return-to-practice courses, and leadership development—helps fill gaps and creates a pipeline of skills tailored to local needs. A workforce plan should couple this with defined career ladders and protected time for professional development so staff can advance without sacrificing patient access.

- Flexible service design and cross-skilling. Encouraging teams to work more collaboratively—shared roles across nursing, therapy, and social care, with cross-skilling to cover urgent needs—can cushion vacancies without compromising safety. A plan that funds time for joint training and flexible team rostering will improve resilience during peak demand or staff shortages.

In practice, these priorities would support the kind of integrated local hubs we’ve promoted previously. If staff feel valued, supported, and fairly compensated for flexible arrangements, they stay longer, share best practices, and deliver timelier care to older residents who often have complex needs. I’ve seen how long-standing staff shortages translate into delayed assessments and avoidable hospital visits; a steadier, well-supported workforce would help shorten the “tell me again” moments patients experience in primary and community care.

To summarise, recruit and retain through flexible, family-friendly work patterns; protect staff wellbeing; fund childcare and practical supports; underpin planning with transparent local data and KPIs; secure multi-year funding; and invest in training and career development. If the NHS can commit to these priorities, we’ll see safer, higher-quality care that’s closer to home for the people who rely on it most.

From our work with residents and frontline teams, I believe an NHS workforce plan should prioritise practical, evidence-based steps that recruit, retain and support staff while safeguarding safe, high-quality care. The aim must be to build a sustainable system where staff feel valued, supported and able to deliver care without burning out. Key priorities would include:

- Flexible, family-friendly working and strong wellbeing support. Offer a real mix of hours—part-time, job-share, phased retirement options, and predictable patterns that fit different life stages. Maintain accessible, proactive mental health services and confidential wellbeing support to prevent burnout and improve morale. In communities where staff can balance work with caring responsibilities or childcare, retention improves and patient care benefits from more stable teams.

- Robust recruitment pipelines and inclusive routes. Expand international recruitment with streamlined visa processes where appropriate, paired with effective induction and local retraining pathways. Strengthen local training pipelines with stronger links to universities and colleges, and expand return-to-practice programs so skilled clinicians can rejoin safely after career breaks. Create visible career ladders that bring in diverse applicants and reduce barriers to entry for carers and other non-traditional routes.

- Retention through career development and sustainable workloads. Provide clear career progression, mentorship, leadership development, and protected time for professional development. Design roles to share workload more evenly across teams and reduce administrative tasks that do not directly improve patient outcomes. Structured, short-cycle appraisals and regular wellbeing check-ins help staff feel valued and supported.

- Safe staffing levels backed by real-time data. Use acuity-based staffing, robust rostering systems and real-time dashboards to ensure safe coverage, with contingency plans for spikes in demand. Transparent staffing information helps both staff and patients understand how care is delivered and where gaps may exist.

- Multidisciplinary, co-located teams and flexible care models. Promote truly multidisciplinary working—nurses, GPs, allied health professionals, social care, mental health—working in integrated hubs or well-connected networks. Flexible rosters that support extended hours without overburdening individuals, alongside telehealth and digital tools, can improve access while protecting staff wellbeing.

- Training, apprenticeships and return-to-practice embedded in workforce design. Prioritise on-the-job training that aligns with local service needs, with clear eligibility and funding. Create streamlined pathways for international graduates and returnees to refresh competencies and re-enter the workforce with confidence.

- Equity, inclusion and support for diverse staff. Proactively address barriers faced by parents, carers, and people from diverse backgrounds; ensure childcare, equitable pay, and inclusive policies are part of workforce planning. A diverse workforce brings different perspectives and improves patient experience, particularly in community settings.

- Strong funding and accountable delivery. Long-term, predictable funding for training, recruitment, retention incentives, and wellbeing services is essential. Workforce plans should include measurable milestones, independent review and public reporting to ensure real progress and course corrections when needed.

Linking this to our broader goals, the workforce plan should align with the push for integrated triage, hub-based care and a stable primary care workforce. When staff have flexible options, good support, and clear career paths, we see lower turnover, more consistent access for patients, and safer care. We are ready to work with commissioners, providers and local communities to test and scale these approaches, monitor outcomes, and ensure an NHS workforce that can deliver timely, high-quality care now and in the future.

From my experience living in rural Wales, any NHS workforce plan must be clearly rooted in local realities and be open to regular checking and adjustment. A plan that looks good on paper won’t help if the staff aren’t there when and where people need them, or if we can’t see how success is being measured. I would want the plan to be built on transparent, localised data, robust modelling, and a small set of clear KPIs with ever-evolving evaluation frameworks. Without this, funding and staffing decisions will feel unsure and it will be hard to tell what actually improved patient care or kept people independent.

What I’d prioritise:
- Localised data, modelling and KPIs with evaluation frameworks: Communities like ours need dashboards showing GP and nurse vacancies, nurse-led and mid-level clinician capacity, urgent care demand, and the impact of new models (mobile clinics, telehealth hubs) on waiting times and travel. A rolling five-year projection would help plan winter spikes and training needs. If the data show gaps, funding decisions must adapt quickly rather than after the event.
- Recruitment and retention that fits rural life: We’ve seen how unpredictable staffing can disrupt access. We also need interpreters and culturally competent staff embedded in teams to close access gaps and sustain high-quality care.

absolutely prioritise safe staffing by a mix of local recruitment and responsibly managed overseas recruitment, with streamlined visa routes, rapid credential recognition, robust integration support, mentoring, and safeguards against draining source countries' health systems; ensure ongoing training and safe staffing levels to maintain high-quality care!

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while maintaining safe, high‑quality care, the workforce plan must prioritise expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams who can safely redistribute GP workload. This means empowering nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied professionals through clearly defined scopes of practice, robust training, and strong supervision with consistent governance. In practice, trained practice nurses handling routine chronic disease reviews and medicines management, with pharmacists contributing medicines optimisation, can free GPs to focus on complex cases if there is reliable escalation and supervision. FROM MY PERSPECTIVE LIVING IN RURAL ENGLAND, ANY NHS WORKFORCE PLAN THAT WANTS TO RECRUIT, RETAIN AND SUPPORT STAFF WHILE KEEPING CARE SAFE AND HIGH QUALITY MUST BE BUILT ON STABILITY, CLEAR CAREER PATHWAYS AND STRONG LINKS TO THE COMMUNITIES IT SERVES. THE PATTERN I’VE SEEN IN PRACTICE IS THAT SHORT-TERM FUNDING OR TINKERING WITH SCOPES OF PRACTICE CREATES MORE CHURN THAN IT CURES. - EXPAND TRAINING CAPACITY WITH PROTECTED PLACEMENTS AND UNIVERSITY-PRACTICE PARTNERSHIPS: WE NEED MORE UNDERGRADUATE, POSTGRADUATE AND APPRENTICESHIP PLACES DEDICATED TO PRIMARY CARE, WITH PROTECTED TIME FOR PLACEMENTS IN REAL PRACTICE SETTINGS. UNIVERSITIES AND NHS PROVIDERS SHOULD CO-DESIGN MULTI-YEAR PARTNERSHIPS THAT GUARANTEE PRACTICE-BASED TRAINING SLOTS, INCLUDING GP, NURSING, PHARMACIST, AND ALLIED HEALTH PROFESSIONAL (AHP) PLACEMENTS. IN MY AREA, WE WOULD WELCOME A STEADY PIPELINE OF STUDENTS AND TRAINEES WHO CAN CONTRIBUTE TO GENERAL PRACTICE WHILE LEARNING THE COMPLEXITIES OF RURAL CARE. THIS SHOULD COME WITH FUNDED SUPERVISION AND CLEAR PROGRESSION ROUTES SO TRAINEES BECOME CONFIDENT, SAFE CLINICIANS WHO STAY ON IN THE LOCAL NETWORK AFTER QUALIFICATION RATHER THAN MOVING AWAY FOR OPPORTUNITIES ELSEWHERE.

- SECURE MULTI-YEAR, RING-FENCED FUNDING TO SUSTAIN WORKFORCE INITIATIVES: POLICY VOLATILITY UNDERMINES MORALE AND PLANNING. A DEDICATED, LONG-TERM FUNDING SETTLEMENT WOULD ALLOW PRACTICES TO INVEST IN TRAINING CAPACITY, STAFF MENTORSHIP, AND INNOVATIVE RECRUITMENT SCHEMES WITHOUT FEARING ABRUPT REVERSALS. RING-FENCED MONEY FOR RECRUITMENT INCENTIVES IN HARD-TO-STAFF RURAL POSTS, FOR POSTGRADUATE TRAINING CREDITS TIED TO LOCAL SERVICE NEEDS, AND FOR PROTECTED TIME FOR SUPERVISION WOULD HELP WITH CONTINUITY OF CARE. THE LESSON FROM PILOTS IS THAT WITHOUT RELIABLE FUNDING, IMPROVEMENTS COLLAPSE WHEN A FUNDING CYCLE ENDS. A MORE PREDICTABLE BUDGET WOULD LET US PLAN LONGER-TERM STAFFING MODELS, SHARE BEST PRACTICE REGIONALLY, AND REDUCE PATIENT RISK DUE TO GAPS IN COVER.

- CLARIFY SCOPE OF PRACTICE, REVALIDATION, INDEMNITY ARRANGEMENTS AND FUND PROTECTED CLINICAL SUPERVISION: AS NEW ROLES EMERGE—SUCH AS PHYSICIAN ASSOCIATES, NURSING ASSOCIATES, AND EXPANDED AHP FUNCTIONS—WE NEED EXPLICIT, CONSISTENT SCOPES OF PRACTICE AND REGULATED PATHWAYS THAT ALIGN WITH PATIENT SAFETY. REVALIDATION PROCESSES MUST BE STREAMLINED AND PREDICTABLE, NOT A MOVING TARGET. INDEMNITY ARRANGEMENTS SHOULD BE FAIR AND COMPREHENSIVE SO STAFF FEEL CONFIDENT TAKING ON EXTENDED ROLES IN PRIMARY CARE SETTINGS. IMPORTANTLY, FUND PROTECTED SUPERVISION TIME SO NEWLY QUALIFIED STAFF AND THOSE MOVING INTO BROADER TASKS HAVE ACCESS TO EXPERIENCED MENTORS. IN PRACTICE, CONFUSION OVER RESPONSIBILITIES CAN SLOW DECISION-MAKING AND IMPACT SAFETY; CLEAR GUIDANCE AND PROTECTED SUPERVISION WILL KEEP CARE SAFE WHILE ENABLING WORKFORCE GROWTH.

- FOCUS ON RETENTION AND WORKFORCE WELLBEING ALONGSIDE UPSKILLING: A PLAN THAT SIMPLY CREATES MORE POSTS WITHOUT SUPPORTING STAFF WILL FAIL. RETENTION REQUIRES FLEXIBLE WORKING ARRANGEMENTS, MEANINGFUL CAREER DEVELOPMENT, MENTORING, AND SUPPORTIVE LEADERSHIP—ESPECIALLY IN SMALL RURAL PRACTICES WHERE WORKLOAD SPIKES CAN BE HIGH. LOCAL CAREER PROGRESSION LADDERS, ACCESS TO CPD, AND OPPORTUNITIES TO ROTATE WITHIN INTEGRATED TEAMS (GPS, NURSES, PHARMACISTS, MENTAL HEALTH WORKERS) WITHOUT LOSING TIES TO THE COMMUNITY MATTER. WHEN STAFF FEEL VALUED AND SUPPORTED, PATIENT SAFETY AND CONTINUITY OF CARE IMPROVE.

- ENSURE ALIGNMENT WITH THE BROADER MODELS OF CARE THAT SUPPORT ACCESS IN RURAL AREAS: TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT STRATEGIES SHOULD DOVETAIL WITH THE OUTREACH, MOBILE AND TELEHEALTH APPROACHES I’VE ADVOCATED PREVIOUSLY. YOU DON’T GROW THE WORKFORCE IN ISOLATION; YOU GIVE CLINICIANS THE TOOLS, TIME AND SUPPORT TO WORK EFFECTIVELY ACROSS LOCAL NETWORKS, CO-LOCATE SERVICES WHERE POSSIBLE, AND MAINTAIN A HUMAN TOUCH IN CARE DESPITE TECHNOLOGICAL ADVANCES. THAT MEANS INVESTING NOT JUST IN PEOPLE BUT IN SUPERVISION, SAFE PROTOCOLS, AND THE INFRASTRUCTURE THAT LETS THEM DO THEIR JOB WELL IN A RURAL SETTING.

ULTIMATELY, THE NHS WORKFORCE PLAN MUST PROVIDE LONG-TERM CERTAINTY, CLEAR ROLES WITH ROBUST SAFETY NETS, AND REAL OPPORTUNITIES FOR CLINICIANS TO DEVELOP AND STAY IN THEIR COMMUNITIES. IF FUNDED AND DESIGNED WITH LOCAL TEAMS AND PATIENTS, IT SHOULD HELP REDUCE AVOIDABLE HOSPITAL VISITS, SHORTEN WAITING TIMES FOR PRIMARY AND MENTAL HEALTH CARE, AND IMPROVE THE OVERALL QUALITY AND SAFETY OF CARE IN RURAL ENGLAND. THE PROOF WILL BE IN STEADY RECRUITMENT, REDUCED VACANCY RATES, AND STAFF REPORTING GENUINE JOB SATISFACTION ALONGSIDE SAFER, HIGHER-QUALITY PATIENT CARE.

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that keeps patients safe while expanding access to GP, community and mental health services. My experience in our area shows that when staffing is stable, well-supported and properly supervised, people get timely help without compromising quality. Conversely, quick fixes or short-term shortages can leave patients with rushed consultations and gaps in care. So the plan should prioritise three things: safe staffing, sustainable funding, and stronger multidisciplinary teams.

- Safe staffing ratios and continuity of care: It is essential to set clear, evidence-based staffing levels for different services and to maintain a stable skill mix across sites. This means not just more bodies, but the right mix of doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and allied health professionals. A key emphasis should be continuity—giving patients a named clinician or a stable team where possible, so long-term conditions are managed consistently and risk is reduced. For example, having a named GP or a small, consistent care team for a patient with multiple conditions reduces missed follow-ups and improves decision-making.

- Robust safety monitoring: Any growth in the workforce must be matched with rigorous safety oversight. We need real-time data dashboards on staffing, patient outcomes, wait times, and staff wellbeing. Regular safety reviews, independent governance checks, and transparent reporting will help catch risks early, prevent burnout, and ensure resources are directed where they will do the most good. This is especially important if we extend clinic hours or rely more on new roles; safety must come first, not be an afterthought.

- Multi-year, ring-fenced funding: A stable, long-term funding settlement is crucial. Short‑term pots create policy volatility, which makes it hard to recruit, train and retain staff. Ring-fenced funding should cover training capacity, career progression, and workforce resilience—such as backfill for training, remote learning, and supported return-to-practice schemes for experienced clinicians who have paused clinical work. Flexible working options and pension considerations for older staff can also help retain experienced clinicians who are central to safe continuity of care.

- Expand and regulate multidisciplinary teams: To safely redistribute GP workload, we should strengthen teams that include nurses, pharmacists, physician associates, paramedics and other allied health professionals. Training and supervision must be embedded so these roles can take on appropriate responsibilities, such as pharmacist-led medicines reviews, nurse-led chronic disease clinics, PAs conducting follow-ups in urgent care, and paramedics supporting same-day access pathways. Clear governance and scope of practice are essential so patients experience seamless, safe care across settings.

- Practical alignment with new models of care: For the proposed co-located hubs and same-day urgent pathways I’ve advocated, a stronger workforce framework will be needed. MDT working, with robust data sharing and joint staffing plans, will enable efficient team-based assessments, faster triage, and safer referrals. This is how we can deliver timely access while protecting clinical quality and patient safety.

In short, I’d like the NHS workforce plan to deliver enough well-supported staff, backed by predictable funding, with teams that work across professional boundaries under strong governance. When done well, this will support our goals of shorter waits, better continuity, and safer, higher‑quality care as we expand access through extended hours, same‑day triage, and integrated community hubs.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while safeguarding care quality, the plan should prioritise several interlinked goals. First, safe staffing ratios that reflect patient complexity, with predictable rosters and protected rest to prevent burnout and preserve standards. Continuity matters too: stable teams and longer attachments to GP practices or community services reduce handovers and mistakes, while a clear escalation path keeps patient risk low. Regular safety monitoring and real-time indicators should flag potential gaps before care is affected. 

Second, targeted competitive pay and incentives are essential to attract staff to underserved areas and high-demand roles. This includes retention payments, relocation support and bursaries for training in nursing, mental health and primary care. In my area, pay gaps and long commutes have pushed experienced colleagues away; a structured package could help retain them.

Third, invest in interoperable IT and secure systems, with staff digital training, while safeguarding alternatives for digitally excluded patients. Shared records and decision-support can speed up access and reduce errors, as long as privacy is protected. 

Finally, maintain a plan for a steady pipeline—funded training places, apprenticeships and clear career progression—to build a resilient workforce able to meet rising demand.

I think any NHS workforce plan should prioritise long-term stability alongside practical steps that help people join, stay and do a high-quality job without burning out. In Wales we’ve seen how short-term policy shifts and unsure funding can push staff to move on or deter new training entrants, so the biggest priority has to be secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding that covers training capacity, workforce development and the modernisation of recruitment across NHS Wales. When budgets are predictable, trusts and local health boards can plan rotations, training slots and supervisor coverage years in advance, which reduces gaps and keeps services safe.

Key priorities I’d want to see:

- Ring-fenced, multi-year funding for workforce initiatives: a clear budget cycle that matches training horizons (e.g., medical, nursing, allied health professions) and supports safe staffing levels. This would shield front-line services from sudden policy shifts that disrupt training placements or temporary staffing.
- Targeted competitive pay and retention incentives: pay supplements or retention payments in underserviced, rural and coastal areas would help attract and keep staff where they’re most needed. I’d also welcome relocation packages and targeted bursaries for students in high-demand roles, so local people can train and work in their communities.
- Expanded training capacity and early exposure: increasing undergraduate and postgraduate places in Wales, plus apprenticeships and work-based routes for pharmacists, nurses, physician associates and other allied roles. If local students can train nearby, they’re more likely to stay locally. I’ve seen local training slots cancelled or delayed due to funding gaps; fixed capacity would make a real difference.
- Strong return-to-practice and CPD pathways: schemes that quickly reintroduce clinicians after a break, with structured bridging and flexible formats, help keep experienced staff in the system. Ongoing CPD should be funded so practitioners can refresh skills without shouldering extra costs.
- Rural and coastal focus: tailored recruitment and retention packages, including housing support, flexible rosters, and remote-working options where appropriate, to improve access in less dense areas. We know access can be uneven in Wales, so this isn’t optional—it’s essential for equity and workforce resilience.
- Multidisciplinary teams that share the load: extend roles for nurse practitioners, physiotherapists, pharmacists, and physician associates in primary care and community settings. Better team working reduces reliance on a single GP and improves safety and access for patients with routine needs.
- Practical support to reduce admin and routine workload: digital tools, streamlined admin processes, and supportive leadership can free clinicians to spend more time with patients and less time on paperwork, which helps retention and job satisfaction.
- Wellbeing and safe staffing safeguards: regular monitoring of staffing levels, manageable caseloads, and access to mental health and occupational health support. Front-line staff repeatedly tell me that feeling supported and safe at work is as important as pay when deciding whether to stay.
- Transparent recruitment pipelines and international collaboration: clear, efficient recruitment processes, with appropriate induction and local settlement support. Where international recruitment is needed, ensure a structured pathway to integration and long-term retention rather than ad-hoc arrivals.
- Local partnerships and community links: collaborate with universities, schools and voluntary sectors to create pipelines that lead to local careers. In our area, community-facing training and volunteering often translates into local recruitment and a more stable workforce.

In practice, these priorities would translate into a healthcare system where services are staffed with purpose-built teams, training slots aren’t repeatedly squeezed, and people who want to work in Wales can do so with confidence they’ll be supported over the long term. That stability is what will deliver consistently high-quality care, reduce avoidable delays and keep families connected to the services they need in their own communities.

Overall, I agree that a workforce plan must be long-sighted, well-funded and equity-focused, with real incentives for nurses, GPs, mental health professionals and allied health workers to move to and stay in Wales. If these elements are in place, we’ll see safer staffing, better patient flow and a more sustainable NHS for the future.

Thank you for the chance to feed in on this. In our work with young people across England, a NHS workforce plan that truly supports recruiting, retaining and developing staff while keeping care safe and high quality is essential. Based on what young people and frontline teams tell us, the following priorities should be at the heart of any credible plan:

- Targeted, competitive pay and retention measures. Pay must reflect local living costs and the pressures of frontline work. Where staff are tempted to move to higher paid roles or agency work, retention payments and year‑on‑year improvements to core pay must be available to make NHS roles financially sustainable in communities that already struggle with access to services. 
- Relocation support to underserved areas. Rural towns and urban neighbourhoods with the greatest gaps in access to GP and mental health services should not be discouraged from recruiting because of housing costs or moving expenses. Relocation packages, housing support and local welcome schemes should be bundled with guaranteed job posts and a clear pathway to progression so staff can settle and stay long‑term.
- Bursaries and student support with service commitments. We need bursaries and funded places that tie graduates into NHS service commitments, with robust return‑to‑practice pathways for those who take breaks for study or personal reasons. Crucially, these should be paired with high‑quality supervision, protected training time and visible career progression so young people can see a realistic route from learning to long‑term front‑line roles.
- Clear, long‑term career pathways and support. A plan must guarantee posts after training, provide structured supervision and rotation through core services, and offer continuing professional development with realistic promotion routes. This helps reduce churn and makes a career in the NHS a stable, attractive option for families and communities that have historically been underserved.
- Safe staffing and workload protection. Across primary care and mental health, safe staffing ratios are non‑negotiable. The plan should reduce reliance on temporary staff by funding stable teams, predictable rosters and reasonable caseloads so staff can deliver high‑quality care without burnout.
- Regional and local workforce planning with accountability. Workforce planning must be rolled out regionally with targeted recruitment drives in areas with the biggest gaps, but backed by shared digital systems for workforce data, so we can spot shortages early and respond quickly. Joined‑up commissioning across health, social care and education will help avoid situations where one service expands while another buckles under pressure.
- Multidisciplinary and new roles. Invest in multi‑disciplinary teams that include GPs, nurses, mental health clinicians, pharmacists, allied health professionals and social care workers. Where appropriate, offer additional roles and training to expand capacity (for example, nurse practitioners or clinical pharmacists) with fair pay and clear boundaries, so patient care remains safe and coherent.
- Flexible, youth‑friendly models of care. For younger patients, services that are accessible evenings and weekends, and that are trauma‑informed and culturally competent, need staff who feel supported and valued. Workforce plans should reflect this with flexible contracts, supportive supervision and career development that recognises the unique needs of younger workers.
- Transparent data and public accountability. Publish wait times, vacancy rates and regional staffing data so communities can see progress and what remains to be done. Public dashboards help build trust and focus accountability on delivering tangible improvements for patients and staff alike.
- Real involvement of young people in design. We’ve seen improvements when young people help shape recruitment, retention, and service models. The plan should include formal mechanisms for youth participation so what is promised actually matches what young people experience in practice.

Taken together, these priorities would make the NHS workforce more sustainable in areas that currently struggle to attract and keep staff, while ensuring high‑quality care for patients. Without targeted financial incentives, relocation support, and strong, long‑term commitments to training, progression and safe staffing, shortages will persist, waits will grow, and trust in services will erode among young people already anxious about accessing timely care.

In our area, a local university has begun placing medical and nursing students in partner GP practices for longer blocks with dedicated tutor time; feedback from students has been positive, and a few have chosen to train and work locally after qualifying. If those models are scaled and funded, we could reduce dependence on agency staff and see more consistent care for patients with chronic conditions and carers who rely on regular check-ins.

Second, provide clear, funded career pathways, with protected continuing professional development and strong mentoring. People respond to good opportunities: they want to know how to move forward, stay up to date, and feel supported as they take on more responsibility or return after a career break. Protected CPD time, formal mentorship schemes, and accessible return-to-practice programmes are vital. I’ve heard from colleagues who paused their clinical work for family reasons or health issues and found it hard to re-enter because their skills weren’t refreshed or they lacked a confident support network. A funded return-to-practice pathway with bite-sized refreshers and a buddy of similar experience can make a real difference, letting skilled clinicians rejoin safely and with confidence. For early-career staff, structured mentoring paired with clearly defined progression milestones would improve retention and wellbeing, reducing avoidable turnover and the costs of recruitment.

Third, tailor incentives to hard-to-fill areas—rural, urban deprived and coastal communities—where staff shortages bite hardest. Housing and transport support is not a luxury; it’s a practical necessity if people are to relocate and stay. In coastal towns like ours, long commutes, high housing costs and limited public transport deter applicants. Targeted relocation grants, affordable housing schemes near practices, and subsidised transport can make post-graduate training and long-term careers feasible locally. Alongside this, flexible rosters, telemedicine options to reduce unnecessary travel, and community-based working patterns could attract staff who might otherwise choose urban centres. I also think professional development opportunities should be available locally; if people can access meaningful CPD without moving away, they are more likely to stay long term.

All of this must be underpinned by robust safety and quality governance. Expanding teams must come with appropriate supervision, clear scope of practice, and consistent appraisal. A multi-disciplinary primary care model—with GPs, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists and mental-health staff working to agreed protocols—can distribute workload more evenly and maintain safety. Investment in digital tools to support training, supervision, and remote learning is important, as is routine monitoring of staffing levels, patient safety indicators and staff wellbeing.

In short, invest in growing our own workforce in primary care, ensure lasting career pathways with protected learning and return-to-practice routes, and tailor incentives to the places most in need. Do that well, and you’ll ease waiting times, improve continuity of care, and help people like me stay independent and supported at home for longer. It’s good value for the NHS and vital for the communities it serves!

I welcome a NHS workforce plan that genuinely prioritises recruiting, retaining and supporting staff while ensuring safe, high‑quality care. Any reform must recognise that technology can and should be a powerful enabler for safer, more efficient services—but not at the expense of patients who are digitally excluded or who rely on face‑to‑face care. In my experience, good digital systems are only as strong as the people who use them and the support they receive to adapt to new ways of working.

What I think should be prioritised:

- Interoperable, secure IT and data sharing across the system. A single, real‑time patient record that follows someone from a GP practice to hospital, Community Health, mental health teams and social care would reduce duplications, errors and wasted time. It must be designed with patient safety at the forefront—robust access controls, audit trails and clear governance so clinicians can rely on the information they see. For example, when records aren’t accessible across teams, I’ve seen delayed decisions and repeated tests; a shared view would keep people moving through the system promptly.

- Staff training and support for digital tools. Invest in practical, role‑specific training, protected time for learning, and a cadre of digital champions within practices and teams. In rural settings, a poorly supported rollout quickly becomes a burden on already stretched staff and disrupts patient care. Ongoing refreshers and easy access to technical help would reduce frustration and improve safety, especially when adopting new decision-support tools or telehealth workflows.

- Safeguard alternatives for those who are digitally excluded. A plan that leans heavily on online systems risks leaving older or less tech‑savvy patients behind. We need reliable non‑digital channels—phone triage that is responsive, in‑person clinics with predictable appointments, and local digital-support points at libraries or community hubs. Devices and connectivity should be available on loan where needed, and staff should be able to assist patients in using basic telehealth options during home visits or outreach sessions.

- Local recruitment, retention and continuity of care. A workforce plan must create stable, locally rooted teams with clear career progression. That means longer‑term contracts where possible, predictable rotas, safe staffing levels, and strong wellbeing support to prevent burnout. Continuity matters for patients with complex needs; frequent turnover disrupts trust and quality of care.

- Practical governance and measurement. Publish local metrics on vacancies, turnover, training uptake, patient safety incidents and patient experience with digital services. Use this data to drive continuous improvement and to show where investment translates into shorter waits, safer care and better outcomes.

- Balance between innovation and accessibility. Roll out interoperable IT in pilots first, with feedback loops to clinicians and patients; avoid “one size fits all” digital platforms. In rural and aging communities, the plan should explicitly fund safe, workable in‑person options alongside digital improvements, ensuring digital tools do not become a barrier to care.

In short, I’m supportive of modernising NHS working practices through interoperable, secure IT and robust staff training, but only if there is equal emphasis on keeping alternatives for digitally excluded patients and on real, local continuity of care. If the plan can deliver reliable staffing, well‑supervised use of technology, and accessible, person‑centred services, it will help us move toward safer, higher‑quality care that serves everyone, especially the elderly and those with mobility challenges.

To recruit, retain and support NHS staff while keeping care safe and high‑quality, the workforce plan should prioritise flexible working, strong wellbeing support and well‑structured multidisciplinary teams. Flexible hours, part‑time roles, job‑share and phased retirement help keep experienced clinicians from leaving entirely and attract a broader range of applicants, including those balancing caring responsibilities. Coupled with accessible childcare and proactive mental health services, these measures reduce burnout and sustain morale.

From my experience, expanding and regulating multidisciplinary teams lightens GP workloads without compromising safety. When a practice uses nurse prescribers, pharmacist medication reviews and physician associates for routine follow‑ups, GPs can concentrate on complex cases and safe triage remains intact. Crucially, these roles must come with solid training, clear supervision and recognised career pathways to ensure confidence and quality.

The plan should fund and grow training pipelines for nurses, pharmacists, PAs and paramedics, with protected time for professional development and strong local hub teams. Data‑driven forecasting and workforce planning are essential to maintain safe staffing levels and continuity of care, including longer appointments for patients with complex needs.

From my perspective living in England and engaging with services that young people rely on, a NHS workforce plan must prioritise long-term stability for front-line teams alongside clear, achievable routes to professional development. The big picture should be: secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements that enable sustained workforce initiatives, training capacity and reduced policy volatility, plus practical, funded career pathways with protected CPD, mentorship and return-to-practice schemes to retain experienced clinicians and those starting out. Here’s how that could translate in practice. 

- Secure multi-year, ring-fenced funding settlements. Short funding cycles make it almost impossible to plan recruitment, backfill training posts, or invest in supervision and supervision. A stable budget would cover recruitment targets, backfill for training and supervision, and capital for training facilities and digital learning platforms. Inconsistent funding means you train people only to lose them to burnout or to better-resourced areas elsewhere. 

- Establish clear funded career pathways. People need to see a real ladder from frontline roles through to advanced practitioner and leadership positions. This should include protected time for study, structured rotations across primary care, community and hospital settings, and guaranteed intake numbers for training posts so progression feels achievable rather than aspirational. 

- Protect CPD and guarantee mentorship. Ongoing professional development is crucial to keep care up to date and clinicians engaged. Protected CPD time, formal mentorship for new graduates, and peer-support networks help new staff settle in, build confidence, and stay in the NHS rather than moving to private work or leaving the service altogether. I’ve seen how meaningful mentorship improves morale and retention in local teams. 

- Prioritise return-to-practice schemes. We must actively facilitate staff who have paused work for family, health or burnout to rejoin with refreshed skills. Return-to-practice programs, up-to-date competencies refreshers, and targeted support reduce talent waste and address gaps more effectively than ad hoc recruitment drives. 

- Focus on safe staffing and wellbeing. Sustainable staffing levels, sensible rosters, supervision, debrief opportunities and access to mental health and wellbeing resources for staff are not luxuries; they underpin safe, high-quality care. Flexible working patterns, reasonable hours, and predictable shifts should be a norm, not an exception, to help retain nurses, therapists and many allied health professionals who balance caring responsibilities. 

- Expand training capacity and placements. Increase clinical placements in primary care, community services, mental health teams, and hospital wards so students and newly qualified staff gain broad, practical experience. More placements reduce bottlenecks and improve readiness to deliver high-quality care on day one. 

- Invest in digital capability. Modern care relies on integrated teams and digital tools. Training in digital records, telemedicine, data protection and cyber security should be embedded so new staff can work confidently across settings without compromising safety. 

- Ensure transparency and accountability. Local workforce dashboards should track vacancies, turnover, CPD uptake and backfill performance. Regular reviews linked to service performance will highlight gaps early and enable corrective action before services suffer. 

In my experience observing youth and primary care services, stable mentorship and clear progression paths have a tangible impact on retention. When a team knows there will be a steady pipeline of trained colleagues stepping up, while every clinician has access to protected CPD and structured mentorship, morale improves and patient care follows. Conversely, frequent policy shifts and short-term recruitment drives lead to churn, gaps in care and increased stress on existing staff. A workforce plan built on long-term funding, predictable career pathways and robust return-to-practice routes would directly support the kind of integrated, timely care I’ve advocated for—where young people can access well-supported, high-quality help close to home, without the anxiety of constant staffing uncertainty.

An NHS workforce plan should prioritise integrating health, social care and community services to spread workload and deliver truly holistic care. The key priorities I’d like to see are:
- Joint funding and shared workforce strategies enabling multi-disciplinary teams (nurses, GPs, mental health specialists, social workers) to co-deliver in hubs or co-located clinics. In our area, a district nurse and a social worker working together has helped keep some patients out of hospital and nearer home.
- Strong recruitment and retention through expanded training places, return-to-practice schemes, CPD and flexible contracts that attract younger staff while offering progression for mid-career professionals.
- Safe, sustainable staffing levels with manageable workloads and protected time for admin, supervision and wellbeing support. This is essential to maintain high-quality care and patient safety.
- Career pathways that enable local recruitment, apprenticeships, and clearer routes between community and hospital roles, supported by robust supervision.
- Digital tools to reduce admin, but with dedicated staff to assist patients who struggle with tech, ensuring no one is left behind.
- Co-commissioning with local authorities to align targets, share back-office functions and standardise quality across settings.
A jointly funded, people-centred plan would make care more resilient and easier for families like mine to access safely.

To recruit, retain and support staff while maintaining safe, high-quality care, the NHS workforce plan should prioritise clear scope-of-practice, robust revalidation and guaranteed indemnity, alongside funded, protected clinical supervision for those taking on new roles. Clear, nationally aligned boundaries for nurses, physician associates, pharmacists and other allied health professionals will reduce confusion, strengthen MDT working and help patients access timely care without compromising safety. Revalidation should reflect expanded competencies, with streamlined appraisals and access to targeted upskilling as staff take on broader duties. Indemnity arrangements must cover expanded roles from the outset—including minor procedures, prescribing and triage decisions—so staff aren’t deterred by fear of liability. Without this, skilled colleagues hold back and patient safety and service quality suffer. Fund protected supervision time so experienced clinicians can mentor new team members, particularly in community and rural settings, and by using telehealth hubs with clear referral and escalation pathways. Provide career ladders, ongoing CPD and predictable staffing budgets to boost retention. In my area, this mix would make new roles feel safe, sustainable and capable of delivering the timely, high-quality care people rely on.
